### [1] [TokenScope: Token-Level Explainability and Interpretability for Code-Oriented Tasks in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01235)
*Amirreza Esmaeili,Fatemeh Fard*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TokenScope is an interactive tool for analyzing decoder-based LLMs during code generation, providing token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information. It supports token replacement, counterfactual branching, and AST-based aggregation to enable systematic investigation of LLM behaviour.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tools for understanding LLM decisions during code generation lack (1) decoding-time signals, (2) fine-grained uncertainty measures, and (3) interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths. This limits the ability of researchers and practitioners to systematically investigate how LLMs make token-level decisions.

Method: TokenScope unifies decoding-time signals (token-level metrics, attention patterns) with structural program analysis via abstract syntax trees (ASTs). It provides interactive features including token replacement, counterfactual branching, and code-aware aggregation, operating on decoder-based LLM architectures.

Result: The paper presents TokenScope as a functioning interactive interpretability tool. It demonstrates the tool's capabilities for exposing token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information during LLM code generation, though specific quantitative experimental results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: By combining decoding-time interpretability signals with program structure analysis, TokenScope enables more systematic and fine-grained investigation of LLM behaviour during code generation than previously possible.

Abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) make token-level decisions during code generation remains a major challenge for both researchers and practitioners. While recent tools provide insights into model internals or generation outcomes, they often lack decoding-time signals, fine-grained uncertainty measures, and interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths. We present TokenScope, an interactive interpretability and analysis tool for decoder-based LLMs that exposes token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information during generation. TokenScope supports interactive token replacement, counterfactual branching, and code-aware aggregation via abstract syntax trees. By unifying decoding-time signals with structural program analysis, TokenScope enables systematic investigation of LLM behaviour during code generation.

</details>


### [2] [Safeguarding LLM Agents from Misalignment through Provenance Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01236)
*Yining She,Yiliang Liang,Eunsuk Kang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ProvenanceGuard introduces a provenance-based framework for detecting when LLM agent tool calls deviate from user intent, reducing misalignment error rates dramatically (42.9%→1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench, 32.1%→17.3% on WorkBench) compared to LLM-as-a-judge baselines, while also lowering false interventions on correct actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents gain access to powerful tools, misalignment—where a proposed tool invocation deviates from user intent—can cause harmful, irreversible consequences. Existing runtime guardrails using LLM-as-a-judge lack a systematic reasoning framework, producing inconsistent, hard-to-audit judgments. The authors are motivated by provenance analysis to create a principled, traceable approach to misalignment detection.

Method: The authors propose (1) a provenance-based conceptual framework that formalizes misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context, and (2) ProvenanceGuard, a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes the agent's action for three types of misalignment before tool execution, only permitting actions deemed aligned with the user's query.

Result: Evaluated on Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench across 10 backbone LLMs, ProvenanceGuard reduced misaligned-trace error rates from 42.9% to 1.8% (Agent-SafetyBench) and from 32.1% to 17.3% (WorkBench). It reduced intervention burden on task-successful traces from 30.5% to 12.8%, with no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces.

Conclusion: Structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents against misalignment, offering both higher detection accuracy and lower unnecessary intervention compared to LLM-as-a-judge approaches.

Abstract: As LLM agents gain increasing access to powerful tools, ensuring that their actions are aligned with the user's intent becomes critical. When an agent's proposed tool invocation deviates from the user's intent -- a phenomenon called misalignment -- it may lead to harmful consequences that are difficult to undo. Existing runtime guardrails rely on an LLM-as-a-judge paradigm that lacks a systematic framework for reasoning about alignment, often producing judgments that are inconsistent or difficult to audit. Motivated by provenance analysis, we propose a provenance-based conceptual framework that formalizes misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context. Building on this framework, we propose ProvenanceGuard, a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes the agent's action for three types of misalignment before the selected tool is executed and only allows the action to take place when it is considered aligned with the user's input query. We evaluated our proposed approach on two different benchmarks, Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench, across 10 backbone LLMs. Compared to the LLM-as-a-judge baseline, ProvenanceGuard reduces error rate on misaligned traces from 42.9% to 1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench and from 32.1% to 17.3% on WorkBench, while reducing intervention burden on task-successful traces from 30.5% to 12.8% and introducing no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces. These results demonstrate that structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents from misalignment.

</details>


### [3] [Kara: Efficient Reasoning LLM Serving via Sliding-Window KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01237)
*Shen Han,Yuyang Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Kara is a sliding-window KV cache compression method that addresses throughput and information loss issues in existing approaches by operating on recently generated context with bidirectional attention scoring and a Token2Chunk module for flexible chunk preservation. It is integrated into KvLLM (built on vLLM) to improve decoding throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KV cache compression methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) threshold-triggered compression policies can hurt throughput and may eliminate entire blocks' KV pairs, causing severe information loss; (2) they retain only isolated KV pairs or rigid fixed-size chunks, failing to preserve flexible-sized semantic chunks at arbitrary positions.

Method: Kara employs a sliding-window approach that compresses only recently generated context during decoding. It uses bidirectional attention within the window to score and select informative KV pairs. A Token2Chunk module expands selected KV pairs into variable-sized chunks for flexible semantic preservation. The method is adapted to PagedAttention and implemented as KvLLM on top of the vLLM inference framework.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements of Kara and KvLLM in terms of both model quality preservation and output throughput.

Conclusion: Kara effectively overcomes the limitations of prior KV cache compression methods by combining sliding-window processing, bidirectional attention scoring, and flexible chunk-based retention, leading to improved throughput and reduced memory usage in LLM inference.

Abstract: Reasoning language models often generate long chain-of-thought (CoT), which accumulates a massive KV cache during the decoding phase and incurs high decoding latency and limited throughput. To address these issues, KV cache compression has emerged as a promising technique for reducing memory overhead by selectively removing unimportant KV pairs while preserving useful ones for subsequent decoding. Nevertheless, we identify two key limitations in existing KV cache compression methods: 1) their threshold-triggered compression policy may provide limited throughput improvement or even reduce throughput, and may fully eliminate KV pairs from certain blocks of the sequence, potentially worsening information loss. 2) they typically retain either isolated KV pairs or fixed-size chunks with rigid boundaries, failing to preserve important flexible-sized chunks at arbitrary token positions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Kara, a sliding-window KV cache compression method that performs decoding-time compression by operating only on the recently generated context. Kara leverages bidirectional attention to score and select informative KV pairs in the window. To enable flexible preservation of important semantic information, we design a Token2Chunk module to expand a subset of selected KV pairs into chunks. Furthermore, we adapt Kara to PagedAttention and develop KvLLM, an inference framework built upon vLLM, which reduces KV cache memory usage and effectively improves output throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements of proposed Kara and KvLLM.

</details>


### [4] [SPARCLE: SPeaker-aware Aligned Representations via Contrastive Language Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01238)
*Priyam Mazumdar,Yurii Halychanskyi,Steven Guo,Mark Hasegawa-Johnson,Volodymyr Kindratenko*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SPARCLE proposes a speaker-aware grapheme representation model that uses contrastive learning to align graphemes with Wav2Vec2 acoustic features conditioned on speaker identity, replacing G2P systems and halving word error rates in low-resource TTS settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grapheme-based TTS models outperform phoneme-based ones at scale but struggle in low-resource settings. Phoneme-based systems rely on G2P systems that fail to capture speaker-specific acoustic variation, while direct grapheme modeling suffers from the one-to-many text-to-acoustics mapping problem, especially with limited data.

Method: SPARCLE (Speaker-Aware Grapheme Representation Model) is trained with a contrastive objective that aligns grapheme representations with Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations, conditioned on speaker identity. The resulting enriched character representations serve as a direct replacement for G2P systems in downstream TTS tasks.

Result: SPARCLE improves TTS generation quality, reducing word error rates (WER) by half in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme-based models.

Conclusion: Conditioning grapheme representations on speaker identity via contrastive alignment with acoustic features effectively bridges the gap between phoneme and grapheme modeling, enabling robust TTS performance even with severely limited data.

Abstract: Recent advances in speech synthesis have shifted from phoneme representations to direct grapheme modeling. While phonemes address the one-to-many mapping between text and acoustics, they rely on grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) systems that fail to capture speaker-specific acoustic variation. Prior work demonstrates that grapheme-based models outperform phoneme-based systems at scale, but not in low-resource settings.
  In this paper, we propose SPARCLE, a speaker-aware grapheme representation model that enriches characters with their precise acoustic realizations. SPARCLE is trained with a contrastive objective to align graphemes with corresponding Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations while conditioned on speaker identity. The resulting model serves as a replacement to G2P systems for downstream text-to-speech (TTS) tasks. We demonstrate that SPARCLE improves generation quality, reducing word error rates by half in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme-based models.

</details>


### [5] [Breaking Safety at the Token Boundary: How BPE Tokenization Creates Exploitable Gaps in LLM Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01239)
*Tung-Ling Li,Hongliang Liu,Yuhao Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Character-level perturbations in prompts bypass LLM safety alignment because BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word tokens unseen during alignment training. The attack flips refusal on 80-100% of prompts, producing harmful outputs in 29-65% of cases across five model families. Defenses via DPO fail; SFT on fragmented prompts closes the gap but causes global refusal collapse on benign prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLMs rely on safety alignment (e.g., RLHF, DPO) to refuse harmful requests, but character-level perturbations (e.g., adding spaces, typos) can bypass these safeguards while keeping prompts human-readable. The authors hypothesize a structural root cause: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word tokens that are absent from alignment training data, creating a distributional blind spot that attackers can exploit.

Method: The paper tests the fragmentation hypothesis end-to-end across five model families (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B). An optimization procedure targets safety-token fragmentation to flip first-token refusal. Activation patching localizes disrupted signals to the last ~30% of layers. A scan of 30,000 alignment prompts confirms zero fragmented inputs (positive-control recall ≥99%). Targeted mutation experiments isolate safety words as the disruption locus. For defense, a 68-cell grid (55 DPO checkpoints) tests closure, and SFT on fragmented prompts is evaluated. The Conv-Benign diagnostic is introduced to distinguish selective repair from global collapse. All attack success rate (ASR) claims use 3-judge calibration.

Result: The fragmentation attack flips first-token refusal on 80-100% of previously refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% of flips yielding genuinely harmful outputs (per-model range: 29-65%). Gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC ranges 0.66-0.98 per model (pooled: 0.84). Activation patching confirms disruption in the last ~30% of layers. The 30K alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts. No DPO configuration achieves seed- and pool-stable ASR closure. SFT on fragmented prompts closes ASR on 3/5 families but only via global collapse, increasing refusal on benign prompts — indicating the missing distribution is necessary but not sufficient under LoRA-16.

Conclusion: BPE tokenization introduces a structural vulnerability in LLM safety alignment: safety-critical words fragment into sub-word tokens not represented in alignment data, enabling reliable jailbreaks via character-level perturbations. Current fine-tuning defenses (DPO, SFT) either fail to close the gap stably or collapse into indiscriminate refusal. The Conv-Benign metric offers a diagnostic for future defenses that might achieve selective repair without global collapse.

Abstract: Character-level perturbations bypass safety alignment in modern LLMs despite leaving prompts human-readable. We identify and test a central structural mechanism: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word pieces, and the three public alignment datasets we surveyed contain no intentionally fragmented inputs. The mechanism is a chain, tested end-to-end on five model families (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B). An optimization targeting safety-token fragmentation flips the first-token refusal trigger on 80-100% of refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% of those flips producing genuinely harmful outputs (per-model 29-65%; gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC 0.66-0.98, pooled 0.84). Activation patching localizes the disrupted signal to the last ${\sim}30\%$ of layers; an alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts among 30,000 examples (positive-control recall $\geq 99\%$ at attack-relevant intensities); and targeted-mutation experiments isolate safety words as the disruption locus. On the defense side, a 68-cell grid (55 trained checkpoints) shows that no DPO configuration achieves seed- and pool-stable ASR closure on the three families with closed pool-size confounds. SFT trained on fragmented prompts closes ASR on 3/5 families but only via global collapse that raises refusal on benign prompts as well, indicating the missing distribution is necessary but not sufficient under the LoRA-16 recipe we tested. To distinguish selective repair from global collapse, we introduce Conv-Benign, a candidate paired diagnostic. All ASR claims are 3-judge-calibrated (cell rankings stable across judges; absolute levels $\pm$18pp; see App.~B.13).

</details>


### [6] [Prompt Framing Distorts Count-Based Evaluation of LLM Error Detection: Evidence from Numeric Anchoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01240)
*Dekun Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper reveals that count-based F1 scores can inflate substantially without genuine improvements in error span localization (termed "F1 Inflation"), demonstrates this via ErrorBench—a controlled prompt-based stress test across six LLMs and 4,290 responses—and recommends avoiding pre-populated error counts while reporting span-aware metrics alongside count-based ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Count-based F1 is widely used as a proxy for LLM error-detection quality in tasks like grammatical error correction and proofreading. The authors identify a critical gap: F1 scores can rise significantly without any improvement in actual span localization, a phenomenon they call "F1 Inflation." This threatens the validity of common evaluation practices where systems might exploit count cues (e.g., pre-populated error counts in prompts) to inflate performance without truly locating errors.

Method: The authors introduce ErrorBench, a controlled stress-test protocol that manipulates prompt conditions to induce count distortion. They evaluate six contemporary LLMs under five prompt conditions, generating 4,290 responses from 143 CoNLL-2014 passages. Two scoring regimes are used: CoNLL-2014 M2-style scoring and strict matching. A 100-passage replication employs the official ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline with multi-reference scoring to validate findings. The Blind-to-Anchored prompt shift is the key manipulation—comparing prompts without error count information against those with pre-populated counts.

Result: Anchored prompts produce up to 0.79 points of F1 Inflation under M2 scoring and up to 0.96 under strict matching. Averaged across six models, the Blind-to-Anchored shift raises Count-F1 by +0.21 while multi-reference ERRANT F0.5 rises by only +0.04, confirming the inflation pattern is robust. GPT/Claude systems show larger count responses (greater inflation), while Gemini-family models exhibit smaller responses under the stress-test protocol.

Conclusion: LLM proofreading and document-review evaluations should avoid pre-populated error counts in prompts and must report span-aware metrics (e.g., ERRANT-based) alongside count-based metrics (e.g., F1) to prevent inflated performance estimates that mask poor localization ability.

Abstract: Count-based F1 is widely used as a proxy for LLM error-detection quality, but this paper shows that it can rise dramatically without a corresponding improvement in span localization, a gap termed F1 Inflation. The paper introduces ErrorBench, a controlled stress-test protocol for prompt-induced count distortion. ErrorBench evaluates six contemporary LLMs under five prompt conditions over 4,290 responses from 143 CoNLL-2014 passages. Under CoNLL-2014 M2-style scoring, anchored prompts produce up to 0.79 points of F1 Inflation, and up to 0.96 under strict matching. A 100-passage replication using the official ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline and multi-reference scoring reproduces the pattern: averaged over six models, the Blind-to-Anchored prompt shift raises Count-F1 by +0.21 while raising multi-reference ERRANT F0.5 by only +0.04. The study finds larger count responses in highly instruction-compliant GPT/Claude systems and smaller responses in the Gemini family under this stress-test protocol. The findings suggest that LLM proofreading and document-review evaluations should avoid pre-populated error counts and should report span-aware metrics alongside count-based metrics.

</details>


### [7] [Mapping Text to Multiplex Graph: Prompt Compression as Lévy Walk-Guided Graph Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01241)
*Yaxin Gao,Yao Lu,Jinhong Deng,Jiaqi Nie,Zhe Tang,Jian Zhang,Zhaowei Zhu,Shanqing Yu,Qi Xuan,Joey Tianyi Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RAGP formulates prompt compression as redundancy-aware graph pruning on a multiplex graph, using Lévy walks to balance local and global exploration, achieving superior compression performance over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt compression methods treat text as flat token sequences and fail to capture the distributed nature of important information, which is spread across multiple locations and connected through both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations.

Method: RAGP constructs a multiplex graph where tokens/sentences are nodes and dependencies are edges, jointly modeling fine-grained attention-based dependencies and coarse-grained semantic relations. It then performs redundancy-aware graph pruning using Lévy walks, whose heavy-tailed step distribution naturally balances local exploitation with global exploration, to efficiently identify non-redundant nodes in the heterogeneous structure.

Result: On LongBench, RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 under a 4× compression ratio, outperforming LLM-based methods like LongLLMLingua (48.8 at 3× compression) and surpassing state-of-the-art vision-based text compression paradigms on multiple tasks.

Conclusion: Modeling prompt compression as graph pruning on a multiplex graph with Lévy walk-based node selection effectively captures distributed important information, yielding better compression ratios and performance than flat token-sequence approaches.

Abstract: Existing prompt compression methods treat text as flat token sequences, failing to capture the distributed nature of important information, which is often spread across multiple locations and connected through both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations. Such relational structure is naturally represented as a graph, where tokens or sentences become nodes and their dependencies become edges. To this end, we propose RAGP, which formulates prompt compression as Redundancy-Aware Graph Pruning on a multiplex graph that jointly models fine-grained attention-based dependencies and coarse-grained semantic relations. To efficiently identify non-redundant nodes in this heterogeneous structure (dense local subgraphs and sparse global connections), we employ Levy walks whose heavy-tailed step distribution naturally balances local exploitation with global exploration. Experiments on LongBench show that RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 under a 4x compression ratio, outperforming existing LLM-based compression methods, such as LongLLMLingua, which attains 48.8 at a 3x compression ratio. Besides, RAGP also surpasses state-of-the-art vision-based text compression paradigms on multiple tasks. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RAGP-B0CB.

</details>


### [8] [Office Comprehension Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01245)
*Firoz Shaik,Mateus Picanço Lima Gomes,Tanvir Aumi,Jingci Wang,Milos Milunovic,Filip Basara,Ivana Jovanovic,Vishwas Suryanarayanan,Neha Nandan Kenkare,Weiyao Xie,Zhipeng Han,Zheng Zhang,Waleed Shahid,Jay Rathi,Russell Scherer,Thong Q. Nguyen,Michael Bentley,Tamara Stankovic,Rasika Chakravarthy,Vishal Chowdhary*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OCB is the first public benchmark evaluating LLMs on native Office document formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) across two tracks: File Fidelity Q&A (structural/visual perception) and Domain Q&A (expert reasoning across 12 industries). Frontier systems achieve only ~59.3% on Domain Q&A, with reasoning depth providing negligible gains within a tier.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks do not evaluate comprehension of native Microsoft Office file formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) despite their ubiquity in professional settings. There is a gap in assessing how well models perceive structural elements (tables, charts, formulas, speaker notes, named ranges) and perform domain-expert reasoning over real-world office documents.

Method: OCB introduces two evaluation tracks: (1) File Fidelity Q&A — tests perception of office-specific artifacts like tables, charts, embedded images, formulas, headers, speaker notes, and named ranges; (2) Domain Q&A — tests multi-step reasoning and cross-document synthesis over real industry documents from 12 professional domains. Evaluation uses atomic, binary-gradable claims decomposed from reference answers, scored independently by an ensemble of LLM judges. The benchmark covers native formats and their variants.

Result: The strongest frontier LLM in its default reasoning mode achieves only ~59.3% on Domain Q&A. Increasing thinking depth within the same product tier yields negligible performance improvement, while upgrading to a higher product tier provides only modest gains.

Conclusion: Native office document comprehension remains a significant challenge for frontier LLMs. OCB provides a rigorous, claim-level evaluation framework and public leaderboard to drive progress in this underexplored area. The dataset, evaluation tooling, and judge prompts are publicly released.

Abstract: We introduce Office Comprehension Bench (OCB), the first public benchmark to jointly evaluate LLM systems on Word, Excel, and PowerPoint comprehension over native file formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) and their variants. OCB consists of two tracks. File Fidelity Q&A tests structural and visual perception of office artifacts - tables, charts, embedded images, formulas, and app-specific elements such as headers, speaker notes, and named ranges. Domain Q&A tests expert-level reasoning grounded in real-world industry documents across 12 professional domains, with queries requiring multi-step analysis and synthesis across documents. Each reference answer is decomposed into atomic, binary-gradable claims, and an ensemble of LLM judges scores responses against each claim independently. Even the strongest frontier system in its default reasoning mode reaches only about 59.3% on Domain Q&A; increasing thinking depth within a tier does not move performance materially, while moving to a higher product tier yields modest gains. We release the dataset, evaluation tooling, judge prompt, and a public leaderboard.

</details>


### [9] [RuleChef: Grounding LLM Task Knowledge in Human-Editable Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01293)
*Ádám Kovács,Nadia Verdha,Gábor Recski*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RuleChef is an LLM-based framework that synthesizes executable rules for NLP tasks (classification, NER, relation extraction) from task descriptions and labeled examples, with iterative refinement via held-out performance and human feedback. It produces fast, deterministic, inspectable rule systems, with LLMs used only at training time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To combine the flexibility and performance of LLMs with the speed, determinism, and interpretability of rule-based NLP systems, while keeping LLM inference costs confined to rule synthesis rather than runtime.

Method: RuleChef takes a task description and labeled examples as input. An LLM generates initial rules, which are iteratively patched based on failure analysis over a held-out split. Human feedback on existing rules can further guide refinement. The framework also supports bootstrapping rules from any existing model's input-output pairs. LLMs are used exclusively during learning, not inference.

Result: Preliminary evaluation was conducted on text classification and NER tasks. No specific quantitative results are reported in this abstract.

Conclusion: RuleChef demonstrates a viable approach for using LLMs to generate interpretable, deterministic rule-based systems for NLP. The framework is released as open-source under Apache 2.0.

Abstract: We present RuleChef, a framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate executable rules for NLP tasks such as text classification, Named Entity Recognition (NER), or relation extraction. Rules are generated based on a task description and a set of labeled examples, then they are iteratively improved based both on additional examples and on human feedback overexisting rules. RuleChef can also be used to bootstrap rules using the observed input-output pairs from any existing model for a given task. LLMs are used only at learning time, synthesizing rules and iteratively patching them based on failures measured on a held-out split. The result of this process is a fast, deterministic, and inspectable rule system. Preliminary evaluation is performed on both classification and NER tasks. We release RuleChef as open-source software under an Apache 2.0

</details>


### [10] [TurnNat: Automatic Evaluation of Turn-Taking Naturalness in Dyadic Spoken Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01345)
*Hao Zhang,Thomas Thebaud,Georgi Tinchev,Venkatesh Ravichandran,Laureano Moro-Velazquez*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TurnNat is a likelihood-based framework for automatically evaluating turn-taking naturalness in two-channel spoken dialogue, using a causal prediction model to measure timing atypicality via negative log-likelihood, validated on a human-judged perturbation benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing turn-taking evaluation relies on subjective human judgments or narrow timing metrics that cannot unify heterogeneous timing failures under one framework, limiting systematic assessment of full-duplex spoken dialogue systems.

Method: TurnNat trains a causal turn-taking prediction model on natural conversations to estimate future two-speaker voice-activity states. Naturalness is measured as the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of observed future activity. Frame-level NLLs are pooled over turn-taking boundary units (TBUs) at utterance onsets/offsets, then mean and tail TBU scores are aggregated into a dialogue-level naturalness score. A controlled perturbation benchmark with paired natural/perturbed clips, validated by human judgments, is constructed for evaluation.

Result: TurnNat successfully identifies unnatural turn-taking perturbations across heterogeneous timing failures on the constructed benchmark.

Conclusion: TurnNat provides a unified, automatic framework for evaluating turn-taking naturalness, effectively handling diverse timing failures without relying on human judgment or behavior-specific metrics.

Abstract: Turn-taking naturalness is central to full-duplex spoken dialogue systems, yet its automatic evaluation remains limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments or behavior-specific timing metrics, making it difficult to compare heterogeneous timing failures within a unified framework. We propose TurnNat, a likelihood-based framework for automatic turn-taking naturalness evaluation in two-channel spoken dialogue. A causal turn-taking prediction model trained on natural conversations estimates future two-speaker voice-activity states, and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the observed future activity measures timing atypicality. TurnNat pools frame-level NLLs over turn-taking boundary units (TBUs) extracted from utterance onsets and offsets, and aggregates mean and tail TBU scores into a dialogue-level naturalness score. We further construct a controlled perturbation benchmark of paired natural and perturbed dialogue clips, validated by human naturalness judgments. Experiments on this benchmark show that TurnNat successfully identifies unnatural turn-taking perturbations across heterogeneous timing failures.

</details>


### [11] [RusFinChain: A Russian Benchmark for Verifiable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Finance with Fuzzy-Aligned Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01388)
*M. K. Arabov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RusFinChain is the first Russian-language benchmark for verifiable Chain-of-Thought reasoning in finance, featuring 5,280 parameterized examples across 17 domains with gold-standard reasoning chains. Evaluation of 8 LLMs reveals a significant reasoning gap, and novel Fuzzy/Soft-Attention metrics outperform prior metrics in correlating with answer correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial reasoning benchmarks either lack intermediate step-level supervision (FINESSE-Bench relies on multiple-choice) or are limited to English (FINCHAIN). No benchmark exists for verifiable, step-by-step symbolic reasoning in Russian financial contexts, creating a gap for the Russian-speaking NLP and finance communities.

Method: The authors construct RusFinChain with 5,280 parameterized examples generated from executable Python templates spanning 17 financial domains and 172 topics. Each example includes a gold-standard CoT reasoning chain with intermediate numeric values for automatic verification. They introduce two enhanced evaluation metrics: Fuzzy Numeric Alignment and Soft-Attention Alignment. Eight open-weight LLMs are evaluated on a stratified sample of 8,100 responses, with comparisons against the original ChainEval metric using Spearman correlation with final-answer correctness.

Result: Models achieve a Hard F1 of ~0.65 for step alignment but only ~29% final-answer accuracy, revealing a substantial reasoning gap. The proposed fuzzy and soft metrics show stronger Spearman correlation (rho ≈ 0.48) with final-answer correctness than ChainEval (rho ≈ 0.38–0.46), demonstrating superior diagnostic power.

Conclusion: RusFinChain fills a critical language and evaluation gap in financial NLP. The reasoning gap between step-level alignment and end-to-end accuracy highlights that current LLMs struggle with faithful multi-step financial reasoning. The new metrics provide better diagnostic signals for model development. Dataset, code, and evaluation framework are publicly released.

Abstract: Multi-step symbolic reasoning is essential for robust financial analysis, yet most benchmarks neglect intermediate reasoning steps. FINCHAIN introduced verifiable Chain-of-Thought (CoT) evaluation but is limited to English. FINESSE-Bench includes a Russian block but relies on multiple-choice questions without step-level supervision. We present RusFinChain, the first Russian-language symbolic benchmark for verifiable CoT reasoning in finance. It spans 17 domains, 172 topics, and comprises 5,280 parameterized examples from executable Python templates, ensuring contamination-free evaluation. Each example includes a gold-standard reasoning chain with intermediate numeric values for automatic verification. We also introduce enhanced metrics: Fuzzy Numeric Alignment and Soft-Attention Alignment. We evaluate 8 open-weight LLMs on a stratified sample, generating 8,100 responses. Results reveal a substantial reasoning gap: models achieve Hard F1 of ~0.65 for step alignment, but only ~29% of final answers are correct. Our fuzzy and soft metrics show stronger correlation with final-answer correctness (Spearman rho approx 0.48) than the original ChainEval (rho approx 0.38-0.46), demonstrating superior diagnostic power. We release dataset, code, and evaluation framework to foster verifiable financial AI for the Russian-speaking community.

</details>


### [12] [Multi-Objective Exploration and Preference Optimization via Mutual Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01392)
*Hongyan Xie,Yikun Ban,Ruiyu Fang,Zixuang Huang,Deqing Wang,Jianxin Li,Shuangyong Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MI-EPO proposes an information-theoretic framework that unifies multi-objective exploration and alignment by maximizing joint conditional mutual information among responses, preference feedback, and preference vectors, improving controllability and trade-off stability in multi-objective LLM alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multi-objective alignment methods that condition policies on preference vectors suffer from exploration uncertainty: reward distributions of responses generated under different preference vectors can overlap, causing generated responses to fail at effectively aligning with their corresponding preference vectors. This calls for a method that jointly addresses exploration and alignment in a principled manner.

Method: MI-EPO maximizes joint conditional mutual information I(Response; Feedback; Preference Vector | Context), decomposing into objective alignment and preference-aware exploration terms. A probabilistic routing mechanism is incorporated, encouraging the model to generate responses that are both distinguishable across different preference conditions and well-aligned with each respective preference vector.

Result: Experiments on safe alignment and helpful assistant tasks demonstrate that MI-EPO significantly improves alignment between generated responses and preference vectors, yields more controllable outputs, and achieves stable trade-offs across multiple objectives.

Conclusion: MI-EPO provides an effective information-theoretic solution for multi-objective LLM alignment, overcoming exploration uncertainty by explicitly encouraging distinguishable and well-aligned responses under different preference conditions.

Abstract: Aligning large language models with diverse and heterogeneous human values requires multi-objective alignment methods to effectively trade off conflicting preference dimensions. Current methods achieve this trade-off by training policies conditioned on preference vectors and leveraging online direct preference optimization. However, exploration uncertainty can cause the reward distributions of responses generated under different preference vectors to overlap, and the generated responses may fail to effectively align with the corresponding preference vectors. In this paper, we propose Multi-Objective Exploration and Preference Optimization via Mutual Information (MI-EPO), an information-theoretic framework. It unifies multi-objective exploration and alignment by maximizing the joint conditional mutual information among generated responses, preference feedback, and preference vectors. By incorporating a probabilistic routing mechanism, MI-EPO naturally decomposes objective alignment and preference-aware exploration, encouraging the model to generate responses that are distinguishable and aligned with different preference conditions. Experiments on safe alignment and helpful assistant tasks show that MI-EPO significantly improves the alignment between generated responses and preference vectors, makes the outputs more controllable, and achieves stable trade-offs across multiple objectives.

</details>


### [13] [MultAttnAttrib: Training-Free Multimodal Attribution in Long Document Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01420)
*Dang Quang Thien Tran,Quang V. Dang,Vinamra Tyagi,Sai Soorya Rao Veeravalli,Trang Nguyen,Ryan A. Rossi,Franck Dernoncourt,Nedim Lipka,Koustava Goswami,Samyadeep Basu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MultAttnAttrib, a training-free method for generating attributions in multimodal QA systems by leveraging attention head activations during prefill, along with MultAttrEval, the first benchmark dataset for fine-grained multimodal attribution evaluation. The method outperforms prompting-based baselines and matches frontier models like GPT-5.4, while achieving up to 7× faster latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As grounded QA systems proliferate in AI assistants, accurate answer-to-evidence attribution is essential for trust and safety. However, existing attribution research has focused predominantly on unimodal (text-only) settings, leaving multimodal attribution underexplored. There is a need for both effective multimodal attribution methods and dedicated evaluation benchmarks.

Method: The authors propose MultAttnAttrib, a training-free attribution-generation approach that operates by: (1) analyzing the model's attention head activations during the prefill pass, (2) selecting specific attention heads relevant to grounding, and (3) applying calibrated thresholds to pinpoint source evidence spans within multimodal documents. They also introduce MultAttrEval, a manually annotated benchmark dataset providing fine-grained ground-truth attributions for answer components grounded in multimodal source documents.

Result: MultAttnAttrib consistently outperforms various attribution-generation methods, including strong prompting-based baselines, and matches the performance of frontier models such as GPT-5.4. It improves attribution accuracy for both unimodal and multimodal attribution types and produces attributions at up to one-seventh the inference latency compared to prompting on the same base model.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention-based, training-free attribution methods can achieve state-of-the-art performance in multimodal grounding tasks while being significantly more efficient than prompting-based alternatives. The release of MultAttrEval also fills a critical gap as the first dedicated benchmark for multimodal attribution evaluation in long-form documents.

Abstract: As grounded QA systems are increasingly deployed in AI assistants, accurately attributing generated answers to evidence is critical for user trust and model safety. While unimodal attributions have been explored in depth, the multimodal setting remains relatively under-researched. As a result, we introduce MultAttnAttrib, a training-free attribution-generation method that leverages a model's prefill pass, selected attention heads, and calibrated thresholds to locate source evidence within a document. To establish baseline results for the method, we introduce MultAttrEval, a complementary benchmark dataset annotated with fine-grained, ground-truth attributions for answer components grounded in multimodal source documents. To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation dataset designed specifically for multimodal attribution in long-form documents. Experimental results show that MultAttnAttrib consistently outperforms a variety of attribution-generation methods, including several strong prompting-based approaches and matches the latest frontier models such as GPT 5.4. Our method not only substantially improves attribution accuracy for both unimodal and multimodal attribution types, but also produces attributions at up to one-seventh of the direct inference latency compared to prompting on the same base model.

</details>


### [14] [IsoSci: A Benchmark of Isomorphic Cross-Domain Science Problems for Evaluating Reasoning versus Knowledge Retrieval in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01431)
*Samir Abdaljalil,Erchin Serpedin,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ISOSCI is a benchmark of structurally identical science problems across different domains, revealing that ~91% of reasoning-mode gains in LLMs are knowledge-dependent rather than attributable to reasoning itself, challenging the assumed benefits of chain-of-thought for scientific problem-solving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluations conflate reasoning ability with domain knowledge retrieval. The authors seek to isolate whether observed gains from reasoning modes (e.g., chain-of-thought) genuinely reflect improved reasoning or merely better knowledge access, enabling controlled attribution of performance improvements.

Method: Created ISOSCI, a benchmark of isomorphic cross-domain science problem pairs sharing identical logical structure but requiring different domain-specific knowledge. Evaluated five model pairs across four model families, comparing standard vs. reasoning-mode performance to measure knowledge-dependent versus structure-invariant gains. Used Wilson 95% confidence intervals for statistical rigor.

Result: 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains were knowledge-dependent (63/69 gains). Reasoning toggles on highly capable models yielded <5 percentage point accuracy gains across domains. A reasoning-specialized model (o3-mini) outperformed its standard counterpart on GPQA Diamond (+19.2 pp) but underperformed on ISOSCI (-24.7 pp), demonstrating that benchmark choice determines conclusions about reasoning utility.

Conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning provides minimal benefit for short-horizon procedural scientific problem-solving. Apparent reasoning improvements largely stem from enhanced knowledge retrieval rather than structural reasoning capabilities. Benchmark design critically shapes conclusions about LLM reasoning abilities.

Abstract: We introduce ISOSCI, a benchmark of isomorphic cross-domain science problem pairs that separates reasoning ability from domain knowledge retrieval in LLM evaluation. Each pair shares identical logical structure but requires different domain-specific knowledge, enabling controlled attribution of reasoning-mode gains. Across five model pairs spanning four model families, we find that 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains are knowledge-dependent rather than structure-invariant (63/69 gains; Wilson 95% CI [82.3%, 96.0%]), directly challenging the assumption that chain-of-thought reasoning improves short-horizon procedural scientific problem-solving. Reasoning toggles on highly capable models provide less than 5 percentage points accuracy gain across all domains, and a reasoning-specialized model (o3-mini) that outperforms its standard counterpart on GPQA Diamond (+19.2 percentage points) underperforms on ISOSCI (-24.7 percentage points), showing that benchmark choice determines conclusions about reasoning utility. We release ISOSCI at https://huggingface.co/datasets/isosci/isosci

</details>


### [15] [FaithMed: Training LLMs For Faithful Evidence-Based Medical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01440)
*Zhiyun Zhang,Liwen Sun,Xiang Qian,Chenyan Xiong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FaithMed is a framework that applies evidence-based medicine (EBM) principles as process-level criteria, combining clinician-designed rubrics with reinforcement learning (step-level process rewards and advantage grouping) to improve both reasoning faithfulness and task performance in medical LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical LLMs either lack active access to evidence or use retrieved evidence without proper supervision on how evidence should be appraised and applied during reasoning. Faithful, transparent justification grounded in reliable evidence is critical for clinical decisions.

Method: The authors formalize EBM principles as process-level criteria and introduce FaithMed, which combines: (1) clinician-designed, automatically refined rubrics for evidence appraisal, and (2) reinforcement learning with step-level process reward assignment and advantage grouping to supervise the reasoning chain.

Result: Across seven medical benchmarks, FaithMed outperforms agentic-search baselines by +9% on average, outcome-only RL by +5.8%, and raises average EBM rubric scores over agentic-search Qwen3 baselines by +15.5%.

Conclusion: Explicit step-level process supervision improves both task success and the faithfulness of the reasoning process in medical LLMs, demonstrating the value of integrating EBM principles into the training pipeline.

Abstract: Faithful reasoning is essential in medicine, where clinical decisions require transparent justification grounded in reliable evidence. Current medical LLMs either lack active access to evidence or use retrieved evidence without supervising how it should be appraised and applied during reasoning. To address this, we formalize evidence-based medicine principles as process-level criteria and introduce FaithMed, a framework that combines clinician-designed, automatically refined rubrics with reinforcement learning using step-level process reward assignment and advantage grouping. Across seven medical benchmarks, FaithMed improves over agentic-search baselines (+9% on average) and outcome-only RL (+5.8%), while raising average evidence-based medicine rubric scores over agentic-search Qwen3 baselines (+15.5%). This work demonstrates that explicit step-level supervision can improve both task success and the faithfulness of the reasoning process. Code is available at https://github.com/cxcscmu/FaithMed.

</details>


### [16] [Grounded Optimization: A Layered Engineering Framework for Reducing LLM Hallucination in Automated Personal Document Rewriting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01457)
*Shashank Indukuri,Adarsh Agrawal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A five-layer "Grounded Optimization" framework mitigates LLM hallucinations in resume optimization, reducing detected hallucinations from 2.48–5.36 to 0.04–0.24 per resume across multiple models, temperatures, and industries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs used for resume optimization introduce unique hallucination types—anachronistic technology injection, cross-domain terminology contamination, structural mutation, and content fabrication—that generic text-generation safeguards fail to address. These domain-specific failures risk disqualifying candidates via applicant tracking systems.

Method: The authors propose Grounded Optimization, a five-layer defense framework: (1) temporal context validation, (2) deterministic contamination detection, (3) structural invariant enforcement, (4) prompt-level grounding, and (5) an evaluator agent. The framework is evaluated via ablation experiments across three LLMs, four temperature settings, and six layer configurations on 25 synthetic resumes from 14 industries.

Result: Undefended baselines yield 2.48–5.36 detected hallucinations per resume. Temporal hallucinations drop by 50–95% across all conditions. Overall detected hallucinations fall to 0.04–0.24 per resume. Prompt-level grounding alone achieves zero detected hallucinations at low temperature with a strong instruction-following model; deterministic layers become necessary at higher temperatures and with weaker models.

Conclusion: The five-layer Grounded Optimization framework effectively suppresses domain-specific LLM hallucinations in resume optimization. Prompt-level grounding suffices under favorable conditions, but deterministic layers provide essential complementary protection under degraded settings. The contamination taxonomy, evaluation code, and data are publicly released.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to resume optimization for applicant tracking systems, introducing hallucination failures distinct from general text generation: anachronistic technology injection, cross-domain terminology contamination, structural mutation, and content fabrication. We present Grounded Optimization, a five-layer framework combining temporal context validation, deterministic contamination detection, structural invariant enforcement, prompt-level grounding, and an evaluator agent.
  In ablation experiments across three LLMs, four temperature settings, and six layer configurations on 25 synthetic resumes spanning 14 industries, undefended baselines produce 2.48-5.36 detected hallucinations per resume. Among detectors independent of the active defenses, temporal hallucinations are reduced by 50-95% across all conditions; overall detected hallucination rate falls to 0.04-0.24. Prompt-level grounding alone achieves zero detected hallucinations at low temperature with a capable instruction-following model; higher temperatures and weaker models reveal the need for the deterministic layers as a complement. We release the contamination taxonomy, evaluation code, and raw data.

</details>


### [17] [Comparing Architectures for Supervised Political Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01464)
*Anna Golub,Sebastian Padó*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates improvements to text scaling (positioning political actors ideologically) by exploring two questions: whether joint prediction of multiple scales outperforms individual prediction, and whether a hybrid approach between classification and regression yields better results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text scaling is a fundamental yet challenging task in political analysis. Existing NLP methods based on either classification or regression have shown both successes and limitations. The authors aim to consolidate the state of the art by addressing two open methodological questions in the field.

Method: The paper takes a consolidating, experimental approach by systematically comparing: (1) individual vs. joint prediction of ideological scales, and (2) classification-based vs. regression-based methods, with a proposed middle-ground approach bridging the two paradigms.

Result: Not specified in the abstract — results are to be presented in the full paper.

Conclusion: Not specified in the abstract — conclusions are to be presented in the full paper.

Abstract: Text scaling, the task of positioning political actors on an ideological scale, is a fundamental task in political analysis. To ease the need for manual analysis, various NLP methods have been proposed for this task, including classification- and regression-based approaches, showing successes as well as limitations. The goal of our paper is to consolidate the state of the art in this area. We ask two questions: (a) Can the performance of scaling methods be improved by predicting scales not individually but jointly? (b) Is there a middle ground between classification and regression?

</details>


### [18] [From Monolingual to Multilingual: Evaluating Mamba for ASR in South African Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01502)
*Jesujoba O. Alabi,Julian Herreilers,Badr M. Abdullah,Dietrich Klakow*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Evaluates Mamba vs. Conformer for ASR on seven South African languages. Mamba matches Conformer accuracy with better efficiency. Multilingual training improves performance; explicit language embeddings help cross-corpus robustness but not in-domain accuracy. Embeddings act as task-specific control vectors rather than capturing linguistic typology.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ASR research has explored Conformer and Mamba architectures across languages, but their effectiveness for African languages—particularly South African languages—remains underexplored. This gap motivates a systematic comparison and multilingual extension study.

Method: Monolingual ASR experiments on seven South African languages (50 hrs/language) comparing Mamba and Conformer of similar scale. Generalization tested on longer utterances. Multilingual experiments: pooling all languages, then extending with (1) language + language-family embeddings as biases to downsampled acoustic features, (2) multitask learning with CTC ASR + language identification (LID) head. Ablation studies at 5-hr and 10-hr per-language settings, plus embedding analysis.

Result: Mamba achieves comparable ASR accuracy to Conformer with fewer computational resources and faster training. Both models struggle to generalize to speech significantly longer than training samples. Multilingual training consistently outperforms monolingual baselines. Explicit language embeddings do not improve in-domain WER but enhance cross-corpus robustness. In low-resource (5/10 hr) settings, language embeddings provide gains; removing or altering them degrades performance. Embedding analysis reveals they function as task-specific control vectors, not typological similarity encoders.

Conclusion: Mamba is a viable, efficient alternative to Conformer for African-language ASR. Multilingual training is beneficial, but explicit language information primarily aids cross-domain robustness rather than in-domain accuracy. Language embeddings serve as learned control signals rather than encoding phylogenetic linguistic relationships.

Abstract: Recent advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR) have explored different sequence models, including Conformer-based models and newer state space models such as Mamba. Although prior work has evaluated these architectures in multiple languages, their effectiveness in African languages remains underexplored. In this work, we evaluate Mamba for ASR on seven South African languages. In monolingual experiments, each model is trained on 50 hours of speech per language, and we compare Mamba to a Conformer baseline of similar parameter scale. Mamba achieves similar recognition accuracy to Conformer while using fewer computational resources and training faster. We further evaluate generalization in this setting and find that both models struggle to generalize to speech that is much longer than what they were trained on. We then study multilingual ASR using Mamba models, where the baseline is pooling all languages together. On top of this, we tested three extensions: training with language-family information by adding both language and language-family embeddings as biases to the downsampled acoustic representations, and multitask learning with a CTC ASR objective and a language identification (LID) head. We find that multilingual training consistently improves performance over monolingual training. However, adding explicit language information does not improve in-domain performance but does improve cross-corpus robustness. We conducted ablation studies in low-resource multilingual settings using 5-hour and 10-hour per-language training data, where we observed gains from using language embeddings and further demonstrated that removing or altering them hurt model performance. Lastly, we analysed these embeddings and find that they do not capture linguistic similarity in a typological sense, but instead act as task-specific control vectors.

</details>


### [19] [Parameter Golf: What Really Works?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01517)
*Prashanna Mani Paudel,Shivanand Venkanna Sheshappanavar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The Parameter Golf challenge required participants to train a language model under strict constraints (16 MB artifact, <10 min on 8×H100). Analysis of 2,037 pull requests and 1,430 scored submissions reveals a 13.6% BPB reduction (1.2244 → 1.058), achieved through 84 identified optimization techniques, though individual techniques rarely contributed >1% improvement. Most gains diminish in competitive settings, isolating only a few robust methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically understand how far language model performance can be pushed under extreme compute and storage constraints, and to identify which optimization techniques remain effective when stacked together in a competitive, adversarial setting — going beyond isolated ablations.

Method: The authors conducted a post-hoc analysis of the Parameter Golf community challenge. They collected and scored 2,037 pull requests (1,430 valid submissions), taxonomized 84 distinct optimization techniques used by participants, and measured each technique's marginal contribution to bits-per-byte (BPB) reduction. They analyzed how gains from individual techniques shrank when combined in competitive stacks, isolating methods that consistently delivered improvements.

Result: The leaderboard BPB dropped from 1.2244 to 1.058 (13.6% reduction) across three phases. Individual techniques rarely improved BPB by more than 1%. Most techniques showed diminishing returns when combined; only a few methods proved robust across different competitive submission stacks.

Conclusion: Under extreme constraints, cumulative stacking of many small optimizations yields substantial overall gains, but most individual techniques' benefits shrink in competitive settings. The exercise reveals which optimization methods are genuinely robust and composable versus those that are fragile or context-dependent.

Abstract: How far can a language model improve under a strict artifact budget? Parameter Golf posed this question as an open community challenge in which participants trained the best language model, with the complete artifact (training code + compressed weights) required to fit within 16 MB and be trained in under ten minutes on 8xH100 SXM GPUs. Quality was measured in bits-per-byte (BPB), the average number of bits required to encode each byte of unseen text. We analyze 2,037 pull requests and 1,430 clean scored submissions from the contest, build a taxonomy of 84 optimization techniques, and measure each technique's contribution to BPB. The verified leaderboard score dropped from 1.2244 to 1.058 BPB across three phases -- a 13.6% reduction, despite individual techniques rarely improving BPB by more than 1%. We show that most gains in techniques shrink across competitive submissions, isolating the few methods that improve performance across stacks.

</details>


### [20] [Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01538)
*Siddharth Gollapudi,Nilesh Gupta,Prasann Singhal,Sewon Min*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents BlockSearch, a 0.6B LM retriever that enables in-context retrieval over million-token corpora. The authors identify an "attention dilution" failure mode where irrelevant documents overwhelm the softmax denominator at scale, and propose length-aware softmax adjustments and document-level sparse attention to address it. The model matches dense retrieval on standard benchmarks and significantly outperforms on tasks requiring different similarity notions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on language model-based retrieval has focused on proprietary systems or small-scale reranking, leaving corpus-scale in-context retrieval (million-token corpora with length generalization) largely unexplored. The authors aim to systematically study whether LMs can serve as practical retrievers at scale.

Method: The authors introduce BlockSearch, a 0.6B parameter LM retriever with architectural and training modifications for length generalization (up to 10x training length). After diagnosing "attention dilution" — where irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator as corpus size grows — they propose two fixes: (1) length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax, and (2) document-level sparse attention. These enable retrieval at the million-token scale.

Result: At the million-token scale, BlockSearch matches dense retrieval performance on MS MARCO and NQ benchmarks while outperforming the concurrent MSA model despite being 7× smaller. On the LIMIT benchmark (requiring different similarity notions), it achieves 3× higher scores than dense retrieval. Without the proposed fixes, retrieval collapses under extreme extrapolation due to attention dilution.

Conclusion: In-context retrieval is a promising alternative to classical vector-based retrieval, but attention control under extreme context growth emerges as a critical new challenge. The proposed length-aware mechanisms effectively mitigate attention dilution, enabling competitive performance at scale.

Abstract: Language models (LMs) raise an intriguing alternative to vector-based retrieval: conditioning on an in-context corpus and directly generating a relevant answer. However, prior work has largely focused on proprietary systems or the smaller-scale reranking task, leaving corpus-scale in-context retrieval largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of in-context retrieval on two scales practical retrievers demand: million-token corpora and length-generalization far beyond training-time sizes. We first introduce BlockSearch, a 0.6B LM retriever whose architectural and training modifications improve over prior LM baselines and length-generalize up to 10 times beyond its training regime. Nevertheless, retrieval still collapses under more extreme extrapolation. We trace this failure to an attention dilution effect: as the corpus grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, reducing the normalized mass on the gold document even when its pre-softmax score stays high. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention. With these modifications, at the million-token scale, our model matches dense retrieval on widely studied benchmarks (e.g, MS MARCO and NQ), while outperforming the concurrent model MSA despite being 7 times smaller. Furthermore, it significantly outperforms dense retrieval on tasks requiring entirely different notions of similarity, such as LIMIT, achieving a 3 times higher score. Together, our results position in-context retrieval a promising alternative to classical retrieval while emphasizing attention control under extreme context growth as a new challenge.

</details>


### [21] [DiPS: Dialogue Policy Selection for High-Stakes Persuasion Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01557)
*Tianyi Zhang,Mousumi Das,Abrar Anwar,Jesse Thomason,David Traum*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DiPS is a Q-learning framework that dynamically selects persuasion strategies in a fire-rescue evacuation scenario, outperforming zero-shot LLMs and RAG-based approaches in both simulated and real human interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with high-stakes persuasion because individuals have diverse personalities and concerns, requiring tailored strategies rather than uniform approaches. Existing methods lack dynamic, context-adaptive policy selection during ongoing conversations.

Method: The authors propose DiPS (Dialogue Policy Selection), a Q-learning framework applied to a fire-rescue evacuation scenario. A critic is trained to maximize evacuation success probability and selects a persuasion policy at each dialogue turn based on the resident's recent utterances, adapting to the evolving conversational context.

Result: DiPS achieved higher evacuation success rates compared to a zero-shot LLM baseline and a generic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach, validated through both simulated interactions and real human experiments.

Conclusion: Dynamic, turn-level policy selection via reinforcement learning (specifically Q-learning) significantly improves persuasion outcomes in high-stakes, personalized dialogue settings compared to static or generic approaches.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with persuasion in high-stakes scenarios. People's individual personalities and concerns require tailored strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. To address this challenge, we focus on a fire-rescue scenario in which an operator must persuade a resident to evacuate as a high-stakes persuasion domain and propose Dialogue Policy Selection (DiPS), a Q-learning framework to dynamically select persuasion strategies adapted to the evolving conversational context. Specifically, we train a critic, trained to maximize the chance of evacuation success, to select a persuasion policy at each turn based on the resident's recent utterances.We then evaluate DiPS against multiple baselines in both simulated and real human interactions. We find that DiPS achieves higher evacuation success than a zero-shot LLM and generic RAG-augmented approach.

</details>


### [22] [Beyond Skepticism: Evaluating LLMs Pedagogical Intent Reasoning with the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01581)
*Minghao Chen,Ruihan Zhou,Jiayi Tang,Zihan Xu,Bowen Huang,Yuxin Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV) framework, which uses a Bayesian engine (PIIE) to model how LLMs can infer instructors' latent pedagogical intent. Tested on GPT-4o and Claude 3.5, APV significantly improves discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, achieves high human correlation (r=0.958), and generalizes robustly to authentic educational discourse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs' capacity to reason about pedagogical intent in instructional communication is underexplored, especially in domains like translation pedagogy. Existing models lack structured mechanisms to infer why instructors select specific content (genre, stance, incentives), limiting their reliability in AI-assisted learning systems.

Method: The APV framework formalizes communicative vigilance as an adaptive learning optimization mechanism. Its core is the Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE), which models how instructors maximize pedagogical utility in content selection and how vigilant learners inversely infer latent instructional configurations (genre, stance, incentives). Evaluation uses a three-tier hierarchy: distinguishing instructional genre, reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and generalizing to authentic educational discourse.

Result: APV achieves strongest discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, correlates highly with human judgments (r=0.958), and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade.

Conclusion: APV provides a unified framework for assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives, advancing more reliable AI-assisted learning systems.

Abstract: The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) to reason about pedagogical intent within instructional communication remains underexplored, particularly in educational domains such as translation pedagogy. To address this, we propose the \textbf{Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV)} framework, a novel computational formalism that reframes communicative vigilance as an adaptive mechanism for optimizing learning through intent inference. APV formalizes the problem via a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE), which models how instructors select content to maximize pedagogical utility and how vigilant learners should inversely reason about latent instructional configurations -- encompassing genre, stance, and incentives. We evaluate APV through a three-tier hierarchy: distinguishing instructional genre, reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and generalizing to authentic educational discourse. Experiments on leading LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) show that APV substantially improves model vigilance. It achieves the strongest discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, correlates highly with human judgments ($r=0.958$), and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade. This work establishes a unified framework for assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives, advancing the development of more reliable AI-assisted learning systems.

</details>


### [23] [ProWAFT: A ROMA-LPD Instance for Workload-Aware and Dynamic Fault Tolerance in FPGA-Based CNN Accelerators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01602)
*Xinxin Chen,Haoran Qiao,Yiming Guo,Kecheng Luo,Siyuan Feng,Jingwen Ma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ProWAFT is a proactive, workload-aware fault-tolerance framework for SRAM-based FPGA CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR, balancing latency, energy, and reliability risk under transient faults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SRAM-based FPGAs are attractive for energy/latency-constrained CNN inference at the edge, but transient faults (e.g., SEUs) cause silent errors. Existing solutions — static always-on redundancy (TMR) and reactive recovery — suffer from high overhead or unacceptable critical-path latency. A smarter, workload-adaptive fault-tolerance mechanism is needed.

Method: ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and partial reconfiguration overhead, then selects TMR configurations per reconfigurable partition to minimize a composite objective (latency + energy + reliability risk). It leverages partial reconfiguration on Xilinx FPGA fabric to dynamically apply TMR only where and when beneficial. Evaluated on ZCU104 with six reconfigurable regions using a 500-task trace (ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-Lite) under time-varying SEU injection.

Result: ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost than both static TMR and reactive reconfiguration, maintains high task success rate and near-baseline throughput, with low online decision-making overhead.

Conclusion: Proactive, workload-aware selective TMR via partial reconfiguration effectively balances reliability, performance, and energy for FPGA-based CNN inference at the edge, outperforming both always-on and purely reactive approaches.

Abstract: SRAM-based FPGAs provide an attractive platform for energy- and latency-constrained CNN inference at the network edge, yet transient faults can lead to silent errors that compromise reliability. Always-on redundancy (e.g., full TMR) improves correctness but incurs substantial performance and energy overhead, while reactive recovery may introduce unacceptable latency on the critical path. We propose \textbf{ProWAFT}, a proactive workload-aware fault-tolerance framework for FPGA-based CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable partitions. ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and reconfiguration overhead, and selects configurations that minimize a composite objective over latency, energy, and reliability risk. Implemented on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 platform with six reconfigurable regions and evaluated on a 500-task trace derived from ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-Lite under time-varying SEU injection, ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost than static TMR and reactive reconfiguration while maintaining high task success rate and near-baseline throughput with low online decision overhead.

</details>


### [24] [When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01727)
*Xu Guo,Jian Tong,Zhihui Lu,Qipeng Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper isolates Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), where the seed-question pool and teacher model are held constant while only the per-question response budget varies. The authors adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, empirically validate it, and show that FSS is a bounded scaling axis — at large budgets, adding seed questions (Source Expansion) outperforms spending budget on more responses per question.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scaling studies conflate two distinct routes for scaling synthetic data: Source Expansion (SE) and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS). FSS remains underexplored because prior work typically expands the source as data grows. The authors aim to isolate and characterize FSS as a distinct scaling axis.

Method: The authors isolate FSS by fixing the seed-question pool and teacher model, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). They adapt the rectified scaling law to the FSS setting, deriving it from how repeated sampling progressively covers a fixed source distribution. The derived form is fit on low budgets and used to predict performance at held-out high budgets. They also compare SE vs. FSS at matched total-sample budgets, and test alternative synthesis protocols within the FSS regime.

Result: The derived scaling law, fit on low budgets, accurately predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher-student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets, but SE outperforms FSS at large budgets. Within FSS, neither synthesizing additional questions from existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain Rejection Sampling at matched budgets.

Conclusion: FSS is a bounded scaling axis and serves as a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. Source Expansion is the more effective route for scaling synthetic data at large budgets. Code and data will be released.

Abstract: Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS by holding the seed-question pool and teacher model fixed, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). We adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, the derived form, fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher--student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets; at large budgets, adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses. Within FSS, however, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.

</details>


### [25] [Rethinking Speech-LLM Integration for ASR: Effective Joint Speech-Text Training by Interleaving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01733)
*Ruchao Fan,Yiming Wang,Rui Zhao,Liliang Ren,Keqi Deng,Xiaoyang Chen,Ali Zare,Bo Ren,Yuxuan Hu,Junkun Chen,Yan Huang,Yelong Shen,Jinyu Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: JSTIP is a pretraining strategy that interleaves speech and text at word/segment levels within aligned pairs, improving ASR entity recognition and domain adaptation while reducing the speech-text modality gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As supervised ASR data scales up, the benefit of LLM priors diminishes, and naive joint speech-text training underutilizes textual knowledge. The authors aim to better harness textual pretraining for ASR.

Method: Proposes Joint Speech-Text Interleaved Pretraining (JSTIP), which constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences within aligned pairs. Designed for speech-LLM architectures accepting continuous inputs.

Result: On 38k hours of ASR data, JSTIP consistently improves entity accuracy over ASR-only and joint speech-text baselines. It matches entity recognition performance using only domain text (vs. synthetic speech-text pairs), simplifying domain adaptation, and is competitive with open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems on medical entity recognition. Zero-shot SQA shows interleaving reduces modality gap and preserves LLM generative priors.

Conclusion: Interleaved pretraining effectively bridges the speech-text modality gap and retains the LLM's generative prior, which likely explains entity recognition gains. JSTIP also enables simpler domain adaptation via text-only data.
