Abstract: Speech-LLM integration has shown promising results by leveraging extensive textual pretraining, yet its specific benefits for automatic speech recognition (ASR) remain unclear. We observe that as supervised ASR training data increases, the contribution of LLM priors becomes less evident, and simple speech-text joint training under-utilizes textual knowledge. We therefore propose Joint Speech-Text Interleaved Pretraining (JSTIP), an ASR-oriented pretraining strategy that constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences within aligned pairs for speech-LLM architectures that accept continuous inputs. Experiments on 38k hours of ASR data show consistent entity accuracy improvement compared to ASR-only and joint speech-text training baselines. JSTIP achieves on-par entity recognition performance using domain transcription text compared to synthetic speech-text pairs, simplifying domain adaptation. Benefiting from textual pretraining and domain text data, JSTIP is competitive with open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems in medical entity recognition. The zero-shot speech question answering behaviors further suggest that interleaving reduces the speech-text modality gap and preserves the LLM generative prior, which is likely the reason for the entity improvements on the ASR task.

</details>


### [26] [HaloGuard 1.0: An Open Weights Constitutional Classifier for Multilingual AI Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02079)
*Navaneeth Sangameswaran,Preetham S,Ashmiya Lenin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HaloGuard 1.0 is an open-weights input safety guard model using a constitutional-classifier paradigm. It achieves state-of-the-art prompt-safety performance at ~1/10th the size of leading alternatives, driven by a 46-policy safety constitution with 2,940 subcategories, paired counterfactual data generation, two-tier harmless design for false-positive reduction, and multilingual coverage across 46 languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current open guard models for input/prompt safety are very large and lack structured, transparent safety governance. There is a need for a smaller, highly performant, open-weights guard that explicitly encodes its safety policies in a human-readable constitution, handles multilingual content without treating non-English languages as inherently adversarial, and systematically reduces both false positives and false negatives.

Method: The approach centers on a **safety constitution** (46 policies, 2,940 subcategories) that drives synthetic data generation. Key techniques include: (1) **one-to-one paired counterfactuals** that hold topic and vocabulary constant while flipping harmful/harmless intent; (2) a **two-tier harmless design** separately targeting boundary false positives and baseline false positives; (3) **balanced multilingual materialisation** across 46 languages, treating language as a surface form on both sides of the safety boundary; and (4) an **always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol** for continuous hardening against content-level and agentic attacks.

Result: On seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B achieves an average F1 of 90.9 (best among evaluated open guards), outperforming models up to 27B parameters (>30× larger), with FPR of 4.3 and FNR of 9.5. The 4B variant reaches F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, using extra capacity for precision. Structured adjudication of remaining failures suggests most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model errors.

Conclusion: The constitutional-classifier paradigm, with structured synthetic data generation and multilingual balance, enables compact open guard models (<1B parameters) to outperform models over 30× larger on prompt-safety benchmarks. The approach demonstrates that explicit policy grounding, counterfactual training, and careful false-positive management yield state-of-the-art safety classification with transparent, auditable decision boundaries.

Abstract: We present HaloGuard 1.0, an open-weights implementation of the constitutional-classifier paradigm for input safety. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on English and multilingual prompt-safety benchmarks at roughly one-tenth the model size of current leading open guard models. The safety constitution is the organising structure of the corpus: a natural-language constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation, with exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic and vocabulary fixed while flipping intent, a two-tier harmless design that separately targets boundary and baseline false positives (FPs), and balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages that treats language as a surface form appearing on both sides of the boundary rather than as an adversarial signal. Across seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B attains the best average F1 (90.9) of any open guard we evaluate, outperforming baselines up to 27B parameters (over 30 times larger) while holding false-positive rate (FPR) to 4.3 and false-negative rate (FNR) to 9.5. The HaloGuard 1.0-4B variant reaches average F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, spending its extra capacity on precision rather than recall. A structured adjudication of the remaining failures indicates that most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses. An always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol continuously hardens the guard against both content-level and agentic attacks. We release the models as open weights.

</details>


### [27] [PARTREP: Learning What to Repeat for Decoder-only LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01792)
*Andikawati P Widjaja,Yongjun Kim,Hyounghun Kim,Jaeho Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PartRep selectively repeats only high-NLL (less predictable) tokens instead of the entire prompt, reducing KV cache and prefill costs while retaining most reasoning gains from full prompt repetition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decoder-only LLMs suffer from asymmetric information flow via causal attention, where later tokens have richer context than earlier ones. Full prompt repetition mitigates this but doubles KV cache and quadruples prefill attention cost, making it impractical for long-context settings.

Method: PartRep uses token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) to select the most informative tokens for repetition, based on the hypothesis that less predictable tokens benefit more from late-position grounding. A lightweight gating network, trained to predict high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states, enables token selection during mid-prefill via early exit, avoiding the cost of a full forward pass for scoring.

Result: Across eight benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, RULER, etc.) and three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most of full repetition's gains while using only 59.4% of the KV cache and 79.0% of the prefill FLOPs.

Conclusion: Selective token repetition based on NLL is an effective and efficient alternative to full prompt repetition, addressing the causal attention asymmetry in decoder-only LLMs with significantly reduced computational overhead.

Abstract: While decoder-only LLMs excel at a vast array of natural language tasks, it suffers from an asymmetric information flow induced by causal attention: later tokens are richer in contextual grounding than earlier ones. A simple and effective remedy is prompt repetition -- just appending a second copy of prompt before generation can redistribute grounding across positions and improve reasoning performance. However, full repetition of the original prompt doubles the KV cache footprint and quadruples attention cost during prefill, making it impractical for long-context settings. We propose PartRep, a selective augmentation method that appends only the most informative tokens -- rather than the entire prompt. We use token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) as a selection signal, motivated by the hypothesis that less predictable tokens are less recoverable from surrounding context and therefore benefit more from late-position repetition. To avoid the heavy cost of a full forward pass for scoring, we train a lightweight gate that predicts high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states, enabling token selection during mid-prefill via early exit. Across eight benchmarks (including MMLU, GSM8K, and RULER) and three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most of the gains of full repetition while using only 59.4\% of its KV cache and 79.0\% of its prefill FLOPs.

</details>


### [28] [On the Limits of Steering Vectors for Preference-Aligned Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01802)
*Melanie Subbiah,Zara Hall,Kathleen McKeown*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Steering vectors for controlled text generation face significant generalization limits across traits, tasks, and multi-trait composition, challenging their viability as a general-purpose preference alignment tool.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite growing interest in steering vectors as interpretable, training-free mechanisms for controlled text generation, their practical generality across different traits, downstream tasks, and compositional settings has not been systematically evaluated.

Method: Using the PLUME writing personalization benchmark, steering vectors were extracted for various preferences and evaluated on summarization and email-writing tasks using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct. The study examines three dimensions: (1) trait expressibility across different traits, (2) transferability from positive/negative style examples to downstream tasks, and (3) multi-trait composition using common vector composition methods.

Result: Steering effectiveness varies substantially across traits. Transfer from source style examples to downstream writing personalization tasks causes degradation in steering effectiveness. All multi-trait composition methods exhibit significant drops in trait expression as more vectors are added, with an inherent tradeoff between coherence and expressibility requiring per-setting hyperparameter tuning.

Conclusion: Steering vectors face meaningful limitations as a general-purpose tool for preference alignment, with their effectiveness being highly contingent on the specific trait, task context, and composition strategy employed.

Abstract: Steering vectors have emerged as a promising approach to controlled text generation, offering interpretable, training-free mechanisms for shaping model outputs. However, their practical generality remains poorly understood. We study the limits of steering vector generalization along three dimensions: trait expressibility, task transfer, and multi-trait composition. Using the PLUME writing personalization benchmark, we extract steering vectors for a range of preferences and evaluate them on summarization and email-writing tasks across two open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct). We find that steering effectiveness varies substantially across traits. We further show that steering effectiveness can degrade when vectors extracted from positive and negative style examples are transferred to downstream writing personalization tasks. Finally, we compare common methods for composing multiple steering vectors and find that all methods suffer significant drops in trait expression as more vectors are added, with a tradeoff between coherence and expressibility that requires per-setting hyperparameter tuning. Taken together, our results suggest that steering vectors face meaningful limits as a general-purpose tool for preference alignment.

</details>


### [29] [PairCoder++: Pair Programming as a Universal Paradigm for Verified Code-Driven Multimodal and Structured-Artifact Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01883)
*Junhao Chen,Xiang Li,Mingjin Chen,Boran Zhang,Henghaofan Zhang,Yibin Xu,Yuehan Cui,Fangsheng Weng,Fei Ma,Qi Tian,Ruqi Huang,Hao Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PairCoder introduces a dual-agent pair programming framework (Driver + Navigator) for code-generation LLMs, where the Navigator reviews outputs against toolchain verification evidence. Across 17 benchmarks and 7 models, it substantially improves verifiable artifact generation (e.g., Blender executability from 0.20→0.78, TikZ compile rate +10–30 points), at ~7× single-model cost. Gains concentrate where the toolchain provides informative feedback; performance ties or mildly regresses otherwise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-pass LLM inference for code-driven artifact generation (charts, CAD, 3D scenes, etc.) is brittle because the compiler/renderer/simulator that validates the output is invisible to the model. The model cannot see diagnostics, execution results, or rendered outputs to correct errors iteratively.

Method: PairCoder frames verification-grounded review as two-agent pair programming: a Driver agent writes the program, and a Navigator agent reviews it against toolchain evidence (diagnostics, execution results, side-by-side renderings of current vs. target artifacts). The two agents switch roles when errors persist. The method is evaluated across 17 public benchmarks, seven models from three vendors, using full official metric suites.

Result: PairCoder improves essentially every benchmark with verifiable artifacts. Key results: Blender scene executability rose from 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rates improved by 10–30 points on every model. Cost is 2.9–9.2× single model (≈7× overall). Improvements are concentrated where the toolchain provides an informative oracle and baseline headroom exists; performance ties or mildly regresses where the oracle is weak.

Conclusion: Pair programming with toolchain-grounded review is a reliable recipe for verified code-driven generation. The method's effectiveness depends on the quality of the toolchain oracle, suggesting future work should focus on strengthening verification feedback loops.

Abstract: Code is the medium through which large language models generate structured artifacts: charts, scientific figures, vector graphics, CAD models, 3D scenes, and hardware designs are all produced by writing programs. In this regime single pass inference is brittle, because the compiler, renderer, or simulator that decides whether the artifact exists is invisible to the model. We present PairCoder, which grounds review in the toolchain and realizes it as two agent pair programming: a Driver agent writes the program, a Navigator agent reviews it against verification evidence (diagnostics, execution results, and renderings of the current artifact beside the target), and the two switch roles when errors persist. Across 17 public benchmarks and seven models from three vendors, PairCoder improves essentially every benchmark whose artifact is verifiable, on full official metric suites rather than execution alone (for example, Blender scene executability 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rate up 10 to 30 points on every model), at 2.9 to 9.2 times single model cost (about 7 times overall). The improvements concentrate where the toolchain provides an informative oracle and the baseline leaves headroom, and the method ties or mildly regresses where the oracle is weak; we frame pair programming as a reliable recipe for verified code driven generation.

</details>


### [30] [The Grammar Does the Work: Functional vs. Lexical Dependency Length Minimization Across Universal Dependencies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01899)
*Kim Gerdes*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Dependency length minimization operates on two distinct levels: grammar-driven optimization keeps functional dependencies universally short and invariant, while processing-driven optimization governs lexical dependencies, which are longer, more variable, and constrained by word-order typology.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous DLM studies report only a single mean dependency distance per language, obscuring variation across syntactic relation types. The authors aim to reveal how DLM operates differentially on functional versus lexical dependencies across a large, typologically diverse sample.

Method: Analysis of 122 languages using two dependency annotation schemes (UD and SUD, version 2.17), comparing mean dependency distances across functional (det, case, aux) and lexical (nsubj, obj, obl) relation types, and examining the influence of word-order typology.

Result: Functional dependencies are universally short (mean 1.71, σ = 0.33) and invariant across languages. Lexical dependencies are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable (σ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. This asymmetry persists in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92).

Conclusion: Grammar does the core work of minimization by scaffolding sentences with local functional attachments, while processing pressures determine the ordering of lexical heads.

Abstract: Dependency length minimization (DLM) is a well-documented processing universal, but previous studies report a single mean dependency distance (MDD) per language, obscuring variation across syntactic relation types. We analyze 122 languages in UD and SUD (version 2.17), showing that DLM operates on two distinct levels. Grammar-driven optimization targets functional dependencies (det, case, aux), which are universally short (mean 1.71, $σ$ = 0.33) and invariant across typologically diverse languages. Processing-driven optimization operates on lexical dependencies (nsubj, obj, obl), which are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable ($σ$ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. This asymmetry holds in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92). We conclude that ''the grammar does the work'' of minimization by scaffolding sentences with local functional attachments, leaving processing pressures to determine the ordering of lexical heads.

</details>


### [31] [TUDUM: A Turkish-Thinking Reasoning Pipeline for Qwen3.5-27B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01927)
*Baran Bingol,Bahaeddin Turkoglu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TUDUM adapts a Qwen 27B model to produce Turkish-language reasoning traces via SFT and GRPO-style RL, achieving more consistent Turkish thinking behavior but with mixed benchmark results—improved reasoning style at the cost of reduced accuracy compared to the base model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing thinking models tend to process Turkish prompts internally in English, producing reasoning traces (the `<think>` block) in English and only translating the final answer. The authors aim to make the full explicit reasoning chain genuinely Turkish, treating the `<think>` block as a trainable behavioral target rather than merely localizing outputs.

Method: The pipeline starts from `unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B` and proceeds in two stages: (1) Supervised fine-tuning with LoRA adapters on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples to instill Turkish-language chain-of-thought behavior; (2) GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment to recover and enhance reasoning performance.

Result: SFT successfully produced shorter, more consistently Turkish reasoning traces with reduced thinking exhaustion and response length, but degraded benchmark accuracy. RL partially recovered mathematical performance—notably AIME24 at the best early checkpoint—but did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and failed to exceed the base model on the Macro-6 average.

Conclusion: The contribution is framed as a technically honest pipeline and evaluation for Turkish-native reasoning, not as a state-of-the-art claim. The RL-tuned step-50 model is publicly released. The work highlights the trade-off between language-consistent reasoning behavior and benchmark performance.

Abstract: This paper presents TUDUM (Türkçe Düşünen Üretken Model), a project pipeline for adapting a Qwen-family 27B thinking model toward Turkish reasoning. The central problem is not only to answer Turkish prompts in Turkish, but to make the explicit reasoning trace itself Turkish. A thinking model may translate a Turkish prompt into an English-centered internal or visible scratchpad, solve the problem mostly in English, and only localize the final answer. TUDUM instead treats the generated <think>...</think> block as a trainable behavior. The pipeline starts from the project base checkpoint unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B, applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples using LoRA adapters, and then applies GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment. The results are mixed. SFT made the model shorter and more consistently Turkish in its reasoning behavior, with large reductions in average response length and thinking exhaustion, but reduced benchmark accuracy. RL recovered some mathematical performance, especially AIME24 at the best early checkpoint, yet did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and did not exceed the base model on the reported Macro-6 average. The contribution is therefore best framed as a technically honest Turkish-thinking reasoning pipeline and evaluation, not as a claim of state-of-the-art Turkish reasoning. The released step-50 model is publicly available.

</details>


### [32] [AIriskEval-edu: New Dataset for Risk Assessment in AI-mediated K-12 Educational Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01934)
*Javier Irigoyen,Roberto Daza,Francisco Jurado,Julian Fierrez,Ruben Tolosana,Alvaro Ortigosa,Enrique Blas,Aythami Morales*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces AIriskEval-edu-db2, a dataset of 1,639 explanations (785 with structured explainability annotations) from 170 ScienceQA questions across K-12 subjects, designed for training LLM-based auditors to detect and explain pedagogical risks along five dimensions: factual precision, depth/completeness, focus/relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. Experiments compare proprietary frontier models against a fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B for risk detection and explainability, testing whether local models can match or exceed larger models while preserving data privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a growing need for automated, explainable pedagogical risk assessment in K-12 educational content to ensure quality and safety. Existing approaches lack structured datasets that combine risk taxonomies with fine-grained explainability annotations, and privacy concerns limit the use of cloud-based proprietary LLMs in educational settings.

Method: The authors construct AIriskEval-edu-db2 by curating 170 ScienceQA questions across science, language arts, and social sciences. For each question, one human teacher explanation and 11 LLM-simulated teacher profile explanations (each tied to a distinct pedagogical risk) are provided. A five-dimension risk rubric is defined, aligned with educational standards. A subset of 785 explanations receives structured explainability annotations (risk localization + risk description) via a semi-automatic pipeline validated by expert teachers. Validation experiments benchmark state-of-the-art proprietary models against a supervised fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B on both risk detection and explainability tasks.

Result: The paper presents the dataset and the experimental framework; specific quantitative results from the validation experiments are not detailed in the abstract, though the abstract indicates the experiments evaluate whether the fine-tuned local model can approach or surpass frontier models.

Conclusion: AIriskEval-edu-db2 provides a novel resource for developing explainable, privacy-preserving pedagogical risk auditors. Fine-tuning smaller, locally deployable models on this dataset may offer a viable alternative to proprietary LLMs for educational auditing tasks.

Abstract: This work introduces AIriskEval-edu-db2, a new dataset designed to train and evaluate auditors based on LLMs for an explainable pedagogical risk assessment in instructional content for grades K-12. The dataset comprises 1,639 explanations from 170 curated ScienceQA questions, covering science, language arts, and social sciences. For each question, the dataset includes an explanation written by a human teacher alongside 11 explanations generated by LLM-simulated teacher profiles associated with distinct pedagogical risks. We propose a comprehensive risk rubric aligned with established educational standards that covers five complementary dimensions: factual precision, depth and completeness, focus and relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. A key contribution is the addition of 785 explanations with structured explainability annotations, including risk localization and risk description. The annotations are produced through a semi-automatic process with expert teacher validation. Finally, we present validation experiments comparing state-of-the-art proprietary models with a lightweight local Llama 3.1 8B model in both the pedagogical risk detection and the explainability assessment. These experiments evaluate whether supervised fine-tuning on AIriskEval-edu-db2 enables a locally deployable model to approach or outperform stronger frontier models while preserving privacy in educational auditing and assessment tasks.

</details>


### [33] [NAVER LABS Europe Submission to the Instruction-following 2026 Short Track](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01960)
*Marcely Zanon Boito,Hemant Yadav,Jean-Luc Meunier,Ioan Calapodescu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NAVER LABS Europe presents an improved multi-stage training pipeline for joint ASR, ST, and SQA, featuring SpeechMapper for speech-to-LLM projection using only ASR data, and a synthetic SQA dataset (fakACL) built from LLM-generated scientific talks. The system ties for first in the IWSLT 2026 short track while being more compact than prior work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To advance instruction-following speech processing by jointly handling ASR, speech translation (ST), and speech question answering (SQA) under constrained settings, while improving upon last year's first-place system with a more compact model and weaker LLM backbone.

Method: The authors propose a multi-stage training pipeline with two key innovations: (1) SpeechMapper — a speech-to-LLM embedding projector trained solely on ASR data, replacing the previous speech projector; (2) fakACL — a synthetic SQA dataset of artificial scientific presentations generated by prompting the LLM backbone, segmenting the output, and synthesizing speech via SeamlessM4T-large-v2. The system processes English speech into Chinese, Italian, and German for all three tasks.

Result: The combined SpeechMapper and fakACL contributions yield a system that outperforms the previous year's best short-track system, ties for first place in the overall IWSLT 2026 short track ranking, and achieves this with a considerably more compact model using a weaker LLM backbone.

Conclusion: An improved speech projection mechanism (SpeechMapper) trained with only ASR data, combined with domain-specific synthetic data (fakACL), enables state-of-the-art instruction-following speech processing that surpasses prior systems in both performance and efficiency.

Abstract: In this paper, we describe NAVER LABS Europe's submission to the instruction-following speech processing short track at IWSLT 2026. We participate again in the constrained setting, developing systems capable of jointly performing ASR, ST, and SQA from English speech into Chinese, Italian, and German. Building on our previous submission, ranked first in last year's short track, we update our multi-stage training pipeline by replacing the speech projector with SpeechMapper, a method for learning a speech-to-LLM embedding projector using only ASR data. In addition, we introduce a synthetic SQA dataset, fakACL, composed of artificially generated scientific presentations. This dataset is built by prompting the LLM backbone, segmenting the generated talks, and synthesizing speech with SeamlessM4T-large-v2. The combination of an improved speech projection mechanism and domain-specific synthetic data allows our model to outperform last year's best short-track system, while being considerably more compact and relying on a weaker LLM backbone. This year's results place our system tied for first place in the overall short track ranking.

</details>


### [34] [Beyond Supervised Clarification: Input Rewriting with LLMs for Dialogue Discourse Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01964)
*Yiming Liu,Ziyue Zhang,Zhichao Xu,Xin Yu,Yingheng Tang,Tianyu Jiang,Jie Cao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper re-examines input clarification for dialogue discourse parsing under realistic zero-shot conditions and finds that unsupervised rewriting often causes more harm than good. The key insight is that clarification should be treated as a selective intervention problem requiring rewritability prediction before editing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work shows supervised clarification models improve dialogue discourse parsing (DDP) by rewriting fragmentary utterances. However, real deployment lacks clarification supervision, requiring zero-shot prompting or parser feedback. The authors investigate whether such unsupervised clarification actually works in practice.

Method: The authors evaluate last-utterance clarification across three SDRT datasets (STAC, Molweni, DISRPT) with multiple frozen parsers, comparing zero-shot prompted clarifiers, best-of-N rewriting, and a parser-aware clarifier trained with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) to reduce regressions via conservative abstention.

Result: Parser-agnostic rewriting introduces more regressions than repairs; edits that fix some issues disrupt discourse cues the parser relies on. A best-of-8 rewriting analysis reveals many errors are fundamentally unrepairable through input rewriting. The GRPO-trained clarifier reduces regressions by up to 37% through abstention but still cannot produce selectivity-aware clarifications that consistently improve parsing.

Conclusion: Clarification should be reframed as a selective intervention problem. The critical missing capability is rewritability prediction — deciding whether an utterance can be repaired before intervening. This is essential for input-side optimization of frozen discourse parsers and for improving agentic NLP pipelines broadly.

Abstract: Rewriting inputs to improve frozen downstream models has become a common strategy in modern NLP pipelines. Prior work on incremental dialogue discourse parsing (DDP) shows that supervised clarification models can rewrite fragmentary or underspecified utterances, such as resolving ellipsis or references, to improve parsing accuracy. In this work, we revisit this idea under realistic deployment conditions, where no clarification supervision is available and the clarifier must rely on zero-shot prompting or feedback from a frozen parser. Across three Segmented Discourse Representation Theory (SDRT) datasets and multiple parsers, we find that last-utterance clarification is far less reliable than suggested by supervised settings. Parser-agnostic rewriting often introduces more regressions than repairs, as edits that enable fixes also disrupt discourse cues relied upon by the parser. A best-of-8 rewriting analysis further reveals a practical ceiling: a large fraction of errors are not repairable through input rewriting alone. A parser-aware clarifier trained with GRPO reduces regressions by up to 37% by learning conservative abstention, yet still fails to produce selectivity-aware clarifications that consistently improve parsing. Together, these findings recast clarification as a selective intervention problem. We identify rewritability prediction, deciding whether an utterance is repairable before intervention, as the key missing capability for input-side optimization of frozen discourse parsers, and a critical direction for improving agentic pipelines more broadly.

</details>


### [35] [Towards a Phonology-Informed Evaluation of Multilingual TTS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01965)
*Sneha Ray Barman,Neeraj Kumar Sharma,Shakuntala Mahanta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A classifier-based auditing framework reveals that Meta's MMS TTS fails to faithfully produce Assamese ATR vowel harmony in ~33% of tokens, despite sounding natural — exposing a gap between intended and produced phonology that standard MOS cannot detect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard TTS evaluation metrics like MOS assess naturalness but fail to test whether systems preserve linguistically meaningful sound contrasts (e.g., those distinguishing words from grammatical forms). There is a need for diagnostic tools that audit phonological faithfulness in TTS output.

Method: A classifier-based framework is proposed: a phonological feature classifier is trained on human speech and then transferred to TTS-synthesized speech with minimal loss. The classifier's predictions on synthesized speech are compared against both underlying phonological specifications and human speech benchmarks to audit faithfulness. The method is demonstrated on Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony using Meta's MMS TTS.

Result: The classifier transfers from human to synthesized speech with minimal performance loss. The audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels surface as [-ATR] in approximately one-third of TTS tokens, despite carrying an underlying [+ATR] specification — a systematic bias absent in human speech. At the word level, classifier-predicted ATR labels classify harmony patterns more accurately than transcription-based labels, indicating a mismatch between intended and actually produced phonology.

Conclusion: The framework provides task-specific diagnostics for phonological faithfulness in TTS and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues, offering a principled complement to coarse-grained naturalness evaluations like MOS.

Abstract: Neural TTS systems can sound natural across languages, but naturalness does not guarantee the preservation of sound contrasts that distinguish words from their grammatical forms. Standard metrics like MOS do not test for this. We propose a classifier-based framework that audits TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns using human speech as a benchmark. Testing Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony with Meta's MMS TTS, we show that a classifier trained on human speech transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The faithfulness audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens despite an underlying [+ATR] specification, a bias absent in human speech. At the word level, predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a gap between intended and produced phonology. The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.

</details>


### [36] [Object Aligner: A Configurable JSON Schema Similarity Score for Graphs, Applied to LLM Prompt Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01972)
*Jan Drchal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Object Aligner (OA) is an open-source Python library for deterministically scoring JSON output against a gold reference. It recursively aligns JSON trees (Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections, sequence alignment for ordered ones), awarding partial credit per schema annotations. Its key contribution, referential alignment, handles graph/hypergraph-structured data with arbitrary identifiers by approximating a bijection via Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement, making the score relabeling-invariant. OA also emits ranked repair suggestions and improves performance as a reward signal in prompt optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing JSON evaluation methods are inadequate: exact match is brittle, text similarity ignores structure, and LLM judges are expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. Moreover, prior similarity metrics assume flat trees and break on graph- or hypergraph-structured data keyed by arbitrary identifiers. A deterministic, structure-aware, schema-driven, and relabeling-invariant scoring method is needed.

Method: Object Aligner scores two JSON objects by recursively aligning their trees: the Hungarian algorithm handles unordered collections (sets, JSON objects), while sequence alignment handles ordered lists. Configuration is entirely via JSON Schema extensions, requiring no code. The key innovation, referential alignment, infers a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers using Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement (approximating graph isomorphism), yielding relabeling-invariant scores. An order-sensitive regime supports ranking/planning tasks. The alignment process also localizes mismatches, enabling free ranked repair suggestions. OA is integrated as a reward inside the GEPA prompt optimizer.

Result: When used as a reward signal within the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all evaluated datasets.

Conclusion: Object Aligner provides a deterministic, schema-configurable, and structure-aware alternative for JSON evaluation that handles complex graph-structured data with referential alignment. It eliminates the need for brittle exact matching, structure-oblivious text similarity, or expensive LLM judges, while offering practical benefits like repair suggestions and prompt optimization utility.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often asked to produce JSON conforming to a fixed schema, powering information extraction, tool calling, agentic planning, and knowledge-graph construction. Measuring how closely an output matches a gold reference is essential yet surprisingly hard: exact match is brittle, text similarity ignores structure, and an LLM judge is expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. We address this with Object Aligner (OA), an open-source Python library that scores two JSON objects deterministically by recursively aligning their trees (the Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections, sequence alignment for ordered ones) and awarding partial credit at the granularity the schema declares. The Object Aligner is configured entirely through a set of JSON Schema extensions, so adapting it to a new task involves annotating a schema rather than writing code. Complex structured data, however, are rarely flat trees: records may form graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, breaking the assumptions of prior similarity metrics. Our central contribution, referential alignment, closes this gap by inferring a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers and scoring every reference through it, so the score is invariant to relabeling. Since recovering this bijection exactly is graph isomorphism, the Object Aligner approximates it with Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement. An order-sensitive sequence regime targets ranking and planning. Since the same alignment localizes every mismatch, the Object Aligner emits ranked repair suggestions at no extra cost. Used as a reward inside the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all datasets.

</details>


### [37] [Using embeddings to predict spoken word duration and pitch in Mandarin monosyllabic words](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02002)
*Xiaoyun Jin,Mirjam Ernestus,R. Harald Baayen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Contextualized embeddings (CEs) from Mandarin conversational speech predict both f0 contours and spoken word duration. The study demonstrates that CEs predict duration for 7470 monosyllabic CV tokens significantly above chance at both type and token levels, and these predicted durations are precise enough to convert time-normalized f0 contours back to absolute time, outperforming permutation baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed CEs predict time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words. However, whether CEs also encode durational information — and whether this information is precise enough to reconstruct f0 contours on an absolute millisecond time scale — remains unexplored. This study aims to fill that gap.

Method: 7470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words were extracted from a spontaneous speech corpus. Contextualized embeddings were used to predict spoken word duration. Predictive performance was evaluated against both type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines. Predicted durations were then used to back-transform time-normalized f0 contours (in [0,1]) to absolute time (ms scale), and the resulting contours were compared to empirical contours and a permutation baseline.

Result: CEs predicted word duration significantly above chance at both the type level and the individual token level. The predicted durations were sufficiently precise that back-transformed f0 contours on the ms time scale approximated empirical contours and outperformed the permutation baseline.

Conclusion: Contextualized embeddings encode not only tonal/prosodic trajectory information but also fine-grained temporal (durational) information about spoken words in spontaneous Mandarin speech, enabling accurate reconstruction of f0 contours in absolute time.

Abstract: Time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words in conversational speech have been shown to be predictable in part from their contextualized embeddings (CEs). The present study investigates whether CEs also predict spoken word duration for 7470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words extracted from a Mandarin corpus of spontaneous speech. We show that CEs indeed are predictive for duration, above chance level, not only at the type level, but also at the level of individual tokens, as indicated by the results obtained with the type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines. We also show that the predicted durations are sufficiently precise to back-transform predicted f0 contours in [0,1] normalized time to contours on the ms time scale. The resulting predicted contours approximate empirical contours and also outperform a permutation baseline.

</details>


### [38] [EduArt: An educational-level benchmark for evaluating art history knowledge in large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02007)
*Gianmarco Spinaci,Lukas Klic,Giovanni Colavizza*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EduArt is a bilingual, 871-question benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs on art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning. It reveals that while frontier models saturate multiple-choice accuracy, performance collapses on open-ended formats like error identification, demonstrating that single-format benchmarks overestimate model capabilities and that knowledge retrieval and knowledge deployment are dissociable skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM benchmarks aggregate performance across domains, masking discipline-specific behavior. Existing art-focused evaluations rely on synthetic questions without item-level psychometric reporting. The authors argue that understanding how models actually perform on real educational art-history tasks—across formats, languages, and image conditions—is essential before responsibly deploying them in art-historical scholarship.

Method: The authors constructed EduArt, a benchmark of 871 human-authored questions drawn from Italian secondary-school exercises and US AP Art History exams, covering two languages and seven formats (multiple choice, open completion, error identification, in-text word placement, etc.). Twelve multimodal LLMs from six provider families were tested under two conditions: answer-only and written-justification. Item properties were analyzed using Classical Test Theory (discrimination indices), and a logistic regression isolated the independent effects of format, language, image presence, and model on accuracy.

Result: The benchmark exhibited strong psychometric properties (mean discrimination = 0.514; 82.3% of items classified as good discriminators). Six models reached near-ceiling multiple-choice accuracy (>94%), but performance dropped dramatically on open-ended formats: Claude Opus 4.6 fell to 23.9% on open completion; Claude Sonnet 4.6 fell to 6.2% on error identification. Format was a strong independent predictor of accuracy. The motivation condition produced predominantly negative, model-family-dependent shifts in accuracy.

Conclusion: Art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy that knowledge in generative tasks are distinct capabilities in current multimodal LLMs. Single-format benchmarks (especially multiple-choice) systematically overestimate what models can reliably do. Mapping the full capability profile across formats is a prerequisite for responsible use of these models in art-historical scholarship, where tasks require content production and manipulation rather than passive recognition.

Abstract: Large language models now score near ceiling on general benchmarks, but these aggregate measures reveal little about how models behave within single disciplines. Existing art-focused evaluations rely on synthetic questions and rarely report item-level properties. This paper introduces EduArt, an educational-level benchmark for art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs. EduArt comprises 871 human-authored questions from Italian secondary-school exercises and US Advanced Placement Art History exams, spanning two languages and seven formats from multiple choice to in-text word placement and error identification. Twelve models from six provider families were evaluated under a default answer-only condition and a motivation condition requiring written justification, and characterized using Classical Test Theory and a logistic regression isolating the effects of format, language, image presence, and model. The benchmark showed strong psychometric properties (mean discrimination 0.514, 82.3 percent good discriminators), while multiple-choice accuracy saturated near ceiling for six models, showing recognition formats alone cannot distinguish frontier models. Format was a strong independent predictor of accuracy: models exceeding 94 percent on multiple choice fell to 23.9 percent on open completion (Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2 percent on error identification (Claude Sonnet 4.6). The motivation condition changed accuracy in a predominantly negative, family-dependent direction. These dissociations indicate that art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy it are distinct capabilities, and that single-format benchmarks overestimate what models can reliably do. Mapping this capability profile is a precondition for responsible use of multimodal LLMs in art-historical scholarship, where tasks demand producing and manipulating content rather than selecting from fixed options.

</details>


### [39] [OpenSafeIntent: Evaluating Intent-Calibrated Safe Completion Across Dual-Use Prompt Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02047)
*Rheeya Uppaal,Seungwoo Lyu,Selina Sung,Junjie Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OpenSafeIntent introduces a benchmark of controlled prompt-sets with benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task to evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts, revealing that prompt-level safety metrics mask critical failures in intent-calibrated safe completion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current safety evaluations rely on isolated prompts, which fail to capture whether models appropriately adjust their behavior when the same underlying task is framed with different intents. The authors argue that safe completion should be measured as intent-calibrated behavior — maintaining helpfulness for benign uses while refusing harmful ones — rather than as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff averaged over independent prompts.

Method: The authors construct OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark where each datapoint consists of matched benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of an identical underlying task. This controlled design enables direct comparison of model behavior across intent shifts. They evaluate a broad suite of models, testing calibration of assistance, robustness to paraphrasing of dual-use prompts, reliability of high-level answers on risky topics, and the effect of reframing ambiguous requests into safer tasks.

Result: Key findings: (1) prompt-level safety hides failures — models often fail to remain safe across matched intent variants; (2) dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrase; (3) high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe; (4) responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks are substantially less likely to cross the safety boundary.

Conclusion: Safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants rather than as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent prompts. The benchmark exposes systematic weaknesses in current safety alignment that single-prompt evaluations miss.

Abstract: Safe completion requires models to provide useful assistance without enabling harm, but this behavior is difficult to evaluate with isolated prompts. We introduce OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark of controlled prompt-sets that vary intent while holding the underlying task fixed. Each datapoint contains benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task. This design lets us evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts, rather than merely appearing safe on average. Across a broad model suite, we find that prompt-level safety hides important failures: models often fail to remain safe across matched intent variants, dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrase, high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe, and responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks are substantially less likely to cross the safety boundary. Our results suggest that safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants, not as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent prompts.

</details>


### [40] [SPLIT: Cross-Lingual Empathy and Cultural Grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02049)
*Anna Chorna*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SPLIT is a bilingual (English-Ukrainian) benchmark of 500 prompts across five emotional categories, evaluating three LLMs on empathetic accuracy, linguistic naturalness, and cultural grounding. Results show that most models degrade in Ukrainian, human-AI evaluator agreement is weak on cultural grounding, and producing Ukrainian text does not equate to providing Ukrainian emotional support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in emotional-support and crisis contexts, yet their cross-lingual performance—particularly in low-to-mid-resource languages like Ukrainian—remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks focus on multilingual performance but neglect crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding.

Method: The authors introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark spanning five emotional categories: Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, and Tension. Three LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3) are evaluated across three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. Both human and LLM-as-a-jury evaluation paradigms are employed, comparing English and Ukrainian responses.

Result: Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct exhibit performance degradation when responding in Ukrainian, whereas DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable. Human and AI evaluators show weak agreement on empathy and naturalness but diverge significantly on cultural grounding. The authors argue that generating Ukrainian text is not equivalent to delivering culturally appropriate Ukrainian emotional support.

Conclusion: The findings highlight the need for culturally tailored benchmark designs and stronger emphasis on human-centered evaluation. Cross-lingual emotional support requires more than linguistic translation—it demands cultural attunement that current LLMs and automated evaluators fail to reliably capture.

Abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in emotional-support contexts and crisis-related situations. Nevertheless, their cross-lingual abilities in these circumstances remain underexplored. Existing benchmarks emphasize multilingual performance but rarely examine crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding in low-to-mid-resource languages. We introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark designed to evaluate LLM consistency in generating emotionally grounded responses across five categories: Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, and Tension. We evaluate three technically diverse LLMs across three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. The framework aims to assess and compare the quality of LLM responses in both English and Ukrainian languages, as well as to explore the reliability of the LLM-as-a-jury paradigm. Our findings reveal that Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct degrade when transitioning to Ukrainian, while DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable within our benchmark. We additionally find that human and AI evaluators agree weakly on empathy and naturalness but diverge on cultural grounding. We further argue that producing Ukrainian text is not equivalent to producing Ukrainian emotional support. Our findings may assist in the future development of more culturally tailored benchmark designs, as well as encourage a stronger emphasis on human-centered evaluation.

</details>


### [41] [Unlocking Speech-Text Compositional Powers: Instruction-Following Speech Language Models without Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02214)
*Congrui Du,Yang Zhang,Kaizhi Qian,Shiyu Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SpeechCombine is an instruction-following speech language model trained without any speech instruction tuning. It starts from a text LLM base, performs continuous pre-training on speech (30k hours), and directly combines the resulting weights with the weight difference between the instruction-tuned and base text LLM. This transfers instruction-following capabilities to speech without requiring massive speech-specific instruction data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Instruction tuning for speech language models (SLMs) is significantly harder than for text LLMs because speech sequences are much longer, making large-scale dataset synthesis and training difficult to scale. Existing approaches that replicate the text LLM paradigm of large-scale pre-training plus instruction tuning are impractical for speech.

Method: The method, SpeechCombine, proceeds in two steps: (1) Starting from a text LLM base model, perform continuous pre-training on 30k hours of speech utterances to produce a speech-adapted model. (2) Directly combine the speech-adapted model's weights with the weight difference (delta) between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM — no speech instruction tuning is performed.

Result: The weight combination strategy effectively preserves the knowledge and capabilities of the original text LLM while transferring them to the speech domain. The model achieves instruction-following in speech without any speech-specific instruction tuning.

Conclusion: This work suggests a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech instruction-tuning data, demonstrating that instruction-following capabilities can be modularly transferred from text to speech via weight-space arithmetic.

Abstract: Instruction tuning for speech language models (SLMs) is substantially more challenging than for text-based large language models (LLMs), as it requires learning a new modality and a wide range of speech-specific instructions in addition to those supported by text LLMs. Existing SLM training approaches largely replicate the text LLM training paradigm by synthesizing large-scale speech pre-training and instruction-tuning datasets. However, this strategy is difficult to scale, since speech sequences are significantly longer than text sequences. In this paper, we propose SpeechCombine, an instruction-following speech language model trained without any instruction tuning, using only a single round of speech pre-training on 30k hours of data. Starting from a text LLM base model, we perform continuous pre-training on speech utterances to obtain a speech-adapted model, and then directly combine its weights with the weight difference between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM. Our results show that this simple combination strategy not only preserves the knowledge and capabilities of the original text LLM, but also effectively transfers them to the speech domain. These findings suggest a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech data.

</details>


### [42] [Challenges and Recommendations for LLMs-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Settings and Low-Resource Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02235)
*A. Seza Doğruöz,Xixian Liao,Verena Blaschke,Jakob Prange,Senyu Li,David Ifeoluwa Adelani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A meta-analysis of ACL Anthology papers reveals that LLM-as-a-Judge is rarely applied to low-resource/multilingual settings (only 33 out of 650 papers), and when it is, evaluations suffer from inconsistency, overtrust in LLM judgments, and reliance on single judge models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge is widely adopted for English NLG evaluation due to high human correlation, but its extension to multilingual and low-resource settings is problematic because LLMs have limited proficiency in these languages and there is little human validation. The authors aim to quantify the scope of this practice and identify systemic issues.

Method: The authors conducted a systematic survey of ACL Anthology papers, screening 650 papers that mention LLM-as-a-Judge and identifying only 33 that focus on multilingual or low-resource settings. They then performed an in-depth qualitative analysis of these 33 papers to assess evaluation practices, outcomes, and methodological patterns.

Result: Only 5% (33/650) of LLM-as-a-Judge papers address multilingual/low-resource settings. The analysis reveals three key problems: (1) inconsistent evaluation outcomes, (2) a widespread tendency to overtrust LLM judgments without sufficient human validation, and (3) heavy reliance on a single judge model per study rather than ensemble or comparative approaches.

Conclusion: The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for responsibly deploying LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource contexts, aiming to improve evaluation rigor and reliability across the NLP community.

Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for many natural language generation tasks, due to shortcomings of conventional metrics and high correlations with human judgment, albeit mostly in English. There are now attempts to extend LLM-as-a-Judge to multilingual settings including low-resource languages. However, LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation in these settings. To highlight the scope of the problem and current practices, we explore the use of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators in ACL Anthology papers focusing on multilingual settings and low-resource languages across a diverse set of tasks. Out of 650 papers mentioning LLM-as-a-judge, only 33 of them focus on low-resource or multilingual settings. Our in-depth analysis of these papers indicates inconsistent evaluation outcomes, a tendency to overtrust LLM judgments in multilingual settings, and the widespread reliance on a single judge model per study. To help the NLP community further, we conclude with recommendations about how to use LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings.

</details>


### [43] [BamiBERT: A New BERT-based Language Model for Vietnamese](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02259)
*Dat Quoc Nguyen,Thinh Pham,Chi Tran,Linh The Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: BamiBERT is a new BERT-based pre-trained language model for Vietnamese, trained from scratch on 129GB of general-domain text with 2048-token context length and no external word segmentation. It outperforms PhoBERT across 8 benchmarks, achieving SOTA among base-sized Vietnamese encoders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PhoBERT, the current de facto Vietnamese text encoder, has key limitations that need addressing: reliance on external word segmentation, limited context length, and suboptimal cross-domain generalization. BamiBERT aims to overcome these shortcomings.

Method: BamiBERT is a BERT-based model trained from scratch on a 129GB general-domain Vietnamese corpus for 20 epochs. It supports an extended context length of up to 2048 tokens and operates directly on raw text input without requiring external word segmentation.

Result: Across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks covering 15 metrics, BamiBERT achieves the best score on 11 metrics and second-best on 3 others, establishing a new state of the art among base-sized Vietnamese encoders with strong cross-domain generalization.

Conclusion: BamiBERT sets a new state of the art for base-sized Vietnamese language encoders, demonstrating that eliminating word segmentation dependency, extending context length, and scaling pretraining data yield significant performance gains. The model is publicly released on Hugging Face.

Abstract: In this paper, we introduce BamiBERT, a new BERT-based pre-trained language model for Vietnamese that addresses key limitations of PhoBERT -- the current de facto Vietnamese text encoder. Trained from scratch on a 129GB corpus of general-domain Vietnamese text for 20 epochs, BamiBERT supports an extended context length of up to 2048 tokens and operates directly on raw input, eliminating the need for external word segmentation. Across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks, it achieves the best score on 11 of 15 metrics and the second-best on 3 others, setting a new state of the art among "base"-sized Vietnamese encoders and demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. We release BamiBERT at: https://huggingface.co/Qualcomm-AI-Research/BamiBERT

</details>


### [44] [CheckRLM: Effective Knowledge-Thought Coherence Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02262)
*Dingling Xu,Ruobing Wang,Qingfei Zhao,Yukun Yan,Zhichun Wang,Daren Zha,Shi Yu,Zhenghao Liu,Shuo Wang,Xu Han,Maosong Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CheckRLM is a framework that combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation with reasoning language models to detect and correct factual errors in reasoning chains during inference, using minimal-cost refinements via external knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) improve performance on complex tasks through extended reasoning chains, but these chains frequently contain factual errors, especially in knowledge-intensive tasks. This leads to error accumulation and unreliable outputs.

Method: CheckRLM extracts factual claims from RLM reasoning chains to identify and localize subtle knowledge inconsistencies during inference. Upon error detection, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost yet precise corrections by leveraging external knowledge, ensuring coherence between the reasoning chain and correct knowledge.

Result: Extensive experiments show CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating strong capability in mitigating error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning while maintaining lower costs.

Conclusion: CheckRLM effectively improves the factual reliability of RLMs by integrating timely RAG-based checking and correction, offering a cost-efficient solution to the problem of factual errors in reasoning chains.

Abstract: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) have significantly improved performance on complex tasks by extending the reasoning chain. However, these chains are prone to containing factual errors, particularly in knowledge-intensive tasks. To address this issue, we propose CheckRLM, a framework that improves the reliability of the reasoning process through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by timely checking and correcting factual errors. Specifically, CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning chain to identify and localize subtle knowledge inconsistencies during inference. Upon detection of errors, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost yet precise corrections by leveraging external knowledge, ensuring coherence between the reasoning chain and correct knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, exhibiting a strong capability to mitigate error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning with lower costs. The code and data are available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/CheckRLM.

</details>


### [45] [On the Role of Directionality in Structural Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02307)
*Zichao Wei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A CCG-based symbolic backend with directional types replaces AM-Parser's direction-agnostic algebra, achieving significant gains on SLOG position-shift categories (75.9% vs 70.8% LFEM). Directional representations shift the bottleneck from symbolic to neural layers, with DeBERTa-v3-large further boosting performance to 90.7%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Several SLOG test categories explicitly require directional distinctions (e.g., modifier position shifts, argument extraction positions), yet the prior SOTA AM-Parser uses an AM algebra whose operations do not encode direction. This structural mismatch limits performance on directionally-sensitive categories, motivating a redesign of the symbolic backend with inherently directional representations.

Method: The authors redesign the symbolic backend around CCG (Combinatory Categorial Grammar) directed types, implementing deterministic CKY parsing with a single linear decoder comprising only 30K learnable parameters. The neural encoder remains BERT-base (later upgraded to DeBERTa-v3-large). The approach replaces AM-Parser's direction-agnostic AM algebra operations with CCG's inherent directional type system.

Result: Under BERT-base, the CCG system achieves 75.9±6.4% LF exact match vs AM-Parser's 70.8±4.3%. Gains are asymmetric: the CCG system outperforms AM-Parser on all 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp), while AM-Parser outperforms on all 6 recursive-depth categories. With DeBERTa-v3-large, performance reaches 90.7±4.9%, with the largest encoder gains in recursive-depth categories — complementary to the directionality gains.

Conclusion: Directional representations successfully shift the bottleneck from the symbolic layer (where AM-Parser exhibited a 0% category ceiling on certain SLOG categories) to the neural layer. This reframed bottleneck then becomes addressable through standard encoder scaling, evidenced by the complementary gains from DeBERTa-v3-large on recursive-depth categories.

Abstract: Several SLOG test categories explicitly involve directional distinctions (modifier position shifts, argument extraction positions), yet AM-Parser, the previous SOTA, uses an AM algebra whose operations do not encode direction. We redesign the symbolic backend around CCG directed types (deterministic CKY + single linear decoder, 30K learnable parameters). Under the same BERT-base encoder, the system achieves 75.9$\pm$6.4% LF exact match, surpassing AM-Parser (70.8$\pm$4.3%). Per SLOG's own category groupings, gains are highly directional: the CCG system outperforms AM-Parser on all 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp), while AM-Parser outperforms on all 6 recursive-depth categories. Replacing the encoder with DeBERTa-v3-large yields 90.7$\pm$4.9%, with the largest encoder gains in recursive-depth categories, complementary to directionality's gains. Directional representations shift the bottleneck from the symbolic layer (AM-Parser's 0% category ceiling) to the neural layer, which improves with encoder upgrades.

</details>


### [46] [World Wide Models: Literary Tools for Cultural AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02369)
*Nina Begus*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that LLMs represent a massive, automated, monolingual cultural force, and contends that literary disciplines—through narratology, critical theory, world literature, and translation studies—offer essential tools for developing culturally literate AI and addressing structural monolingualism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs stage an unprecedented form of cultural encounter that is massive, automated, and structurally monolingual. The motivation is to demonstrate that literary and critical theory tools are now indispensable for building culturally literate AI, and to bridge the gap between AI development and humanistic disciplines.

Method: The essay develops a layered framework that connects current debates in critical theory with the problem of structural monolingualism in AI. It proposes applying world literature methodologies—specifically macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability—to analyze and address global AI textuality.

Result: The paper does not present empirical results but offers a theoretical framework emphasizing the natural intersections between literature and AI development. It identifies comparative reading, narratological analysis, critical theory, and translation studies as indispensable tools for pluralistic AI interpretation and for countering monolingual bias.

Conclusion: Building culturally literate AI requires integrating literary and humanistic methodologies. A world literature approach—attending to macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability—provides a productive lens for pluralistic interpretations and for addressing the structural monolingualism embedded in current LLM paradigms.

Abstract: LLMs stage a new form of cultural encounter that is massive, automated, and monolingual. Literary disciplines have always negotiated cultural struggles with comparative reading of literature, narratological and poetic analysis, critical theory, world literature, and translation. These tools have now become indispensable for building culturally literate AI. The essay develops a layered framework toward more nuanced textual models and pluralistic interpretations of AI, emphasizing the natural intersections of literature and AI development, connecting current debates in critical theory with structural monolingualism, and suggesting a new application of world literature approaches to address global AI textuality through macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability.

</details>


### [47] [HULAT2 at MER-TRANS 2026: Governed Multi-Agent Simplification for Spanish Easy-to-Read Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02381)
*Lourdes Moreno,Paloma Martínez,Marco Antonio Sanchez-Escudero,Miguel Domínguez-Gómez*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents HULAT2-UC3M's submission to the MER-TRANS 2026 shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation, comparing a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow (RUN1/RUN2) against a generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline (RUN3), finding that signal-guided multi-agent routing outperforms linear regeneration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The work is motivated by the MER-TRANS 2026 shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation, which requires automatic systems to simplify and translate text for accessibility. The authors aim to explore whether multi-agent architectures with internal quality signals can improve over standard regeneration-based approaches for this task.

Method: Three fully automatic Spanish runs were submitted:

- **RUN1**: A LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow using Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2, incorporating parallel generation strategies, internal quality signals, Event-Condition-Action routing, controlled editing, and traceable decisions.
- **RUN2**: Same as RUN1 but with an additional lexical-support layer using glossary and lexical resources.
- **RUN3**: A RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA-based adaptation.

Development-time evaluation included internal signals: semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity, and factual consistency. Official metrics were BLEU-Orig, BLEU-Gold, SARI, and BERTScore.

Result: Official SARI scores: RUN1 (44.0543) > RUN2 (43.1049) > RUN3 (38.5136). The multi-agent routing approach (RUN1/RUN2) significantly outperformed the linear regeneration baseline (RUN3). Notably, the lexical-support layer in RUN2 did not improve reference-based scores over RUN1.

Conclusion: Signal-guided multi-agent routing outperforms linear regeneration for Easy-to-Read translation in this task setting. Adding lexical support did not automatically yield better reference-based scores, suggesting that further segment-level and document-level analysis is needed to properly assess readability, factual consistency, and user-oriented adequacy.

Abstract: This paper describes the participation of HULAT2-UC3M in the Spanish track of MER-TRANS 2026, a shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation. Three fully automatic Spanish runs were submitted. RUN1 and RUN2 used a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow combining Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2, parallel generation strategies, internal quality signals, Event-Condition-Action routing, controlled editing and traceable decisions. RUN1 used the base workflow, while RUN2 activated an additional lexical-support layer based on a glossary and lexical resources. RUN3 was a RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA-based adaptation. The official leaderboard reports BLEU-Orig, BLEU-Gold, SARI and BERTScore. During development, additional internal signals were also inspected, including semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity and factual consistency. According to official SARI, RUN1 was the best HULAT2 run, with 44.0543 points, followed by RUN2 with 43.1049 and RUN3 with 38.5136. These results indicate that, in this task setting, signal-guided multi-agent routing outperformed the linear regeneration baseline. They also show that adding lexical support did not automatically improve reference-based scores. Further segment-level and document-level analysis are required to assess readability, factual consistency and user-oriented adequacy.

</details>


### [48] [Know Your Source: A Public Knowledge Store for Media Background Checks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02383)
*Benjamin Nichols,Michael Schlichtkrull,Nedjma Ousidhoum*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MEDIAREF is a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents designed to enable reproducible, low-cost evaluation of media background check (MBC) generation for source-critical reasoning in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems used for automated fact-checking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG-based automated fact-checking systems often naively assume retrieved evidence is reliable, ignoring conflicting, outdated, or biased sources. While source-critical reasoning via media background checks (MBCs) addresses this, existing MBC generation relies on costly proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility and accessibility.

Method: The authors introduce MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store covering 200 media sources, constructed using a reproducible methodology for building and updating the document collection from web-sourced documents. They evaluate widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task using both automatic metrics and qualitative assessment.

Result: MEDIAREF enables reproducible, low-cost MBC generation and supports higher-quality MBC generation compared to existing approaches, as demonstrated through both automatic and qualitative evaluation of widely used LLMs on the task.

Conclusion: MEDIAREF provides an effective, reproducible, and low-cost alternative to proprietary search APIs for generating media background checks, thereby improving the accessibility and rigor of source-critical reasoning in RAG-based fact-checking pipelines.

Abstract: LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used for automated fact-checking (AFC) and related tasks. By grounding LLM outputs in retrieved evidence, RAG-based systems provide transparent justifications while allowing external information to be updated independently of the underlying model. However, existing approaches often assume retrieved evidence is reliable, although real-world information may be conflicting, outdated, and can originate from unreliable or biased sources. Recent work on *source-critical reasoning* addresses this challenge through media background checks (MBCs) (Schlichtkrull, 2024), which assess the credibility of evidence sources to support downstream fact verification. However, generating MBCs relies on costly proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility. To mitigate this issue, we introduce MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents that enables reproducible, low-cost evaluation of MBC generation across 200 media sources. We describe a reproducible methodology for constructing and updating the collection, assess widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task, and demonstrate that MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation through both automatic and qualitative evaluation.

</details>


### [49] [The Future of NLP may not be at NLP Conferences: Scholarly Migration Patterns in Natural Language Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02416)
*David Jurgens*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NLP research is migrating from traditional *ACL venues to general ML venues, driven partly by a citation premium conferred by ML venues and accelerated by the LLM era.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The blurring of disciplinary boundaries between NLP and general ML, spurred by LLM advances, raises the question of whether the center of gravity in NLP publication venues is shifting. The authors aim to empirically quantify this potential migration.

Method: The authors analyze NLP publications from 2010–2026, examining venue distributions for both established and new authors across pre- and post-LLM eras. They compare shares at flagship *ACL main tracks, Findings tracks, and general ML venues, adjusting for parallel field growth. For newer authors, they track first-author NLP papers and venue affiliation trends (2019–2024). Causal inference techniques are applied to estimate the citation premium of general ML venues and its influence on venue selection.

Result: Established authors lost 19.2 percentage points of share at flagship *ACL main-conference tracks and gained 14.8pp in Findings tracks post-LLM, while general ML venues rose 8.6pp. Among new authors with ≥3 first-author NLP papers, *ACL-dominant share dropped from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), and ML-dominant share rose from 5% to 21%. A significant citation premium for general ML venues was estimated, influencing venue selection.

Conclusion: A significant and measurable shift in NLP publication venues is underway, with work increasingly appearing in general ML venues and Findings tracks at the expense of flagship *ACL main tracks, a trend partially explained by the citation advantage of ML venues.
