Abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has traditionally been published in its core disciplinary venues like ACL. However, advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to a blurring of the disciplinary lines between NLP and general Machine Learning (ML), with authors regularly publishing in venues from both fields. Here, we ask whether the disciplinary center of gravity is shifting. Using NLP research published from 2010 to 2026 and studies of both established and new authors, we find that a migration is taking place. First, comparing the pre- and post-LLM eras, established authors lost 19.2pp of share at flagship *ACL main-conference tracks while gaining 14.8pp in the newer Findings tracks, and general ML venues rose 8.6pp, even when adjusting for parallel growth in the fields. Second, among newer authors who debut with at least three first-author NLP-topic papers, the share whose work appears mostly at *ACL venues fell from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), while the share appearing mostly at general ML venues rose from 5% to 21%. Using causal inference techniques, we estimate that these general ML venues confer a significant citation premium, which influences venue selection. Together, these results point to a significant shift in where NLP research is published.

</details>


### [50] [Language Models as Measurement Apparatus for Culture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02459)
*Kent K. Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper argues that NLP-based cultural measurement is a material-discursive practice where the apparatus (model, data, annotation) co-constitutes cultural reality. Drawing on Barad's "agential cut," it shows design choices create contingent boundaries between instrument and phenomenon, illustrated through case studies on dialogue analysis and apparatus examination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the assumption that NLP models passively record cultural phenomena, and instead demonstrate that the measurement apparatus actively participates in constituting cultural reality. The author aims to establish a theoretically grounded, reflexive framework for cultural NLP research.

Method: A theoretical analysis drawing on Karen Barad's agential realism and the concept of the "agential cut." The argument is illustrated through three case studies on television/film dialogue (measuring structure, interaction, and deviation) and three examinations of the apparatus (erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, agency in agentic workflows).

Result: The analysis demonstrates that (1) design choices in the apparatus create contingent boundaries between phenomenon and instrument, (2) language models have already internalized cultural material they purport to measure, making this boundary entangled from the start, and (3) each methodological choice carries both epistemic and ethical weight.

Conclusion: The paper proposes a research program that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent, treating each agential cut as a conscious commitment that is simultaneously methodological and ethical.

Abstract: Language models are increasingly used to quantify cultural phenomena, but what makes such measurement distinctively cultural? This paper argues that NLP work on culture is a material-discursive practice: the apparatus -- model, data, annotation, evaluation -- participates in constituting the cultural reality it measures, rather than passively recording it. Drawing on Karen Barad's concept of the agential cut -- the contingent boundary between phenomenon and instrument -- I show that the apparatus's substantive design choices draw such boundaries, and that the boundary is entangled from the start because language models have already internalized much of the cultural material they measure. I illustrate this through three case studies on television and film dialogue (measuring structure, interaction, and deviation) and three examinations of the apparatus itself (erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, and agency in an agentic workflow). This big picture analysis proposes a research program that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent, treating each agential cut as a conscious commitment, at once methodological and ethical.

</details>


### [51] [Will Scaling Improve Social Simulation with LLMs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02464)
*Caleb Ziems,William Held,Su Doga Karaca,David Grusky,Tatsunori Hashimoto,Diyi Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether scaling LLMs improves the fidelity of social simulations. Using 85 Qwen3 models (10¹⁸–10²⁰ FLOPs) and 35 larger open-weight models (up to 70B), the authors find strong compute scaling for opinion modeling and behavioral simulation, but weaker scaling for longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented populations. Notably, scaling fails to improve model calibration on human cognitive biases (e.g., risk aversion) and heuristic learning, even with fine-tuning. The conclusion: scale helps in most settings, but key gaps remain, especially in low-resource domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based social simulations show promise but currently lack sufficient fidelity for widespread adoption. The authors aim to determine whether continued scaling of language models will naturally close these fidelity gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and thus requires dedicated research attention beyond simply scaling compute.

Method: The study employs scaling laws methodology across two complementary approaches: (1) training a suite of 85 transformer LLMs based on the Qwen3 architecture on the DCLM web text corpus under fixed compute budgets spanning 10¹⁸ to 10²⁰ FLOPs, and (2) evaluating 35 larger open-weight models up to 70B parameters. Fidelity is assessed across three social simulation sub-domains: opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting. Performance is predicted from loss to establish scaling trends.

Result: Strong compute scaling was observed across all three sub-domains. Behavioral and opinion simulation tasks improve rapidly with scale, especially for populations well-represented in English web corpora. However, longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly, particularly when weakly correlated with general knowledge benchmarks like MMLU. Critically, scaling fails to improve model calibration on human cognitive biases (e.g., risk aversion) and human heuristics (e.g., learning correlated rewards). On these tasks, even fine-tuned models show negligible improvement from 0.5B to 8B parameters.

Conclusion: Scale will improve social simulations in most settings, but important outliers exist. Improvements will be less reliable in low-resource domains. Simulation fidelity is not fully orthogonal to general capabilities, yet certain aspects — particularly those involving cognitive biases and heuristic learning — appear resistant to scaling and warrant dedicated research beyond the current scaling paradigm.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) social simulations are a promising research method, but they are not yet faithful enough to be adopted widely. In this work, we investigate whether the current scaling paradigm in language modeling is likely to close these gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and therefore deserving of more research attention. We use scaling laws to study the relationship between LLMs' compute scale, general capability benchmarks, and the fidelity of social simulation in three representative sub-domains: opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting. Surprisingly, we discover strong compute scaling in all three settings, using a suite of 85 transformer LLMs with the Qwen3 architecture pre-trained on the DCLM web text corpus under fixed-compute budgets from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ FLOPs. Then we evaluate 35 larger and more capable open-weight models up to 70B parameters, allowing us to predict downstream accuracy from loss. This reveals that the majority of behavioral and opinion simulation tasks will rapidly improve with scale, particularly when they involve populations that are well-represented in English web corpora. Longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly, especially when they are less correlated with general knowledge and reasoning benchmarks like MMLU. In behavior simulation, scaling fails to improve model calibration with human cognitive biases like risk aversion, as well as human heuristics like learning correlated rewards from related tasks. On these tasks, even fine-tuned models fail to noticeably scale up performance from 0.5B to 8B parameters. Taken together, we conclude that scale will improve social simulations in most settings, but outliers exist, and improvements will be less reliable in low-resource domains.

</details>


### [52] [Audio-Based Understanding of Audiobook Narration Appeal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02473)
*Shahar Elisha,Mariano Beguerisse-Díaz,Emmanouil Benetos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents the first systematic computational analysis linking audiobook narration qualities (vocal and acoustic features like tone, pace, loudness) to listener appeal, using LibriVox data and proprietary engagement metrics. The study finds that acoustic features robustly predict appeal even after controlling for title effects, and that these effects vary by genre, title, and audience.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Narration is central to the audiobook listening experience, yet no prior systematic computational study has examined how narration qualities influence audiobook consumption and appeal. Understanding these relationships could improve personalization and narrator casting decisions.

Method: The authors extract vocal and acoustic features (tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox audiobooks using pre-trained audio models. They then analyze the relationship between these features and consumption data (view-rate), examining interactions with genre and title. Findings are further validated using proprietary engagement metrics with greater nuance.

Result: Acoustic information alone shows a robust association with audiobook appeal, even after accounting for title effects. The effects of narration qualities vary by genre, title, and audience. These findings hold when validated with proprietary engagement data.

Conclusion: This is the first systematic computational study linking narration qualities, genre, title, and audiobook consumption. It highlights the potential of data-driven insights to improve audiobook personalization and narrator casting, paving the way for future work in computational audiobook analysis.

Abstract: Narration is central to the audiobook listening experience, shaping how listeners engage with and understand the content. This work explores how narration qualities shape an audiobook's appeal, noting that their effects can vary by genre, title, and audience. We extract vocal and acoustic features (e.g., tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox using pre-trained audio models and analyse their relationship with consumption data (specifically, view-rate) and their interplay with genre and title. Despite limited consumption data, we find that acoustic information alone has a robust association with appeal, even after accounting for title effects. We further validate these findings using more nuanced proprietary engagement metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic computational study linking narration qualities, genre, title, and audiobook consumption, highlighting the potential of data-driven insights to improve audiobook personalisation and narrator casting.

</details>


### [53] [Visually Grounded Self-Reflection for Vision-Language Models via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02490)
*Liyan Tang,Fangcong Yin,Greg Durrett*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes VRRL, a reinforcement learning framework that trains vision-language models to perform visually grounded self-reflection. Uses trajectory prefix masking and buffered roll-ins from experience replay to teach models to correct errors by properly attending to visual inputs, significantly improving out-of-distribution accuracy on visual grounding and navigation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LVLMs exhibit self-reflection in chain-of-thought reasoning but fail to properly attend to visual inputs during reflection, especially under distribution shift. This prevents translating corrective feedback into grounded corrections, limiting robustness on OOD images.

Method: VRRL, a reinforcement learning training framework with two components: (1) random masking of trajectory prefixes during training to force recovery from incorrect intermediate predictions, and (2) buffered roll-ins from an experience replay buffer exposing the model to diverse failure states requiring correction.

Result: Off-the-shelf and conventionally fine-tuned models degrade substantially under distribution shift, while VRRL substantially improves average OOD accuracy over standard RL and reflection-oriented fine-tuning baselines on table/chart visual grounding and spatial navigation benchmarks.

Conclusion: Explicitly training LVLMs to recover from errors with grounded visual attention via RL enables effective self-reflection and robust OOD generalization. Trajectory masking and replay-based roll-ins are key mechanisms for eliciting this capability.

Abstract: Large vision-language models can reason over multimodal inputs by generating textual chains of thought (CoT). A key capability exhibited in CoT reasoning is self-reflection: revisiting earlier decisions and correcting previous errors. However, existing LVLMs often fail to properly attend to visual inputs during reflection, limiting their ability to translate feedback into grounded corrections, especially for out-of-distribution images. To address this issue, we propose a novel reinforcement learning training framework VRRL, with two components explicitly designed to elicit visually grounded self-reflection. First, we randomly mask trajectory prefixes during training to emphasize recovery from incorrect intermediate predictions rather than making early mistakes. Second, we introduce buffered roll-ins from an experience replay buffer to expose the model to diverse failure states that it must learn to correct. We evaluate our approach on visual grounding tasks involving tables and charts, as well as spatial navigation benchmarks. While off-the-shelf and conventionally fine-tuned models degrade substantially under distribution shift, our method substantially improves average out-of-distribution accuracy over standard RL and reflection-oriented fine-tuning baselines by using self-reflection effectively.

</details>


### [54] [Reasoning LLM Improves Speaker Recognition in Long-form TV Dramas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02504)
*Yuxuan Li,Lingxi Xie,Xinyue Huo,Jihao Qiu,Jiacheng Shao,Pengfei Chen,Jiannan Ge,Kaiwen Duan,Qi Tian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces DramaSR-532K, a large-scale benchmark for speaker recognition in TV dramas (532K annotated lines, 900+ characters), and DramaSR-LRM, a Large Reasoning Model that uses multimodal tool-use to aggregate contextual cues, outperforming baselines especially on short utterances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form TV drama understanding requires accurate speaker recognition (attributing utterances to characters), but existing methods struggle, especially when acoustic biometrics are unreliable (e.g., short utterances). Comprehensive video understanding necessitates integrating auditory, linguistic, and visual cues.

Method: Two contributions: (1) DramaSR-532K benchmark — 532K annotated dialogue lines from TV dramas spanning 900+ unique characters, designed for multimodal speaker recognition evaluation. (2) DramaSR-LRM — a Large Reasoning Model that autonomously aggregates contextual evidence through multimodal tool-use, synthesizing auditory, linguistic, and visual inputs for high-fidelity speaker attribution.

Result: DramaSR-LRM significantly outperforms existing baselines, with particularly strong gains on short utterances where acoustic biometrics alone are inherently unreliable.

Conclusion: Combining large-scale multimodal benchmarks with reasoning-capable models that leverage tool-use offers a promising direction for robust speaker recognition in complex, long-form video content.

Abstract: Long-form TV dramas present a formidable challenge for comprehensive video understanding, where deciphering complex storyline often relies on \textbf{speaker recognition}, the task of accurately attributing each spoken utterance to its respective character. In this paper, we advance this field through two primary contributions. (1) We introduce \textbf{DramaSR-532K}, a large-scale benchmark comprising 532K annotated dialogue lines across more than 900 unique characters, necessitating the integration of auditory, linguistic, and visual cues for speaker recognition. (2) We propose \textbf{DramaSR-LRM}, a robust approach built upon a large reasoning model (LRM). DramaSR-LRM is designed to autonomously aggregate contextual evidence via multimodal tool-use, synthesizing diverse inputs to achieve high-fidelity attribution. Experimental results demonstrate that DramaSR-LRM significantly outperforms existing baselines, particularly on short utterances where acoustic biometrics are inherently unreliable. \textit{All the data and code will be made publicly available at the project page: https://www.github.com/198808xc/DramaSR-LRM.}

</details>


### [55] [LACUNA: A Testbed for Evaluating Localization Precision for LLM Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02513)
*Matteo Boglioni,Thibault Rousset,Siva Reddy,Marius Mosbach,Verna Dankers*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LACUNA is a benchmark that injects synthetic PII into known model parameters, enabling ground-truth evaluation of unlearning localization. Current SOTA methods achieve good output-level performance but fail at precise parameter-level erasure and remain vulnerable to resurfacing attacks; precise localization dramatically improves robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unlearning benchmarks only evaluate at the output level, leaving it unclear whether unlearning truly erases knowledge from parameters or merely obfuscates it. The success of resurfacing attacks suggests obfuscation, but without ground-truth knowledge of which parameters store targeted information, precise evaluation is impossible.

Method: The authors introduce LACUNA, a testbed that injects PII of synthetic individuals into predefined parameters of 1B and 7B OLMo-based models via masked continual pretraining. This provides ground-truth parameter-level localization, enabling direct measurement of whether unlearning methods target the correct weights. They then benchmark current SOTA unlearning methods and test a simple gradient-based approach when localization is known.

Result: Despite strong output-level performance, current SOTA unlearning methods are highly imprecise in targeting the actual knowledge-storing parameters and remain susceptible to resurfacing attacks. When localization is successful (using ground-truth), even a simple gradient-based unlearning method achieves strong erasure and robustness against resurfacing attacks.

Conclusion: Precise localization is critical for robust unlearning. LACUNA is released to complement behavioral evaluations and drive advances in localization-based unlearning by providing the first testbed with ground-truth parameter-level labels.

Abstract: LLMs memorize sensitive training data, including personally identifiable information (PII), creating a pressing need for reliable post hoc removal methods. Unlearning has emerged as a promising solution, with state-of-the-art(SOTA) methods often following a localize-first, unlearn-second paradigm that targets specific model parameters. However, existing benchmarks evaluate unlearning solely at the output level, leaving open the question of whether unlearning truly erases knowledge from a model's parameters or merely obfuscates it, a concern reinforced by the success of resurfacing attacks. To bridge this gap, we introduce LACUNA: the first unlearning testbed with ground-truth parameter-level localization. LACUNA injects PII of synthetic individuals into predefined parameters of 1B and 7B OLMo-based models via masked continual pretraining, enabling direct evaluation of whether unlearning targets the weights responsible for knowledge storage. We use LACUNA to benchmark current SOTA unlearning methods and find that, despite strong output-level performance, existing methods are highly imprecise and susceptible to resurfacing attacks. We further show that when localization is successful, even a simple gradient-based unlearning method achieves strong erasure and robustness to resurfacing attacks, highlighting the importance of precise unlearning. We release LACUNA to complement behavioral evaluations and drive further advances in robust, localization-based unlearning.

</details>

### [56] [PACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Plausible and Actionable Counterfactual Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01306)
*Pavel Iakovets,Liyanapathiranage Sudeepika Wajirakumari Samarathunga,Martin Thomas Horsch,Fadi Al Machot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PACE is a neuro-symbolic framework that generates counterfactual explanations constrained by domain-specific feasibility rules, using a neural classifier paired with Answer Set Programming (ASP) symbolic reasoning to ensure recommendations are realistic and actionable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations because they lack explicit mechanisms to incorporate domain knowledge and intervention constraints. Neuro-symbolic AI offers a path to combine predictive power with symbolic reasoning over feasible actions.

Method: PACE is a modular, model-agnostic framework with two components: (1) a neural predictive model (multilayer perceptron) for classification, and (2) a symbolic reasoning layer using Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules that encode domain constraints, feasible modifications, and immutable attributes. The case study uses the Adult Income dataset, constraining changes to education, occupation, and working hours.

Result: The case study demonstrates a trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility. Symbolic constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements compared to unconstrained generation.

Conclusion: Neuro-symbolic methods show strong potential for producing transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations in XAI, enabling realistic decision support across various domains.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations explain machine learning predictions by identifying minimal input changes that would alter a model's decision. Although many existing methods successfully generate prediction-changing alternatives, they often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations due to a lack of explicit mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge and intervention constraints. Neuro-symbolic AI offers a promising direction by combining data-driven predictive models with symbolic reasoning capable of representing human-understandable rules and feasible actions. This paper presents PACE, a modular neuro-symbolic framework for generating feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations. The framework separates prediction and reasoning into two components: a neural predictive model for classification and a symbolic reasoning layer that enforces domain-specific constraints during counterfactual generation. By explicitly modeling feasible interventions, the framework produces explanations consistent with domain knowledge while remaining interpretable and actionable. The approach is model-agnostic and adaptable to domains requiring realistic decision support. A case study is conducted on the Adult Income dataset, combining a multilayer perceptron classifier with Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules encoding feasible modifications to education, occupation, and working hours while preserving immutable attributes. Results highlight the trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility and show that symbolic constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements, illustrating the potential of neuro-symbolic methods for transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanation in explainable AI.

</details>


### [57] [Auto-FL-Research: Agentic Search for Federated Learning Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01366)
*Holger R. Roth,Ziyue Xu,Chester Chen,Daguang Xu,Peter Cnudde,Andrew Feng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Auto-FL-Research (AFR) is a constrained coding-agent workflow that automates the search for effective federated learning algorithmic recipes. Evaluated on healthcare FLamby tasks and LEAF benchmarks, AFR discovers performance gains but also reveals that some improvements stem from genuine FL mechanisms, others from hyperparameter tuning, and some from irreproducible artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning research involves many small but consequential algorithmic choices (optimizers, aggregation rules, training schedules, normalization, regularization, architecture) that are expensive to explore manually and hard to compare fairly when changes alter the training/evaluation path.

Method: AFR is a constrained coding-agent workflow where agents propose and implement candidate FL training algorithms (server aggregation, client updates, local objectives, model variants). Task profiles fix the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and final evaluation. Each campaign records scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status.

Result: On five FLamby healthcare tasks and six LEAF profiles, five-seed repeat evaluations show gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles. However, same-budget controls reveal that some gains are genuine FL-recipe changes, others are recovered by fixed-surface scalar tuning, and some fail under repeat or held-out evaluation.

Conclusion: Agent-generated FL candidates can be systematically separated into three categories: repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts. This taxonomy of improvement sources is a key contribution beyond the search framework itself.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) research often depends on many small but consequential algorithmic choices: optimizer variants, server aggregation rules, local training schedules, normalization, regularization, and model architecture. These choices are expensive to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly when candidate changes can also alter the FL training or evaluation path. In this work, we present Auto-FL-Research (AFR), a constrained coding-agent workflow for FL algorithmic recipe search. Agents may propose and implement candidate training algorithms, including server aggregation rules, client update schedules, local objectives, and registered model variants, while task profiles fix the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and final model evaluation. Each campaign records candidate scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status. We evaluate AFR on five healthcare cross-silo FLamby tasks and on grouped-client profiles for the five fixed LEAF datasets plus the LEAF synthetic task. Five-seed repeat evaluations support gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles, while also exposing seed-sensitive and search-selected failure cases. Same-budget controls show that several gains correspond to FL-recipe changes, whereas other improvements are recovered by fixed-surface scalar controls or fail under repeat or held-out evaluation. These mixed outcomes are part of the contribution: they show how agent-generated candidates can be separated into repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts.

</details>


### [58] [The Wiola Architecture for Efficient Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01394)
*Aryuemaan Kumar Chowdhury,Afreen Shaik,Yaparla Bhargavi,Brahma Kumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Wiola is a novel Small Language Model (SLM) built from scratch with five original components — Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (SRPE), Gated Cross-Layer Attention (GCLA), Adaptive Token Merging (ATM), Dual Stream Feed-Forward (DSFF), and WiolaRMSNorm — released in sizes from 120M to 1.5B parameters with full HuggingFace compatibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To design a fully original SLM architecture from first principles that shares no structural lineage with existing model families (GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, Falcon), thereby exploring novel design choices in positional encoding, inter-layer communication, token efficiency, feed-forward computation, and normalization — all aimed at improving coherence, efficiency, and training stability without relying on established architectural templates.

Method: The authors propose five independently novel components: (1) SRPE — 3D helical manifold positional encoding integrating absolute, relative, and hierarchical signals; (2) GCLA — soft cross-attention allowing each decoder layer to access compressed summaries of two preceding layers; (3) ATM — dynamic merging of semantically redundant adjacent tokens at middle layers to reduce attention complexity; (4) DSFF — dual parallel feed-forward streams fused via a learned per-dimension gate, replacing standard MLPs; (5) WiolaRMSNorm — RMSNorm variant with a per-dimension learned offset vector to prevent representation collapse. The model is released in four sizes and systematically compared against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral.

Result: All 22 architectural unit tests pass, and the model is fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem. The paper includes complete mathematical derivations, architectural diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons against baseline models (GPT-2, LLaMA-2, Mistral).

Conclusion: Wiola demonstrates that a fully original SLM architecture — incorporating innovations in positional encoding, cross-layer attention, adaptive token merging, dual-stream feed-forward computation, and modified normalization — can be successfully designed, implemented, and validated entirely from first principles, yielding a functional model family ready for integration into the broader open-source ecosystem.

Abstract: We present Wiola, a fully original Small Language Model (SLM) architecture built from first principles, sharing no structural lineage with any existing model family including GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, or Falcon. Wiola introduces five independently novel components: (i) Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (SRPE), which embeds token positions on a three-dimensional helical manifold combining absolute, relative, and hierarchical positional signals; (ii) Gated Cross-Layer Attention (GCLA), providing each decoder layer with soft cross-attention access to compressed summaries of two preceding layers for inter-layer coherence; (iii) Adaptive Token Merging (ATM), which dynamically merges se mantically redundant adjacent tokens in middle network layers to reduce attention complexity without information loss; (iv) Dual Stream Feed-Forward (DSFF), replacing the conventional MLP with two parallel streams fused by a learned per-dimension gate; and (v) WiolaRMSNorm, a modified normalisation introducing a per-dimension learned offset vector that prevents representation collapse. We provide complete mathematical derivations, architectural block diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral. Wiola is released in four sizes (120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters) and is fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem, with all 22 architectural unit tests passing.

</details>


### [59] [Agent4cs: A Multi-agent System for Code Summarization in Large Hierarchical Codebases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01425)
*Yongjian Tang,Ezgi Sarikayak,Doruk Tuncel,Jie M. Zhang,Thomas Runkler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agent4cs is a multi-agent framework that summarizes large codebases bottom-up using three specialized agents: a summarization agent, a keyword-extraction agent, and a quality-assurance agent — achieving up to 8% improvement in semantic consistency and 38% gains in keyword coverage over structured prompting baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing code summarization tools treat source code as flat text and rely on a single language model, failing to exploit the hierarchical structure and interdependencies within code repositories. This is especially problematic for large, complex, obfuscated, or poorly documented codebases.

Method: A bottom-up multi-agent framework with three agents: (1) a summarization agent that produces robust summaries at each level, (2) a keyword-extraction agent that proactively identifies critical information from subfolders, and (3) a quality-assurance agent that iteratively refines outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness.

Result: Evaluated across 7 frontier models, Agent4cs improved semantic consistency by an average of 8% over two structured prompting baselines with code segments. On real-world datasets, it achieved up to 38% improvement in normalized keyword coverage rate.

Conclusion: The multi-agent, bottom-up architecture of Agent4cs effectively leverages repository structure to produce higher-quality code summaries than flat-text, single-model approaches.

Abstract: Understanding large, complex codebases, especially those with obfuscated structures and incomplete documentation, remains a significant challenge. Existing code summarization solutions often rely on a single language model or coding assistant like Claude Code, and treat source code as flat text, underutilizing the rich interdependencies and hierarchical information within a repository. To address these shortcomings, we propose Agent4cs - a multi-agent framework that summarizes large codebases in a bottom-up fashion, where a summarization agent focuses on producing robust summaries; a keyword-extraction agent proactively identifies critical information from subfolders; and a quality-assurance agent iteratively refines the outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness. Evaluated on 7 frontier models, Agent4cs improves semantic consistency across all folder levels by average 8% compared to two structured prompting baselines with code segments. Furthermore, extensive evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate over the same baselines.

</details>


### [60] [When Should Service Agents Reconsider? Difficulty-Routed Control in Customer-Service Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01426)
*Qian Chen,Chengyuan Liu,Xin Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a difficulty-routed service-control architecture for autonomous customer-service agents that routes operationally complex sessions to an escalated workflow with conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration, concentrating safeguards before consequential backend writes rather than uniformly applying control. Evaluated on retail and airline tasks from τ²-bench, showing improved reliability on conflicted requests without burdening routine sessions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As autonomous customer-service agents shift from conversation to operational execution (refunds, cancellations, order modifications), firms face a service-control problem: balancing fast, low-friction routine service against preventing operational errors when customer instructions, policy constraints, firm records, and backend writes interact in complex ways.

Method: A difficulty-routed architecture: a lightweight router classifies sessions, keeping routine ones on a low-cost baseline path and escalating operationally coupled sessions to a conflict-aware workflow. The escalated path employs conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration, concentrating deliberation and safeguards specifically before consequential backend writes rather than applying uniform control across all sessions.

Result: On retail tasks from τ²-bench, the method consistently improves reliability on requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence confirms stronger control targets conflicted requests. Dialogue and tool-use analysis shows gains stem from evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration — not indiscriminate interaction expansion. Case evidence demonstrates preserved fallback plans, correct record-to-action binding, write sequencing, and multi-entity request decomposition. Airline results extend the logic to reservation operations.

Conclusion: Difficulty-based routing with targeted escalation and pre-write safeguards effectively addresses the service-control problem in operational customer-service agents, improving reliability selectively without penalizing routine service efficiency.

Abstract: Autonomous customer-service agents are shifting from conversational interfaces toward operational execution roles: they retrieve firm records, apply service policies, and execute backend writes such as refunds, cancellations, exchanges, order modifications, and reservation changes. This shift creates a service-control problem: firms must keep routine service fast and low-friction while preventing operational errors on requests where customer instructions, policy constraints, firm records, and backend writes interact. We propose a difficulty-routed service-control architecture that asks when service agents should reconsider before acting. A lightweight router keeps routine sessions on a low-cost baseline path and routes operationally coupled sessions to an escalated workflow. The escalated path uses conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration to concentrate deliberation and safeguards before consequential backend writes, rather than applying additional control uniformly across all service sessions. We evaluate the architecture on human-verified retail and airline tasks from $τ^{2}$-bench. In retail, the method improves reliability consistently on service requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence shows that stronger control is directed toward conflicted requests rather than broadly applied to routine ones. Dialogue and tool-use profiles suggest that gains do not come from indiscriminate interaction expansion or broader tool chains; instead, added turns and tool calls support evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration. Case-level evidence shows that the escalated workflow preserves fallback plans, binds retrieved records to the correct action, sequences writes, and decomposes multi-entity requests. Airline results extend the same service-control logic to reservation operations.

</details>


### [61] [CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01433)
*Samuel Schapiro,Core Francisco Park,Felix Sosa,Lav R. Varshney*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CreativityNeuro is a data-free, contrastive weight steering method that enhances divergent thinking in LLMs, improving creativity metrics by up to 14 percentile points on the DAT and achieving significant gains in originality and surprise on the AUT and Task Task, while reducing mode collapse without requiring retraining or fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer from the "artificial hivemind effect" — a tendency to produce homogeneous, repetitive responses to open-ended prompts. Existing solutions often require behavioral data or gradient-based fine-tuning. The authors aim to mitigate this mode collapse and boost divergent thinking through a lightweight, data-free intervention.

Method: The authors introduce CreativityNeuro, a contrastive weight steering method. It operates directly on model weights (weight-space steering) rather than activations, requiring no behavioral data, retraining, or gradients. The method is evaluated against activation steering baselines across three tasks: the Divergent Association Task (DAT), the Alternative Uses Test (AUT), and the Task Task, including a large-scale human evaluation (N=720).

Result: On the DAT, CreativityNeuro yields up to a 14 percentile-point improvement. In human evaluations on the AUT and Task Task, it significantly boosts originality, surprise, and overall creativity. Across all three tasks, it demonstrably reduces mode collapse. Activation steering matches CreativityNeuro on DAT but fails to transfer to AUT and Task Task, highlighting the superior generalization of weight-space steering.

Conclusion: CreativityNeuro effectively enhances divergent thinking and mitigates mode collapse in LLMs through weight-space contrastive steering, without needing behavioral data, retraining, or fine-tuning. This provides a simple, generalizable method for improving LLM performance in creative, open-ended domains.

Abstract: Divergent thinking is a crucial aspect of creativity, yet large language models (LLMs) tend to consistently generate similar responses to open-ended questions, in what has been termed the artificial hivemind effect. Here, we introduce CreativityNeuro, a data-free method for enhancing divergent thinking in LLMs via contrastive weight steering. We evaluate our method across multiple creativity assessments and report several main findings. On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), a vocabulary-space creativity test, CreativityNeuro improves performance by up to 14 human percentile points. Next, in a large-scale human evaluation (N=720) on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) and the Task Task, CreativityNeuro achieves significant improvements in originality, surprise, and creativity, transferring to longer-form and more open-ended tasks. Importantly, we find that across all three tasks, CreativityNeuro demonstrably reduces measures of mode collapse. Moreover, activation steering achieves comparable performance to CreativityNeuro on the DAT, but it does not transfer to the AUT and Task Task, demonstrating the effectiveness of weight-space steering in generalizing to unseen tasks. In conclusion, CreativityNeuro improves divergent thinking and reduces mode collapse without requiring behavioral data, re-training, or gradient-based fine-tuning, providing a straightforward way to enhance LLM performance in creative domains.

</details>


### [62] [Hardware-Enforced Semantic Coordination for Safety-Critical Real-Time Autonomous Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02376)
*Uwe M. Borghoff,Paolo Bottoni,Remo Pareschi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture using FPGAs to implement coordination semantics directly at the hardware level, ensuring bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees for real-time autonomous AI systems, while keeping semantic reasoning flexible in software.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems increasingly integrate heterogeneous components (LLMs, world models, neural architectures, human operators) that must coordinate under uncertainty in safety-critical, real-time deployments. Current software-mediated coordination cannot provide bounded latency, deterministic coordination, or enforceable safety guarantees — fundamental requirements for such domains.

Method: The authors propose mapping selected coordination mechanisms from the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework onto FPGA primitives. This creates a hardware-native semantic coordination layer that enforces temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware. Semantic reasoning remains software-driven and adaptive, while coordination semantics become deterministic and hardware-enforced.

Result: The paper presents an architectural design rather than empirical results. The key outcome is the conceptual separation of concerns: adaptive semantic reasoning executes in software, while critical coordination semantics (timing, gating, authorization, boundedness) are enforced deterministically via FPGA hardware primitives.

Conclusion: Hardware-enforced semantic coordination addresses a critical gap in safety-critical agentic AI deployment. By offloading coordination guarantees to FPGA hardware while retaining software flexibility for reasoning, the architecture achieves verifiable safety properties without sacrificing the adaptability needed for complex autonomous systems.

Abstract: Recent advances in agentic AI are producing increasingly complex autonomous systems that integrate large language models, world models, optimization engines, specialized neural architectures, autonomous platforms, and human operators. While much current research focuses on improving reasoning capabilities, safety-critical real-time deployment also requires bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous components operating concurrently under uncertainty. Software-mediated coordination presents fundamental limitations in domains where bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees are essential.
  Hence, we propose a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture in which selected coordination semantics are implemented directly at the hardware level via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). The approach builds on the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework, which separates semantic reasoning from interaction management.
  In this approach, selected TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms are mapped onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Focus is not on acceleration, but on enforcing temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware. Semantic reasoning remains adaptive and software-driven, while embedded coordination semantics become deterministic.

</details>


### [63] [Discrete Diffusion Language Models for Interactive Radiology Report Drafting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01436)
*Max Van Puyvelde,Halil Ibrahim Gulluk,Wim Van Criekinge,Olivier Gevaert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper adapts a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model (DiffusionGemma-26B) for medical visual question answering, showing it matches or outperforms its autoregressive counterpart (Gemma-4-26B) while offering 3.5–4.4× faster decoding and a unique any-order infill capability useful for radiology report refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical foundation models are almost exclusively autoregressive, which limits them to left-to-right generation. The authors aim to demonstrate that diffusion language models—which denoise bidirectionally—can match AR performance in the medical domain while providing unique practical advantages such as any-order text infill, which is valuable for real-world clinical report editing where fragments need correction between existing text.

Method: The authors adapt DiffusionGemma-26B, a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, and fine-tune it on medical visual question answering datasets using an identical LoRA recipe as applied to its same-size autoregressive sibling, Gemma-4-26B. Both models are evaluated using a verbosity-robust LLM judge to ensure fair scoring. The diffusion model's bidirectional denoising is also leveraged to demonstrate any-order infill—fixing report fragments and filling text between them.

Result: DiffusionGemma matches or exceeds the autoregressive baseline on all medical VQA benchmarks. The fine-tuned model (3.8B active parameters) is competitive with frontier vision-language models. Decoding is 3.5–4.4× faster than the AR counterpart. Additionally, the any-order infill capability proves effective for radiology report editing, an operation AR models perform poorly.

Conclusion: Diffusion language models are a viable and often superior alternative to autoregressive models for medical vision-language tasks, offering competitive accuracy, faster inference, and unique bidirectional infill capabilities that align well with clinical workflow needs such as standardizing or correcting radiology reports.

Abstract: Diffusion language models, which generate text by denoising a token canvas bidirectionally instead of emitting tokens left to right, have become competitive with autoregressive (AR) generation. Medical foundation models, however, remain almost entirely autoregressive. We adapt a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, DiffusionGemma-26B, and benchmark it against its same-size AR sibling Gemma-4-26B under an identical LoRA recipe on medical visual question answering datasets, scored by a verbosity-robust LLM judge. Diffusion matches or exceeds AR on all of them, and the finetuned model (3.8B active) is competitive with frontier vision-language models; its decoding is also 3.5-4.4x faster. Beyond this parity, the diffusion model offers a drafting capability AR lacks: any-order infill. Because the canvas is denoised bidirectionally, a radiologist can fix report fragments and have the model fill the text between them, an operation inherent to diffusion but not to autoregression, which is subpar at it. This suits real reports, which are often terse or inconsistent across clinicians and institutions.

</details>


### [64] [What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02507)
*Arman Ghaffarizadeh,Danyal Mohaddes,Aliakbar Izadkhah,Shahriar Noroozizadeh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents exhibit significant divergence between public and off-the-record statements when placed in socially structured settings, with decision divergence rising from ~3% to ~40% under alignment-inducing conditions, suggesting emergent social accommodation behaviors driven by relational pressures like career risk or sponsorship obligations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in socially structured environments, their behavior may be influenced by role, audience, and relational context—even without explicit objectives. The authors aim to investigate whether social structure alone can cause agents to strategically alter their public expressions compared to private, off-the-record responses.

Method: A dual-channel debate framework where agents produce both public utterances (shared with the other participant) and off-the-record (OTR) responses (recorded but hidden from the other participant). Experiments span 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations per scenario. Analysis employs four aggregate measures: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses.

Result: In alignment-inducing settings, public-OTR decision divergence rose significantly from a ~3% baseline to approximately 40%. OTR responses sometimes explicitly attributed public accommodation to relational pressures (e.g., career risk, sponsorship obligations). The effect was consistent across all four aggregate analyses.

Conclusion: Agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals to detect emergent objectives shaped by social context. The dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures provide a practical methodology for operationalizing this broader assessment.

Abstract: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. We present a dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures that operationalize this assessment.

</details>


### [65] [Beyond Next-Token Prediction: An RLVR Proof of Concept for Tool-Use Agents on Atlassian Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01465)
*Karthikeya Aditya Vissa,Sankalp Mane,Ananya Mantravadi,Harshit Rajgarhia,Abhishek Mukherji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Applying RLVR (specifically GRPO) to small LLMs (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3.5-4B) in synthetic enterprise API environments (Jira/Confluence) dramatically improves tool-calling accuracy — reward scores rise from 0.35–0.92 to 0.95–1.00 — without any live API, learned judge, or human labels. The approach is limited by the need to hand-craft verifiable reward checkers per endpoint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are trained for next-token prediction, not for correctly sequencing API calls with proper nested arguments. In enterprise SaaS workflows, this mismatch causes silent failures: hallucinated tools, dropped required fields, and premature task termination. The authors investigate whether RLVR applied in the target environment can close this gap.

Method: The authors built five synthetic environments emulating Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs with full schema fidelity. Rewards are computed entirely from tool-call traces using deterministic, verifiable checkers — no live API calls, no learned reward model, no human feedback. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is used to fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B, with scoring done by the same checkers that drive training.

Result: On four non-degenerate reward scenarios, the RL-trained policy improved average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35–0.92 to 0.95–1.00. The largest single gain was on Confluence page creation (0.35 → 1.00). One scenario (ticket-transition) was already saturated by the prompted 4B baseline.

Conclusion: This is positioned as a preliminary step toward outcome-optimized small models for niche enterprise APIs. Two key limitations: (1) hand-crafting verifiable rewards doesn't scale beyond the few endpoints reported, and (2) one scenario showed ceiling effects where the baseline already maxed out the reward.

Abstract: Large language models are trained to predict the next token, not to act inside a specific API. In niche enterprise SaaS workflows -- where success means hitting the right endpoint with the right nested arguments in the right order -- this objective mismatch shows up as silent failures: dropped required fields, hallucinated tools, or early stops after a single read. We ask whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), applied directly in the target environment, closes the gap. As a proof of concept we build a suite of five synthetic environments emulating the Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs at schema fidelity; rewards are computed entirely from the tool-call trace, with no live API, no learned judge, and no human label in the loop. Scoring prompted Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B on the same checkers that drive GRPO training, we find that on the four scenarios whose rewards are non-degenerate the RL-trained policy lifts average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35--0.92 to 0.95--1.00, with the largest single gain on Confluence page creation ($0.35 \rightarrow 1.00$). We position this as a preliminary step toward outcome-optimised small models for niche enterprise APIs, and foreground two limitations a workshop reader should weigh: hand-crafting verifiable rewards does not scale beyond the handful of endpoints reported here, and one of our five scenarios (ticket-transition) has a saturating reward shape that the prompted 4B already maxes out.

</details>


### [66] [World Feedback for Clinical Agents: Diagnosing RL in FHIR Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01470)
*Ananya Mantravadi,Harshit Rajgarhia,Prasanna Desikan,Abhishek Mukherji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedAgentBench-v3 fixes a silent-finish ceiling in prior benchmarks, but RL training on clinical protocol tasks hits two structural barriers — capability ceilings (zero base performance) and format-knowledge gaps (undiscoverable clinical codes) — requiring a hybrid SFT+RL strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical protocol-execution tasks (checking lab values, applying thresholds, structuring FHIR orders) are well-suited for RL from world feedback because clinical SMEs can encode decision logic into a verifier that grades unlimited rollouts. However, existing benchmarks (MedAgentBench v1/v2) suffer from a 41.7% silent-finish ceiling where doing nothing yields high reward, undermining RL as a training paradigm. The authors aim to construct a sound benchmark and systematically identify what structural barriers prevent pure RL from succeeding on clinical agent tasks.

Method: The authors first audit MedAgentBench v1/v2 to quantify the silent-finish ceiling, then construct MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3) with 508 tasks and a reduced 8.9% ceiling. They train Qwen3-8B using pure RL and compare against rule-based SFT. Through systematic analysis, they classify 20 task types along two barriers: a capability ceiling (10/20 types with 0% base performance, yielding zero gradient for RL) and a format-knowledge barrier (3/20 types requiring exact clinical codes that cannot be discovered via exploration). They propose a three-way taxonomy — decision, format-knowledge, and lookup tasks — to predict RL learnability.

Result: Pure RL on MAB-v3 achieves 18.2% pass@1 versus 34.1% for rule-based SFT, with the 15.9 percentage-point gap fully attributable to the two identified barriers. The decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy accurately predicts which task types are amenable to RL. The prescribed remedy is SFT to inject undiscoverable clinical codes, followed by RL to learn conditional decision logic.

Conclusion: RL from verifier-based feedback is a promising paradigm for clinical agent training, but only after structural barriers are addressed: benchmarks must be audited for silent-finish ceilings, and training must combine SFT for format-knowledge injection with RL for decision-boundary learning. The proposed taxonomy provides a diagnostic framework for predicting RL applicability to clinical tasks.

Abstract: Clinical protocol-execution tasks -- checking a lab value, applying a threshold, placing a correctly structured FHIR order -- are natural candidates for RL from world feedback: once clinical SMEs encode decision logic into a verifier, that verifier grades unlimited rollouts without per-episode annotation. But applying RL requires a sound feedback channel and sufficient base capability. We audit MedAgentBench v1/v2, find a 41.7\% silent-finish ceiling that makes inaction the RL dominant strategy, and construct \textbf{MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3)} (508 tasks, 8.9\% ceiling). Training Qwen3-8B exposes two structural barriers: a \emph{capability ceiling} (10/20 task types have 0\% base performance, zero gradient) and a \emph{format-knowledge barrier} (3/20 types require exact clinical codes undiscoverable by exploration). Pure RL reaches 18.2\% pass@1 vs.\ 34.1\% for rule-based SFT; the 15.9~pp gap is attributable entirely to these barriers. A decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy predicts RL learnability and prescribes the fix: SFT to inject codes, RL to learn conditionals.

</details>


### [67] [Procedural Memory Distillation: Online Reflection for Self-Improving Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01480)
*Ye Liu,Srijan Bansal,Bo Pang,Yang Li,Zeyu Leo Liu,Yifei Ming,Zixuan Ke,Shafiq Joty,Semih Yavuz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PMD introduces a co-evolving procedural memory scaffold that captures cross-episode signals (successful strategies, persistent failure modes, recurring patterns) from rollouts at three abstraction levels, then distills this memory into policy weights via a memory-conditioned self-teacher, yielding 3.8–13.6% gains over SDPO while leaving no memory overhead at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLVR and self-distillation methods like SDPO use only episode-level verifier signals and discard rich procedural information within rollouts. Crucially, cross-episode signals — which strategies work consistently, which failures persist, which patterns recur — are lost because episode-local updates cannot capture them. The authors aim to retain and reuse this procedural knowledge across episodes and epochs.

Method: PMD organizes procedural memory at three levels: (1) raw trajectories, (2) self-reflected strategies and lessons, and (3) higher-level behavioral patterns recurring across problems — all extracted online from the model's own rollouts. A memory-conditioned self-teacher uses this accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts. The core design is co-evolution: policy rollouts update the memory, and memory shapes the supervision that updates the policy. The memory is fully absorbed into policy weights, yielding a memory-free model at inference.

Result: On Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD surpasses SDPO by 3.8–5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9–13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Ablation confirms co-evolution is critical: freezing either memory or policy causes over 10% degradation across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.

Conclusion: Co-evolution between policy and procedural memory enables the student to progressively internalize cross-episode procedural knowledge, yielding substantial gains over episode-local methods like SDPO without inference-time memory overhead.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), along with recent selfdistillation variants such as SDPO, evaluates each rollout against a verifier and updates the policy from that episode-level signal. However, the richer procedural information in the rollout is rarely retained or reused. Across episodes and epochs, the model repeatedly encounters related problems under a changing policy, producing cross-episode signals that episode-local updates cannot capture: which strategies consistently pass verification, which failure modes persist, which patterns recur. We propose Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), which converts these crossepisode signals into reusable procedural memory and distills it into the policy's weights during training. This memory functions as a training scaffold, absorbed into the policy itself, yielding a memory-free model at inference. PMD organizes the memory at three levels of abstraction: raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies and lessons, and higher-level behavioral patterns that recur across problems, all extracted online from the model's own trajectories. A memory-conditioned self-teacher draws on the accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts, enabling student to progressively internalize procedural knowledge within its parameters. The central design principle is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update the memory, and memory shapes the supervision that updates the policy. Empirically, across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8-5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9-13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Co-evolution powers these gains: freezing either the memory or the policy trails PMD by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.

</details>


### [68] [The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01507)
*Jiacheng Miao,Jonathan K Pritchard,James Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI agents given different personas can reproduce the analytical variation seen among human researchers, revealing that divergent conclusions often stem not from flawed analyses but from selective exploration of defensible methodological choices. The authors introduce m-value and Agentic Bootstrap to quantify where a reported analysis falls within the distribution of plausible analyses, turning this into a credibility criterion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Empirical research suffers from "forking paths" — different defensible analytical choices leading to different conclusions from the same data. These paths are hidden and difficult to observe systematically, making it hard to assess whether a reported finding reflects selective reporting from a large space of reasonable analyses. The authors seek to make this problem explicit and measurable.

Method: The authors deploy AI agents with different personas (e.g., political ideologies) to analyze the same datasets across four high-stakes domains. They compare AI-generated analytical variation against a benchmark study where 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset. They introduce two methodological innovations: (1) the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path yields a claim at least as extreme as the reported one; and (2) Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by having AI agents sample plausible analysis paths from the multiverse of defensible analyses.

Result: AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates from the immigration study. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, 86% of AI reports passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review, indicating analyses were methodologically defensible. Applied to the human study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05).

Conclusion: The central challenge in empirical research is often not flawed analyses but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of defensible analytical choices. AI agents can amplify this problem by making exploration inexpensive and scalable. Scientific evidence should be evaluated by a finding's position within the distribution of plausible analyses, not just by the single reported analysis. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable, providing a new criterion for scientific credibility.

Abstract: Empirical research rarely admits a unique analysis. Different analytical choices can lead to different conclusions from the same data, yet these hidden forking paths are difficult to observe. We show that AI agents capture much of the analytical variation among human researchers while making these paths explicit. Across four high-stakes domains, assigning different personas is sufficient for AI agents to report divergent, often opposing, conclusions from the same data and question, with findings systematically aligned with those beliefs. In a study in which 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, it is difficult to identify clear issues in each analysis based on the final AI reports: 86% passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. These findings suggest that the central challenge is often not flawed analyses, but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents may amplify this longstanding problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. To address this, we introduce the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one. We further introduce Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Scientific evidence should therefore be evaluated not only by a single reported analysis but also by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and turns it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

</details>


### [69] [Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01510)
*Natalie Grace Brigham,Eugene Bagdasarian,Tadayoshi Kohno,Franziska Roesner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Janus is a modular playground for designing and evaluating user-involved permission management in AI agent systems. It implements six permission assistants spanning a design space defined by key user-involvement axes, evaluates them across scenarios, and finds that no single design is universally optimal — user input strengthens security, AI augmentation reduces cognitive load, and permission fatigue must be accounted for.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on behalf of users create unresolved questions about permission management — specifically, what role users should play. Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains underexplored, motivating a systematic framework for designing and evaluating user-involved permission schemes.

Method: The authors introduce Janus, comprising Janus-Core (a modular agentic system supporting a spectrum of permission management designs) and Janus-Harness (an automated evaluation framework). They define a conceptual model identifying key design axes for user involvement, implement six permission assistants that span the resulting design space, and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders.

Result: User input significantly strengthens privacy and security; AI augmentation of user decisions helps reduce cognitive load; realistic user behaviors like permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. Critically, no single permission management design performs optimally across all contexts.

Conclusion: The findings motivate a more principled, context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is released publicly to support further research into user-involved permission management for AI agents.

Abstract: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

</details>


### [70] [Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01511)
*Hongyang He,Jiuming Liu,Victor Sanchez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Semi-CoT proposes reusing chain-of-thought reasoning traces as pseudo-labels for semi-supervised learning. It samples multiple reasoning chains per unlabeled question, filters via entropy-based answer consistency, and uses low-entropy chains as training demonstrations. Pilot experiments show the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs (91-100%), but downstream gains are modest, with negative transfer on some tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CoT methods use reasoning chains only as inference-time prompts and discard them afterward. The authors identify an untapped opportunity: these generated reasoning traces could serve as semi-supervised learning signals to improve model training, extending self-training from inference-time refinement to training-time pseudo-supervision.

Method: Semi-CoT operates in three stages: (1) For each unlabeled question, sample multiple pseudo chain-of-thought reasoning traces from the model. (2) Estimate answer-level semantic entropy by clustering outputs based on their final answers; low entropy indicates high answer consistency. (3) Select low-entropy chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations and use them for semi-supervised student training.

Result: On four math reasoning datasets (AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, MultiArith), the entropy gate achieves pseudo-answer precision between 91.36% and 100%. Semi-CoT yields small improvements on SVAMP and GSM8K, but shows negative transfer on AQuA and hits a ceiling on MultiArith.

Conclusion: Unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals via entropy-based filtering. However, effectively leveraging these signals for training gains remains an open challenge, requiring stronger demonstration selection methods or improved student training strategies.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

</details>


### [71] [OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01531)
*David Courtis,Wenhao Li,Scott Sanner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPINE-World is an LLM agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models online from pixel-rendered environments by coupling two cooperating agents in a hypothesis-test loop: one acts in the environment, the other synthesizes a code-based world model via replay verification and planning, using a novel Bayesian "ontology error" metric to guide exploration. It solves 20/25 ARC-AGI-3 games without per-game training, achieving 78.4 action-efficiency against a human baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing world model approaches suffer from a trade-off: deep network-based models are flexible but data-hungry and generalize poorly out-of-distribution, while program-synthesis approaches (CEGIS) are data-efficient and reusable but fail to scale to pixel-rendered environments where object structure must be flexibly hypothesized rather than given. The authors aim to bridge this gap.

Method: OPINE-World couples two cooperating LLM agents: (1) an actor agent that interacts with the environment, and (2) a synthesizer agent that builds a programmatic world model in code using replay verification and model-based planning. The system operates in a hypothesis-and-test loop, steering exploration using a novel Bayesian metric called "ontology error," which quantifies the adequacy of the hypothesized object-type vocabulary relative to observed transitions.

Result: Evaluated on ARC-AGI-3 (a benchmark withholding object vocabulary, goals, and action semantics), OPINE-World solves 20 out of 25 games with no per-game training, achieving an action-efficiency score of 78.4 compared to the human baseline.

Conclusion: Programmatic world model learning can be successfully extended to pixel-rendered domains with unknown object structure by combining LLM-based code synthesis with Bayesian exploration guidance, yielding strong sample efficiency and generalization without per-task fine-tuning.

Abstract: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

</details>


### [72] [Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01567)
*Oskar J. Hollinsworth,Ann-Kathrin Dombrowski,Sam Adam-Day,Adam Gleave,Chris Cundy*

Main category: cs.AI
