TL;DR: The paper scales SOLiD (a lie-detector-based oversight method) to larger LLMs and realistic preference-learning settings, finding that undetected deception decreases with model scale. However, distribution shift between detector training and deployment data can cause impractical false positive rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is expensive to monitor and prevent. SOLiD was proposed as a scalable oversight mechanism using lie detectors to flag responses for human review, but its effectiveness at larger scales and in realistic settings was unknown.

Method: The authors scale SOLiD to models ranging from 1B to 405B parameters and evaluate it across diverse, realistic preference-learning settings. They test whether human labelers can be removed from the fine-tuning phase and examine sensitivity to distribution shifts between detector training data and preference-training data.

Result: Undetected deception drops from 34% (1B models) to 14% (405B models) at a 99% detector true positive rate. Human labelers can be removed entirely from fine-tuning without statistically significant increase in deception. However, distribution shift between detector training and deployment data can drive false positive rates to impractical levels.

Conclusion: SOLiD exhibits favorable scaling properties with model size and can operate without human labelers during fine-tuning, but its practical deployment is critically constrained by sensitivity to distribution shift, which must be addressed for real-world use.

Abstract: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

</details>


### [73] [Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02245)
*Seren Yenikent,Jack Vinijtrongjit,Katherine Ng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Copewell is a multi-agent AI swarm system for mental wellness that combines multi-source assessment, emotion routing via Russell's Circumplex Model, and dual-mode intervention (conversational + sensory protocols) — all built with privacy-first, ethics-embedded architecture from the ground up.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Nearly one billion people suffer from mental health disorders, with 75% in low- and middle-income countries receiving no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost, and stigma. Existing AI wellness tools are single-mode conversational interfaces with high abandonment rates, lacking measurable, immediate relief tailored to dynamic emotional states.

Method: Copewell introduces three innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework fusing self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to reduce algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping via Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery blending conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. The architecture also features a privacy-first design, a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design input from mental health practitioners.

Result: Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment have informed design decisions and surfaced directions for future empirical evaluation. Quantitative clinical outcomes are not yet reported; the contribution is primarily architectural and sociotechnical.

Conclusion: Copewell demonstrates how responsible AI principles — equity, safety, and ethics — can be operationalized from inception through deliberate technical architecture, contributing to discourse on human-centered, ethical AI for mental wellness in underserved contexts.

Abstract: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design informed by mental health practitioners. Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. This work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

</details>


### [74] [EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01584)
*Mahyar Ghazanfari,Amin Tabrizian,Armin Mehrabian,Peng Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A knowledge-graph-grounded pipeline using heterogeneous GNNs and a three-agent LLM system generates and evaluates Earth science hypotheses from NASA datasets, producing 160 plausible, novel research hypotheses across multiple domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation relies on unstructured literature and free-form text, lacking structured grounding in curated scientific knowledge. This work aims to ground hypothesis generation in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph to produce more structured, verifiable, and domain-relevant hypotheses.

Method: A heterogeneous graph neural network (GNN) trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate NASA dataset pairings. A three-agent LLM pipeline then filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses from top-ranked pairings. The system is evaluated via a 2×2×2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, comparing model-predicted novel pairings against held-out real co-usages from the literature.

Result: Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produced 160 hypotheses spanning ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol-cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Novel dataset pairings were rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages. The factorial experiment revealed that hypothesis rankings remain stable across models, but absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, exposing limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

Conclusion: Grounding hypothesis generation in structured knowledge graphs yields scientifically coherent yet unexplored dataset combinations. However, reliance on a single LLM judge introduces evaluation instability, suggesting multi-judge or human-in-the-loop evaluation is necessary for robust assessment of generated hypotheses.

Abstract: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

</details>


### [75] [Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01590)
*Junyi Wen,Ruiyan Zhuang,Yongjia Xu,Pengtu Li,Rui Zou,Hongyi Chen,Chingman Wan,Puxu Yang,Wuhui Chen,Yanlin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hawk is a training-free framework that uses three hardware-aware knowledge modules (Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis, Bottleneck-Aware Retrieval, and Effect-Driven Distillation) to improve LLM-generated NPU kernel code, boosting generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieving up to 2.2x speedup over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs fail at generating NPU kernel code because they lack hardware-specific priors about implicit hardware constraints and memory hierarchies. Naive code transplantation from similar kernels compiles but causes runtime crashes and performance degradation by violating underlying hardware constraints.

Method: Hawk integrates three modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis with Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation coupling error context to executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval using 2D-Retrieval that projects queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation using LLM-driven semantic arbitration to prune errors and consolidate redundancies based on empirical execution feedback — all without training.

Result: On real-world NPU workloads, Hawk improves generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieves up to 2.2x execution speedup compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: Hawk demonstrates that training-free, hardware-aware knowledge integration can effectively bridge the gap between LLM code generation capabilities and the stringent requirements of NPU kernel development, substantially improving both correctness and performance.

Abstract: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [76] [Safe and Adaptive Cloud Healing: Verifying LLM-Generated Recovery Plans with a Neural-Symbolic World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01595)
*Junyan Tan,Haoran Lin,Siyuan Guo,Yichen Fang,Xinyue Luo,Tianyu Shen,Zeyu Qiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PASE introduces a self-healing framework for cloud AI systems that reframes fault recovery as neuro-symbolic program synthesis. It tightly couples an LLM-based Plan Synthesis Engine, a Neural-Symbolic World Model for verification, and a DRL-trained Meta-Prompt Optimizer in a reason-plan-verify-adapt loop, achieving 40%+ reduction in recovery time over SOTA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fault recovery approaches for cloud AI systems combine LLMs and DRL in sequential, loosely coupled architectures that fail to fully exploit LLM generative and reasoning capabilities. There is a need for a tighter integration that enables dynamic, context-aware recovery beyond predefined action spaces.

Method: PASE reconceptualizes fault recovery as neuro-symbolic program synthesis with three tightly integrated components: (1) an LLM Plan Synthesis Engine that generates structured recovery plans from semantic primitives; (2) a Neural-Symbolic World Model that simulates and verifies plan feasibility; (3) a Meta-Prompt Optimizer trained via DRL to generate optimal prompts guiding the LLM's planning. These form a reason-plan-verify-adapt loop.

Result: On a real-world cloud fault injection dataset, PASE outperforms SOTA methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in previously unseen fault scenarios.

Conclusion: PASE advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning, model-assisted verification, and meta-learned guidance, demonstrating that tight neuro-symbolic integration significantly improves self-healing performance in complex cloud environments.

Abstract: As the scale and complexity of cloud-based AI systems continue to escalate, ensuring service reliability through rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery has become a critical challenge. While existing approaches integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic understanding and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for policy optimization, they often rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize the generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift with PASE, a Planning-Aware Semantic self-healing engine, a novel fault self-healing framework that reconceptualizes recovery as a neuro-symbolic program synthesis task. PASE employs an LLM as a core Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from a library of semantic primitives. A Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility through simulation, while a Meta-Prompt Optimizer, trained via DRL, learns to generate optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning process. This tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop enables dynamic, context-aware recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces. Experiments on a real-world cloud fault injection dataset demonstrate that PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios. Our framework advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance.

</details>


### [77] [SemHash-LLM: A Multi-Granularity Semantic Hashing Framework for Document Deduplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01601)
*Xinyi Fang,Kejian Tong,Jiabei Liu,Tao Ning,Yuhang He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SemHash LLM is a multi-granularity document deduplication framework that combines semantic projection hashing, attention-weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM adjudication to achieve high-quality duplicate detection at scale with under 1% neural verification cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale document deduplication requires both semantic equivalence preservation (distinguishing truly duplicate content from superficially similar documents) and computational efficiency over massive corpora. Existing methods struggle to balance these demands, often either missing semantically equivalent duplicates or incurring prohibitive computational costs.

Method: A cascaded multi-granularity framework operating at character, token, and document levels: (1) Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in a distilled LLM embedding space; (2) Attention-weighted MinHash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content; (3) Contrastive boundary learning establishes adaptive decision boundaries; (4) Gated fusion combines signals across granularities; (5) Uncertainty estimation gates selective LLM-based adjudication as a final high-precision verification stage, applied to only the most ambiguous candidates.

Result: SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality while requiring neural (LLM-based) verification on less than 1% of candidates, demonstrating effective candidate reduction through the cascaded filtering pipeline.

Conclusion: The multi-granularity, cascaded approach effectively balances semantic precision with computational efficiency, making large-scale semantic deduplication practical. The sub-1% LLM verification cost suggests the earlier pipeline stages successfully handle the vast majority of cases, reserving expensive neural inference for only the most uncertain boundary cases.

Abstract: Large scale document deduplication must preserve semantic equivalence while remaining efficient over massive corpora. We present SemHash LLM, a multi granularity framework that unifies semantic projection hashing, attention weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM based adjudication. The method combines character, token, and document level signals through gated fusion, then applies a cascaded filtering pipeline for efficient candidate reduction. Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space, while attention weighted Min- Hash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content. Adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation further improve robustness across template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments. Experiments show that SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality with less than one percent neural verification cost.

</details>


### [78] [Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Product Improvement: A Case Study of Manga Sales in Japan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01610)
*Keita Kinjo,Takeshi Ebina*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanation (PBCE), which reformulates counterfactual explanations as a profit maximization problem. Unlike traditional CE methods that require exogenous target specification and an abstract distance metric, PBCE directly optimizes profit while reinterpreting distance as the economic cost of modifying product attributes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CE methods suffer from two key limitations in regression settings: (1) they require an arbitrarily specified target output value whose validity is unaddressed, and (2) the distance function lacks a practical, real-world interpretation. Moreover, current methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, despite real-world decision-making being inherently objective-driven.

Method: The authors formulate counterfactual explanation as a profit maximization problem within management and marketing contexts. The PBCE framework eliminates exogenous target specification by setting profit maximization as the primary optimization objective. The distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing economic grounding.

Result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the abstract focuses on the problem formulation and proposed framework rather than empirical results.

Conclusion: PBCE addresses critical gaps in counterfactual explanation for regression by aligning the CE objective with real-world decision-making goals — profit maximization — and by giving the distance metric an economically meaningful interpretation as attribute modification cost.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanation (CE) is widely used to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models and support data-driven decision-making based on model predictions. However, existing CE methods typically require two exogenously specified inputs: a desired output value (target) and a distance function that quantifies changes in explanatory variables. In regression settings, neither the validity of target specification nor the practical interpretation of the distance metric has been sufficiently addressed. Furthermore, most existing CE methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, even though real-world decision-making often requires explicit objective maximization. To address these limitations, we formulate CE as a profit maximization problem in management and marketing contexts and propose a framework termed profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE). PBCE eliminates the need for exogenous target specification by directly maximizing profit as the primary optimization objective. Concurrently, the distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing a clear and economically grounded interpretation.

</details>


### [79] [Scaling with Confidence: Calibrating Confidence of LLMs for Adaptive Test Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01612)
*Xuqing Yang,Yi Yuan,Shanzhe Lei,Xuhong Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C3RL is a reinforcement learning method that jointly optimizes response correctness and confidence calibration in LLMs, improving calibration without sacrificing accuracy. The authors further introduce CAS, an adaptive inference-time strategy that uses calibrated confidence scores to allocate compute, surpassing majority voting while reducing inference budget by up to 12.33×.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RL training for LLMs rewards only response correctness, causing models to become poorly calibrated—they grow overconfident and hallucinate when uncertain. There is a need to incentivize accurate confidence expression alongside correctness.

Method: C3RL integrates three reward signals: correctness reward, calibration reward (penalizing confidence-accuracy mismatch), and a dataset-informed reference accuracy reward. Following C3RL training, CAS uses the verbalized confidence scores to adaptively allocate inference-time compute, e.g., triggering additional sampling or verification only for low-confidence responses.

Result: C3RL improves calibration across 8 text and multimodal datasets without degrading accuracy, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art on both performance and calibration. CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while cutting inference budget by up to 12.33×.

Conclusion: The synergy of C3RL and CAS enables more reliable, resource-efficient LLM deployment by ensuring models know when they are uncertain and adaptively scaling compute accordingly.

Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced their performance on reasoning and question-answering tasks. However, prevailing RL reward designs typically prioritize response correctness, neglecting to incentivize models to express their confidence accurately. This leads to a critical problem: performance gains are often accompanied by poor calibration between confidence and accuracy, misleading models to overconfidently hallucinate when uncertain. To address this limitation, we propose $\textbf{C}$orrectness and $\textbf{C}$onfidence $\textbf{C}$alibration $\textbf{R}$einforcement $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textbf{C3RL}$), a novel RL algorithm integrating correctness, calibration and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards together. Comprehensive evaluation across 8 text and multimodal datasets demonstrates that C3RL enhances calibration without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method in both performance and calibration metrics. Utilizing the well-calibrated verbalized confidence from C3RL, we further introduce $\textbf{C}$onfidence-based $\textbf{A}$daptive Test Time $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{CAS}$), an adjustable inference-time strategy that allocates computational resources based on response confidence. Experiments show that CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing the inference budget by up to 12.33 times. We believe the synergy of C3RL and CAS paves the way for deploying more reliable and resource-efficient LLMs. The code, data and models will be released.

</details>


### [80] [Spatial Support Matters: Geometry-Aware Graph Fusion for Rainfall Field Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01621)
*Low Jun Yu,Niramay Kachhadiya,Herath Mudiyanselage Viraj Vidura Herath,Sanka Rasnayaka,Lucy Amanda Marshall*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a geometry-aware heterogeneous graph neural network for rainfall reconstruction that explicitly models measurement supports (0D points, 1D paths, 2D grids) as distinct node layers with cross-support message passing. It reduces RMSE by 23.2% over IDW and shows fusion benefits depend on gauge spacing relative to spatial correlation length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real rainfall sensing systems operate on incompatible spatial supports — gauges (0D points), microwave links (1D paths), and radar/satellite (2D grids). Existing heterogeneous graph methods reconcile these in feature space but discard the geometry of the measurement support, losing critical spatial constraints that could improve reconstruction fidelity.

Method: The authors propose a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous GNN with distinct node layers per support type (0D point, 1D line, 2D grid). Cross-support message passing fuses information across these layers into a point-support prediction layer. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, enabling reconstruction at arbitrary user-defined target locations. The model is evaluated on data from Singapore and Sydney.

Result: On Singapore data, the method reduces RMSE by 23.2% over inverse-distance weighting and consistently outperforms convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. The Sydney generalization study reveals that multi-support fusion helps most when gauge spacing is large relative to the field's spatial correlation length, and offers little gain when the field is already well-resolved.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling measurement support geometry in heterogeneous GNNs significantly improves fine-scale rainfall reconstruction. The benefit of multi-support fusion is conditional on the sampling density relative to spatial correlation structure, providing practical guidance for sensor network design and deployment. Code and models will be open-sourced.

Abstract: Fine-scale rainfall reconstruction is critical for urban flood modeling, but real rainfall sensing systems observe the field through incompatible spatial supports: gauges measure points, microwave links measure paths, and radar/satellite products measure gridded areas. These differences in measurement support impose geometrically distinct constraints on the rainfall field, yet existing heterogeneous graph approaches reconcile such sources in feature space, giving each its own embedding while discarding the geometry of its support. We propose a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network that represents each observation according to its support type (0D point, 1D line, or 2D grid) as a distinct node layer, and fuses them through cross-support message passing into a point-support prediction layer from which the field is reconstructed. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, allowing the same trained model to reconstruct the field at user-defined target locations or display grids. On Singapore data, the proposed method reduces RMSE by 23.2\% over the classical interpolation baseline, inverse-distance weighting, and consistently outperforms other neural architectures such as convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study using data from Sydney, Australia lets us characterize when multi-support fusion helps: the available skill appears to depend on gauge spacing relative to the spatial correlation length of the field, so fusion delivers the largest gains where the field is under-sampled relative to its correlation length and little when it is already resolved. Code and models will be open-sourced upon paper acceptance.

</details>


### [81] [Autonomous discovery of traffic laws with AI traffic scientists](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01639)
*Xingyuan Dai,Yue Liu,Xiaoyan Gong,Qinghai Miao,Junyou Shang,Yutong Wang,Chao Guo,Yonglin Tian,Yizhang Chai,Chao Xiang,Yisheng Lv,Fei-Yue Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrafficSci is an agentic AI system that autonomously discovers traffic laws by integrating evidence scoping, hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. It rediscovers three known traffic laws and identifies a new intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior across multiple cities and datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traffic-law discovery has traditionally been expert-driven, requiring manual identification of candidate regularities from heterogeneous data or intervention experiments. While autonomous AI has succeeded in controlled lab settings (e.g., molecular biology), extending such systems to complex, open-ended transportation domains remains an unsolved challenge.

Method: TrafficSci frames traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow with three core components: (1) evidence scoping — gathering and curating heterogeneous observational data; (2) critic-judge hypothesis induction — generating candidate laws via a critique-and-evaluation loop; and (3) observational-interventional validation — testing hypotheses against both existing data and targeted intervention experiments. The system is evaluated across four case studies spanning population, network, control, and trajectory scales.

Result: TrafficSci successfully rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies a previously unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, which holds statistical consistency across eight cities and two different trajectory datasets.

Conclusion: TrafficSci demonstrates a viable pathway for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled laboratory domains to complex urban systems, enabling autonomous, auditable formulation and validation of universal traffic laws.

Abstract: Universal traffic laws describe recurrent patterns in congestion, mobility and driving behavior across cities, providing a scientific basis for transportation planning, management and control. Their discovery, however, remains expert-driven, requiring candidate regularities to be identified from heterogeneous observational evidence or validated through intervention experiments. Although autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems have advanced scientific discovery in controlled laboratory settings, extending them to complex transportation domains remains a challenge. Here we present TrafficSci, an agentic AI system that formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow integrating evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. Across four case studies spanning population, network, control and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets. TrafficSci provides a route for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled domains to complex urban systems.

</details>


### [82] [ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01919)
*Jiankai Jin,Xiangzheng Zhang,Zhao Liu,Wenzhuo Xu,Dongdong Yang,Deyue Zhang,Quanchen Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ElephantAgent is a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against tool and memory poisoning attacks in agentic systems, using replicated trusted hardware and a linearizable ledger to verify state digests and enable post-hoc audit and recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic systems increasingly rely on external tools and persistent memory, which introduce new attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks can covertly bias agent behavior by manipulating tool descriptors or memory contents. The core problem is the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state during planning and execution.

Method: ElephantAgent extends prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble) to the evolving contextual state of agents. It defines contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context (tool state, memory). Before each query, it recomputes a digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. Replicated trusted hardware maintains a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions, detecting out-of-band tampering. For in-band semantic abuse, it provides Historical Traceability for conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.

Result: The paper presents the ElephantAgent protocol design, demonstrating that Contextual State Continuity can be enforced via digest verification against a trusted, linearizable ledger, and that Historical Traceability enables audit and rollback capabilities for in-band attacks.

Conclusion: Contextual State Continuity is a viable defense primitive against contextual state poisoning in agentic systems. By combining digest verification, replicated trusted hardware, and historical traceability, ElephantAgent addresses both out-of-band tampering and in-band semantic abuse, providing a foundation for verifiable agent execution integrity.

Abstract: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, these external dependencies introduce novel attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks show that maliciously crafted tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. These threats reflect a deeper issue: the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning and execution. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against contextual state poisoning. Inspired by prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble), ElephantAgent extends this protection to the evolving contextual state of agentic systems. We define the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's entire context (e.g., tool state and memory). Before processing each query, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. Using replicated trusted hardware, ElephantAgent maintains a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions and detects out-of-band state tampering. To handle in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent additionally provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.

</details>


### [83] [Diverse Evidence, Better Forecasts: Multi-Agent Deliberation Under Information Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01661)
*Yuante Li,Yicheng Tao,Kate Zhang,Taozhi Wang,Gefei Gu,Yaxin Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-agent LLM forecasting systems fail to improve over single agents when all agents receive identical evidence, due to herding. The authors propose designed information asymmetry—partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets—and instantiate it in InfoDelphi, achieving 12–18% Brier score improvement and 4–8 pp accuracy gains on the PolyGym benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent forecasting systems give all agents identical evidence, causing deliberation to degrade into herding rather than genuine belief revision. This eliminates the potential benefit of multiple agents and leaves performance barely above a single-agent baseline. The authors identify the lack of input diversity across agents as a fundamental, overlooked design gap.

Method: The authors propose **designed information asymmetry**: evidence is split into a shared public subset (common to all agents) and disjoint private subsets (unique to each agent). This is instantiated in **InfoDelphi**, which comprises three components: (1) relevance-aware evidence routing to assign private evidence, (2) rationale-based iterative deliberation where agents exchange reasoned arguments, and (3) confidence-weighted aggregation of final predictions. A theoretical analysis shows the decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation.

Result: On **PolyGym**, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by **12–18% in Brier score** and **4–8 percentage points in accuracy**. Ablation studies confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing input diversity as the critical enabler.

Conclusion: Diversity of input, rather than deliberation alone, is the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning. Designed information asymmetry is a principled and effective mechanism to achieve this diversity, substantially improving forecasting performance over both single-agent and homogeneous-information multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used for forecasting future events, as deliberation among multiple LLMs is believed to improve reasoning and calibration. Yet existing approaches overlook a critical design choice: what information each agent receives. When all agents are given identical evidence, deliberation collapses into herding rather than genuine belief revision, leaving multi-agent systems little better than a single agent. We identify this as a fundamental gap and propose designed information asymmetry to close it: by partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets, each agent holds exclusive knowledge that can only reach others through deliberation. We theoretically show that this decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation, and instantiate it in InfoDelphi, a framework combining relevance-aware evidence routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. On PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions derived from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12--18% in Brier score and 4--8 percentage points in accuracy. More detailed experiments confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing diversity of input as the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning.

</details>


### [84] [Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01674)
*Yufan Lu,Xinhui Liu,Chenyang Xu,Yuxi Zhou,Hao Wang,Shenda Hong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A frozen ECG foundation model backbone is extended with incremental source-specific classifiers and a lightweight router. Without source metadata at deployment, top-2 margin fusion of routed experts achieves near oracle performance, with autonomous source inference identified as the remaining bottleneck.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-source ECG deployment, new data sources must be incorporated without retaining or replaying raw ECGs from earlier sources. Standard approaches either freeze a backbone with isolated per-source classifiers (requiring source metadata at test time) or risk parameter interference during fine-tuning. The core challenge is enabling source-agnostic deployment — selecting the right expert without knowing which source a sample comes from.

Method: The authors propose an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each new domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert. A lightweight MLP router is trained only on retained training features and domain labels from sources seen so far — raw ECGs are never replayed. At inference, rather than hard-routing to a single expert, a validation-calibrated margin rule fuses predictions from the two most likely experts (top-2 margin fusion). Experiments span CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing datasets across three domain arrival orders.

Result: Source-aware expert selection achieves 0.7915±0.0036 Macro-F1, closely matching an offline independent-head reference (0.7885±0.0009). Without source IDs, MLP routing reaches 0.7756±0.0027 and top-2 margin fusion reaches 0.7782±0.0022 — a small gain (+0.0026) with a 95% CI including zero. The top-2-to-oracle gap remains 0.0111–0.0133 across three domain orders.

Conclusion: Source-aware expert retention is effective when source IDs are available. For source-agnostic deployment, top-2 margin fusion provides only marginal improvement over hard MLP routing, and the primary bottleneck is autonomous source inference rather than expert fusion strategy. The method is not memory-free since frozen training features must be retained for router updates.

Abstract: In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

</details>


### [85] [Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01690)
*Joshua Penman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Language models exhibit "Negation Neglect," failing to internalize explicit annotations that documents are fictional. The authors introduce Goggles, a gradient-intervention module that imparts an epistemic frame during LoRA finetuning, enabling models to correctly flag claims as fictional ~91% of the time (vs. ~9% for data-annotation baselines) while preserving general capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When finetuning LMs on documents explicitly labeled as fictional, models still absorb and believe the core claims—a phenomenon termed "Negation Neglect" (only ~9% correct identification). This poses a safety risk: models trained on misaligned or synthetic data may inadvertently adopt undesirable behaviors. The authors seek a method to train on potentially harmful data without the model internalizing the demonstrated behaviors.

Method: Goggles is a learned module that operates on gradients during supervised finetuning rather than modifying the data itself. During LoRA-based finetuning, Goggles edits the gradients to impart a chosen "epistemic frame"—the stance the model takes toward the nature of the documents. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to unseen documents. The architecture is frame-agnostic (tested with fiction and "AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" frames).

Result: With Goggles, models correctly flag fictional claims ~91% of the time (vs. ~9% baseline with explicit annotation). GPQA and TruthfulQA performance matches or exceeds baseline, indicating capability preservation. The imparted epistemic frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, whereas prior interventions revert. The approach generalizes to other frames beyond fiction.

Conclusion: Goggles offers a viable path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without the model absorbing the demonstrated behaviors, by intervening on gradients rather than data annotations to impose a protective epistemic frame that proves robust to further training.

Abstract: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

</details>


### [86] [COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01709)
*Zongxia Li,Dawei Liu,Fuxiao Liu,Yuhang Zhou,Xiyang Wu,Jingxi Chen,Jing Xie,Xiaomin Wu,Lichao Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: COMFYCLAW introduces an agent framework that evolves reusable skills from past workflow executions, using typed graph editing and VLM-based visual verification to iteratively improve ComfyUI image generation workflows, outperforming non-evolution baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As agents are increasingly used for recurring, domain-specific workflows, they lack mechanisms to remember workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from prior runs. This gap limits agent reliability and efficiency in repeated visual workflow construction tasks.

Method: COMFYCLAW formulates ComfyUI workflow construction as typed graph editing with stage-organized tools and automatic rollback of invalid edits. A region-level VLM verifier translates visual output failures into actionable repair suggestions. Crucially, it maintains a progressively disclosed skill library that distills trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from prior runs into reusable Agent Skills.

Result: Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, surpassing a verifier-only baseline lacking skill evolution. Human annotators also preferred COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution.

Conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction, enabling agents to learn from past failures and user preferences.

Abstract: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

</details>


### [87] [Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02389)
*Thomas Winninger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes applying traditional software engineering management practices (access control, coding conventions, tool-enforced policies) to constrain coding agents, demonstrating that a constrained substrate plus a simple CLI tool dramatically improves a small reviewer model's ability to detect backdoors in Python code (recall: 54.5% → 90.9%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unconstrained coding agents introduce security vulnerabilities, degrade codebase scalability, and overwhelm human reviewers. The bottleneck is no longer agent capability but human oversight. The authors argue that instead of complex agentic scaffolding, proven organizational practices from managing human engineering teams can be transferred directly to agent governance at lower token cost.

Method: A controlled experiment where a small reviewer model (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase with 11 inserted backdoors. Two conditions are compared: (1) unconstrained agent with no tools, and (2) a constrained substrate with a ~200-line `docs` CLI tool. The substrate enforces access control, network policies, and coding conventions, while the CLI provides structured codebase documentation. Effects of substrate and tools are measured independently.

Result: Backdoor detection recall improved from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate + `docs` CLI). The substrate and the tooling contributed independently to the gains. Python was chosen deliberately because its minimal default guarantees maximize the marginal benefit of substrate-level oversight; the approach generalizes to languages like Rust.

Conclusion: Traditional software engineering governance mechanisms — access control, network policies, convention enforcement — transfer effectively and cheaply to coding agent management. Constraining agents via a well-designed substrate, rather than relying solely on increasingly complex agentic scaffolding, yields substantial improvements in scalable oversight and security review outcomes.

Abstract: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

</details>


### [88] [Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01710)
*Yongqin Zeng,Sicheng Pan,Jiale Wang,Hai-tao Zheng,Hong-Gee Kim,Chunxia Ma,XiuTeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Generic TB-Coverage, a coverage-aware expert pruning method for MoE language models that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2, C4) and preserves high-utility experts per corpus via a fixed-budget coverage rule, outperforming existing methods especially under aggressive pruning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparsely activated MoE models contain structured redundancy among routed experts, but existing pruning methods rely on a single aggregated importance score that biases retention toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. Moreover, downstream calibration data may not always be available, creating a need for effective pruning using only generic corpora.

Method: Generic TB-Coverage: profiles per-expert utility separately on each generic corpus (WikiText2 and C4), then enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that ensures high-utility experts from each corpus are preserved before constructing the final pruning mask, rather than collapsing expert utility into a single score.

Result: Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets, the method improves average accuracy on six zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. Gains are largest at aggressive pruning levels (25% and 50% retain).

Conclusion: Preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. The method demonstrates that strong pruning performance can be achieved with fixed budgets and no downstream calibration data.

Abstract: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

</details>


### [89] [Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01715)
*Xudong Wu,Jian Qian,Pangpang Liu,Vaneet Aggarwal,Jiayu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a robust Plackett-Luce objective for listwise preference optimization that handles ranking-label uncertainty via a tractable total-variation robustification, reducing inner maximization from factorial to linearithmic complexity, with strong theoretical guarantees in both offline and online settings, and empirical improvements in LLM alignment under noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing robust preference optimization focuses on pairwise settings and places robustness at coarse levels (dataset/prompt/pair). Real-world listwise ranking labels suffer from annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy feedback, and reward-model noise, creating a need for robustness at the ranking-label level within the listwise Plackett-Luce framework.

Method: The authors propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective that decomposes into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction. The worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting implicit scores in ascending order, reducing inner maximization from $K!$ to $O(K \log K)$. This structure is analyzed in both offline (fixed-list, convex, projected stochastic subgradient) and online (policy-induced, weak convexity, Moreau-envelope stationarity) settings.

Result: Offline: convex objective with $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity to global $\epsilon$-suboptimality. Online: $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity under weak convexity. Experiments show robust correction preserves clean-label performance while improving robustness under noise; online alignment yields more reliable reward-model-ranked candidate expansion and improves both reward-model and GPT-4 judge scores.

Conclusion: The proposed tractable robust Plackett-Luce objective effectively addresses ranking-label uncertainty in listwise preference optimization, offering strong theoretical convergence guarantees and practical improvements in LLM alignment robustness under both offline and online settings.

Abstract: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

</details>


### [90] [DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01729)
*Yueming Huang,Wenhan Yao,Fen Xiao,Xiarun Chen,Weiping Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A novel clean-label backdoor attack (DRL-CLBA) for speech classification that uses DDPG reinforcement learning and deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers, bypassing defenses without requiring poisoned labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor attacks on speech classification either rely on poisoned labels (detectable via manual inspection) or use static triggers (vulnerable to defenses). There is a need for a clean-label, sample-specific attack that can evade both manual data inspection and automated backdoor defenses.

Method: The authors propose DRL-CLBA with three core components: (1) Deep audio steganography to imperceptibly embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchor points; (2) Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning to optimize target samples toward trigger-bearing anchors in the model's deep latent space, enabling clean-label (label-migration-free) poisoning; (3) The framework trains the backdoor without altering the original labels of poisoned samples.

Result: Evaluated across three datasets and four DNN architectures, DRL-CLBA achieves high attack success rates. It effectively bypasses defenses including fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature detection, while maintaining clean label integrity.

Conclusion: DRL-CLBA exposes critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems by demonstrating that clean-label, sample-specific backdoor attacks are feasible and resistant to multiple defense mechanisms, highlighting a significant security gap in current speech classification models.

Abstract: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

</details>


### [91] [Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01734)
*Simon Guilloud,Sankalp Gambhir,Samuel Chassot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A case study on reformalization — porting formal proofs between different proof assistants — demonstrated through three translations of the Jordan Curve Theorem (Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, HOL Light→Agda), analyzing pipeline design choices for practical use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoformalization has focused on translating natural language into formal proofs, but a practical and underexplored variant is reformalization: translating an existing formal proof from one proof assistant to another. This is motivated by the growing diversity of proof assistants and the desire to reuse formal developments across systems without manual re-engineering.

Method: The authors conduct a case study involving three concrete reformalization tasks of the Jordan Curve Theorem: (1) Mizar to Lean, (2) HOL Light to Lean, and (3) HOL Light to Agda. They analyze the results and extract general pipeline design choices — such as how to handle logical framework mismatches, translation of tactic scripts vs. declarative proofs, and semantic alignment of libraries — that affect the success of practical reformalization.

Result: Three successful reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem were completed across different proof assistant pairs. The analysis reveals that pipeline design choices (e.g., direct translation vs. semantic reconstruction, handling of dependent types, library alignment strategies) significantly impact the feasibility and quality of the resulting formalizations.

Conclusion: Reformalization is a viable and valuable paradigm distinct from natural-language autoformalization. The case study demonstrates that careful pipeline design is critical, and the lessons learned can guide future tool-building efforts for inter-proof-assistant translation.

Abstract: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

</details>


### [92] [Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01740)
*Blair Hudson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a meta-benchmarking framework that maps 452 public benchmarks to 41 work activities and 38 banking business domains, using a multiplicative weighting scheme and Elo tournament to produce cross-benchmark-comparable scores for financial-services model selection, demonstrated on 288 models from 25 organizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public LLM leaderboards optimize for global average performance and fail to capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work, causing models that excel on general benchmarks to underperform on domain-specific tasks like compliance reasoning or multi-turn customer interactions.

Method: A meta-benchmarking framework that organizes 452 public benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates them into 38 BIAN banking business domains (sales, operations, risk, support). A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination × coverage × recency) computed over a rolling model window rewards benchmarks that separate top models, are widely reported, and remain actively used. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, yielding cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalization; business-domain scores are weighted averages of constituent work-activity Elos.

Result: The framework is demonstrated on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models from 25 organizations as of June 2026, producing work-activity and business-domain Elo scores that enable domain-specific model comparison beyond saturated legacy benchmarks.

Conclusion: The meta-benchmarking approach provides a reproducible, governance-oriented alternative to generic leaderboards for financial institutions, with full methodology, taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations documented for adoption by similar organizations facing model selection challenges.

Abstract: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

</details>


### [93] [Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01754)
*Sung June Kim,Sangpil Kim,Honglak Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Phi-Nav is an on-policy framework for Vision-Language Navigation that uses hindsight reasoning to generate synthetic instructions for exploratory trajectories, bridging the semantic gap between off-expert-demonstration paths and original instructions through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy exploration in VLN exposes agents to broader state distributions but creates a semantic mismatch between actual trajectories and original language instructions. This gap leaves exploratory trajectories without appropriate textual supervision, limiting the effectiveness of on-policy learning.

Method: Phi-Nav employs a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: (1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration where the agent samples trajectories with expert action feedback; (2) a hindsight speaker model that synthesizes path-level instructions grounded in the collected visual observations; (3) a second imitation pass that treats the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration, converting semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals.

Result: Phi-Nav achieves competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines.

Conclusion: Semantic exploration is essential for VLN, and Phi-Nav offers an effective data-efficient solution for training embodied agents with limited expert demonstrations by leveraging hindsight instruction synthesis.

Abstract: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

</details>


### [94] [Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01764)
*Mingzhe Du,Luu Anh Tuan,Tianyi Wu,Renyang Liu,Zhijiang Guo,Dong Huang,See-Kiong Ng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mastermind is a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific execution for repository-level vulnerability reproduction. A trainable planner learns reusable strategies via SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains local records. With GPT-5.5, it achieves 84.5% pass rate on CyberGym, outperforming baselines (60–77%), and the same planner transfers effectively to other frozen executors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents for repository-level vulnerability reproduction fail not due to incorrect action execution but because they choose the wrong strategy. Strategy is identified as the optimal learning unit: compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse. Existing approaches lack a mechanism to learn and transfer these high-level strategies independently of the executor.

Method: Mastermind introduces a dual-loop architecture: (1) a strategy learning loop where a trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and milestone-based Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), trained independently of the executor; (2) an experience loop that maintains task-local strategy records to guide subsequent attempts. The planner is executor-agnostic, enabling strategy improvements to benefit multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capabilities.

Result: Evaluated on CyberGym with 260 training and 200 held-out tasks. With GPT-5.5 as frozen executor, Mastermind achieves 84.5% pass rate vs. open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner transfers to GPT-5.4 mini (45.0% → 60.0%) and GLM 5.1 (58.5% → 71.0%), demonstrating cross-executor transferability.

Conclusion: Learning high-level strategies, rather than full action trajectories, is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale software engineering agents. The separation of strategy learning from execution enables broad applicability across different LLM backends.

Abstract: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

</details>


### [95] [SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01766)
*Chunjiang Liu,Xiaoyuan Wang,Haoyu Chen,Yizhou Zhao,Ming-Hsuan Yang,László A. Jeni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework that generates dynamic, editable 4D scenes (3D + time) from text prompts using Blender, employing a planner-coder-reviewer workflow, a layered scene protocol with deterministic verification, and runtime-state inspection tools. It introduces 4DBuildBench for evaluating physical consistency and visual fidelity, outperforming prior baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-agent systems for text-to-3D focus on static output, while dynamic 4D scenes involving liquids, particles, rigid bodies, and articulated mechanisms remain unexplored. Dynamic scenes are valuable for editable content creation and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two key challenges motivate this work: (1) an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in one coherent scene; (2) verifying motion correctness from rendered video is significantly harder than judging a single static image.
