Method: The authors propose SimWorlds, a multi-agent framework with four core components: (1) Blender-specific procedural knowledge integrated into the agents; (2) a planner-coder-reviewer workflow that drives a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages; (3) a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier to ensure structural coherence; and (4) a runtime-state inspection tool suite that detects mechanism failures invisible in rendered images. They also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for evaluating both visual fidelity and physical consistency of procedurally generated dynamic 3D scenes from text.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that SimWorlds outperforms existing baselines for dynamic Blender generation, as measured on the 4DBuildBench benchmark.

Conclusion: The SimWorlds framework advances text-to-4D scene generation by addressing the unique challenges of dynamic scene construction—multi-physics coordination and motion verification—through a structured multi-agent architecture with deterministic verification, setting a new state-of-the-art on the 4DBuildBench benchmark.

Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

</details>


### [96] [Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01767)
*Xinyuan Song,Zekun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WM-SAR repairs failed planning graphs by identifying the causal error-amplifying subgraph rather than scanning for visible symptoms, achieving superior stabilization under realistic token budgets compared to engineering correctors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As agent planning scales to workflows with thousands of steps, failures propagate within large planning graphs. Full-graph replanning after every mistake is computationally prohibitive, consumes excessive context, and degrades long-context retrieval. A missing component is a world-model corrector that can repair failed planning graphs in place without full replay.

Method: Two families of correctors are compared: (1) Engineering correctors that scan nodes/edges, select suspicious local regions, and invoke an LLM for repair; (2) WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair), which works backward from subgraph amplification to identify nodes and edges that persistently re-amplify error, sending only that causal subgraph to the LLM for targeted repair.

Result: Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and provides the LLM a cleaner repair target.

Conclusion: Causal subgraph identification via error amplification tracing is more effective and efficient than symptom-based scanning for repairing large-scale agent planning graphs, enabling scalable persistent workflows without full-graph replay.

Abstract: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

</details>


### [97] [Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01773)
*Yujin Yang,Heejung Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework combining small language models with formal concept analysis uses FCA as a symbolic verification loop to validate knowledge expansions, achieving moderate F1 scores in a rare ataxia domain while maintaining inspectability of all decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models can propose ontological structures from text, but their outputs are often unsupported or inconsistent. A verifiable, inspectable method is needed to validate knowledge expansion in ontology construction.

Method: A retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework where formal concept analysis (FCA) proposes implications over a growing formal context from seed attributes. An SLM oracle (grounded via retrieval) validates each implication or returns counterexamples, and also handles incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals. All accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections remain inspectable.

Result: In a rare ataxia domain (Orphadata), 10-seed runs achieved relation F1 of 0.29–0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22–0.30. Larger seed sets increased the number of evaluated implications and often improved implication F1. Lower implication F1 reflects stricter evaluation: one missed/extra relation can affect multiple implication judgments. Ablations showed incidence judgments in fixed object-attribute settings can improve closure-based implication scores, though identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even with fixed candidates.

Conclusion: Combining retrieval-augmented SLMs with FCA-based symbolic verification yields inspectable, moderately accurate ontology construction. The framework's transparency and the strictness of implication evaluation are key strengths, though challenges remain in positive object-attribute identification.

Abstract: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

</details>


### [98] [Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01774)
*Maximo Rulli,Thomas Fontanari,Simone Petruzzi,Federico Alvetreti,Giorgio Strano,Donato Crisostomi,Giorgos Nikolaou,Tommaso Mencattini,Andrea Santilli,Emanuele Rodolà,Simone Scardapane,Alessio Devoto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) encode a latent representation of denoising progress within their residual streams, despite lacking explicit timestep conditioning. This signal is decodable via probing, steerable along a low-dimensional subspace to modulate confidence/entropy, and exhibits structured geometric properties in activation space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on timesteps unlike standard diffusion models, raising the question of whether and how they internally represent denoising progress. Understanding this mechanism is crucial for interpretability and control of these emerging models.

Method: The authors use linear probes trained on residual stream activations across layers to decode the latent diffusion timestep. They then perform activation steering along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep to modulate the model's notion of denoising progress. Finally, they analyze the geometric properties of the identified representation in activation space.

Result: Probes reliably extract timestep information across layers, confirming DLMs encode denoising progress. Steering along the identified subspace produces predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. The representation exhibits structured and interpretable geometric properties.

Conclusion: DLMs internally represent denoising progress in a structured, decodable, and steerable manner within their residual streams, providing insights into how these models process the generation trajectory without explicit timestep conditioning.

Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

</details>


### [99] [Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01793)
*Yunhao Feng,Ruixiao Lin,Ming Wen,Qinqin He,Yanming Guo,Yifan Ding,Yutao Wu,Jialuo Chen,Yunhao Chen,Xiaohu Du,Jianan Ma,Zixing Chen,Zhuoer Xu,Xingjun Ma,Xinhao Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Vera is an automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage pipeline (risk discovery, combinatorial test case generation, and adaptive sandbox execution) to uncover vulnerabilities. Evaluated on four production agent frameworks, it achieved 93.9% attack success rates under multi-channel attacks and produced Vera-Bench, a benchmark of 1600 executable safety cases across 124 risk categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety testing for LLM agents relies on expert-designed violations and hard-coded evaluation rules, making testing costly to scale and maintain as agents evolve. There is a need for automated, extensible safety evaluation infrastructure grounded in software engineering testing principles.

Method: Vera implements a three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) Literature-driven exploration continuously mines emerging risks and structures them into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and execution environments. (2) Combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions generates executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate based on observable artifacts. (3) Adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes, where a control agent orchestrates multi-turn interaction using runtime observations, and evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call traces rather than model self-reporting.

Result: Evaluation across four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code) revealed substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings, was released publicly.

Conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. Vera demonstrates that automated, evidence-grounded testing pipelines can effectively uncover safety vulnerabilities that would be missed by static or self-reported evaluation approaches.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

</details>


### [100] [MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01814)
*Lihui Luo,Joongwon Chae,Ziyan Chen,Yang Liu,Siyi Cheng,Weihan Gao,Zelin Zeng,Xiaoming Yin,Samaneh Beheshti Kashi,Dongmei Yu,Lian Zhang,Jing Sui,Zeming Liang,Jiansong Ji,Peter E. Lobie,Peiwu Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MMIR-TCM is a multimodal AI framework for TCM tongue diagnosis that combines a training-free segmentation module, a fine-tuned MLLM (Qwen3-VL), and a RAG component. It was trained/evaluated on a newly introduced large-scale dataset (MedTCM) and assessed with a novel domain-specific metric (TDEU), outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional TCM tongue diagnosis suffers from subjectivity and poor reproducibility. Multimodal AI for tasks like syndrome differentiation is hindered by (1) the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual clinical reasoning, and (2) the absence of large-scale, standardized multimodal datasets.

Method: The MMIR-TCM framework uses a three-stage pipeline: (1) Memory-SAM, a training-free memory-augmented segmentation module for robust tongue extraction; (2) a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL MLLM for generating structured tongue diagnosis; and (3) a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The authors also introduce MedTCM, a large-scale multimodal dataset, and TDEU, a new evaluation metric that incorporates semantic understanding and diagnostic importance weighting.

Result: MMIR-TCM significantly outperformed leading models including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on the TDEU metric, demonstrating superior clinical accuracy in tongue diagnosis and clinical decision support tasks.

Conclusion: By combining memory-augmented segmentation, fine-tuned MLLMs, and retrieval-augmented generation within a unified framework, MMIR-TCM effectively bridges the visual-textual semantic gap in TCM diagnosis. The introduction of MedTCM and TDEU further provides foundational resources for advancing multimodal AI research in traditional medicine.

Abstract: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

</details>


### [101] [Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01903)
*Zihao Xu,Yuekang Li,Gelei Deng,Yi Liu,Zhenchang Xing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HECATE is the first tool to measure complexity in LLM-integrated applications across both prompt and code layers. Using a Hoare-logic-inspired "Prompt-as-Specification" formalism, it generates 52 candidate metrics from 25 complexity dimensions. After empirical validation against maintenance activity in 18 repositories, only 10 metrics survive — 7 of which are newly introduced "structural breadth" metrics that count distinct elements (LLM call sites, prompt templates, memory attributes) rather than size. Prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when controlling for code-level metrics, establishing prompt complexity as an independent dimension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing complexity metrics operate exclusively at the code level, yet LLM-integrated applications derive much of their runtime behavior from natural language prompts. This fundamental disconnect means current metrics overlook a critical layer of behavioral logic, creating a gap in our ability to assess and manage complexity in this emerging class of software.

Method: The authors propose HECATE, grounded in a "Prompt-as-Specification" formalism inspired by Hoare logic, treating each prompt as a behavioral specification. They identify 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies, generating 52 candidate metrics (spanning prompt-layer, code-layer, and hybrid metrics). These are evaluated against 118 components from 18 open-source repositories, using maintenance activity from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity. Metrics that lose significance after controlling for code size are discarded. The surviving metrics undergo further validation on 20 held-out components from 6 unseen repositories.

Result: Only 10 of 52 candidate metrics survive the size-controlled significance test. Seven are newly introduced metrics measuring "structural breadth" — counts of structurally distinct elements such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates. Three surviving conventional metrics are RFC (which also exhibits breadth-oriented character), and Halstead N and V (which survive only as residual effects of size). The top-performing new metrics exceed all three conventional ones. Prompt-layer metrics retain significance even with the strongest code-level metric as a covariate. The two best-performing metrics generalize to held-out repositories.

Conclusion: Prompt complexity constitutes an independent dimension of software complexity in LLM-integrated applications, one that cannot be reduced to code-level metrics. Structural breadth — counting distinct elements rather than measuring volume — proves more meaningful than sheer size for predicting maintenance effort. HECATE demonstrates that prompt-layer metrics are both empirically valid and practically useful for assessing maintainability in this new application paradigm.

Abstract: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

</details>


### [102] [Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01829)
*Alex Brooker,Tim Hughes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 multiple-choice questions evaluating LLMs on aviation-specific operational knowledge (ICAO/FAA regulations, ground operations, scenarios). Even the strongest model (2026) reaches only 82.7% accuracy versus ~95% expert baseline, revealing a persistent reliability gap that the authors argue must be addressed before deploying LLMs in non-safety-critical aviation roles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose LLM benchmarks fail to assess whether models reason safely and correctly about domain-specific aviation operational knowledge. Given aviation's high-stakes, regulated nature, this gap poses consequential risks for proposed LLM deployments in business operations such as documentation, training, and customer-facing assistants.

Method: The authors created Pre-Flight, a 300-question multiple-choice benchmark covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge, and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners (air traffic management, ground operations, commercial flying). Models were evaluated using the Inspect framework under a standard multiple-choice protocol, with a rolling leaderboard maintained as new models release. An informal expert baseline (~95%) was established via a low-sample quiz at an aviation conference.

Result: The strongest model evaluated (released 2026) achieved 82.7% accuracy, improving only gradually from ~75% in early 2025. A substantial gap persists below the ~95% expert reference level.

Conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation benchmarks like Pre-Flight are a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations. The dataset, evaluation harness, and results are publicly released via inspect_evals.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

</details>


### [103] [Actual causality in fault trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01840)
*Georgiana Caltais,Milan Lopuhaä-Zwakenberg,Mariëlle Stoelinga*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper bridges fault tree analysis with Halpern & Pearl's actual causality theory, providing a complete classification of causal notions in terms of fault tree structure and showing how minimal cut sets correspond to actual causes, thereby enabling fault trees to answer "why" questions in failure diagnostics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fault trees are well-established for answering "what can go wrong?" via minimal cut set analysis, but they are not traditionally used to answer "why has it gone wrong?" — a question fundamental to failure diagnostics. The authors aim to extend the utility of fault trees by grounding them in a formal theory of actual causality.

Method: The authors apply Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality to fault trees. They analyze both the graph-theoretic structure and the logical (Boolean) structure of fault trees to classify each notion of actual causality — such as being a cause, a sufficient cause, a necessary cause, etc. — in terms of structural properties of the fault tree. They also investigate the relationship between minimal cut sets and actual causes.

Result: A complete classification is achieved: each distinct notion of actual causality from Halpern & Pearl's framework is characterized in fault tree terms. Furthermore, minimal cut sets are shown to give rise to actual causes, establishing a formal link between the two frameworks.

Conclusion: Fault trees can be systematically repurposed from mere risk assessment tools into formal diagnostic engines. By mapping actual causality notions onto fault tree structures and leveraging minimal cut sets as actual causes, one can rigorously answer retrospective "why" questions about system failures.

Abstract: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

</details>


### [104] [CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01846)
*Fangfei Li,Chenyang Zhao,Long Wang,Feng Tian,Zhiyue Zheng,Lv Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CLAP is a closed-loop framework for domain-agent post-training that converts noisy business data into structured training/evaluation artifacts and uses offline gates plus application-chain replay to decide adapter release readiness, revealing that SFT yields mixed gains across manufacturing batches and that RAG-based adapters improve factual extraction at the cost of latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Domain agents deployed in industrial settings face four key challenges: noisy business data, uncertain post-training performance gains, mismatch between offline evaluation and real application performance, and risks associated with releasing adapters into production. Existing approaches lack an integrated methodology to manage the full data-training-evaluation-release lifecycle.

Method: CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training) comprises: (1) converting raw business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records; (2) data validation and target/evidence normalization; (3) reward/KL divergence diagnosis; (4) offline gating mechanisms; and (5) application-chain replay for final adapter suitability assessment. Experiments use QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT and GRPO, tested on five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches with a 3B backbone model, including RAG-oriented adapter variants.

Result: Across five manufacturing batches, LoRA-SFT yields modest average improvements: overall score (+0.0098), pass rate (+0.0240), and evidence accuracy (+0.0280), with reductions in hallucination and wrong facts. However, only 3 of 5 batches improve, with some showing regression. GRPO exposes high KL-divergence risks. Application-chain replay demonstrates that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; a RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value accuracy, core fields, and answer-evidence document/page matching over base+RAG, though at increased latency.

Conclusion: Domain-agent post-training should be managed through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release closed loop rather than relying solely on training completion or a single offline metric. The CLAP framework provides a systematic approach to decision-making about adapter deployment, accounting for performance variability, safety risks, and application-level trade-offs such as the latency-accuracy balance.

Abstract: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

</details>


### [105] [Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01859)
*Joshua Adrian Cahyono*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Safety training for LLMs is predominantly English-centric, creating an epistemic gap where models confidently produce harmful outputs on low-resource/mixed-language inputs. The authors introduce STEER, a gradient-guided attack that iteratively translates refusal-triggering words into low-resource languages, achieving up to 96.7% attack success rate and transferring even to GPT-4o-mini.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety alignment in LLMs is conducted primarily on English data, and it is unclear whether these safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages or code-switched inputs. The authors hypothesize an "epistemic gap": models confidently generate harmful responses when inputs fall outside the distribution of their safety training.

Method: STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement): a gradient-guided attack that (1) identifies tokens/words contributing most to the model's refusal behavior using gradient signals, then (2) iteratively translates those high-contribution words into low-resource languages, suppressing refusal while preserving the harmful intent of the original prompt. Evaluated on six open-source 8B models against baselines including random code-switching and GCG.

Result: STEER achieves attack success rates up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and GCG. The generated prompts transfer to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% ASR without white-box access, indicating the vulnerability is architecture-agnostic.

Conclusion: Safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. The authors argue for broader multilingual coverage during alignment and explicit mechanisms to detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

Abstract: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

</details>


### [106] [CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01870)
*Dawei Ren,Yan Zhang,Hongying Tang,Qiaoling Zhou,Jianpo Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CamoNAS introduces a neural architecture search framework with frequency-aware dual-stream design for camouflaged object detection, automatically discovering optimal cell operations and downsampling paths to achieve state-of-the-art results across four benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional COD models rely on manually designed architectures and heuristic multi-scale feature fusion, which may be suboptimal. There is a need for systematic architecture search to discover better network designs tailored specifically for the challenges of camouflaged object detection.

Method: CamoNAS employs a hierarchical NAS framework that jointly searches cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths. It also uses an RGB-frequency dual-stream architecture where a learnable wavelet transform complements the standard RGB spatial stream, enhancing sensitivity to frequency-domain cues critical for detecting camouflaged objects.

Result: CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON.

Conclusion: The strong results validate NAS as an effective paradigm for COD, demonstrating that automatically searched architectures with frequency-aware designs can outperform hand-crafted models in locating and segmenting camouflaged objects.

Abstract: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

</details>


### [107] [SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01874)
*Jiayin Zhu,Kelong Mao,Yudong Guo,Dengbo He,Sulong Xu,Simiu Gu,Yutao Yue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillCoach introduces self-evolving rubrics to evaluate LLM agent skill-use along four process dimensions—selection, following, composition, and reflection—rather than relying solely on coarse outcome verifiers, enabling better evaluation and training signal quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In realistic skill repositories with overlapping skills, agents can succeed accidentally (via trial and error, skipping steps, incorrect composition, or omitting checks) despite flawed skill-use. Final verifier success is too coarse to distinguish genuine skill mastery from accidental task completion, and this weak signal hampers both reliable evaluation and effective training.

Method: SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real agent rollouts, evaluating trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It retains the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, decoupling process quality from accidental success. The evolved rubrics self-improve iteratively and serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories.

Result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality over outcome-only signals, expose failures that final accuracy would otherwise mask, and provide stronger supervision for training than outcome-only filtering.

Conclusion: Process-oriented rubrics derived from rollouts offer a superior evaluation and training paradigm for agentic skill-use, distinguishing competent execution from lucky outcomes and enabling more targeted skill improvement.

Abstract: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

</details>


### [108] [Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01893)
*Tianjian Yang,Meng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AUF (Accepted-Until-First-Failure) modifies the cross-entropy loss for block drafters in speculative decoding by truncating supervision at the first predicted rejection, improving emitted length from 2.40 to 2.61 on DFlash without altering the inference pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard block drafters are trained with full-block cross-entropy that supervises all positions, but during inference, tokens after the first rejection are discarded. This creates a train-test mismatch. The authors use teacher-forced learning as motivation: supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix rather than the full block.

Method: AUF modifies the cross-entropy loss support for mask-only block drafters (like DFlash and Domino) by truncating it at the drafter's first predicted failure — the first position where the drafter's argmax disagrees with the target. This is a single, detached change: no auxiliary objectives, no verifier rollouts, no inference pipeline changes, and no alteration to the exactness contract. The mask-only architecture lacks an input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates prefix-sensitive supervision purely on the loss side.

Result: On Qwen3-8B across six benchmarks, AUF raises DFlash's average emitted length τ from 2.40 to 2.61 (gains on every benchmark) and improves Domino's two-branch head from 2.56 to 2.68. Two key findings: (1) a decay-only baseline achieves higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse; (2) once AUF truncates the support, standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

Conclusion: Truncating cross-entropy support at the first predicted failure is a simple, effective way to align block drafter training with the inference-time acceptance mechanism. The findings suggest that token accuracy on the full block is a misleading proxy for speculative decoding quality, and that acceptance-aware supervision subsumes the role of position-based decay weighting.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

</details>


### [109] [ContextSniper: AntTrail's Token-Efficient Code Memory for Repository-Level Program Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01916)
*Chiwang Luk,Matin Mohammad Najafi,Zhifeng Jia,Wei Yang,Xiuchang Li,Jinwei Zhu,Yang Ren,Lei Chen,Gao Cong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ContextSniper is a token-efficient code memory layer for LLM-based repository-level program repair that reduces token usage by 39–52% and cost by 27–36% with only a marginal 2% drop in resolution rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents for program repair waste large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is interleaved with irrelevant code and logs. A more precise evidence selection mechanism is needed to reduce token consumption without substantially degrading repair performance.

Method: ContextSniper, part of the AntTrail agent memory engine, implements a Sniper feature with four stages: (1) retrieving candidate code and runtime evidence, (2) ranking candidates using hybrid retrieval signals, (3) filtering long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and (4) returning compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. Evaluated on SWE-bench Lite across 50 task runs per condition using OpenClaw and Claude Code host agents.

Result: With OpenClaw: 51.5% token reduction, 36.4% cost reduction; resolution rate dropped from 26.0% to 24.0%. With Claude Code: 38.9% token reduction, 27.3% cost reduction; resolution rate dropped from 32.0% to 30.0%.

Conclusion: ContextSniper achieves substantial token and cost savings while preserving near-original resolution rates, demonstrating that precision evidence selection with intention-aware filtering is an effective strategy for efficient LLM-based program repair. The approach is open-sourced for further validation.

Abstract: Large language model agents can repair real repository issues, but they often spend large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is mixed with irrelevant code and logs. This paper presents ContextSniper, AntTrail's token-efficient code memory layer for repository-level program repair. As the coding specialization of AntTrail's broader agent memory engine, ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature for precision evidence selection: it retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks it with hybrid retrieval signals, filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. We evaluate ContextSniper on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code, using 50 task runs per host-agent condition. ContextSniper reduces total token use by 51.5% and logged cost by 36.4% for OpenClaw, and reduces total token use by 38.9% and estimated cost by 27.3% for Claude Code. Submitted-resolution rates decrease slightly, from 26.0% to 24.0% for OpenClaw and from 32.0% to 30.0% for Claude Code. ContextSniper's pilot testing scripts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Calluking/ContextSniper

</details>


### [110] [A-TMA: Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01935)
*Zitong Shi,Yixuan Tang,Anthony Kum Hoe Tung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces "ghost memory," a failure mode in LLM agent memory systems where outdated, current, and transitional facts coexist and confuse answers. The authors propose ATMA, a state-aware overlay that labels records by temporal state (current/historical/transition), and LTP, a benchmark for measuring ghost memory failures, demonstrating significant accuracy gains when ATMA is applied to existing memory systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents with long-term memory must track changing user facts, but current memory systems fail to distinguish between what is true now, what was true before, and what changed. This "ghost memory" problem causes stale and conflicting facts to mislead retrieval and answer generation. Moreover, final QA accuracy metrics obscure where failures actually occur across the memory pipeline.

Method: The authors propose a three-level framework for analyzing memory systems: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer-time resolution. They introduce ATMA, a state-aware overlay that (1) retains superseded and transition records in the memory bank, (2) builds evidence packets with explicit state labels (current, historical, transition) aligned to the query's requested temporal view, and (3) exposes these labels during QA. They also construct LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict-heavy benchmark, and evaluate using both LTP and the existing LoCoMo benchmark.

Result: On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improved conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over baseline Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raised temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. Gains are host-system-dependent but consistently demonstrate that explicit state roles reduce memory failures otherwise hidden by final QA accuracy.

Conclusion: Memory systems for LLM agents should be evaluated and optimized across three decoupled levels (bank, retrieval, answer resolution). Explicit temporal state labeling via ATMA significantly mitigates ghost memory failures, and dedicated benchmarks like LTP are essential for diagnosing where these failures occur rather than relying solely on end-to-end QA accuracy.

Abstract: Long term memory lets LLM agents act as persistent assistants, but user facts change. A useful memory system must know what is true now, what used to be true, and what changed. We study \emph{ghost memory}, a state coordination failure in which old, current, and transition facts coexist in the memory bank, remain mixed during retrieval, and mislead the answer model. We argue that memory systems should be understood and optimized from three levels: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer time resolution. We propose ATMA, a state aware overlay for existing memory systems. ATMA keeps superseded and transition records in the bank, builds evidence packets for the query's requested state view, and exposes current, historical, and transition labels to QA. We further call for decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval, and answer level failures, since final QA accuracy can hide where ghost memory occurs. To make this failure measurable, we build LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict heavy benchmark for ghost memory, and evaluate on LoCoMo for long conversation generalization. On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. The gains are host dependent, but they indicate that explicit state roles can reduce memory failures hidden by final QA accuracy.

</details>


### [111] [Atomic Task Graph: A Unified Framework for Agentic Planning and Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01942)
*Yue Zhang,Sihan Chen,Ziwen Huang,Hanyun Cui,Kangye Ji,Zhi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATG is a graph-based control framework that explicitly models subtask dependencies as directed acyclic graphs, enabling parallel execution, targeted failure repair, and intermediate result reuse — all with smaller 7B-8B backbone models, outperforming larger-model baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agents improve via scaling (costly) or fine-tuning (poor generalization). Prompt-based methods are training-free but leave subtask dependencies implicit in text, preventing reuse of verified intermediate results and efficient error recovery.

Method: ATG maintains an explicit directed acyclic graph (DAG) representing task dependencies. During planning, it recursively decomposes high-level tasks into subtasks, producing an evolving DAG sequence. During execution, independent DAG branches run in parallel. On failure, ATG traces graph evolution history to localize errors and repairs only the affected subgraph, preserving validated regions.

Result: ATG with 7B-8B backbone models consistently outperforms strong baselines in both success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks.

Conclusion: Explicit graph-based dependency modeling enables smaller LLM agents to achieve superior performance through parallelism, reuse, and precise error localization — offering a cost-effective alternative to scaling or fine-tuning.

Abstract: LLM-based agents have shown strong potential for solving complex multi-step tasks, yet existing performance improvements often rely on either scaling to larger backbone models or task-specific fine-tuning. The former incurs substantial computational costs, while the latter typically generalizes poorly across different tasks. Although prompt-based control is training-free and broadly applicable, existing methods still leave input-output dependencies between subtasks implicit in textual trajectories, making verified intermediate results difficult to reuse. To address these limitations, we propose Atomic Task Graph (ATG), a unified control framework for planning and execution. Specifically, ATG maintains an explicit graph to expose dependencies and support reuse. During planning, it recursively decomposes a high-level task into subtasks, forming a sequence of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) whose evolution can be traced. During execution, the dependencies exposed by ATG allow independent branches to be executed in parallel, thereby improving execution efficiency. When failures are detected, ATG leverages the graph evolution history to localize the error source and repair only the affected region, preserving validated regions unchanged. Experiments show that ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks using only 7B-8B backbones.

</details>


### [112] [OntoLearner: A Modular Python Library for Ontology Learning with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01977)
*Hamed Babaei Giglou,Jennifer D'Souza,Andrei Aioanei,Nandana Mihindukulasooriya,Sören Auer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OntoLearner is a unified framework for ontology learning that provides 180 ontologies, standardized benchmarks, and LLM-driven pipelines. A large-scale evaluation of 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs reveals that the primary bottleneck in OL is not model capability but a structural mismatch between model knowledge encoding and ontological organization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ontology learning research is fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices, lacking shared infrastructure for systematic benchmarking and ontology access. This fragmentation has left central challenges unaddressed.

Method: The authors introduce OntoLearner, a modular, cross-domain framework that unifies ontology access, LLM-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking. It releases 180 machine-readable ontologies across 22 domains with train/dev/test splits for term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction. A large-scale empirical study evaluates 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs.

Result: Failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication. The primary bottleneck is a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it, not model capability per se.

Conclusion: Effective ontology learning is achievable through cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking. The findings reframe OL's central challenge away from model scaling toward structural alignment between neural representations and ontological structures.

Abstract: Ontology learning (OL) aims to automatically construct structured knowledge models from text, yet progress remains fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices. Despite decades of research, OL lacks a shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation and ontology access. This absence has hindered progress and fragmented research, leaving the central challenges of OL largely unaddressed. We introduce OntoLearner, a modular, cross-domain, and first-of-its-kind framework that unifies ontology access, large language model (LLM)-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking. OntoLearner releases 180 machine-readable ontologies spanning 22 domains and provides pipeline-ready datasets with train/dev/test splits for three core OL tasks: term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction. Using this infrastructure, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of OL, evaluating 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across domains and tasks. The results converge on a finding that reframes the central challenge of OL: failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication. The primary bottleneck is not model capability, but a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it. These findings establish that effective OL is reachable through the cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking enabled by OntoLearner. OntoLearner is open-source (MIT license) at https://github.com/sciknoworg/OntoLearner/.

</details>


### [113] [Multimodal Knowledge Edit-Scoped Generalization for Online Recursive MLLM Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01978)
*Siyuan Li,Youyuan Zhang,Ruitong Liu,Junxi Wang,Jing Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ScopeEdit addresses the problem of semantic scope control in online multimodal knowledge editing by decomposing each edit into a local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch, using orthogonal low-rank spaces and Sherman-Morrison recursions for constant per-edit overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal knowledge editing methods focus on edit reliability and stability but fail to control the semantic boundary of edits. The authors identify a "scope gap": instance-level success does not guarantee transfer to valid cross-modal variants, nor does it prevent leakage to unrelated inputs. Edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers, motivating explicit scope control.

Method: ScopeEdit formulates Edit-Scoped Generalization and proposes a scope-aware online editor with two branches: (1) a modality-local absorption branch for stable edit absorption, and (2) an evidence-gated shared generalization branch that propagates edits across modalities only when visual and textual evidence align. Both branches use scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces with branch-wise preconditioners updated via Sherman-Morrison recursions for constant per-edit overhead.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, multiple MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures demonstrate that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality while preserving edit reliability, stability, and online efficiency.

Conclusion: ScopeEdit successfully bridges the scope gap in online multimodal knowledge editing by introducing explicit semantic boundary control through its dual-branch architecture, achieving better cross-modal generalization without sacrificing locality, reliability, or efficiency.

Abstract: Online multimodal knowledge editing requires injecting a continual stream of visual-textual corrections into multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with bounded overhead and minimal disruption to unrelated behaviors. Existing editors mainly emphasize edit reliability and long-horizon stability, but rarely control the semantic boundary of each edit. Our pilot analyses of post-edit behaviors and internal neuronal activities reveal a scope gap behind reliable edits: instance-level success neither guarantees transfer to valid cross-modal variants nor prevents leakage to unrelated inputs, while edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers. Therefore, we formulate Edit-Scoped Generalization, reframing online MLLM editing from merely correcting an instance to controlling the propagation boundary of each edit. To this end, we propose ScopeEdit, a scope-aware online editor that decomposes each update into a modality-local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch. The local branch supports stable edit absorption, whereas the shared branch enables cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence are sufficiently aligned. Both branches perform scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces and maintain branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman--Morrison recursions, yielding constant per-edit overhead. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures show that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality, while preserving edit reliability, stability and online efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/lab-klc/ScopeEdit.

</details>


### [114] [Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01988)
*Xue Qin,Simin Luan,Cong Yang,Zhijun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a method for memory consolidation in autonomous agents that preserves cryptographic identity integrity. Instead of modifying the agent's core planner, consolidation is treated as a deterministic function mapping episodic memory to a separate semantic knowledge layer, leaving the identity hash unchanged. This ensures auditable knowledge accumulation without violating audit contracts or certified identity commitments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-running adaptive agents face a structural tension: conventional memory consolidation (fine-tuning, prompt rewriting, policy distillation, reflection appending) inherently mutates the agent, violating cryptographic identity commitments required in regulated autonomic deployments where agents operate under audit contracts tied to a certified identity.

Method: The authors formalize agent representation with a manifest whose hash-input set excludes a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer (M^sem). A deterministic aggregation function f: M^ep → M^sem transforms episodic memory into auditable database rows with explicit confidence scores and supporting-event provenance. Identity invariance is proved via a structural lemma confirming that the identity hash reads only from an invariant input set.

Result: Synthetic experiments demonstrate: (1) per-field correctness of the aggregation output, (2) byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and (3) a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. An embodied service agent serves as the running case study.

Conclusion: The proposed construction provides a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents where lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, resolving the tension between consolidation and identity integrity in regulated deployments.

Abstract: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

</details>


### [115] [Traceable Fault Diagnosis for Battery Energy Storage Systems via Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent O&M Assistant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01992)
*Jiangdi Ru,Bing Li,Yage Huang,Ding Wang,Keru Hua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This digest presents a traceable fault-diagnosis assistant for large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESSs) that uses retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning to integrate operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation, with preliminary evaluation on routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing BESS monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations but lack the explanatory capability to determine whether specific anomalies (voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, or thermal abnormality) require intervention, creating a gap between alarm detection and actionable O&M decisions.

Method: The authors propose a traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant employing retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning with four key components: (1) BESS-specific task routing to direct queries, (2) schema-constrained natural-language database access for structured operational data, (3) hybrid text-image retrieval for integrating documentation and visual evidence, and (4) evidence-based answer synthesis for generating diagnostic reports.

Result: Preliminary internal evaluation results are reported for three capabilities: task routing accuracy, database access performance, and diagnostic reasoning quality.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-agent assistant improves diagnostic reliability and traceability for BESS O&M by connecting heterogeneous data sources through retrieval-augmented reasoning, though full-scale validation remains as future work.

Abstract: Large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESSs) require O&M decisions that combine alarms, cell-level measurements, device topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, and maintenance documents. Monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations, but they often cannot explain whether voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, or thermal abnormality needs intervention. This digest presents a traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant that uses retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning to connect operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation. Reliability is improved through BESS-specific task routing, schema-constrained natural-language database access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based answer synthesis. Preliminary internal evaluation is reported for routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning.

</details>


### [116] [InduceKV: Fixed-Footprint Continual Adaptation of Multimodal LLMs via Inducing KV Memories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02010)
*Qianyu Chen,Ziteng Feng,Canran Xiao,Runxuan Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InduceKV is a fixed-footprint continual adaptation method for multimodal LLMs that stores selected training prefixes as compact KV-cache memory entries, using bilevel selection to maximize task coverage under a strict memory budget, outperforming PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines across multiple continual learning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal LLMs face continual distribution shifts from new tasks and domains, but existing adaptation methods accumulate state over time (growing replay buffers, repeated parameter updates), violating deployment memory constraints. The authors address the problem of fixed-footprint continual adaptation: achieving continual improvement while keeping the adaptation state under a fixed memory budget, with the backbone frozen and updates externalized.

Method: InduceKV stores each selected training prefix as an attention-ready memory entry comprising a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise KV payloads that are appended to the self-attention cache during inference. Under a strict memory budget, it constructs a compact inducing set via bilevel selection: a lightweight calibration module is trained for retrieval, while memory entries are selected to jointly optimize current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention (preserving past knowledge), and coverage in the frozen retrieval embedding space.

Result: InduceKV consistently outperforms PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning. Ablations confirm gains are not attributable to a stronger backbone, replay alone, or an unbounded candidate pool, with backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, and scalability diagnostics supporting the findings.

Conclusion: Fixed-footprint continual adaptation is a viable and effective paradigm for multimodal LLMs. By externalizing task-specific updates as retrievable KV-cache memory with principled bilevel selection, InduceKV achieves strong continual adaptation performance without violating deployment memory budgets, offering a practical path toward lifelong multimodal model improvement.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models must adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet continual improvement under bounded deployment footprint remains difficult because repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores can accumulate adaptation state over time. We study fixed-footprint continual adaptation: the deployed adaptation state is kept under a fixed memory budget, while the backbone model is left unchanged and task-specific updates are externalized. We propose InduceKV, a retrieval-based method that stores each selected training prefix as an attention-ready memory entry, consisting of a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise key--value (KV) payloads that can be appended to the model's self-attention cache. Under a strict memory budget, InduceKV constructs a compact inducing set through bilevel selection: a lightweight calibration is fit for retrieval, while the selected memory balances current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in the frozen retrieval space. Across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning, InduceKV consistently improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets. We further report backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, and scalability diagnostics, showing that the gains are not due to a stronger backbone, replay alone, or an unbounded candidate pool.

</details>


### [117] [Hidden Forgetting in Continual Multimodal Learning: When Accuracy Survives but Grounding Fails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02020)
*Qianyu Chen,Canran Xiao,Runxuan Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reveals that continual learning in multimodal LLMs suffers from "hidden evidence-use forgetting" — models retain correct answers but silently shift their grounding evidence. The authors propose RCL, a replay-free framework that freezes the previous model as a reference and uses counterfactual channel interventions to preserve evidence-reliance patterns, improving both performance and grounding stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard continual learning metrics for MLLMs only check whether answer accuracy is preserved, ignoring whether the model's multimodal grounding (how it uses visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence) remains stable. The authors identify that models can maintain answer correctness while silently shifting evidence reliance — a failure mode they term "hidden evidence-use forgetting" — which undermines interpretability and robustness.

Method: RCL (Reliance-Constrained Continual Learning) freezes the pre-adaptation checkpoint as a behavioral reference teacher. It estimates both teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles via counterfactual channel interventions (ablating each modality channel and measuring prediction change). The framework then jointly optimizes three objectives: task learning loss, prediction preservation (standard distillation), and reliance preservation (aligning student reliance profiles to the teacher's), all without added inference cost.

Result: Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and a custom evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, RCL consistently outperforms replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines in final performance and forgetting metrics. Critically, it substantially reduces modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates, demonstrating that preserving evidence pathways is achievable and beneficial.

Conclusion: Robust continual multimodal learning demands preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves. RCL demonstrates that reliance-constrained optimization via frozen behavioral references and counterfactual interventions effectively mitigates hidden evidence-use forgetting without inference overhead.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models must continually adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet standard continual learning metrics mainly measure whether old answers remain correct, leaving the stability of multimodal grounding largely unexamined. We study this overlooked failure mode and ask whether a continually adapted MLLM can preserve not only what it answers, but also how it uses visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence. We identify \emph{hidden evidence-use forgetting}, where answer accuracy is retained while the model silently shifts toward different or less grounded evidence channels, and propose \textsc{RCL}, a replay-free reliance-constrained continual learning framework. \textsc{RCL} freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation without adding inference-time cost.
