Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and an evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, \textsc{RCL} consistently improves final performance and reduces forgetting over replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines, while substantially lowering modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates. These results suggest that robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves.

</details>


### [118] [PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02032)
*Yueqi Song,Lintang Sutawika,Jiarui Liu,Lindia Tjuatja,Jiayi Geng,Yunze Xiao,Daniel Lee,Aditya Bharat Soni,Vincent Lo,Xiang Yue,Graham Neubig*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PACE selects a small subset of cheap, non-agentic benchmarks whose aggregate scores reliably predict performance on expensive agentic benchmarks (SWE-Bench, GAIA, etc.), achieving under 4% MAE and >0.80 Spearman correlation at <1% of the full evaluation cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full agentic benchmark evaluation (e.g., SWE-Bench, GAIA) is prohibitively expensive — costing thousands of dollars and days to run — while non-agentic benchmarks are fast and cheap. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling accurate prediction of agentic performance from a small set of atomic evaluations.

Method: PACE constructs a proxy benchmark by: (1) curating a pool of candidate instances from 19 existing non-agentic benchmarks spanning atomic capabilities; (2) fitting a regression that maps model scores on a compact subset of these instances to the target agentic benchmark score; (3) selecting the subset via two complementary strategies — target-relevance local selection (instances most correlated with the target) and globally informative global selection (instances that capture diverse capability signals across models). The resulting concrete proxy is called PACE-Bench.

Result: Evaluated across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks, PACE-Bench achieves LOOCV MAE under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at less than 1% of full agentic evaluation cost. The selected proxy instances also reveal which specific skills each agentic benchmark demands.

Conclusion: PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing without the overhead of full agent evaluation. The framework demonstrates that expensive agentic benchmarking can be effectively approximated by a carefully curated, low-cost proxy.

Abstract: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA can be expensive, time-consuming, and requires complex infrastructure. A single evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days to complete. In contrast, non-agentic LLM benchmarks that test individual capabilities (e.g., reasoning, code generation) are fast and cheap to run. In this paper, we investigate whether performance on expensive agentic benchmarks can be accurately predicted by the performance on a small, carefully selected subset of atomic evaluation instances. We introduce PACE, a framework that constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict model performances on agentic benchmarks. Given a pool of candidate instances spanning atomic capabilities, PACE fits a regression that maps a model's scores on a compact subset of source instances to its score on the target agentic benchmark. The subset itself is curated by combining two complementary instance-selection strategies, target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. We apply PACE to the 4 target agentic benchmarks in this paper, which yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy benchmark that we evaluate in the paper. Experiments across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks show that PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) mean absolute error (MAE) under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at much less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. We further analyze the selected proxy instances, revealing which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands. PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing, without the overhead of full agent evaluation.

</details>


### [119] [Algebraic Model Counting for Global Analysis of Optimal Decision Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02069)
*Hiroki Arimura*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ADTC is a formal framework that unifies optimization, counting, and sampling of optimal/near-optimal decision trees via sum-of-products computation over semirings, achieving O*(n^O(Δ)) time complexity, and uses model behavior tensors to capture trade-offs between accuracy, size, and fairness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires exhaustive global analysis of the hypothesis space, which is doubly exponential for decision trees. Existing methods lack a unified algebraic framework for simultaneously handling diverse analytical tasks like optimization, counting, and sampling over near-optimal trees.

Method: The authors propose Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC), inspired by Algebraic Model Counting in knowledge representation. ADTC reformulates analytical tasks as sum-of-products computations over a semiring R. A dynamic programming algorithm achieves O*(n^O(Δ)) time. For multi-criteria constraints, model behavior tensors aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring, constructing a model profile that reveals global trade-offs.

Result: The dynamic programming algorithm runs in O*(n^O(Δ)) time despite the doubly exponential hypothesis space. The software implementation, emtrees, is demonstrated on real-world datasets, showing how ADTC enables evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

Conclusion: ADTC provides a principled algebraic approach to exhaustive decision tree analysis, enabling practitioners to make evidence-based model selections by examining the full landscape of accuracy, size, and fairness trade-offs rather than relying on single optimal solutions.

Abstract: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space. We propose a formal framework for the exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees, called Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC). Inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC) in knowledge representation, ADTC reformulates diverse analytical tasks, such as optimization, counting, and sampling, into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring $R$. While the hypothesis space of decision trees is doubly exponential with respect to the maximum depth $Δ$, our dynamic programming algorithm achieves $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ time complexity in the number of features $n$, where $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors. To handle complex constraints consisting of multiple tree metrics, we introduce model behavior tensors that aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring. This algebraic approach efficiently constructs a model profile that captures the global landscape and trade-offs between criteria such as accuracy, size, and fairness. We demonstrate the utility of our software, emtrees, on real-world datasets, illustrating how ADTC facilitates evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

</details>


### [120] [Evidence-State Rewards for Long-Context Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02073)
*Ya Gao,Pekka Marttinen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Maven introduces a reinforcement learning framework for long-context reasoning that rewards stateful evidence navigation (add, link, drop actions) via an editable evidence memory, outperforming outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-context RL methods only reward final answers or static evidence extraction, providing no feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state during reasoning.

Method: Maven uses an editable evidence memory with answer-conditioned evidence-state value. It rewards three action-level state transitions in GRPO: (1) add actions credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, (2) link actions rewarded by evidence synergy, and (3) drop actions rewarded by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence.

Result: Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER across Llama and Qwen models, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention.

Conclusion: Long-context RL benefits more from optimizing stateful evidence navigation than from one-shot evidence extraction.

Abstract: Long-context reasoning requires models to locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Existing long-context RL methods usually reward final answers or static evidence extraction, offering little feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state. We propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with an editable evidence memory. Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add actions are credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These rewards are assigned to the corresponding action spans in GRPO. Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention. Our results show that long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

</details>


### [121] [SUNTA: Hierarchical Video Prediction with Surprise-based Chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02087)
*Tomoshi Iiyama,Masahiro Suzuki,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SUNTA improves hierarchical state-space models by using prediction errors (surprise) to determine chunk boundaries, employing decoupled training and internal inconsistency as a surprise metric, achieving accurate predictions over 250 timesteps while baselines fail within 10.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing HSSMs rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, which misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of data. Prediction-error-driven chunking is more principled, but integrating surprise-based segmentation into HSSMs causes hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and lacks surprise signals during open-loop prediction.

Method: SUNTA (Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction) uses: (1) a decoupled training strategy that preserves surprise signals by avoiding end-to-end training pitfalls; (2) internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts, enabling surprise-driven segmentation even during open-loop prediction.

Result: On video prediction tasks in both 2D and 3D environments, SUNTA uniquely maintains accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, while all baseline methods degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

Conclusion: Prediction-error-driven chunking is a superior principle for temporal abstraction in HSSMs. The proposed decoupled training and internal inconsistency metric effectively resolve the key challenges of hierarchical collapse and missing surprise signals, enabling significantly longer-horizon prediction.

Abstract: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon prediction by segmenting sequences into temporal chunks. However, their performance hinges on how chunk boundaries are determined. While prior HSSMs typically rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, these methods often misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data. We argue that chunking should instead be driven by prediction errors, which more directly indicate when longer-range context becomes necessary. Nevertheless, integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces critical challenges, including hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction. To address these issues, we propose Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA), a method that employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts. Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

</details>


### [122] [ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02116)
*Misha Sulpovar,Benn R. Konsynski,Qaish Kanchwala,Gabe Goodhart*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ContextNext is an open specification and reference implementation for "context governance" — a layer beneath RAG that provides provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, and point-in-time reconstruction for AI-consumable knowledge. Experiments show governed selection outperforms BM25 on answer quality (97% vs 93-90%) at lower token cost, and deterministic selectors achieve perfect Jaccard stability (1.0) versus non-deterministic dense+HNSW retrieval (mean 0.611).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous AI agents increasingly rely on external knowledge stores, but current retrieval pipelines lack durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, and point-in-time reconstruction. This gap means organizations cannot reliably reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent's output or whether those versions were authorized at consumption time. The authors formalize this problem as "context governance."

Method: ContextNext introduces a governance layer beneath retrieval comprising: typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, MCP source nodes for live data, and audit traces of agent context consumption. Two controlled experiments evaluate: (1) a stale-version attack isolating governance-versus-retrieval failure modes, comparing governed selection against BM25 sparse retrieval; and (2) a retrieval-determinism experiment over 1,060 documents comparing deterministic selectors, BM25, and dense+HNSW baselines.

Result: In the stale-version attack experiment, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25: 97% answer-quality pass rate versus 93-90%, at roughly one-third the input-token cost. In the determinism experiment, both deterministic selectors and BM25 yield stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while dense+HNSW is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210).

Conclusion: Context governance addresses failure modes that retrieval quality alone cannot resolve. The results demonstrate that a dedicated governance layer — ensuring approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified artifacts — improves both reliability and efficiency over retrieval-only approaches. The authors release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

Abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly depend on external knowledge stores, yet most retrieval pipelines provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. We formalize this as context governance and present ContextNext, an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults. ContextNext does not replace Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); it supplies the governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
  The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes for live data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and audit traces of agent context consumption. These mechanisms let organizations reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent output and whether those versions were AI-eligible when consumed.
  We report first empirical results from two controlled experiments. In a stale-version attack isolating the governance-versus-retrieval failure mode, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval, with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while a dense+HNSW baseline is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210). These results suggest that context governance addresses failure modes retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. We release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

</details>


### [123] [Enhancing Fitness Intelligence through Domain-Specific LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02118)
*Xingtao Zhao,Tian Yang,Han Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FitOne introduces a series of domain-specialized LLMs (8B and 32B) for scientific fitness coaching, built on Qwen3 via a three-stage post-training pipeline (continual pre-training, SFT, RL). The models achieve up to 12.73% improvement on professional fitness exams while retaining general capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is expensive and inaccessible because it relies on human professionals. General-purpose LLMs fail in complex SFC scenarios due to insufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, motivating the need for specialized fitness LLMs.

Method: FitOne is built on Qwen3 foundation models using a three-stage post-training pipeline: (1) continual pre-training, (2) supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (3) reinforcement learning (RL). All stages use large-scale, high-quality datasets constructed through rigorous knowledge engineering. Two model scales are produced: 8B and 32B parameters.

Result: On ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS professional fitness certification exams, FitOne-8B achieves improvements of 10.09% and 12.73%, while FitOne-32B achieves 9.29% and 7.01% over Qwen3 base models, respectively. Both models retain strong general capabilities in knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Ablation studies confirm each training stage is necessary and the pipeline effectively balances domain expertise with general ability retention.

Conclusion: FitOne demonstrates that a carefully designed multi-stage post-training pipeline can produce LLMs with strong domain specialization in fitness coaching without sacrificing general capabilities, advancing LLM systems toward reliable fitness intelligence and offering a blueprint for domain-specific LLM development.

Abstract: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is typically delivered by human professionals, making it costly and inaccessible to many. While recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) show considerable promise for more inclusive fitness coaching, directly deploying prevailing general-purpose LLMs in SFC reveals critical limitations. These models often lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. In this paper, we introduce FitOne, a series of fitness LLMs (with 8B and 32B parameters) designed to improve reliability and domain specialization for SFC applications. Built upon the Qwen3 foundation models, FitOne is developed through a three-stage post-training pipeline consisting of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of FitOne on professional fitness certification exams, including ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS, as well as general capabilities such as knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Experimental results show that, while retaining strong general capabilities, FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. Furthermore, in-depth ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage, highlighting the pipeline's effectiveness in balancing domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. We believe this research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and will inspire future research on developing domain-specific LLMs.

</details>


### [124] [Coding-agents can replicate scientific machine learning papers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02134)
*Atharva Hans,Ilias Bilionis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper-replication is a coding-agent workflow that structures scientific ML paper replication around verifiable claim targets, requiring agents to record evidence, run experiments, link outputs to provenance, and pass validation checks before completion. Evaluated across 12 runs on 4 papers, all workspaces passed completion gates with full target coverage, though runs varied in target decomposition, numerical fidelity, and evidence-acceptance rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current coding agents can be prompted to replicate scientific ML paper claims, but they lack reliable mechanisms to preserve progress, verify that generated evidence actually supports paper claims, or ensure completion depends on workspace evidence rather than agent assertions. There is a need for structured workflows that make replication accountable and evidence-driven.

Method: The authors introduce Paper-replication, a workflow implemented as a coding-agent skill. The workflow requires the agent to: (1) decompose each selected paper claim into discrete targets with recorded evidence; (2) reconstruct the paper's method; (3) run computational experiments; (4) link generated outputs to provenance and compare them against the paper's claims; (5) record where matched evidence appears in the replication report; and (6) pass validation checks before completion. The system was evaluated on 12 independent runs across 4 scientific ML papers, with all 158 recorded targets matched against report coverage.

Result: All twelve workspaces passed the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets were matched with report coverage. However, repeated runs exhibited variability across several dimensions: how papers were divided into targets, numerical fidelity to source papers, elapsed replication time, number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence acceptance, and the rules used to accept evidence.

Conclusion: Paper-replication successfully shifts completion dependence from agent's final messages to verifiable workspace evidence and validation checks. The workflow ensures accountability in automated scientific replication, though inherent variability across runs highlights the non-deterministic nature of LLM-based replication and the need for structured evidence-tracking.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning papers typically make computational claims, e.g., that the relative mean square error is less than 5% or that the 95% predictive credible interval covers the test data. A coding agent can be prompted to replicate those claims from paper materials alone, but the prompt does not by itself reliably preserve progress or check whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims. We introduce Paper-replication, a workflow that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, and implement it as a coding-agent skill. The workflow makes the agent record those targets, reconstruct the paper's method, run computational experiments, link generated outputs to provenance and comparisons with the paper's claims, record where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and pass validation checks before completion. We evaluate Paper-replication on twelve independent runs across four scientific machine learning papers. All twelve workspaces pass the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets are matched with report coverage. Even in this completed workspace state, repeated runs differ in how papers are divided into targets, in numerical fidelity to the source papers, in elapsed replication time, in the number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence is accepted, and in the rules used to accept evidence. Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than on the agent's final message.

</details>


### [125] [A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02141)
*Shuo Ren,Yaohui Han,Yifan Shi,Libo Shen,Haodong Lu,Dongfang Wu,Rongliang Fu,Bei Yu,Tsung-Yi Ho*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A$^{2}$utoLPBench is a generative benchmark for evaluating LLM-driven agents on linear programming word problems. Unlike static datasets, it generates fresh problems with answers known by construction (no solver or human annotation needed), offers adjustable difficulty via (n,m) parameters, and is resistant to training-data leakage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static LP-from-text benchmarks suffer from fixed size, fixed difficulty, and vulnerability to training-data leakage. Human authoring is costly and limits scale. A generator-based benchmark that produces fresh, verifiable problems on demand addresses all these limitations simultaneously.

Method: The benchmark generates LP problems by reverse construction: first selecting a feasible point and dual, then synthesizing a problem for which that point is provably optimal with a known objective value. The ground-truth answer is correct by construction, requiring no solver invocation or human labeling. The evaluation environment includes a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image with agent-facing instructions, enabling any LLM agent to run and obtain a calibrated score with a single command. Difficulty is parameterized by (n,m), and fresh problems can be drawn from post-cutoff seed ranges to prevent leakage.

Result: The benchmark provides an unlimited supply of fresh problems, repeatable scores across independent batches, low per-problem cost relative to human authoring, and resistance to training-data contamination. The calibrated scoring mechanism ensures comparability across different agents and runs.

Conclusion: A$^{2}$utoLPBench demonstrates that generative benchmarking with construction-guaranteed ground truth is a viable and superior alternative to static datasets for evaluating LLM agents on structured reasoning tasks like linear programming.

Abstract: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

</details>


### [126] [A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02175)
*Samiha A. Ismail,Fan X. Chen,Ali Merali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A small, clinician-authored evaluation dataset (5 scenarios, 184 weighted MECE criteria across 4 specialties) reveals that frontier models (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieve only 32.4–41.7% on highest-weighted critical criteria versus 80–90% on low-stakes criteria, with 52% of critical criteria unsatisfied by any model — an inversion of clinical priority. The paper proposes a scalable pipeline for rubric-based benchmarking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are saturated and fail to capture open-ended clinical reasoning. Even rubric-based benchmarks like HealthBench leave substantial room (32% top score on Hard subset), motivating the need for deliberately difficult, clinically authentic, and defensibly graded evaluation datasets that probe genuine clinical competence rather than test-taking ability.

Method: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios across anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics were created, each paired with an atomic, weighted, MECE (Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive) rubric (25–62 criteria per task; 184 total) derived from a clinician-drafted golden answer. Three frontier models were evaluated against these rubrics. Three LLM autoraters were validated against expert clinician labels on 552 graded criteria to assess scalability.

Result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. Critical (weight-5) criteria passed at only 32.4–41.7%, while weight-1 criteria passed at 80–90%. 56 of 108 critical criteria (52%) were met by no model. LLM autoraters reproduced expert labels at 92.8–94.7% agreement, supporting automated grading feasibility.

Conclusion: The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: models perform best where stakes are lowest and worst where they are highest, raising significant safety concerns. The five-task dataset demonstrates a scalable, defensible evaluation pipeline suitable for expansion into a large-scale benchmark for open-ended clinical reasoning.

Abstract: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

</details>


### [127] [UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02186)
*Temitayo Olamilekan Ogunsusi,Lijun Qian,Xishuang Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UA-ChatDev introduces uncertainty quantification into multi-agent LLM-based software development, using token-level log probabilities and phase-aware threshold calibration to trigger retrieval-based verification when confidence is low, thereby mitigating hallucination propagation across development phases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent software development frameworks treat all intermediate agent outputs as equally reliable, making them susceptible to hallucination propagation—where erroneous decisions from early phases cascade to downstream agents and degrade final software quality.

Method: UA-ChatDev integrates a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism using token-level log probabilities to assess agent response confidence, combined with phase-aware threshold calibration that selectively activates retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels during agent interactions.

Result: Experiments on the SRDD benchmark show UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms both single-agent and existing multi-agent frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Ablation studies and communication analyses confirm that uncertainty-aware interactions improve code execution reliability.

Conclusion: Incorporating uncertainty awareness into multi-agent software development frameworks effectively reduces hallucination propagation and enhances the reliability of autonomously generated software.

Abstract: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

</details>


### [128] [Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02210)
*Ravi Kant Sharma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes GRV, a runtime framework that intercepts AI/ML inference outputs in autonomous telecom networks, evaluates decisions across weighted dimensions to assign a criticality level, and applies graduated validation mechanisms (logging, bounds checking, independent validation, multi-agent consensus) before execution, with cross-agent conflict detection and regulatory conformance logging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fully autonomous telecom networks (Levels 4-5) require AI/ML agents to make real-time decisions without human oversight, yet no standardized runtime mechanism exists to validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous or malicious autonomous decisions.

Method: The GRV framework intercepts AI inference outputs pre-execution and scores them across six weighted dimensions: action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns. The resulting criticality score triggers one of four graduated validation mechanisms: execute-with-logging (low), bounds checking (moderate), independent agent validation (high), or multi-agent consensus (critical). It also includes cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging aligned with EU AI Act Article 14. An O-RAN deployment model is provided.

Result: The paper presents the GRV architecture, algorithmic procedures, and an O-RAN deployment model, along with a threat coverage evaluation demonstrating effectiveness against known AI/ML attack vectors in telecommunications.

Conclusion: The GRV framework fills a critical standardization gap by providing a systematic, graduated runtime validation mechanism for AI/ML-driven decisions in autonomous networks, reducing risk while maintaining operational velocity and supporting regulatory compliance.

Abstract: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

</details>


### [129] [Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02234)
*Zhanming Shen,Jintao Tong,Shaotian Yan,Chen Shen,Hao Chen,Wentao Ye,Xiaomeng Hu,Rui Miao,Haobo Wang,Junbo Zhao,Gang Chen,Jieping Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) fails on long chain-of-thought models because teacher supervision is dominated by reference-specific shortcuts that promote rote memorization rather than transferable reasoning. The authors decompose the supervision signal, isolate the non-transferable reference-induced component, and use pointwise mutual information (PMI) to distill only the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction — achieving consistent improvements across four long-CoT models while preserving reflective reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD — distilling from a teacher with reference solution access onto a student's self-generated trajectories — succeeds on standard LLMs but consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, producing marginal gains at best and destabilizing the reflective reasoning these models rely on. The paper seeks to diagnose why this failure occurs and to develop a fix.

Method: 1) Signal decomposition: The teacher's token-level supervision is decomposed into a reference-induced component (non-transferable, drives rote memorization of shortcuts) and a question-conditioned component (inference-transferable, but ignored or opposed). 2) Isolation via reference-only teacher: A reference-only teacher (model conditioned on the reference without the question) is constructed to capture the non-transferable component; subtracting it yields the question-conditioned residual. 3) PMI-based distillation: Pointwise mutual information transforms this residual into a well-formed target distribution that the student distills from, effectively filtering out reference-induced shortcuts.

Result: Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets show consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving natural epistemic behavior (reflective reasoning capability) throughout training.

Conclusion: OPSD fails on long-CoT models because reference-specific shortcuts dominate the teacher signal. By isolating the reference-induced component and using PMI to distill only the transferable correction, the proposed method achieves robust improvements without compromising reflective reasoning.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

</details>


### [130] [AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02255)
*Xiangchen Cheng,Yunwei Jiang,Jianwen Sun,Zizhen Li,Chuanhao Li,Xiangcheng Cao,Yihao Liu,Fanrui Zhang,Li Jin,Kaipeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a bounded memory contract for long-horizon LLM agents where each decision uses typed retrieval from a fresh prompt, avoiding raw transcript accumulation. Tested on the challenging game Slay the Spire 2, a skill-layer ablation shows directional improvement (3/10 vs 6/10 wins), and the authors release a reproducible testbed with 298 trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agents use an append-only memory contract where all past observations, tool calls, and reflections are concatenated into every prompt. This creates a jumbled context where individual memory components cannot be isolated or ablated, making it impossible to study which memory mechanisms actually drive agent performance.

Method: The authors introduce a bounded memory contract: each decision is made from a fresh user message assembled via typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. They instantiate this in a harness for Slay the Spire 2 (a stochastic deck-building game requiring hundreds of decisions per run) and instrument ablation experiments, specifically testing the effect of triggered strategic skills by comparing a no-store baseline against a skill-enabled variant, using a fixed-A0 configuration.

Result: The no-store baseline wins 3/10 games; adding the strategic skill layer raises this to 6/10. While not statistically decisive (Fisher exact p≈0.37), the result is directionally positive. Frontier LLMs on a public benchmark score zero wins at the lowest difficulty, and human win rate is 16%, confirming the task is hard but not saturated.

Conclusion: The bounded contract enables clean ablation of individual memory layers, offering a validated methodology for studying how explicit memory shapes long-horizon LLM-agent decisions. The authors release a reproducible testbed including 298 completed trajectories, frozen snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts to support further research.

Abstract: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

</details>


### [131] [A Hippocampus for Linear Attention: An Exact Memory for What the Recurrent State Forgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02303)
*Wanyun Cui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HOLA combines a compressive linear-attention state with a bounded exact KV cache to overcome the "lossy memory" problem in recurrent models, achieving better perplexity than a full Transformer++ and superior long-context needle recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Linear-attention and state-space models compress all prefix information into a fixed-size recurrent state, which enables O(1) memory but suffers from catastrophic forgetting: when many key-value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and retrieval degrades. The authors seek to remedy this without sacrificing the memory efficiency of linear attention.

Method: HOLA augments standard delta-rule linear attention with a bounded, exact KV cache — a semiparametric test-time memory inspired by Complementary Learning Systems theory. The cache uses a write rule without learned eviction: tokens are stored when their prediction residual norm (beta * ||e||) is large, i.e., when the state cannot easily absorb them. At read time, a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma mechanism retrieves from the exact cache, producing sharp, high-fidelity recall rather than soft averaging over the compressive state.

Result: At 340M params trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA reduces Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (−16.1%), surpassing a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88). LAMBADA perplexity improves from 30.95 to 30.26. HOLA achieves the best linear-model in-context retrieval and remains far more robust than GDN or a recency-cache baseline on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall up to 32k tokens (16× training length).

Conclusion: A hippocampal-style exact memory cache effectively compensates for the representational bottleneck of compressive recurrent states, yielding a linear-complexity model that matches or exceeds full-attention perplexity while maintaining superior long-range retrieval robustness.

Abstract: Linear-attention and state-space language models compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, yielding O(1) memory at the cost of a lossy exact memory: when many key--value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, we give linear attention a hippocampal complement. HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) keeps the usual delta-rule state as a compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory: the state models linearly compressible structure, while the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state. The cache writes without a learned eviction module, keeping tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state; a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read then turns these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging. At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), and improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26. It also achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains much more robust than GDN or a matched HOLA+recency cache on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x its training length).

</details>


### [132] [Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02329)
*Haonan Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an autonomous research agent that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism. The agent autonomously maps the literature, calibrates methods via reproduction, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes a grounded manuscript across 47 sessions with over 2,100 literature consultations. Fault tolerance is achieved through fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review. The work establishes structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the key mechanism for grounding, laying foundations for autonomous research in high-stakes physical sciences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier physical science poses categorically different challenges from ML sandboxes: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are underdocumented, and calibration lacks execution feedback, instead requiring external literature anchors. Existing unscaffolded agents cite but do not genuinely confront literature, hallucinating plausible but unverifiable results from internal priors. This necessitates a grounded autonomous pipeline that numerically confronts published references for calibration.

Method: A multi-phase pipeline operating over a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers. The agent: (1) maps the corpus to conceive a research direction; (2) calibrates methodology by reproducing published references; (3) conducts novel first-principles computations; (4) writes a publication-grade manuscript. It runs across 47 fresh-context sessions across six phases, sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy (fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, adversarial review). Two paired failure modes — a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation — test the grounding mechanism. Pilot stage requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures (operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction).

Result: The pipeline produced a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism, grounded in literature throughout. The pre-architecture baseline and no-pilot ablation successfully isolated structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The agent demonstrated that fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review provide fault tolerance by catching errors that any single session would miss. Pre- and post-pilot stages were fully autonomous.

Conclusion: Structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints is the operative mechanism for grounding autonomous research agents in physical sciences. The characterized failure modes, primitives, and quantified intervention pattern provide a foundation for extending autonomous research to high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics, where execution-based calibration is unavailable and literature grounding is essential.

Abstract: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors. We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses; pre- and post-pilot stages are fully autonomous, and pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures - operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction. Two paired failure modes - a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation - isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.

</details>


### [133] [DRIFTLENS: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02374)
*Xi Fang,Weijie Xu,Yingqiang Ge,Yuhui Xu,Stephanie Eckman,Chandan K. Reddy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Personalizing LLMs with user-attribute memory causes measurable shifts in reasoning trajectories (not just final answers). The authors introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework to quantify this "reasoning drift," find it is substantial across models and attributes, and show that post-training interventions (GRPO/DPO) reduce but do not eliminate it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While personalization in LLMs is known to change what models say, no prior work has systematically studied whether injecting user attributes into memory reshapes *how* the model reasons—i.e., the step-by-step justifications—especially on open-ended questions lacking ground-truth answers. The authors aim to characterize and measure this as a potential failure mode.

Method: They propose DRIFTLENS, a framework that: (1) maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category, and (2) measures the divergence between a model's reasoning trajectory with no memory versus its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. The framework is ground-truth-free, validated against pragmatic-noise baselines, and tested across four LLMs and ten user-attribute categories (age, occupation, disability, etc.). They further evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for drift reduction.

Result: User-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. Both GRPO and DPO reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; their effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model- and reward-dependent.

Conclusion: Memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized LLMs. The work highlights a new axis of safety/alignment concern beyond surface-level response changes.

Abstract: Personalization changes what a model says to a user; we show that it can also change the reasoning trajectory used to justify the response. Modern LLMs personalize interactions by storing user attributes, preferences, and prior context, then injecting this information into future prompts. We study whether such memory reshapes reasoning on open-ended questions where no single ground-truth answer exists. To quantify this effect, we introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between a question's no-memory trajectory and its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. We first validate that DRIFTLENS distinguishes content-free pragmatic noise from substantive reasoning changes. Across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories, including age, occupation, and disability, user-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. We then evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for reducing drift. Both reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model-and reward-dependent. These results suggest that memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized language models.

</details>


### [134] [Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02432)
*Manuel Alonso-Carracedo,Ruben Fernandez-Boullon,Pedro Celard,Francisco J. Rodriguez-Martinez,Lorena Otero-Cerdeira*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) for automated grading of Linux command-line exam responses using a four-level cognitive taxonomy. Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-enhanced prompting achieved the highest agreement with human experts (ICC=0.888). The study finds rubric quality matters more than model choice, and question complexity reliably predicts grading difficulty, establishing a principled framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rising enrollments in computing education make manual grading of command-line examinations increasingly difficult. Existing rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. The authors aim to determine whether frontier LLMs can approximate expert human judgment in grading short Linux/bash responses, and to establish a principled framework for identifying which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading.

Method: The study tested four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) on 1,200 real student responses from second-year Computer Engineering students. Grading was structured around a four-level cognitive taxonomy (L1: information retrieval, L2: basic file manipulation, L3: structural operations, L4: advanced system management). Two prompting conditions were compared: a minimal baseline prompt and a rubric-enhanced prompt. Three expert instructors independently graded all responses to establish ground truth. Agreement was measured using ICC(3,1), Mean Absolute Error, and Bland-Altman analysis.

Result: Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the strongest performance (ICC(3,1)=0.888, MAE=0.10, Bland-Altman bias=-0.014). Agreement between LLMs and human experts declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher cognitive levels (L3 and L4). Rubric quality had a larger effect on agreement than the choice of model provider; structured prompts consistently improved performance across all models. Question complexity proved to be a reliable predictor of grading difficulty for LLMs.

Conclusion: LLMs can approximate expert grading for command-line examinations, particularly at lower taxonomy levels, but human review remains necessary for higher-complexity questions. The taxonomy-based framework provides a transferable, principled method for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading. The authors also contribute reusable evaluation protocols and prompt templates for practitioners.

Abstract: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper evaluates whether four frontier Large Language Models (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) can approximate expert judgment when grading short Linux/bash command responses. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). The models were tested with two prompt variants, a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version, on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students independently graded by three expert instructors. Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher levels. Across all models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement. These results show that question complexity is a reliable predictor of the difficulty LLMs face in grading accurately, and they establish a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while also providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

</details>


### [135] [EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02440)
*Zhilin Wang,Han Song,Runzhe Zhan,Jusen Du,Jiacheng Chen,Tianle Li,Qingyu Yin,Yulun Wu,Zhennan Shen,Tong Zhu,Yanshu Li,Guanjie Chen,Derek F. Wong,Yafu Li,Yu Cheng,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoPolicyGym introduces a controlled benchmark for evaluating how autonomous agents iteratively improve executable policies under a fixed interaction budget, with GPT-5.5 achieving top performance across all 16 environments. The benchmark enables trajectory-level diagnostics revealing that strong policy evolution depends on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and efficient feedback utilization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of autonomous agents that learn from feedback either reduce performance to a single final score or conflate policy improvement with open-ended software engineering tasks. There is a need for a controlled, diagnostic evaluation setting that isolates the iterative policy evolution process itself.

Method: The authors propose Autonomous Policy Evolution, a setting where a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. They instantiate this via EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark comprising compact interactive RL environments, and evaluate agents on how they iteratively improve explored policies. Trajectory-level diagnostics analyze budget allocation, feedback-to-parameter conversion, and mechanism discovery.

Result: GPT-5.5 achieved the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Trajectory-level analyses revealed that strong autonomous policy evolution depends on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback, not merely on isolated task wins.

Conclusion: EvoPolicyGym provides a rigorous, diagnostic framework for evaluating autonomous policy evolution, demonstrating that effective agents must go beyond isolated successes to develop robust feedback utilization strategies and task-specific mechanisms within constrained interaction budgets.

Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

</details>


### [136] [Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02396)
*Thomas Winninger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper adapts the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm with probe-informed initialization to efficiently identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in LLMs (both reasoning and non-reasoning models) in seconds, outperforming existing computationally expensive methods on ablation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for extracting multi-dimensional behavior subspaces (e.g., refusal) in LLMs are computationally expensive, especially problematic for reasoning models that produce long reasoning traces. There is a need for faster, scalable alternatives.

Method: The authors adapt the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm — chosen for its computational efficiency — and augment it with a probe-informed initialization strategy. They apply this to identify the refusal subspace in both reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models.

Result: RFM identifies the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, dramatically faster than alternatives. It also demonstrates superior performance on the ablation task compared to competing methods.

Conclusion: RFM shows promise as a cheap, scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods. Further work is needed to understand the relationships between subspaces found by different methods.

Abstract: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

</details>


### [137] [Text-Driven 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis in Non-Manhattan Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02407)
*Xianhui Meng,Zirui Song,Yuchen Zhang,Li Zhang,Yongxuan Lv,Xiuying Chen,Kun Wang,Yan Luo,Kai Chen,Hangjun Ye,Long Chen,Jun Liu,Xiaoshuai Hao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SPG-Layout is a text-driven framework for generating physically plausible indoor scenes in non-Manhattan environments, using statistical priors of object distributions and a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes large objects to reduce geometric violations and improve physical fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based 3D indoor synthesis methods perform well in Manhattan (orthogonal) environments but fail in non-Manhattan settings because they cannot adequately model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, resulting in high geometric violations and low physical plausibility.

Method: SPG-Layout employs two key components: (1) statistical priors of object distributions to guide training and enhance environmental understanding, and (2) a hierarchical layout strategy that mirrors human design workflows by placing large objects first to minimize layout violations. These components are synergized for balanced semantic realism and physical plausibility.

Result: A new benchmark of 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments was constructed. Extensive experiments show SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods in both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments.

Conclusion: SPG-Layout effectively addresses the challenge of indoor scene synthesis in non-Manhattan environments by integrating statistical priors and hierarchical layout planning, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code will be publicly released.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 3D indoor synthesis for Manhattan environments. However, existing methods often fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan settings, primarily because they struggle to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose SPG-Layout, a novel text-driven framework designed to generate physically plausible indoor scenes within complex non-Manhattan environments. Specifically, we first utilize statistical priors of object distributions to guide the training process, enhancing environmental understanding and fidelity. Furthermore, mirroring human design workflows, we adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes the placement of large objects, thereby substantially minimizing layout violations. By synergizing these components, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility. To evaluate performance in these complex settings, we constructed a new benchmark comprising 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods across both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments. The code will be publicly released.

</details>


### [138] [Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02510)
*Mona Schirmer,Metod Jazbec,Alexander Timans,Christian Naesseth,Maja Waldron,Eric Nalisnick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A simple threshold-based real-time safety monitor for LLM outputs, calibrated via risk control, performs competitively with more complex sequential hypothesis testing monitors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs still produce unsafe outputs despite alignment training, necessitating online output monitoring that can raise alarms when safety guarantees break down.

Method: A real-time monitor that converts a verifier signal from an external model into a binary alarm via thresholding, with the threshold calibrated using risk control techniques.

Result: The simple threshold-based monitor matches or rivals the performance of more sophisticated monitors employing sequential hypothesis testing on mathematical reasoning and red teaming benchmarks.

Conclusion: Complex monitoring strategies based on sequential hypothesis testing may be unnecessary; a straightforward thresholding approach with proper risk-controlled calibration can suffice for real-time LLM safety monitoring.

Abstract: Despite alignment training, LLMs remain prone to generating unsafe outputs at deployment time. Monitoring outputs online and raising an alarm when safety can no longer be assumed is therefore critical. We study a simple real-time monitor that turns a verifier signal from an external model into an alarm decision by thresholding, with the threshold calibrated via risk control. In experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets, we show that this simple design is competitive with more advanced monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.

</details>


### [139] [G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02491)
*Timo Bertram,Sidhant Bhavnani,Richard Freinschlag,Erich Kobler,Andreas Mayr,Günter Klambauer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces G-RRM, a neuro-symbolic approach that integrates symbol-equivariant recurrent reasoning models (SE-RRMs) with classical symbolic solvers. Neural guidance yields significant speedups only when (1) the search space is expansive and (2) the solver can dynamically override imperfect neural hints. Backtracking and Glucose 4.1 benefit substantially, while CaDiCaL 3.0.0 does not due to overhead and rigid adherence to hints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SE-RRMs show improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes, but their solution proposals are not globally guaranteed. The authors investigate whether these neural models can effectively guide classical symbolic solvers to improve search efficiency, and under what conditions such neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

Method: The authors propose G-RRM, a neuro-symbolic framework where SE-RRMs generate full solution proposals that guide symbolic solvers (backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0) on constraint satisfaction problems like Sudoku. They systematically test conditions under which guidance helps, varying problem size (9×9 and 25×25 Sudoku) and solver architecture to assess conflict counts, wall-clock speedups, and statistical significance.

Result: On 9×9 Sudoku (91.1% SE-RRM accuracy), backtracking accelerates by 33.3× and Glucose 4.1 by 1.70× (median, p<0.001). On perfect-hint 25×25 grids, Glucose 4.1 retains a 1.17× speedup. CaDiCaL 3.0.0 shows no significant speedup (median 1.02×, n.s.) and a small significant mean slowdown (0.90×), attributed to runtime overhead and inability to overwrite branching hints. Two necessary conditions emerge: expansive combinatorial search space and dynamic overwriting capability.

Conclusion: Neural guidance via G-RRM can yield substantial speedups, but its efficacy is not universal. Practical gains depend critically on problem difficulty (search space size) and solver flexibility in handling imperfect hints. The results delineate clear regimes where neuro-symbolic integration is beneficial versus where it incurs overhead without payoff.

Abstract: In this work, we focus on SE-RRMs, a symbol-equivariant instantiation of RRMs that exhibits improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes. We propose a neuro-symbolic approach, ``Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models'' (G-RRM), which integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems. SE-RRMs act as neural solvers that generate full solution proposals and guide classical symbolic solvers, such as backtracking or SAT-based methods like Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0, that produce globally correct solutions. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers. %
Our experiments show that the efficacy of G-RRM depends on two conditions: first, the problem instances must have an expansive combinatorial search space to expose potential gains, and second, the solver architecture must be capable of dynamically overwriting its branching choices to recover when neural hints are imperfect. When these conditions hold, guidance drives median conflict counts to zero and yields significant wall-clock speedups: on $9\times9$ Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves $91.1\%$ of instances, backtracking accelerates by $33.3\times$ and Glucose 4.1 by $1.70\times$ (median, $p<0.001$), with Glucose 4.1 retaining a $1.17\times$ speedup on perfect-hint $25\times25$ grids. In contrast, CaDiCaL 3.0.0, whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects the injected branching hints rather than overwriting them, shows no significant speedup (median $1.02\times$, n.s.) and even a small significant mean slowdown ($0.90\times$) on $9\times9$. These results delineate the regimes in which neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

</details>


### [140] [ReContext: Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02509)
*Yanjun Zhao,Ruizhong Qiu,Tianxin Wei,Yuanchen Bei,Zhining Liu,Lingjie Chen,Ismini Lourentzou,Hanghang Tong,Jingrui He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RECONTEXT is a training-free inference method that uses recursive evidence replay based on model-internal relevance signals to improve LLM long-context reasoning. It constructs a query-conditioned evidence pool and replays it before generation, supported by an associative memory theoretical framework. Experiments on 128K-context datasets show consistent improvements across multiple model backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
