On the sign axis, imbalanced updates collapse either entropy or weight geometry. On the difficulty axis, hard-problem focus sharpens signal but costs sample size. Both trade-offs shift during training: exploration favors balance and hard focus; exploitation favors suppression and medium focus. This motivates FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), a self-adapting advantage that reads training dynamics to schedule the gradient weight automatically. FADE reaches peak pass@1 20k steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2k steps earlier at the 32B , while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.

</details>


### [164] [Towards Learning Representations of Policies in Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01498)
*Kevin Wang,Kevin Yang,Arjun Prakash,Amy Greenwald*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates self-supervised learning methods for generating useful policy embeddings in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games, introducing dataset creation techniques, embedding methods, and downstream evaluation tasks, with experiments on Kuhn and Leduc Poker demonstrating that even basic methods yield meaningful behavioral representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically explore whether self-supervised learning can produce useful policy representations (embeddings) that capture behavioral patterns in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games, an area where such systematic comparison has been lacking.

Method: The authors propose three components: (1) methods to create policy datasets for a given game, (2) self-supervised techniques to learn policy embeddings from those datasets, and (3) downstream tasks to evaluate representation quality. Experiments are conducted on Kuhn Poker and Leduc Poker as benchmark domains.

Result: Even basic embedding methods produce policy representations that contain useful behavioral information, as demonstrated by performance on the downstream evaluation tasks. This represents one of the first systematic comparisons of self-supervised learning for policy representation learning in games.

Conclusion: Useful behavioral representations can be learned via self-supervised methods for policies in imperfect-information games, and the released codebase provides a foundation for future extensions in this research direction.

Abstract: We investigate the problem of learning useful policy representations (embeddings) in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. We make three contributions: First, we introduce methods of creating datasets of policies for a given game. Second, we propose methods to learn policy representations. Third, we introduce downstream tasks to evaluate the effectiveness of such representations.
  We evaluate each dataset method, embedding method, and downstream task on Kuhn and Leduc Poker. Although our methods are very basic, we demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning policy representations in games. Our code is available at https://github.com/VitamintK/ssl-project for others to extend.

</details>


### [165] [The risk of KV cache compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01520)
*Lukas Haverbeck,Carmen Amo Alonso,Andres Felipe Posada-Moreno,Sebastian Trimpe,Marco Pavone*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper establishes a theoretical framework for KV cache compression by characterizing its minimax risk in terms of intrinsic compressibility, providing principled design guidelines that map to efficient prefill and autoregressive decoding, and demonstrating practical effectiveness on LongBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer inference on long sequences is bottlenecked by softmax attention's repeated reads from large KV caches. While KV cache compression is a prevalent practical solution, its design is largely empirical, and existing theory only provides worst-case impossibility results without constructive guidance for when and how accurate compression is achievable.

Method: The authors characterize the minimax risk of KV cache compression as a function of the cache's intrinsic compressibility, revealing conditions under which accurate compression is possible. From this analysis, they derive design principles for compression under causal masking that map efficiently to both prefill and autoregressive decoding stages, and instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm with minimax-optimal guarantees.

Result: The proposed algorithm achieves minimax-optimal risk for KV cache compression and demonstrates promising empirical performance on the LongBench benchmark in targeted experiments.

Conclusion: The work bridges theory and practice by providing a principled, theoretically-grounded avenue for KV cache compression with formal guarantees, moving beyond purely empirical approaches.

Abstract: Transformer inference on long sequences is expensive because softmax attention repeatedly reads from a large KV cache. The prevalent approach to this bottleneck is KV cache compression, which replaces the full cache with a compact summary. Despite its practical importance, the design of such summaries is largely driven by empirical experimentation. On the theoretical side, existing results show that KV cache compression can be impossible in the worst case, but offer little systematic guidance for designing algorithms in regimes where accurate compression is possible. We bridge this gap by characterizing the minimax risk of KV cache compression in terms of the intrinsic compressibility of a cache, revealing when and how accurate compression is possible. These results yield novel design principles for KV cache compression under causal masking that map efficiently to prefill and autoregressive decoding while achieving minimax-optimal risk. We instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm and report promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments. Overall, our results provide a principled avenue for practical KV cache compression with theoretical guarantees.

</details>


### [166] [kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02072)
*Mahmoud Abdelfattah,Hamid Nasiri,Peter Garraghan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: kNNGuard is a training-free guardrail for LLMs that classifies prompts as safe/unsafe using multi-layer k-nearest neighbors on hidden activations. It matches or exceeds fine-tuned guardrails on F1 while being 2.7–10× faster, and supports rapid domain adaptation by simply updating a small labeled prompt bank.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM guardrails rely on fine-tuned classifiers that suffer from low generalization, high inference latency, and costly retraining for domain adaptation. A training-free, low-latency, and easily adaptable alternative is needed for production deployment.

Method: kNNGuard uses a small bank of ~50 labeled safe/unsafe prompts. For each input, it extracts hidden activations from multiple layers of an off-the-shelf LLM, then performs k-nearest neighbor classification by fusing scores from both activation-space and embedding-space distances. No gradient updates or fine-tuning is required. Domain adaptation involves only updating the labeled bank, which takes under 10 seconds.

Result: Across six domains covering topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 versus fine-tuned SOTA guardrails. It runs 2.7× faster than the best comparable guardrail and 10× faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier. The labeled bank can be constructed in under 10 seconds, orders of magnitude faster than established guardrail training pipelines.

Conclusion: kNNGuard demonstrates that training-free, activation-space-based classification is a viable and efficient alternative to fine-tuned guardrails, offering strong performance, low latency, and rapid domain adaptability suitable for production LLM systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

</details>


### [167] [Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01523)
*Jiatong Li,Samuel Yeh,Sharon Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recurrent memory agents suffer from context-length degradation due to memory retention collapse. The authors propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free architecture that partitions memory into independent heads with a select-then-update strategy, preventing overwriting. MHM-LRU substantially improves retention and accuracy on 100K–1M token benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recurrent memory agents that consolidate long contexts into fixed-size memory windows suffer systematic end-to-end performance degradation as context length grows. The authors diagnose that memory retention — the ability to preserve previously stored information across updates — is the dominant bottleneck, caused by monolithic memory designs where every update risks overwriting prior content.

Method: The authors propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free framework that partitions memory into multiple independent heads. A stage-wise select-then-update strategy ensures that at each step, only one head is updated while others are structurally protected from overwriting. As a lightweight instantiation, MHM-LRU (Least-Recently-Updated) guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead by always selecting the least recently updated head for the next write.

Result: On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improved memory retention rate from under 30% to 73.96%. Gains in both retention and end-to-end accuracy were observed across the 100K–1M token range, generalizing across model families, scales, and task types.

Conclusion: Architectural optimization via multi-head partitioning with overwrite protection is a practical, cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory, shifting the retention burden from model behavior to structural design.

Abstract: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

</details>


### [168] [Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01528)
*Abdullah Al Tasim,Wei Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage learning pipeline combining a wind estimator (attention-augmented GRU) with a PPO-based flight controller reduces trajectory tracking error by 48% for small multirotors in turbulent boundary-layer winds, with graceful degradation beyond the training distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small multirotor aircraft operating in the atmospheric boundary layer face turbulent winds comparable to their airspeed, causing trajectory tracking degradation that defeats conventional feedback control. There is a need for controllers that can perceive and exploit wind information to maintain robust tracking performance.

Method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) An attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on simulated flights through von Kármán turbulence (with power-law shear and veer) estimates the horizontal wind vector from onboard kinematics and dynamics. (2) A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) controller uses the frozen wind estimator's output for flight control. Ablation study decomposes improvement into kinematic and wind-perception components.

Result: The wind estimator achieves per-flight RMSE of 0.40 m/s and direction error of 3.2° on unseen wind regimes, with a skill score of 0.861 on vertical ascent profiles. The PPO controller reduces horizontal tracking error by 48% vs. a wind-blind PD baseline across 4–12 m/s mean winds, winning 100% of evaluation episodes. The perception component's contribution grows with wind speed, approaching half the total benefit in strong winds. The controller degrades gracefully at 13–15 m/s while the baseline fails catastrophically.

Conclusion: Integrating learned wind perception into an RL flight controller yields substantial and robust tracking improvements for small multirotors in turbulent conditions. The wind-perception benefit scales with wind speed in line with aerodynamic drag scaling, and the approach generalizes beyond its training distribution, suggesting practical viability for real-world boundary-layer operations.

Abstract: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

</details>


### [169] [Privacy-Preserving and Verifiable Approximate Distributed Coded Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02187)
*Xavier Martínez-Luaña,Alba Gude-Santos,Manuel Fernández-Veiga,Rebeca P. Díaz-Redondo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A model-agnostic framework combining privacy-enhancing coded computing (GPBACC) with robust aggregation (for federated learning) and lightweight verification techniques (for decentralized learning) to jointly defend against privacy leakage and malicious attacks across distributed learning paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing defenses for distributed machine learning address privacy and malicious manipulation in isolation, are tailored to specific paradigms or architectures, and fail to handle the distinct adversarial surfaces of federated vs. decentralized learning within a unified framework.

Method: The authors propose a unified framework combining GPBACC (a model-agnostic privacy-enhancing coded computing technique) with: (1) robust aggregation strategies for federated learning to mitigate malicious participants, and (2) approximate decode-and-compare plus group testing for decentralized learning to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without a trusted aggregator. Evaluation is attack-driven, implementing representative privacy and malicious attacks to empirically measure leakage reduction and resilience.

Result: The combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries in both federated and decentralized settings.

Conclusion: Privacy-enhancing coded computing (GPBACC), when paired with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning across diverse learning paradigms.

Abstract: Distributed machine learning enables collaborative model training without centralizing data, but it also exposes learning processes to privacy leakage and malicious manipulation. Existing defenses typically address these threats in isolation and are often tailored to specific learning paradigms or model architectures, limiting their applicability in realistic deployments. In particular, federated learning and decentralized learning exhibit distinct adversarial surfaces that are rarely addressed within a unified framework. In this paper, we present a model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that jointly addresses privacy preservation and malicious behavior across both federated and decentralized settings. Our approach combines paradigm-specific defense mechanisms with GPBACC, a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary machine learning models. For federated learning, we integrate robust aggregation strategies to mitigate the impact of malicious participants, while for decentralized learning we employ approximate decode-and-compare and group testing techniques to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without relying on a trusted aggregator. Crucially, we evaluate the proposed framework through an explicit, attack-driven analysis. We implement representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors, and empirically demonstrate that the combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries. These results suggest that privacy-enhancing coded computing, when combined with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning.

</details>


### [170] [Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01537)
*Hongbo Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a certified sensing clock derived from the validity horizon of a world model, providing a drift-aware rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. The method uses on-manifold Lyapunov rates calibrated with native rollout-drift envelopes to produce deployable deadlines, validated on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model and a synthetic theorem-bed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Certified world models can estimate how long predictions stay valid, but there lacks a principled operational rule for translating this validity horizon into a concrete sensing schedule. Existing approaches using Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, motivating the need for a drift-aware deployment method that carries guarantees to the actual deployment distribution.

Method: Starting from an audited equivariant world model, the authors derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals. They show that deployable deadlines must be drift-aware by combining on-manifold Lyapunov rates with calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes. The resulting clock is evaluated on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model (controlling held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violations) and a cue-conditioned theorem-bed synthetic bench that isolates scheduling rules by sharing the exact model across schedulers.

Result: On the frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In the synthetic theorem-bed, the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budgets. Limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term.

Conclusion: The primary contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and a drift-aware deployment method. The authors explicitly do not claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers, but rather establish a principled, certificate-carrying mechanism for deciding when to re-sense.

Abstract: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

</details>


### [171] [Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01548)
*Ege Onur Taga,Yilin Zhuang,M. Emrullah Ildiz,Petros Mol,Abhimanyu Das,Karthik Duraisamy,Samet Oymak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EFE is a framework that uses LLM-based evolution to automatically discover preprocessing transformations (as Python programs) for structured data. Applied to time-series (EFE-Time) and tabular data (EFE-Tab), it improves forecasting accuracy by up to 19% and enhances or matches feature engineering baselines while preserving interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as search operators in evolutionary optimization, but existing work lacks a principled framework for using LLM-driven evolution to discover data preprocessing transformations that integrate seamlessly into ML pipelines and improve both accuracy and interpretability on structured data.

Method: EFE represents preprocessing transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, enabling direct insertion into ML pipelines. Candidate programs are evolved using LLMs as mutation/recombination operators, guided by dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream validation performance. Two instantiations: EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations for time-series foundation models (e.g., Chronos-2); EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add interpretable features and remove redundant ones for tabular prediction.

Result: EFE-Time reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) by ≥3% on average across datasets, with up to 19% improvement on COVID-Deaths using Chronos-2. EFE-Tab matches or outperforms existing LLM-based feature engineering methods, and is especially effective with decision trees where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while maintaining interpretability.

Conclusion: LLM-based evolution can simultaneously improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically engineering features for structured data. EFE provides a general, pipeline-compatible framework that proves effective across time-series forecasting and tabular prediction tasks.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

</details>


### [172] [X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01553)
*Leyan Li,Rennong Yang,Zhenxing Zhang,Liping Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: X-LogSMask introduces a logarithmic structural mask for Graph Transformers that directly injects normalized graph topology into attention logits. Different attention heads receive different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix, giving each head a defined structural radius. The method achieves SOTA on 13 of 20 benchmarks while preserving the standard Transformer architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Transformers use all-to-all self-attention poorly suited to graph data, which has sparse, structured, multi-scale interactions. Existing Graph Transformers address this via structural encodings, hybrid message-passing, or learned attention constraints, but these add complexity and reduce interpretability. The authors aim to incorporate graph topology into attention in a simple, interpretable, and architecture-preserving manner.

Method: X-LogSMask is a multi-head logarithmic structural mask that converts symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix entries into attention logit modifiers. The logarithmic transform acts as a topology-aware gating signal: structurally disconnected nodes are suppressed while feature-dependent attention is preserved for connected nodes. Different heads receive different powers (k) of the normalized adjacency matrix, giving each head a defined structural radius and enabling multi-hop propagation within a single layer. The authors also show a standard Transformer encoder can be viewed as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative.

Result: Transformers with X-LogSMask achieved state-of-the-art performance on 13 out of 20 benchmarks spanning node, edge, and graph-level tasks. The method remained competitive even in a lightweight one-layer configuration.

Conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without modifying the Transformer architecture. X-LogSMask demonstrates that injecting symmetrically normalized graph topology via logarithmic masking suffices for strong graph representation learning.

Abstract: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

</details>


### [173] [Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01571)
*Aria Masoomi,Mahsa Bazzaz,Adel Javanmard,Vahab Mirrokni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the geometric properties of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories in LLM hidden states, introducing effective dimension as a complexity measure and showing that kinematic features of these trajectories can predict solution correctness early in generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While extensive research has focused on the content and length of CoT reasoning chains, the internal geometric structure of these reasoning trajectories in the model's hidden state space remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to establish whether geometric properties of CoT trajectories can reveal insights about task difficulty and solution quality.

Method: The authors formalize each CoT reasoning chain as a discrete curve in ℝ^d (the hidden state space) and analyze it using three classes of geometric functionals: spectral (effective dimension d_ρ via eigenvalue spectrum flatness), positional (mean position, dispersion, initial/current states), and kinematic (mean velocity, mean speed, speed dispersion). They provide theoretical justification linking flatter eigenvalue spectra to harder tasks, and apply these measures to MATH500 mathematical reasoning problems.

Result: The effective dimension d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy from hard MATH500 problems, confirming the theoretical prediction that flatter spectra (higher effective dimension) correlate with task difficulty. Kinematic features can predict solution correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens, and these correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty.

Conclusion: The shape of a model's internal CoT reasoning trajectory serves as a principled lens into both task hardness and solution quality. These findings suggest potential applications in early-stopping strategies and provide a new geometric framework for understanding LLM reasoning processes.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

</details>


### [174] [BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01600)
*Zewen Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling in LLM agents via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF). Experiments with GPT-4o show that inter-agent communication causes significant output homogenization in both text and image modalities, group size moderates coupling direction (K=5 homogenizes, K=3 diversifies), cross-model replication reveals extreme variation, and coupling is stateless — driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as communicating agents in multi-agent systems, it is critical to understand whether inter-agent communication causes outputs to converge toward homogeneity, potentially reducing diversity and introducing systemic risks in collaborative AI systems.

Method: The authors propose BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol that measures representational coupling using the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF), defined as the ratio JSD_cond / JSD_baseline, where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. Controlled experiments were conducted using GPT-4o (N=30, ~9,900 API calls) across text and image communication tasks, with no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls. They also varied group size (K=3 vs. K=5), performed cross-model replication, and tested for stateful vs. stateless coupling dynamics.

Result: Five key findings: (1) Text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803, d=1.30, p<0.001); (2) Image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834); (3) Group size moderates coupling direction — K=5 yields homogenization, K=3 yields CAF > 1.0, suggesting diversification; (4) Cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034–0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) Coupling is stateless, driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence.

Conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, carrying direct implications for multi-agent system design. The BOUNDARY_SYNC protocol offers a principled framework for diagnosing and mitigating unwanted homogenization in communicating AI agents.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

</details>


### [175] [SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01609)
*Saoud Aldowaish,Yashwanth Karumanchi,Kai-Chen Chiang,Mohammed Ayman Habib,Finn Murphy,Rishen Cao,Morteza Fayazi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SINA is a fully automated, open-source pipeline that converts circuit schematic images (both IC- and PCB-level) into machine-readable netlists using deep learning for component detection, connected-component labeling for connectivity inference, OCR for reference designator extraction, and a VLM for designator assignment, achieving 96.67% netlist generation accuracy — a 2.72× improvement over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Analog and mixed-signal EDA lacks machine-readable circuit design knowledge. Schematic images in papers, textbooks, and websites represent a vast repository of validated designs, but current image-to-netlist conversion methods fail to generalize across IC and PCB domains, struggle with component recognition, connectivity inference, and cannot reliably distinguish crossing wires from connected junctions.

Method: SINA integrates four key modules in a fully automated pipeline: (1) deep learning-based component detection for robust identification of circuit elements, (2) connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, (3) OCR for extracting component reference designators, and (4) a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. It also includes a dedicated crossing-wires detection mechanism to differentiate wire intersections from actual connections. Netlist correctness is validated using graph isomorphism techniques.

Result: SINA achieves an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, representing a 2.72× improvement over state-of-the-art approaches, with generalization across both IC- and PCB-level schematics.

Conclusion: SINA significantly advances the state of the art in schematic image-to-netlist conversion by delivering high accuracy, cross-domain generalization, and robust handling of crossing wires versus junctions, thereby enabling better utilization of existing circuit design knowledge for AI-driven EDA tools.

Abstract: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

</details>


### [176] [MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01627)
*Wenbo Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a multimodal framework for cold-start protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction that combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four biomedical knowledge graphs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA). A bridge reconstruction objective and pair-level gating mechanism enable effective integration of sequence and graph evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets under both novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cold-start PPI prediction — where candidate proteins lack observed interaction edges during training — is a challenging setting where topology-based methods fail due to missing network context. The authors aim to address this by leveraging complementary multimodal biomedical knowledge beyond the PPI network itself.

Method: The framework, called \method, has three key components: (1) a region-aware protein sequence encoder that extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions; (2) graph attention encoders that learn modality-specific protein embeddings from four biomedical knowledge graphs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA); and (3) a bridge reconstruction objective that regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, plus a pair-level gating module that adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair.

Result: Experiments on two benchmark datasets under both novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings demonstrate that \method consistently outperforms competitive sequence-based, network-based, and knowledge-graph baselines across five metrics: ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

Conclusion: The proposed multimodal framework effectively addresses the cold-start PPI prediction problem by integrating sequence and biomedical knowledge graph modalities, with the bridge reconstruction and gating mechanisms providing robust regularization and adaptive evidence fusion, leading to consistent performance gains over existing methods.

Abstract: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

</details>


### [177] [DeadPool: Resilient LLM Training with Hot-Swapping via Zero-Overhead Checkpoint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01646)
*Haotian Xie,Junlin Chen,Mingkai Zheng,Lishan Yang,Zhao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DeadPool is a fault-tolerance mechanism for LLM training that uses hot-swapping of failed nodes with spares, leveraging off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing and runtime communicator reconstruction to achieve zero overhead during error-free execution and sub-40-second recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM training at scale (tens of thousands of GPUs over months) inevitably encounters hardware/software failures. Existing fault-tolerance solutions either impose significant overhead during normal (failure-free) operation or suffer from long recovery latency — especially under permanent node failures. There is a need to simultaneously optimize both dimensions.

Method: DeadPool employs two key techniques: (1) Off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing that provides spatial redundancy by asynchronously writing checkpoints to peer-node memory, overlapping entirely with computation for zero overhead. (2) A communicator reconstruction protocol that dynamically replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime without terminating the entire job. Recovery uses these in-memory checkpoints to rebuild lost states with minimal recomputation.

Result: Evaluated on up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with models up to 65B parameters, DeadPool demonstrates zero checkpoint overhead during error-free execution and hot-swapping recovery in under 40 seconds.

Conclusion: DeadPool successfully resolves the trade-off between failure-free overhead and recovery latency, achieving both zero-overhead normal execution and extremely fast recovery from permanent node failures in large-scale LLM training.

Abstract: State-of-the-art large language model (LLM) training takes tens of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) for months and encounters failures across the software and hardware stack. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms either impose non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency, particularly under scenarios where a small subset of compute nodes experience permanent failures. %The tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency forms a space forms a Pareto frontier We present DeadPool to simultaneously address both optimization objectives. DeadPool incorporates a fault-tolerance mechanism that restores LLM training via hot-swapping, namely by replacing failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the complete job. The hot-swapping of DeadPool is enabled by two ideas: First, it exploits an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy. Second, it introduces a communicator reconstruction protocol that replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime. DeadPool efficiently overlaps the in-memory checkpointing with computation, thus introducing zero overhead during error-free execution. Upon permanent node failures, DeadPool can rebuild memory states with minimal recomputation by leveraging in-memory checkpoints. We evaluate DeadPool across scales (up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs) and LLMs (up to 65B parameters), and observe zero checkpoint overhead with hot-swapping recovery completing in under 40 seconds. These results show that DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost.

</details>


### [178] [CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01656)
*Jueqi Wang,Zachary Jacokes,John Darrell Van Horn,Kevin A. Pelphrey,Michael C. Schatz,Archana Venkataraman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CALM aligns brain ROI and genetic pathway data from disjoint unimodal populations in a shared latent space using linear projections, enabling interpretable cross-modal associations. It outperforms baselines and reveals immune/metabolic pathway–cortex links in autism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most large-scale datasets are unimodal (imaging only or genetics only), yet understanding neuropsychiatric disorders requires studying brain–gene interactions. No existing framework effectively learns interpretable associations between these modalities from completely separate populations.

Method: CALM learns linear projections that map brain ROI features and genetic pathway features into a shared latent space. The projections are trained to: (1) align class-conditional latent distributions across modalities, and (2) ensure group separability (discriminability between diagnostic groups). The linear nature of the projections directly yields interpretable pathway–ROI association weights. Training uses only unimodal datasets; evaluation is on a held-out paired dataset.

Result: CALM generalizes to unseen paired data, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. Learned ROI–pathway associations are stable compared to a paired baseline. In autism spectrum disorder, CALM identifies immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions, consistent with established literature.

Conclusion: CALM enables leveraging large unimodal repositories to study cross-modal brain–gene interactions in brain disorders, opening new avenues for integrative analysis without requiring costly paired multimodal data.

Abstract: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway--ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

</details>


### [179] [Message Passing Based Two-Timescale Bayesian Learning for Joint Channel and Memory Hardware Impairments Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01660)
*Wei Xu,An Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an MP-TTBDL framework using RGRU to model hardware impairment memory, combining Turbo-OAMP for channel estimation and DAMP for impairment calibration via EP, achieving robust channel estimation under hardware impairments in massive MIMO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers cause inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling that severely degrade channel estimation. These impairments drift slowly over time while channels vary rapidly, creating a two-timescale tracking problem that conventional compensator-then-estimate approaches handle poorly.

Method: An RGRU models intra-slot hardware impairment memory. A two-timescale Bayesian framework assigns a fast-varying Markov prior to the sparse channel and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior to network parameters. The multi-slot factor graph is solved via message passing: inter-slot messages are closed-form; the intra-slot graph is partitioned into a Turbo-OAMP-based channel tracking module and a DAMP-based impairment calibration module, which iteratively exchange extrinsic information through EP.

Result: Simulations demonstrate that MP-TTBDL robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensator-followed-by-estimation baselines across diverse online impairment scenarios and SNR conditions.

Conclusion: The MP-TTBDL framework effectively handles the two-timescale nature of channel variation and hardware impairment drift in massive MIMO, providing robust and accurate joint tracking through the integration of model-based message passing and deep learning.

Abstract: Hardware impairments in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. This paper employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model the intra-slot memory of the hardware impairments and proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework for joint channel and impairment tracking. Owing to small-scale fading, the wireless channel varies rapidly across slots, whereas hardware impairments drift slowly due to hardware aging and environmental variations. To capture these distinct physical timescales, a fastvarying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are assigned to the sparse channel and the network parameters, respectively. Based on a multi-slot factor graph formulation, a message-passing algorithm is developed. Specifically, the inter-slot messages admit closed-form updates, while the intra-slot factor graph, due to its complex recurrent structure, is partitioned into a channel tracking module and an impairments calibration module. The channel tracking module performs sparse channel estimation via turbo orthogonal approximate message passing (Turbo-OAMP), and the impairments calibration module updates the impairment parameters via a specially designed deep approximate message passing (DAMP) procedure, with the two modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation (EP) until convergence. Simulation results show that the proposed framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions.

</details>


### [180] [Revisiting Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01665)
*Hao Zhou,Xiaoyu Wang,Chang Yao,Mingli Song,Yuanyu Wan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes two FTRL-type algorithms for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication, addressing the full-information and bandit settings. The bandit algorithm significantly improves both regret bounds and communication costs over existing OGD-type methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work on D-OCO with compressed communication relies exclusively on OGD-type algorithms, while the best exact-communication D-OCO uses FTRL-type methods. There exists a gap: no FTRL-based compressed communication algorithms exist, despite FTRL's superior elegance and theoretical properties in the exact setting.

Method: The authors leverage FTRL's dual update mechanism to seamlessly integrate communication compression via average consensus techniques. Two algorithms are designed: one for the full-information setting and one for the bandit setting, both using compressed communication within the FTRL framework.

Result: The full-information algorithm matches existing regret bounds of OGD-type compressed methods. The bandit algorithm significantly improves upon both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

Conclusion: FTRL-type algorithms with compressed communication are not only feasible but advantageous for D-OCO. The dual update structure of FTRL makes it particularly well-suited for incorporating communication compression, especially yielding notable gains in the bandit setting.

Abstract: Decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) is a popular framework for distributed applications with streaming data. To tackle the communication bottleneck, previous studies have investigated D-OCO with compressed communication and proposed several algorithms that are variants of online gradient descent (OGD). However, for D-OCO with exact communication, the best existing algorithms are variants of follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In this paper, for the first time, we propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. Compared with OGD-type algorithms, our algorithms are more elegant in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. The key insight is that the dual update mechanism of FTRL allows us to make a simple application of the technique for average consensus with communication compression. More specifically, our first algorithm considers the full-information setting, and can match the existing regret bounds. Our second algorithm is designed for the bandit setting, and can significantly improve both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

</details>


### [181] [UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01670)
*Ronghui Xu,Tongxin Wu,Guozhen Zhang,Yihan Li,Chenjuan Guo,Bin Yang,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UniWind is a day-ahead wind power forecasting model that combines a physics-informed physical prior estimator with a latent state encoder and state-aware power corrector. It uses site-calibrated monotonic warping and shared physical power curves to create a soft upper-bound envelope, then applies knowledge-guided state routing to correct for operational states like shutdowns and curtailment. The model demonstrates strong accuracy and zero-shot cross-farm generalization on 20+ real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing physical models adapt poorly across wind farms, while data-driven models conflate meteorological effects with latent operational state-induced deviations (e.g., shutdowns, curtailment). There is a need for a model that combines physical constraints with data-driven learning to disentangle available wind power from operational artifacts.

Method: UniWind consists of three components: (1) a Physical Prior Estimator that builds a site-calibrated physical prior via site-conditioned monotonic warping and a shared physical power curve, constrained by a physical upper bound as a soft envelope of available power; (2) a Latent State Encoder that models operational-state embeddings; (3) a State-aware Power Corrector that uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction to transform the physical prior into final forecasts.

Result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate UniWind's accuracy and robustness, outperforming both purely physical and purely data-driven baselines.

Conclusion: UniWind effectively integrates physics-informed priors with learnable latent state modeling, achieving accurate day-ahead wind power forecasting while generalizing robustly across wind farms in zero-shot settings.

Abstract: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

</details>


### [182] [SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01678)
*Mingkai Zheng,Junlin Chen,Haotian Xie,Zhao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCAPE is a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM pre-training that uses first-moment statistics from AdamS to enable aggressive gradient sparsification (90–99%) with delayed, overlapped mask synchronization, achieving up to 43.3% wall-clock time reduction while preserving model quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Communication dominates LLM pre-training cost under data-parallel and sharded training. Existing solutions are insufficient: raw gradient sparsification is unstable with Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, and quantization savings are bounded by bit width with additional runtime overhead. A method is needed that achieves aggressive communication reduction without sacrificing training stability or model quality.

Method: SCAPE exploits AdamS's stable first-moment estimates to derive sparsification masks instead of using noisy raw gradients. Key techniques: (1) mask generation from first-moment statistics partitioned across workers to align with optimizer sharding, (2) one-step delayed mask usage so synchronization overlaps with computation, and (3) reconstructing second-moment update quantities from a single synchronized sparse buffer to eliminate an extra collective communication. Implemented in Megatron-LM.

Result: Evaluated on GPT-345M (OpenWebText) and Llama-500M (SlimPajama-6B) with 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs. SCAPE maintains training stability, validation loss, and downstream accuracy under 90% and 99% sparsity. For Llama-500M, end-to-end wall-clock time reduced by up to 43.3% versus dense AdamW/AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, per-step speedup reaches 3.26× compared to dense AdamS.

Conclusion: SCAPE demonstrates that first-moment-based sparsification can drastically reduce communication overhead in distributed LLM training while preserving convergence and model quality, outperforming both gradient sparsification and quantization-based approaches in the Adam-style optimizer regime.

Abstract: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

</details>


### [183] [WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01686)
*Tzu-Heng Huang,Aditya Goyal,John Cooper,Frederic Sala*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WARP recovers the domain mixture weights of a fine-tuned model's training data directly from its weights by interpolating between base and fine-tuned models to simulate the training trajectory and extracting geometric features from weight space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation model training data recipes (e.g., domain mixture weights) are rarely disclosed, creating an asymmetry where researchers can study models but lack visibility into their training distributions. Prior methods like membership inference operate at the sample level and cannot characterize global corpus composition.

Method: WARP interpolates between base and fine-tuned model weights via model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints approximating the training trajectory. These reveal a geometric footprint of training data in weight space. Geometric features are extracted from these simulated footprints and mapped to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures.

Result: On controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming both membership inference baselines and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

Conclusion: WARP demonstrates that global training data composition can be effectively inferred from model weights alone, exposing a previously unrecognized privacy/transparency implication of public model release.

Abstract: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

</details>


### [184] [Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01689)
*Long Minh Bui,Tuan Anh Le Van,Tung Phi Duc,Phi Le Nguyen,Jana Doppa,Trong Nghia Hoang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a Product-of-Experts framework, where each single-task model acts as an energy-based expert. It identifies a mismatch between the implicit Gaussian assumptions in existing methods and the empirically observed heavy-tailed residuals, and proposes a Cauchy-based heavy-tailed PoE design that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solution spaces, which provide limited statistical guidance on how useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks. The authors aim to provide a principled statistical framework for model merging that better captures the empirical behavior of parameter residuals.

Method: The authors formulate model merging under a Product-of-Experts (PoE) scenario, where each single-task solution defines an energy-based model (EBM) over merged parameters. They show existing methods emerge as special cases with implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals. Observing that residuals are empirically heavy-tailed, they propose a heavy-tailed PoE design using Cauchy experts with provably convergent inference.

Result: Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The Cauchy-based heavy-tailed PoE design better captures observed residual behavior compared to implicit Gaussian assumptions in prior methods.

Conclusion: The probabilistic inference perspective via PoE-EBM provides a principled and flexible framework for model merging. Moving from light-tailed Gaussian to heavy-tailed Cauchy expert models yields substantial empirical gains, suggesting that better statistical modeling of parameter residuals is key to improved merging performance.

Abstract: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

</details>


### [185] [A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01693)
*Jianfeng Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A proof-oriented tutorial introducing diffusion models from the sampling perspective, bridging classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers with error analysis and inference-time control, aimed at graduate students with probability background.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide beginning graduate students with a unified, rigorous introduction to diffusion models through the lens of sampling theory, filling the gap between classical stochastic sampling methods and contemporary diffusion-based generative modeling.

Method: The material is structured in a layered pedagogical fashion: core definitions and identities are proved in full, representative estimates are derived under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems are presented with proof roadmaps. The exposition traces a single conceptual arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, error analysis, and inference-time control techniques.

Result: A self-contained educational resource that requires only probability background (no prior exposure to SDEs, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models) and builds up to state-of-the-art research-level understanding.

Conclusion: Diffusion models can be understood coherently as an evolution of classical sampling dynamics, and this perspective enables a rigorous, accessible pedagogical framework suitable for graduate-level instruction.

Abstract: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

</details>


### [186] [Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01694)
*Xiong Xiong,Ruonan Zhai,Zheng Zeng,Sheng Zhou,Rongchun Hu,Zichen Deng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FS-PIELM addresses spectral bias in physics-informed extreme learning machines by shifting the mean of Gaussian weight distributions (rather than scaling variance) to target high-frequency PDE solutions. The linear variant (FS-PIELM-L) achieves 1–5 orders of magnitude accuracy improvement across seven benchmark problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-informed neural networks struggle with high-frequency PDE solutions due to spectral bias — the preferential learning of low-frequency components. Existing methods that multiply random weights by a scaling factor amplify variance quadratically, causing instability. A more principled approach is needed to enable high-frequency learning while preserving computational efficiency and numerical stability.

Method: The FS-PIELM framework uses an additive weight initialization mechanism: instead of scaling random weights, it translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping variance fixed at unity. Two variants are proposed: (1) FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes per neuron, and (2) FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for robustness. The method retains the extreme learning machine paradigm — only a single linear solve is required. Theoretical analysis bounds the frequency variance, showing it approaches unity regardless of target frequency, unlike the quadratic growth in scaling-based methods.

Result: FS-PIELM-L achieves the best accuracy in six out of seven benchmark cases, with improvements ranging from one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The method succeeds across six equation types (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) on both regular and complex geometries.

Conclusion: The additive mean-shift strategy for weight initialization effectively mitigates spectral bias without the variance amplification problems of scaling-based approaches. FS-PIELM combines high accuracy for high-frequency PDEs with the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, making it a practical and theoretically grounded solution.

Abstract: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization.
