Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

</details>


### [187] [Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01736)
*Nikolai Smolyanskiy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem of offline checkpoint selection for latent world models, where validation loss metrics fail to detect closed-loop performance collapse. The authors propose the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) — measuring how much the reward predictor depends on the observable subspace — and combine it with structural regularizers into a Composite ROF (CROF) score. CROF-selected checkpoints yield a model-based A2C policy that outperforms model-free A2C by ~24.5 return points with ~65× fewer environment interactions on LunarLander v3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE continue improving long after closed-loop performance degrades in world-model training, making reliable offline checkpoint selection a critical unsolved problem. There is no existing diagnostic that reliably predicts downstream policy performance from validation-time metrics alone, especially in environments with shaped rewards.

Method: The authors train an RSSM world model on Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, using per-checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. They evaluate 40 candidate metrics against this oracle, drawn from optimal-control theory (including observability, controllability, and stability measures). The Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) emerges as the strongest single predictor. ROF is combined with three structural regularizers into a composite score (CROF) for offline checkpoint ranking. Model-based A2C and zero-shot CEM-MPC policies are then trained using the CROF-selected world model.

Result: ROF is the strongest individual predictor of closed-loop quality among 40 evaluated metrics. The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65× fewer real-environment interactions. The same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy, demonstrating generalization across different downstream control strategies.

Conclusion: Structural diagnostics from optimal-control theory — particularly reward observability — can reliably predict closed-loop world-model quality from validation-time data alone, solving the checkpoint selection problem that naive loss-based methods fail to address.

Abstract: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

</details>


### [188] [Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01746)
*Kanishka Reddy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a finite-lag operator geometry framework for analyzing recurrent neural network hidden states, decomposing transport dynamics into conditional spread, coherent displacement, and circulation components with proven covariance and stability properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recurrent neural representations are inherently trajectories, yet existing geometry tools only capture static snapshots. Infinitesimal methods like carré-du-champ fail to detect deterministic recurrent motion over finite time lags. There is a need for a principled geometric framework that operates directly on observed source-successor pairs to quantify directed, lagged flow in hidden state space.

Method: The authors develop finite-lag operator geometry centered on the conditional transport law Q_Δ(dy|x) estimated via a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this, they derive: (1) a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ that decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, (2) an antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ summarizing directed lagged flow. They prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates all quantities.

Result: Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance-matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture-dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction proves to be metric- and resolution-dependent.

Conclusion: The finite-lag operator geometry successfully captures directed recurrent dynamics that infinitesimal methods miss, providing a covariant, stable, and interpretable toolkit for comparing RNN architectures beyond task performance alone.

Abstract: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

</details>


### [189] [Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01752)
*Cheng Wan,Quyu Kong,Feng Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS), a novel framework for modeling cumulative conditional intensity functions (CCIFs) of temporal point processes, overcoming three structural deadlocks (convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and CCIF modeling violations) inherent in existing Monotone Neural Network (MNN) parameterizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CCIF parameterizations for temporal point processes uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which suffer from three critical structural deadlocks: (1) convexity restrictions that limit flexibility, (2) saturation limits that constrain dynamic range, and (3) fundamental violations of CCIF modeling requirements. These limitations severely restrict representational capacity for modeling complex temporal dynamics.

Method: The authors propose Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS), a framework that decouples CCIF modeling into distinct interpolation and extrapolation components. The interpolation component provides strong fitting accuracy for observed data ranges, while the extrapolation component supports robust out-of-distribution generalization, reducing the irreducible approximation gaps inherent in MNN-based approaches.

Result: Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that MAS achieves superior performance compared to existing MNN-based methods for CCIF modeling in temporal point processes.

Conclusion: MAS resolves the fundamental structural bottlenecks of MNN-based CCIF parameterizations by leveraging separate interpolation and extrapolation mechanisms, offering a more flexible, efficient, and theoretically grounded framework for modeling complex temporal dynamics in point processes.

Abstract: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS). By leveraging distinct interpolation and extrapolation components, MAS provides a flexible and efficient framework for modeling CCIFs. Theoretically, MAS's interpolation provides strong fitting accuracy, while its extrapolation supports robust generalization, reducing the irreducible approximation gaps of MNNs. Extensive experiments show that MAS achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

</details>


### [190] [Role-Aware Neural Convex Divergence Heads for Asymmetric Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01762)
*He Huang,Lu Shen,Yunfeng Huang,Li Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning, applying source/target-role projections before an input-convex neural Bregman divergence. It outperforms symmetric distances and plain ICNN-Bregman heads on semantic/ontology benchmarks while remaining interpretable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard distance heads (Euclidean, cosine, Mahalanobis) are symmetric and cannot capture directed relations like lexical entailment, sentence entailment, ontology hierarchies, and citation links. Unstructured neural scorers can model directionality but lack geometric interpretability. The paper aims to bridge this gap with a structured, asymmetric, and interpretable distance module.

Method: The authors propose a role-aware neural convex divergence head. It first applies distinct source-role and target-role projections to the input representations, then evaluates an input-convex neural network (ICNN)-parameterized Bregman divergence in the projected space. This yields a nonnegative, asymmetric score. The paper provides theoretical analysis including projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature characterization.

Result: Across ten random seeds on lexical, sentence, and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while maintaining zero observed negative divergence rate. However, on large fixed-feature citation prediction tasks, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy, identified as a boundary case.

Conclusion: The role-aware neural convex divergence head is best understood as a structured, interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter, offering a favorable trade-off between geometric structure and directional modeling capacity.

Abstract: Many representation learning problems involve directed relations, such as lexical entailment, sentence entailment, ontology hierarchy, and citation links. Standard Euclidean, cosine, and Mahalanobis heads are symmetric, while generic neural scorers can model directionality but provide limited geometric structure. This paper proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning. The head applies source- and target-role projections before evaluating an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, yielding a nonnegative structured score in the role-projected space. We characterize its projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature. Experiments on lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed graph benchmarks compare symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads, and the proposed role-aware variant. Across ten random seeds on the main semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while preserving zero observed negative divergence rate. The results also identify a boundary case: on large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy. Overall, the proposed head is best understood as a structured and interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter.

</details>


### [191] [Denser $\neq$ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01763)
*Meng Wang,Haohan Zhao,Wenzhuo Liu,Lu Yang,Geng Liu,Haiyang Guo,Guo-Sen Xie,Gaofeng Meng,Hongbin Liu,Fei Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO) accelerates in-domain specialization but causes stronger forgetting and potential collapse in continual post-training compared to conservative on-policy RL methods like GRPO. Dense self-distillation induces larger parameter/response drift and amplifies formatting artifacts via self-reinforcing loops, suggesting it should not be used as a default stabilizer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent work has optimistically framed on-policy self-distillation as an effective approach to mitigate forgetting during continual post-training of foundation models. This paper challenges that view, seeking to rigorously evaluate whether SDPO truly serves as a reliable stabilizer or whether its benefits are limited to narrow conditions.

Method: The authors conduct experiments using self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO) and compare it against on-policy reinforcement learning methods (specifically GRPO) in continual post-training settings. They analyze parameter-space drift, response-space drift, and the emergence of high-frequency formatting artifacts through the self-reinforcing teacher-student loop.

Result: SDPO accelerates in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well-aligned, but struggles with out-of-distribution generalization. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can collapse, while GRPO adapts more conservatively and preserves prior capabilities better. Denser self-distillation causes larger drift in both parameter and response spaces and amplifies formatting artifacts through self-reinforcement.

Conclusion: On-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can be useful for accelerating specialization under stable, reliable token-level supervision, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training.

Abstract: Continual post-training enables foundation models to acquire new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Recent work suggests that on-policy learning can mitigate forgetting, with on-policy self-distillation emerging as a particularly attractive approach. In this work, we revisit this optimistic view through self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO). Our experiments show that SDPO can accelerate in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well aligned, but it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can even collapse, whereas on-policy reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO adapt more conservatively and better preserve prior capabilities. Further analyses reveal that denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and can amplify high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher--student loop. These findings suggest that on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL.

</details>


### [192] [Set Diffusion: Interpolating Token Orderings Between Autoregression and Diffusion for Fast and Flexible Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01775)
*Marianne Arriola,Volodymyr Kuleshov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Set diffusion introduces a new class of language models that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets with a set-causal diffusion architecture supporting KV caching, enabling arbitrarily-ordered decoding with better speed-quality tradeoffs than prior diffusion LMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrete diffusion models are constrained to fixed-length generation without KV caching, while block diffusion's fixed-size sequential blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. There is a need for a diffusion-based LM that supports efficient caching, flexible decoding orders, and variable-length generation.

Method: The authors propose set diffusion with two key components: (1) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets rather than fixed-size blocks, and (2) a set-causal diffusion architecture that enables KV cache updates after every inference step, supporting arbitrarily-ordered token set decoding (e.g., sliding-window sets).

Result: Set diffusion achieves superior speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models, and demonstrates stronger infilling performance than block diffusion.

Conclusion: By moving from fixed-size blocks to flexible token sets with KV caching support, set diffusion unlocks faster inference and any-order decoding, representing a significant step forward for diffusion-based language modeling.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion models have steadily improved in quality relative to autoregressive (AR) models. However, these models are normally constrained to fixed-length generation and do not support key-value (KV) caching. Block diffusion partially bridges diffusion and AR by generating token blocks left-to-right, but its fixed-size sequential blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. Here, we present a new class of language models, set diffusion, comprised of (i) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets and (ii) a set-causal diffusion architecture that supports KV cache updates after every inference step. By factorizing over token sets instead of fixed-size blocks, tokens can be decoded in arbitrarily-ordered sets, including sliding-window sets, enabling faster inference and support for any-order decoding. Set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models while offering stronger infilling performance than block diffusion. We provide the code, along with the model weights and blog post on the project page: https://m-arriola.com/setdlms/

</details>


### [193] [EHHN: An Event-driven Heterogeneous Hypergraph Network for Object-Centric Next Activity Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01785)
*Jiaxing Wang,Kaitao Chen,Zhubin Han,Chenyu Hou,Bin Cao,Jing Fan,Ji Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EHHN proposes a heterogeneous hypergraph network for next-activity prediction in object-centric event logs, using dual-stream micro-spatial and macro-evolution architectures, achieving SOTA accuracy with up to 24× GPU memory reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing next-activity prediction methods either flatten OCELs (losing cross-object context) or use pairwise graph relations (failing to capture higher-order multi-object interactions). No prior method jointly models event-driven object state changes, inter-event timing, and global execution patterns.

Method: EHHN represents prediction prefixes as heterogeneous hypergraphs with event-object hyperedges and lifecycle hyperedges. A dual-stream architecture processes these: (1) a micro-spatial stream models event-driven object-state evolution via hypergraph message passing, and (2) a macro-evolution stream captures temporal dynamics using retrieved global prototypes. The two streams are fused for prediction.

Result: On four public OCEL benchmarks against nine baselines, EHHN achieves best accuracy and macro F1-score on all datasets, improving up to 8.1 and 12.4 percentage points over strongest baselines, while reducing peak GPU memory up to 24× compared to the strongest OCEL-native graph baseline.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous hypergraph modeling with dual-stream micro-macro learning effectively captures both fine-grained object-state evolution and global temporal patterns in object-centric processes, enabling accurate and memory-efficient next-activity prediction.

Abstract: Next activity prediction helps service-oriented processes anticipate upcoming steps before delays, exceptions, or service-level risks occur. Most existing methods assume classical single-case event logs, whereas real service processes often involve events shared by multiple typed business objects. Object-centric event logs (OCELs) capture such interactions, but current predictors remain limited. Flattening-based approaches lose cross-object context, and native OCEL graph-based approaches encode multi-object events through pairwise relations. Existing models also do not jointly capture event-driven object state changes, inter-event timing, and global execution patterns. We propose EHHN, an Event-driven Heterogeneous Hypergraph Network for object-centric next activity prediction. EHHN represents each prediction prefix as a heterogeneous hypergraph, where event--object hyperedges bind retained co-participating objects and a lifecycle hyperedge groups the primary object's observed lifecycle events. Based on this representation, EHHN uses a dual-stream architecture in which a micro-spatial stream models event-driven object-state evolution and a macro-evolution stream captures temporal dynamics using retrieved global prototypes. The two streams are fused to predict the next activity. Experiments on four public OCEL benchmarks against nine baselines show that EHHN achieves the best accuracy and macro F1-score on all datasets, with improvements of up to 8.1 and 12.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines. Compared with the strongest OCEL-native graph baseline, EHHN also reduces peak GPU memory by up to 24 times. Code is available at https://github.com/chenkaitao1112/EHHN.

</details>


### [194] [EPnG: Adaptive Expert Prune-and-Grow for Parameter-Efficient MoE Fine-tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01789)
*Ahin Lee,Sehyun Yun,Taesik Gong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EPnG adaptively prunes under-utilized and grows high-importance experts in MoE models based on router gate probabilities, achieving full fine-tuning comparable performance while updating only 0.55%-0.72% of parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE models have redundant experts and uniform parameter allocation, making adaptation costly. Existing PEFT methods (e.g., LoRA) ignore MoE routing dynamics, resulting in suboptimal resource utilization.

Method: EPnG (Expert Prune-and-Grow): an adaptive framework that prunes under-utilized experts and expands high-importance experts via rank growth with orthogonal initialization, guided by router gate probabilities, while maintaining a fixed parameter budget.

Result: On OLMoE and Qwen1.5-MoE benchmarks, EPnG consistently outperforms LoRA under the same budget and matches full fine-tuning performance while updating only 0.55%-0.72% of parameters (140x-180x fewer).

Conclusion: Aligning PEFT with MoE routing dynamics yields a more effective and scalable fine-tuning strategy, demonstrating that adaptive expert-level capacity reallocation is superior to uniform parameter allocation.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale efficiently but remain costly to adapt due to redundant experts and uniform parameter allocation. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA ignore MoE routing dynamics, leading to suboptimal resource use. We propose EPnG, an adaptive prune-and-grow framework that reallocates LoRA capacity based on expert importance derived from router gate probabilities. EPnG prunes under-utilized experts and expands high-importance experts via rank growth with orthogonal initialization, while maintaining a fixed parameter budget. Across OLMoE and Qwen1.5-MoE, EPnG consistently outperforms LoRA under the same budget and achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning while updating only 0.55%-0.72% of parameters (up to 140x-180x fewer). These results demonstrate that aligning PEFT with MoE routing yields a more effective and scalable fine-tuning strategy.

</details>


### [195] [Single-Channel EEG-Based Cognitive Load Assessment in Online Learning: A Hybrid Deep Learning Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01795)
*Rowan Hussein,Mohamed Ouf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using a consumer-grade single-channel EEG device, a hybrid CNN+LSTM+Attention model achieves up to 78.5% within-subject accuracy in distinguishing easy vs. difficult educational video content, outperforming conventional feature-based classifiers (55%). The authors release a reproducible evaluation pipeline and an open-source tool for visualizing cognitive load heatmaps over video timelines, while advocating for subject-independent evaluation as the standard for this task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In remote online learning, instructors lose the visual cues normally available in classrooms to gauge when students find content difficult. The authors investigate whether low-cost, consumer-grade EEG can fill this gap by automatically detecting cognitive load from brain signals during video-based learning, enabling scalable, non-intrusive monitoring of learner difficulty.

Method: The study uses the publicly available Wang et al. dataset with nine participants (one excluded for noise). A hybrid deep learning architecture combining CNN, LSTM, and Attention mechanisms is implemented, fusing raw EEG waveform data with band-power features. Regularization via dropout and L2 is applied to mitigate overfitting. Within-subject classification is performed, and the authors construct an open-source pipeline supporting reproducible evaluation. They also build a notebook-based tool that records EEG, runs inference, and produces a heatmap visualization of estimated cognitive load over the video timeline.

Result: The CNN+LSTM+Attention model achieves up to 78.5% within-subject accuracy vs. 55% for conventional feature-based classifiers. Without regularization, a large train-validation accuracy gap is observed; dropout and L2 stabilize validation accuracy at roughly 68–73%. The authors caution that within-subject results are optimistic given the small sample (n=9) and argue for subject-independent evaluation as the standard benchmark.

Conclusion: Single-channel consumer EEG shows promise as a feasibility-level tool for discriminating cognitive load during educational video viewing, but is not yet deployable. Future work should adopt subject-independent evaluation protocols, and the released pipeline and visualization tool aim to facilitate reproducible research and practical exploration by educators.

Abstract: Monitoring cognitive load during online learning could help instructors identify content that learners find difficult, but remote settings remove the visual cues that support this judgement in a classroom. We study whether a single-channel, consumer-grade EEG device (the NeuroSky MindWave Mobile 2) can distinguish easy from difficult educational-video content, using the publicly available dataset of Wang et al. [24] (ten learners, one excluded for excessive noise, leaving nine). We implement a hybrid CNN+LSTM+Attention model that combines the raw waveform with band-power features. In a within-subject setting, the model reaches up to 78.5% accuracy, compared with 55% for conventional feature-based classifiers; regularization (dropout and L2) closes the large gap between training and validation accuracy that we observe without it, keeping validation accuracy stable at roughly 68-73%. We are deliberately cautious about these numbers: with only nine subjects, within-subject evaluation is optimistic, and we argue that subject-independent evaluation -- in which no learner appears in both training and test data -- should be the standard for this task. To that end we release a reproducible evaluation pipeline. We frame the work as a feasibility study rather than a deployable system, and pair it with an open, notebook-based tool that records EEG, runs inference, and visualizes estimated cognitive load as a heatmap over the video timeline to help educators locate potentially challenging segments.

</details>


### [196] [Expander Sparse Autoencoders: Parameter-Efficient Dictionaries for Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01799)
*Rodrigo Mendoza-Smith*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Expander SAEs replace the dense decoder of TopK sparse autoencoders with a sparse, expander-graph-structured decoder, dramatically reducing learned parameters and storage while retaining most of the fidelity. The approach traces a clean storage--fidelity frontier, with theoretical guarantees for sparse code identifiability and OMP support recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard SAEs use a dense decoder matrix of size m×n, costing O(mn) learned values—prohibitively expensive at large feature counts. The authors seek to reduce this parameter and storage cost while preserving the sparse-coding inference quality.

Method: The decoder W (and its tied encoder) is constrained to be supported on a left-d-regular expander graph mask (d ≪ m), learning only d·n values instead of m·n. The matching-pursuit correlation step W^T r in OMP becomes an O(dn) gather-and-reduce. Theoretical analysis provides sufficient conditions (expansion and column flatness) for noiseless k-sparse code identifiability and exact OMP support recovery.

Result: On Pythia-70M/160M, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.2-1B residual-stream activations, varying d reveals a consistent storage--fidelity frontier. At the most compressed setting (Qwen2.5-3B, d=7), the method uses 293× fewer learned decoder values than the dense baseline while recovering 84% of the dense CE-loss reduction. Control experiments attribute gains primarily to sparse, diverse decoder support structure rather than merely fewer parameters; comparing sparse and dense decoders at matched parameter counts reveals a residual gap partly due to encoder amortisation.

Conclusion: Expander SAEs offer a highly parameter-efficient alternative to dense SAEs, achieving strong fidelity with orders-of-magnitude fewer decoder parameters. The work establishes both empirical storage--fidelity Pareto frontiers and theoretical recovery guarantees, with the sparse support structure—not just parameter count—driving the improved tradeoff.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose internal activations of neural networks into sparse linear combinations of learned features by fitting an overcomplete dictionary $\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ with $m<n$, and inferring a sparse code $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ from $\mathbf{h}\approx\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$. This inference problem closely resembles the canonical setup of compressed sensing, but dense decoders requires $O(mn)$ learned values, which becomes costly at large feature counts. We introduce Expander SAEs: TopK SAEs whose decoder and tied encoder are supported on a left-$d$-regular expander mask with $d\ll m$, learning only $dn$ decoder values while keeping the sparse-coding problem $(m,n,k)$ fixed. The same structure reduces storage and turns the matching-pursuit correlation step $\mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{r}$ in OMP into an $O(dn)$ gather-and-reduce operation. Our experiments show that across Pythia-70M/160M, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.2-1B residual-stream activations, varying $d$ traces a consistent storage--fidelity frontier, and that at the most compressed modern-LM setting, Qwen2.5-3B with $d=7$ uses $293\times$ fewer learned decoder values than the full dense decoder while retaining $84$% of dense CE-loss recovered. Control experiments show that the improved storage--fidelity tradeoff is driven by sparse, diverse decoder support structure rather than by fewer learned decoder values, and that when sparse and dense decoders are compared at matched parameter count, part of the remaining gap comes from encoder amortisation. On the theoretical side, we show that expansion and column flatness are sufficient for identifiability of noiseless $k$-sparse codes, and we derive complementary sufficient conditions under which OMP recovers the support exactly.

</details>


### [197] [Do LLMs Truly Generalize in the Molecular Domain? A Perturbation-Based Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01800)
*Jiatong Li,Weida Wang,Changmeng Zheng,Shufei Zhang,Yatao Bian,Xiao-yong Wei,Qing Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether molecular LLMs can generalize beyond local neighborhoods of their sequence-based representations. Using a Molecular Perturbation framework with controlled Graph Edit Distance, the authors find that even single-atom edits cause substantial performance drops, revealing fragile local trust regions. In-Context Tuning (ICT) on structurally similar molecules partially mitigates this fragility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs applied to molecular discovery operate on discrete sequential tokens (e.g., SMILES strings), but chemical space has rigid topological constraints. There is a fundamental gap between the probabilistic, sequence-based nature of LLMs and graph-structured molecular representations. The authors aim to systematically probe whether molecular LLMs truly learn meaningful chemical manifolds or merely exploit local sequence neighborhoods.

Method: The authors propose a Molecular Perturbation framework that generates syntax-valid structural variants of training molecules under controlled Graph Edit Distance (GED). By applying single or few atomic edits (additions, deletions, substitutions), they measure how model performance degrades across common molecular tasks, quantifying the extent of the local trust region. They further evaluate In-Context Tuning (ICT), where predictions are anchored on structurally similar molecules, to test whether it confers robustness against these perturbations.

Result: Even a single graph edit causes substantial performance drops on standard molecular prediction tasks, indicating a narrow local trust region and high sensitivity to minor structural changes. In-Context Tuning (ICT) partially expands this local trust region, offering improved stability against structural variation, though the effect is only partial.

Conclusion: Molecular LLMs exhibit fragile generalization confined to narrow local neighborhoods in chemical space. The sequence-based tokenization fails to capture robust topological invariance. ICT offers a promising direction for stabilizing molecular LLMs by leveraging structural similarity to anchor predictions, but more work is needed to achieve broader generalization.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in molecular discovery, yet a gap remains between their probabilistic nature over discrete sequential tokens and the rigid topological constraints of chemical space. This raises the question of whether molecular LLMs can generalize beyond the local neighborhoods induced by their sequence-based representations. To systematically investigate this question, we introduce a Molecular Perturbation framework that generates syntax-valid structural variants of training molecules under controlled Graph Edit Distance (GED) to probe the manifold regularity of molecular LLMs. Our analysis shows that even a single edit can cause substantial performance drops on common molecular tasks, revealing a narrow local trust region and fragile sensitivity to structural changes. Since similar molecules tend to exhibit similar properties, In-Context Tuning (ICT), which anchors predictions on structurally similar molecules, offers a natural way to mitigate such fragility. Our experiments also examine whether ICT confers robustness under controlled structural perturbations, and the results suggest that it can partially expand the local trust region and offer a promising direction for stabilizing molecular LLMs against structural variation.

</details>


### [198] [Gaming Consensus: Coordinated Manipulation in Crowdsourced Fact-Checking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01824)
*Nikil Roashan Selvam,Jay Baxter,Sophie Hilgard,Brad Miller,Keith Coleman,Ellen Vitercik,Sanmi Koyejo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the matrix factorization-based bridging algorithms used in crowdsourced fact-checking systems (like X's Community Notes and Meta's equivalent), demonstrating that coordinated users can manipulate latent representations to fabricate synthetic consensus. The authors find up to 10.7% of low-quality notes can be elevated above consensus thresholds with fewer than 10 ratings, uncover a counterintuitive vulnerability where "Not Helpful" ratings can increase helpfulness scores, and present mitigations deployed in X's algorithm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crowdsourced fact-checking systems relying on bridging-based consensus (rather than majority voting) are increasingly deployed by major platforms, but the only publicly disclosed implementations use matrix factorization. The security of these algorithms against strategic manipulation by coordinated actors is not well understood, creating a risk that adversarial groups could undermine the integrity of decentralized content moderation at scale.

Method: The authors conduct a dual theoretical and empirical analysis of the core matrix factorization component in bridging algorithms. Empirically, they use historic production data from X's Community Notes to simulate coordinated voting attacks that exploit latent representations. Theoretically, they derive properties showing how rating trajectories can be manipulated, including a proof that "Not Helpful" ratings can paradoxically increase helpfulness scores. They also construct a cost model to quantify the effort required for manipulation.

Result: Up to 10.7% of lower-quality notes could be manipulated above consensus thresholds using fewer than 10 strategically placed ratings. A counterintuitive vulnerability exists where marking a note as "Not Helpful" can increase its helpfulness score due to the geometry of latent factor updates. The cost model demonstrates that synthetic consensus fabrication is feasible with relatively low effort. Mitigations were developed and deployed within X's Community Notes algorithm to address these findings.

Conclusion: Bridging-based matrix factorization algorithms, while effective for crowdsourced fact-checking under normal conditions, contain structural vulnerabilities that can be exploited by coordinated actors to fabricate consensus. The findings underscore the need for robust defenses — which the authors have already operationalized at X — and highlight the broader challenge of designing manipulation-resistant decentralized content moderation systems.

Abstract: Crowdsourced fact-checking systems have been adopted by major social media companies such as X, Meta, TikTok and Google with the aim of combating misleading information at scale without relying on centralized editorial control. These systems have been developed around a common underlying concept: a bridging mechanism that identifies notes flagging misleading information when they receive support from people with different perspectives rather than simple majority support. To our knowledge the only publicly disclosed bridging algorithms deployed for fact-checking are based on matrix factorization, as deployed by both X and Meta, augmented with additional components addressing abuse, targeted manipulation, and contributor brigades. This work examines the core matrix factorization portion of these systems, presenting theoretical and empirical evaluations of the degree to which coordinated users could vote strategically by leveraging the latent representations to fabricate the appearance of synthetic consensus within the bridging mechanism. Using historic production data, we find that up to 10.7% of lower quality notes could be manipulated above consensus thresholds using less than 10 ratings. We complement these findings with a theoretical analysis, revealing counterintuitively that rating a note as "Not Helpful" can increase its helpfulness score, as well as a cost model quantifying manipulation effort. We have developed and deployed mitigations within X's Community Notes algorithm to address synthetic consensus.

</details>


### [199] [Many Voices, One Reward: Multi-Role Rubric Generation for LLM Judging and Reward Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01830)
*Dazhi Fu,Jiuding Yang,Yiwen Guo,Jicong Fan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MRRG proposes a multi-role rubric generation framework that elicits evaluation criteria from complementary perspectives to address "dimensional blind spots" in single-evaluator rubric generators, producing auditable scorers for preference validation and RLVR reward signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing annotation-free rubric generators rely on a single generic evaluator, which creates "dimensional blind spots" — overlooked dimensions of human preference that compromise the reliability of reward and preference signals for LLM evaluation and optimization.

Method: A training-free, reference-free framework (MRRG) that: (1) elicits evaluation criteria from multiple complementary roles/perspectives, (2) consolidates these criteria into a unified auditable rubric-based scorer, (3) uses the scorer for pairwise preference validation and as a reward signal for GRPO-style Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).

Result: MRRG consistently outperforms single-role rubric generation baselines on preference validation benchmarks across multiple backbone models. In RLVR experiments, MRRG provides stronger reward signals that improve open-ended generation quality.

Conclusion: Multi-role elicitation effectively mitigates dimensional blind spots in rubric generation, yielding more reliable and comprehensive evaluation criteria that benefit both preference judgment and RL-based LLM optimization.

Abstract: Reliable reward and preference signals are critical for evaluating and optimizing large language models on open-ended tasks. Rubric-based judges offer a transparent way to decompose such judgments into explicit evaluation criteria, but existing annotation-free rubric generators typically rely on a single generic evaluator. As a result, they may overlook important dimensions of human preference, a failure mode we term dimensional blind spots. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-Role Rubric Generation (MRRG), a training-free and reference-free framework that elicits evaluation criteria from multiple complementary roles and consolidates them into an auditable rubric-based scorer. This scorer can be used both to validate pairwise preferences and to provide rewards for GRPO-style Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). Experiments on preference validation benchmarks show that MRRG consistently outperforms single-role rubric generation baselines across multiple backbone models. Further RLVR experiments demonstrate that MRRG yields a stronger reward signal for improving open-ended generation.

</details>


### [200] [Adaptive Group-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Time-Series Rehabilitation Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01838)
*Emmanuel C. Chukwu,Rianne M. Schouten,Monique Tabak,Mykola Pechenizkiy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage framework for group-based counterfactual explanations in multivariate IMU time-series. Shapley-Adaptive ranking preserves validity but lacks group sparsity; Learnable Gate methods with jointly optimized relevance gates achieve superior modality-group sparsity, temporal smoothness, and clinically aligned corrective guidance on rehabilitation data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinicians interpret rehabilitation movement via semantic muscle-group and joint-segment abstractions, but existing channel-level counterfactual methods produce scattered, biomechanically incoherent explanations that are hard to interpret in clinical practice.

Method: A two-stage framework: (1) Shapley-Adaptive (SA) group ranking to assess whether ranking alone can enforce group sparsity while preserving validity; (2) Learnable Gate (LG) methods that introduce trainable per-group relevance gates jointly optimized with perturbation masks to explicitly select salient groups. Evaluated on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset with multi-sensor IMU data.

Result: SA ranking preserves counterfactual validity but fails to achieve group-level sparsity. LG methods substantially improve modality-group sparsity over the M-CELS channel-level baseline while maintaining or improving validity, temporal smoothness, and generation efficiency. Exercise-specific analyses yield concise, muscle-level corrective guidance aligned with clinical reasoning.

Conclusion: Group-structured counterfactual generation enhances interpretability without sacrificing counterfactual quality, enabling more actionable explanations for rehabilitation movement analysis and bridging the gap between channel-level explanations and clinician reasoning.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CEs) for multivariate time-series classifiers are often difficult to interpret in domains where experts reason in terms of semantic feature groups rather than individual channels. In rehabilitation movement analysis with multi-sensor inertial measurement units (IMUs), clinicians interpret motion through muscle-group and joint-segment abstractions; yet, most existing counterfactual methods operate at the channel level, producing scattered and biomechanically incoherent explanations. We propose a two-stage framework for group-based counterfactual generation in high-dimensional IMU data. We first show that Shapley-Adaptive (SA) group ranking preserves counterfactual validity but fails to enforce group-level sparsity, motivating the need for explicit group selection. We then introduce Learnable Gate (LG) methods, which incorporate trainable per-group relevance gates jointly optimized with perturbation masks. Experiments on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset demonstrate that LG substantially improves modality-group sparsity compared to the channel-level M-CELS baseline while maintaining or improving validity, temporal smoothness, and generation efficiency. Exercise-specific analyses further show that group-structured counterfactuals yield concise, muscle-level corrective guidance aligned with clinical reasoning. Overall, the proposed framework enhances interpretability without sacrificing counterfactual quality, enabling more actionable explanations for rehabilitation movement analysis.

</details>


### [201] [Decomposer: Learning to Decompile Symbolic Music to Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01849)
*Yewon Kim,Apurva Gandhi,David Chung,Graham Neubig,Chris Donahue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decomposer is a post-training framework that recovers executable Strudel music programs from symbolic MIDI input, combining supervised fine-tuning on a synthetic corpus (Strudel-Synth) with reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI to optimize both reconstruction faithfulness and code readability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recovering high-level musical instructions (executable, editable programs) from symbolic music performances is a challenging inverse problem. Strudel, as a low-resource music programming language, lacks naturally paired MIDI-code data, and naive optimization for faithful MIDI reconstruction leads to unreadable note-by-note transliteration rather than structured, editable programs.

Method: A two-stage post-training approach: (1) Construct Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus of paired Strudel programs and their rendered MIDI, used for supervised fine-tuning; (2) Apply reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI data with rewards that jointly optimize for MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability/diversity.

Result: Decomposer achieves substantially higher MIDI reconstruction faithfulness compared to closed-source LLMs, while producing code that is more readable and diverse than output from heuristic converters, as evaluated on both synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks.

Conclusion: The two-stage post-training framework effectively addresses the decompilation of symbolic music into editable programs even in low-resource language settings, balancing reconstruction accuracy with code quality through synthetic data and RL-based refinement.

Abstract: Musical performance involves executing a set of high-level musical instructions, yet recovering those instructions from the performance is a challenging inverse problem. We present Decomposer, a post-training framework for symbolic music decompilation: the task of recovering executable, editable music programs from symbolic music. We instantiate the task as MIDI-to-Strudel decompilation, where the model takes symbolic MIDI as input and produces a program in Strudel, a music programming language, that reconstructs the input when executed. The task poses two challenges: Strudel is a low-resource language with little naturally paired MIDI-code data, and optimizing faithful reconstruction of MIDI alone can collapse to unreadable note-by-note transliteration. We address these challenges in two stages. First, we construct Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus of paired Strudel programs and rendered MIDI, and use it for supervised fine-tuning. Second, we refine the model with reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI, optimizing rewards for both MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability. Our evaluation across synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks shows that Decomposer achieves substantially higher MIDI reconstruction faithfulness than closed-source LLMs while producing more readable and diverse code than the heuristic converter.

</details>


### [202] [Learning the Supports for Categorical Critic in Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01880)
*Jen-Yen Chang,Takayuki Osa,Tatsuya Harada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a dynamic support-learning method for histogram-based distributional RL (HL-Gauss) that jointly learns the support bounds and categorical value representation, forming a tighter upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error than fixed-support HL-Gauss, and matches or improves performance on continuous-control tasks without requiring a pre-specified support interval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HL-Gauss reframes value regression as classification by encoding scalar Bellman targets as Gaussian-smoothed categorical targets, but requires pre-defining a fixed support interval. This is problematic in RL due to non-stationary and stochastic target values, making prior specification of bounds difficult and potentially suboptimal.

Method: The authors derive an objective that jointly learns the lower and upper support bounds alongside the categorical value representation. They prove this objective forms an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error, and theoretically show this bound is tighter than that of HL-Gauss with a fixed, non-learned support.

Result: The proposed method enables stable adaptation of the support interval and matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control tasks while improving performance on a subset, all without requiring a manually pre-specified support interval.

Conclusion: Dynamically learning the support bounds for histogram-based distributional value functions is both theoretically sound (tighter upper bound) and empirically effective, eliminating a key practical limitation of HL-Gauss in RL.

Abstract: Value functions are an essential component in actor-critic based deep reinforcement learning (RL). Conventionally, these functions are trained as a regression task by minimising the mean squared error (MSE) relative to bootstrapped target values. Meanwhile, in distributional RL, a distribution of returns is modelled based on the distributional Bellman operator. This work investigates the Gaussian Histogram Loss (HL-Gauss), a recent approach that reframes value estimation as classification by encoding each scalar Bellman target as a Gaussian-smoothed categorical target. Despite its potential, applying histogram-based losses to RL presents inherent challenges, most notably the requirement to pre-define a fixed support interval, which is often complicated by the non-stationary and stochastic nature of target values typically found in RL tasks. In this work, we propose an approach that dynamically learns the lower and upper bounds of the support instead of assigning them beforehand. We derive an objective that jointly learns these bounds whilst learning the categorical representation of the scalar values, and we show that this objective forms an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error. Our theoretical analysis further shows that this bound is tighter than that of non-learned supports of HL-Gauss. Empirically, the proposed objective enables stable adaptation of the support interval and matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control tasks whilst improving on a subset, without requiring a pre-specified support interval.

</details>


### [203] [Regularized Variational and Spectral Log-Density-Ratio Estimation in the Gaussian Location Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01895)
*Francis Bach*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares two estimators for log-density-ratio estimation under ridge regularization in a Gaussian location model: a variational KL-based estimator and a spectral estimator. It derives high-dimensional asymptotic equivalents for both, showing the variational estimator is better with many observations, while the spectral estimator is favored in low-data regimes due to lower variance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Log-density-ratio estimation is a fundamental task in statistics and machine learning (e.g., for two-sample testing, classification, and generative modeling). The paper seeks to rigorously compare two competing regularized estimation approaches — variational (KL-based) and spectral (moment-based) — in high-dimensional settings where both sample size and dimension grow proportionally. Understanding which estimator performs better under different sample-size regimes is the core motivation.

Method: The authors work in the Gaussian location model with common covariance, reduced by affine invariance to q ~ N(0,I), p ~ N(Δ,I). They analyze: (1) a variational estimator minimizing empirical KL divergence with an L2 penalty on the nonconstant coefficient, and (2) a spectral estimator from [1] that solves a continuum of ridge-regularized least-squares problems. High-dimensional asymptotic equivalents are derived: the variational limit via the Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem (CGMT), yielding a scalar entropy minimization; the spectral limit via deterministic equivalents for resolvents of weighted sums of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices. Population risks are compared under fixed-signal aspect-ratio sweeps with optimized regularization. Nuclear-norm penalization is also explored for feature learning.

Result: In the well-specified setting, the variational estimator achieves lower population risk when observations are abundant. The spectral estimator is favored in the low-observation regime because its covariance-based construction has intrinsically lower variance. The nuclear penalty extension offers a partial analysis pathway for feature learning, though full theoretical treatment remains open.

Conclusion: There is no uniformly superior estimator: the choice between variational and spectral approaches depends on the sample-size-to-dimension ratio. The variational estimator benefits from correct model specification when data are plentiful, while the spectral estimator's moment-based construction provides robustness through reduced variance when data are scarce. Nuclear penalization offers a promising direction for incorporating structure beyond isotropic regularization.

Abstract: We study ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimation in the Gaussian location model with a common covariance matrix. By affine invariance, the model is written as q $\sim$ N(0, I), p $\sim$ N($Δ$, I), with linear features, where $Δ$ is a mean vector. The variational estimator is the empirical Kullback-Leibler (KL) log-normalized fit with a squared L2-penalty on its nonconstant coefficient, and the spectral estimator recently introduced in [1] replaces a single variational problem by a continuum of ridge-regularized least-squares problems. We derive high-dimensional deterministic asymptotic equivalents when the numbers of observations and dimension tend to infinity with fixed ratios. The regularized variational limit is characterized by a scalar entropy minimization problem derived from the convex-Gaussian-min-max theorem (CGMT), while the regularized spectral limit follows from deterministic equivalents for resolvents of weighted sums of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices. We use these formulas to compare population risks, with experiments focused on fixed-signal aspect-ratio sweeps and optimized regularization. Our conclusion is that with many observations, under the criteria and asymptotic regimes analyzed here, the well-specified variational estimator has the smaller risk, while with fewer observations, the spectral estimator is favored because its covariance-based construction has lower variance. We also study how a nuclear penalty can be used and partially analyzed to perform feature learning.

</details>


### [204] [Rank-Then-Act: Reward-Free Control from Frame-Order Progress](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01897)
*Yuriy Maksyuta,George Bredis,Ruslan Rakhimov,Daniil Gavrilov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RTA learns control policies from expert videos by training a VLM as a progress scorer via ordinal ranking, then uses Spearman correlation between predicted and true frame indices as a reinforcement learning reward, achieving strong results on discrete and continuous control benchmarks without environment rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning control policies from expert demonstrations without explicit environment rewards is challenging. Existing video-based methods often rely on absolute scalar rewards that suffer from calibration issues and poor transfer. The authors aim to replace explicit reward design with a scalable, ordinal supervision signal derived purely from video progress rankings.

Method: The framework has two stages: (1) Offline VLM training using GRPO over shuffled frame sequences to produce a progress-based ordinal scorer that recovers temporal ordering from visual semantics. (2) A correlation-based reward function for RL where Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices over an interaction window yields a bounded, scale-invariant reward signal, decoupling reward learning from absolute calibration.

Result: RTA matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines on discrete control (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control (PointMaze, MetaWorld) benchmarks. A single pretrained progress scorer transfers effectively across tasks.

Conclusion: Correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design with strong cross-task transfer properties.

Abstract: We introduce Rank-Then-Act (RTA), a framework for learning control policies from expert video demonstrations without environment rewards. RTA trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) offline as a progress-based ordinal scorer, using a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective over shuffled frame sequences, which forces the model to recover temporal ordering from visual semantics rather than trivial time cues. Importantly, instead of using the scorer directly as a scalar reward model, we propose a correlation-based reward function for reinforcement learning: at each interaction window, we compute the Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices, yielding a bounded, scale-invariant learning signal. This design decouples reward learning from absolute calibration and enables stable transfer across tasks and environments. We evaluate RTA on discrete control benchmarks (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control tasks (PointMaze, MetaWorld). RTA consistently matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines, while demonstrating strong cross-task reuse of a single pretrained progress scorer. Our results suggest that correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design.

</details>


### [205] [SABER: A Semantic-Aligned Brain Network Analysis Framework via Multi-scale Hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01901)
*Yidan Xu,Xiangmin Han,Rundong Xue,Huihui Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A semantic-aligned brain network framework that integrates LLM-derived semantics at ROI-level, multi-scale hypergraph, and decision-level alignment stages, achieving SOTA on ABIDE and ADHD-200 with improved stability and interpretability, especially in small-sample settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing brain disease diagnosis methods treat LLM-derived semantics merely as auxiliary features or supervision, limiting their direct role in decision-making and constraining classification stability and robustness.

Method: The proposed framework operates in three stages: (1) ROI-level semantic incorporation via global self-attention to enrich node representations with whole-brain context; (2) multi-scale hypergraph construction to explicitly model functional subnetworks and multi-ROI interactions, overcoming locality limitations of traditional GNNs and capturing high-order dependencies; (3) a decision-level semantic alignment mechanism that selectively injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations, allowing semantics to directly guide predictions without perturbing the underlying network structure.

Result: Experiments on public brain network datasets ABIDE and ADHD-200 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, enhanced stability, and improved interpretability, with particularly strong results in small-sample settings.

Conclusion: The proposed semantic-aligned brain network framework effectively bridges brain connectivity patterns with high-level semantic knowledge from LLMs, enabling semantics to directly participate in decision-making. This yields superior diagnostic performance, robustness, and interpretability compared to approaches that relegate semantics to auxiliary roles.

Abstract: Effective brain disease diagnosis requires the synergy of brain connectivity patterns and high-level semantic knowledge. Existing methods, however, largely treat semantics from large language models (LLMs) as auxiliary features or supervision, limiting their direct role in decision-making and constraining classification stability and robustness. To overcome this, we propose a semantic-aligned brain network framework that actively integrates LLM-derived semantics into the prediction process. Specifically, ROI-level semantics are first incorporated via global self-attention to enrich node representations and provide whole-brain context. Multi-scale hypergraphs are then constructed to explicitly model functional subnetworks and multi-ROI interactions, addressing the locality limitations of traditional GNNs and capturing high-order dependencies. Finally, a decision-level semantic alignment mechanism selectively injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations, enabling semantics to directly guide predictions without perturbing the underlying network structure. Experiments on public brain network datasets ABIDE and ADHD-200 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, enhanced stability, and improved interpretability, particularly in small-sample settings.

</details>


### [206] [Population-Based Multi-Objective Training of Discriminators for Semi-Supervised GANs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01907)
*Francisco Sedeño,Francisco Chicano,Jamal Toutouh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an evolutionary multi-objective training strategy for semi-supervised GANs, maintaining a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance to balance classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination, demonstrating improved robustness on MNIST with limited labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training of semi-supervised GANs (SSL-GANs) is often unstable due to the difficulty of balancing the supervised classification loss and the unsupervised adversarial loss within a single scalar objective. The authors aim to address this instability by reformulating discriminator learning to better serve both roles: accurate classification and effective real/fake discrimination for generator training.

Method: The method frames discriminator learning as a multi-objective optimization problem with two objectives: (1) supervised classification accuracy on labeled data, and (2) unsupervised real/fake discrimination on both labeled and unlabeled data. A population of discriminators is maintained and ranked using Pareto dominance, allowing diverse trade-offs between the two objectives. Variants include an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation to isolate the effect of multi-objective selection.

Result: Experiments on MNIST with limited labeled samples show that the proposed approach yields improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN baselines. The elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy among all tested configurations.

Conclusion: Multi-objective evolutionary optimization provides a viable and effective alternative to scalarized loss aggregation in SSL-GAN training, leading to more stable training and better classifier performance, particularly with the elitist selection strategy.

Abstract: Semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (SSL-GANs) can exploit large unlabeled datasets while retaining a classifier in the discriminator, but their training is often unstable. This paper proposes a population-based evolutionary training strategy in which discriminator learning is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem. Instead of aggregating the supervised and unsupervised components of the SSL objective into a single scalar loss, the method maintains a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance, enabling the exploration of different trade-offs between classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination. This formulation aims to improve both roles of SSL-GANs: learning accurate classifiers and training generators capable of producing realistic samples. We analyze several variants, including an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation, to assess the role of multi-objective selection. Experiments on MNIST with limited labels show improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN state-of-the-art baselines, while the elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy.

</details>


### [207] [Zeus: Towards Tuning-Free Foundation Model for Time Series Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01918)
*Yisong Fu,Zezhi Shao,Chengqing Yu,Yujie Li,Yongjun Xu,Xueqi Cheng,Fei Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Zeus is a tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model using a multi-scale Transformer with U-shaped hierarchy and Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM) to handle heterogeneous tasks (forecasting, imputation, classification, etc.) without task-specific fine-tuning, achieving competitive zero-shot performance across five tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TS foundation models excel at zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific fine-tuning for other tasks (e.g., imputation, classification). Zeus aims to bridge this gap by enabling a single unified model to generalize across diverse time series tasks in a completely tuning-free manner.

Method: Zeus combines two key innovations: (1) a multi-scale Transformer with point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy to balance fine-grained fidelity with long-sequence computational efficiency; (2) Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified pretraining strategy that accommodates heterogeneous task inductive biases — extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction — within a single framework.

Result: Extensive experiments across five representative time series tasks show that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free settings, matching or outperforming task-specific models without any fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Zeus demonstrates strong potential as a general-purpose Time Series Foundation Model, proving that a single tuning-free architecture can unify diverse time series analysis tasks by addressing multi-scale representation and heterogeneous inductive biases.

Abstract: We present Zeus, a unified tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) that delivers superior performance across diverse analysis tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike prior studies that primarily focus on zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other tasks, Zeus bridges this gap by addressing two fundamental challenges in multi-task generalization. First, to reconcile point-level granularity with long-sequence scalability, Zeus incorporates a multi-scale Transformer featuring point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy, effectively balancing fine-grained fidelity with computational efficiency. Second, to accommodate varying inductive biases across different tasks, Zeus introduces Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified strategy that supports heterogeneous tasks (e.g., extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction) within a single framework. Extensive experiments across five representative tasks demonstrate that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free settings, underscoring its potential as a general-purpose TSFM.

</details>


### [208] [Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01940)
*Zhiren Gong,Zihao Zeng,Chau Yuen,Wei Yang Bryan Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Standard first-order ablation scoring fails when models self-repair using dormant backup components. The authors propose Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free conditional scoring method that measures how much a unit's ablation effect grows after a primary set is removed, exposing second-order interactions. CoAx achieves 0.91 ROC-AUC on GPT-2-small IOI backup recovery (vs. 0.33 baseline), transfers across eight models, and improves attribution, capability knockout, and structured pruning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer models exhibit self-repair: when a primary component is ablated, dormant backup components activate to compensate. First-order ablation scoring—measuring each unit's effect in isolation—fails to identify these backups because they appear irrelevant in the intact model and their importance only emerges after the primary is removed. This leads to misleading component importance estimates, particularly problematic for circuit discovery, capability knockout, and model pruning.

Method: The authors reframe backup discovery as "conditional circuit completion" and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx). CoAx is a label-free, output-grounded score that quantifies how much each remaining unit's ablation effect increases once a primary set has been removed. Specifically, it measures the conditional growth in ablation effect: Δ = effect(ablate unit | primary removed) − effect(ablate unit | intact model). This captures second-order interactions that single-unit scores discard. The method requires no labeled data and uses only output distributional change as the signal.

Result: On the GPT-2-small Indirect Object Identification (IOI) circuit, CoAx achieves 0.91 ROC-AUC for backup-head recovery, dramatically outperforming the first-order baseline (0.33) and self-repair-aware gradient-based scores (best 0.82). Counterfactual patching confirms the recovered heads causally carry the repair. CoAx transfers successfully to induction-head backup discovery across eight models. The recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify components essential for capability knockout, and enable repair-aware structured pruning from 124M to 7B parameter scales.

Conclusion: Component importance is not merely an isolated-unit property. In robust circuits with self-repair mechanisms, the components that truly matter can only become visible under the interventions that make them necessary. Conditional interaction scoring like CoAx is essential for accurate mechanistic interpretability in transformer models, with practical implications for attribution, knockout, and pruning.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability often relies on component-level interventions to discover how a model produces a behavior. This guides attribution, capability knockout, and model pruning downstream to operate by scoring each unit by the effect of ablation in isolation. Such first-order scoring is natural when component importance is additive, but becomes misleading when a transformer self-repairs: after a primary component is removed, a dormant backup can take over, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup itself appears irrelevant on the intact model. We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed. This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

</details>


### [209] [Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sentiment analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01943)
*Giacomo Cappiello,Filippo Caruso,Xing Liang,Dimitrios Makris*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid quantum-classical neural networks achieve comparable accuracy to classical models on COVID-19 tweet sentiment analysis and significantly outperform them in transfer learning to SMS spam detection (+15pp on spam class), suggesting richer representational capacity and better generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum machine learning (QML) offers potential advantages via the expressive power of parameterized quantum circuits, but its applicability to real-world NLP tasks like sentiment analysis remains underexplored. This work investigates whether hybrid quantum-classical architectures can match or exceed classical performance on text classification, and whether they exhibit distinct and beneficial learning dynamics.

Method: Text from a COVID-19 tweets dataset is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward neural networks and hybrid models that integrate parameterized quantum circuits into the architecture.
