The models are evaluated on in-domain sentiment analysis and then further assessed via transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task to probe generalization capability.

Result: Hybrid models achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline on the primary sentiment analysis task while displaying distinct learning dynamics in validation loss and accuracy, suggesting richer representational capacity. In the transfer learning setting, hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, raising spam-class accuracy from 66% to 81% — a 15-percentage-point improvement, indicating enhanced generalization.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of using QML for NLP tasks and suggest that hybrid quantum-classical models may offer generalization advantages, with further potential as quantum hardware continues to mature.

Abstract: Quantum machine learning has recently emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages the expressive power of quantum circuits to address complex learning tasks. In this work, we investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in natural language processing. We focus on a dataset of tweets related to COVID-19, where the textual content is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Our results show that hybrid models can achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline, while exhibiting distinct learning dynamics, especially in terms of validation loss and accuracy, that suggest a richer representational capacity. Moreover, when applying transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task, the hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, achieving an accuracy increase of 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class, demonstrating enhanced generalization. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing QML for natural language processing and point toward the potential advantages of hybrid models as quantum hardware continues to advance.

</details>


### [210] [A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01958)
*Koki Konishi,Masataka Ushiku,Yuta Saito*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A/B testing can paradoxically yield higher algorithm selection error than offline evaluation because its sample mean estimator lacks positive correlation between estimates. The authors propose a novel estimator that introduces a hypothetical middle algorithm and uses stepwise shared-data estimation to induce beneficial correlation, halving the required A/B testing data while maintaining the same selection accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline evaluation is safer than A/B testing but suffers from lower estimation accuracy, so final decisions still rely on A/B testing. The authors challenge this conventional wisdom by revealing that A/B testing can actually produce higher selection error rates due to the absence of positive correlation in its estimator, and seek to improve A/B testing-based algorithm selection.

Method: The proposed estimator introduces a hypothetical middle algorithm M and estimates performance differences (A vs. M, M vs. B) stepwise using shared data at each step, analogous to offline evaluation techniques. This intentionally induces positive correlation between estimates, reducing critical selection errors (underestimating superior algorithms and overestimating inferior ones). The optimal middle algorithm is derived via variance analysis, and bias-variance trade-offs are analyzed relative to existing methods.

Result: Experiments on real-world data show the proposed estimator achieves the same selection error rate as conventional A/B testing approaches while requiring only 50% of the data.

Conclusion: Positive correlation between performance estimates is critical for reducing selection errors in algorithm comparison, and it can be intentionally engineered in A/B testing through stepwise estimation with a middle algorithm. This significantly improves data efficiency without sacrificing selection accuracy.

Abstract: A/B testing is the gold standard for selecting the better algorithm in online services. While offline evaluation has attracted attention as a safer alternative due to the high experimental costs and the potential risk of degrading user experience and revenue in A/B testing, it is widely recognized that the estimation accuracy of offline evaluation is substantially lower. As a result, final selection decisions are typically made through A/B testing. Contrary to this conventional view, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon in which A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation. This occurs because the sample mean estimator used in A/B testing does not induce positive correlation, which is crucial for reducing critical selection errors, namely underestimating the truly superior algorithm and overestimating the truly inferior one. In contrast, offline evaluation methods unintentionally generate this beneficial correlation by relying on shared offline data when estimating and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms. Building on this insight, we propose an estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation to improve algorithm selection in A/B testing. The key idea is to introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm and to estimate the performance difference between algorithms A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This approach enables the application of offline evaluation techniques in each step, thereby inducing positive correlation and reducing critical selection errors. Furthermore, we derive the optimal middle algorithm regarding the resulting variance and analyze its advantages over existing methods through bias-variance analysis. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.

</details>


### [211] [Probabilistic Low-Voltage Peak Load Forecasting with Time Series Foundation Models Evaluated on Application-Oriented Metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01966)
*Benedikt Kaas,Manuel Treutlein,Hannes Benedikt Gerber,Oliver Neumann,Cheewan Phatthanakhuha,Oliver Resch,Ralf Mikut,Veit Hagenmeyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The study evaluates short-term net load forecasting for 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, comparing Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, and TabPFN-TS against six baselines. Chronos-2 performs best; foundation models adapt well under missing weather covariates. A new application-oriented metric connects peak prediction quality to grid planning cost-risk trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current low-voltage load forecasting methods demand substantial manual effort, lack uncertainty quantification and reliable peak prediction, and are rarely evaluated against real grid operational requirements. With increasing electrification and decentralized generation, robust and automated forecasting is critical for distribution grid planning and operation.

Method: The authors benchmark three time series foundation models — Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, and TabPFN-TS — against six conventional baseline models on short-term net load forecasting across 200 real-world low-voltage feeders. An ablation study removes weather covariates to assess model robustness to increased uncertainty. They also introduce a novel application-oriented metric that directly links peak forecasting accuracy to the cost-versus-failure-risk trade-off in grid asset planning and operation.

Result: Chronos-2 achieves superior overall forecasting performance among all tested models. The ablation study reveals that time series foundation models effectively adapt to the increased uncertainty when weather covariates are omitted, despite weather information being important. The proposed metric successfully captures the practical implications of peak forecast errors for grid planning.

Conclusion: Time series foundation models, particularly Chronos-2, represent a promising direction for low-voltage net load forecasting, offering strong predictive accuracy, inherent adaptability under uncertainty, and reduced manual effort. The application-oriented evaluation framework provides a meaningful bridge between forecast quality and real-world grid decision-making.

Abstract: Low-voltage load forecasting is an important component in current and future energy systems with a high degree of electrification and decentralized generation. However, current forecasting methods require significant manual effort, often lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and they are often not adequately evaluated in terms of grid requirements. In the present study, we provide an extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts of 200 real-world low-voltage feeders with a focus on the rapidly evolving time series foundation models. Our study compares Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to six baseline models and demonstrates superior performance, in particular for Chronos-2. An ablation study, in which weather covariates are omitted, shows that time series foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty, despite the importance of weather information. A novel application-oriented metric links the model's forecasting capabilities in peak prediction to the trade-off in grid asset planning and operation between cost reduction and minimizing the risk of failure.

</details>


### [212] [Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01984)
*Tasnim Shahriar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A controlled comparison of nine lightweight CNN architectures across three datasets reveals that newer models provide selective rather than universal gains. EfficientNet-B0 emerges as the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option, appearing on every accuracy-resource Pareto frontier, while EfficientNetV2-S and RepViT-M1.0 lead on specific datasets. GMACs do not reliably predict measured latency across different hardware environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Claims that newer lightweight CNNs improve both predictive performance and deployment efficiency lack rigorous controlled evaluation. The authors aim to provide a systematic, apples-to-apples comparison under a shared downstream protocol to identify which architectures deliver genuine, consistent gains versus situational advantages.

Method: Nine lightweight CNN model packages (including EfficientNet variants, MobileNet variants, RepViT, and SqueezeNet) are compared on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet using a unified downstream training protocol. Metrics include top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency (on NVIDIA L4 GPU and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU), peak CUDA allocated tensor memory, and Pareto frontier analysis. Both pretrained and random-initialization (scratch) training regimes are evaluated.

Result: EfficientNetV2-S achieves highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%); RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 trails the best by only 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 points while using ~79% fewer parameters and ~86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S, appearing on every Pareto frontier. MobileNetV3-Small surpasses MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all datasets (gains of 2.55, 1.76, 0.99 points under random init). EfficientNet-B0 pretrained advantage is substantial (3.29–17.54 points over scratch training). SqueezeNet1.1 has fewest parameters and lowest CUDA memory but weakest accuracy. Latency rankings diverge significantly between L4 GPU and CPU environments.

Conclusion: Newer lightweight CNN designs provide selective rather than universal improvements. EfficientNet-B0 represents the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget choice. GMACs are an unreliable proxy for real-world inference latency, and practitioners should benchmark on target hardware. Pretraining confers substantial accuracy advantages that scratch training cannot recover even with extended epochs.

Abstract: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

</details>


### [213] [Liquid Latent State Dynamics for Interpretable Turbofan Degradation Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01986)
*Weizhi Nie,Weijie Wang,Yuting Su*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a liquid neural network with a disentangled latent state for aircraft engine prognostics, separating degradation from operating conditions. It improves sensor forecasting and learns a more interpretable degradation trajectory, though RUL regression still favors a GRU baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multivariate time-series prognostics models are evaluated on point prediction accuracy but fail to learn coherent, interpretable internal degradation processes. There is a need for latent dynamics models that both forecast accurately and expose a meaningful health-state representation.

Method: A liquid neural network encodes a sensor history window into a latent state factorized into degradation and condition components. The degradation component is supervised by RUL, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses; the condition component uses condition prediction and decorrelation losses to prevent operating-condition leakage. Evaluation uses the C-MAPSS benchmark (FD001–FD004) with sensor forecasting RMSE, degradation-axis Spearman correlation, and RUL regression as metrics.

Result: The disentangled liquid model reduces overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 (GRU baseline) to 0.2266, with largest gains on multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The degradation state achieves an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960, indicating a clearer temporal degradation axis. However, direct RUL regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline.

Conclusion: Liquid latent dynamics with disentanglement can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and interpretable health-state modeling. The approach is more effective as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor, suggesting promise for inspectable prognostics.

Abstract: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated by point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process. We study liquid neural networks as latent dynamics models for aircraft engine health monitoring on the C-MAPSS benchmark. The proposed model encodes a history window into a latent state, evolves that state with a liquid transition model, and decodes future sensor observations. To separate health evolution from operating-condition variation, the latent state is factorized into degradation and condition components. Remaining useful life, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses supervise the degradation component, while condition prediction and decorrelation losses discourage operating-condition leakage. Across FD001--FD004, the full disentangled model improves overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 for a GRU baseline to 0.2266, with the largest gains on the multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state also forms a clearer temporal degradation axis, reaching an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct remaining-useful-life regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, indicating that the proposed representation is currently more effective as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor. These results suggest that liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling.

</details>


### [214] [Fast and Accurate Anomaly Detection in Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02046)
*Emanuele Mele,Massimo Cafaro,Angelo Coluccia,Italo Epicoco*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm for time series is proposed, combining Haar discrete wavelet transform with a specially designed t-test. It is theoretically grounded and experimentally validated across 343 datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world anomaly detection suffers from severe class imbalance (anomalies are rare) and a scarcity of labeled anomalous data, making supervised methods impractical. Unsupervised methods avoid labeling but often produce high false positive rates in safety-critical applications. There is a need for an unsupervised method that is both theoretically sound and empirically robust.

Method: The authors propose an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm for time series data that leverages the Haar discrete wavelet transform for signal decomposition and a custom-designed t-test for statistical anomaly scoring. The theoretical properties of the t-test are formally established.

Result: Extensive experimentation across 343 datasets shows the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.

Conclusion: The Haar wavelet-based t-test method provides a theoretically grounded, effective unsupervised solution for time series anomaly detection, achieving superior performance over existing approaches on a large-scale empirical evaluation.

Abstract: Anomaly detection is a critical and evolving field in Machine Learning, with applications targeting different domains such as cybersecurity, finance, healthcare, manufacturing and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. Traditionally, anomaly detection algorithms have been designed using both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. The fundamental challenge in real-world anomaly detection scenarios is related to the inherent class imbalance (anomalies are typically rare) and, for supervised methods, to the scarcity of labelled anomalous data. Indeed, labelling is both expensive and time-consuming. Conversely unsupervised methods do not require labelling, but may suffer from high false positive rates when deployed in safety-critical applications. In this work we introduce a novel unsupervised algorithm for anomaly detection in time series based on the Haar discrete wavelet and a suitably designed $t$-test. We establish the theoretical foundation of the proposed $t$-test and, through extensive experimentation across 343 datasets, demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.

</details>


### [215] [A Memory Efficient Unified Algorithm for Online Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02050)
*Yuval Ran-Milo,Angelos Assos,Elad Hazan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies online prediction for unknown linear dynamical systems (LDS), focusing on systems with low "instability complexity" (k unstable/non-semisimple modes). The authors present a unified algorithm using only Õ(k) learnable parameters and prove matching lower bounds, showing k is the right complexity measure. Experiments confirm superiority over prior methods at equal parameter budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stabilizing unknown LDS from observations is challenging. The authors aim to achieve sublinear regret in online prediction with memory adapting to intrinsic dynamical complexity rather than full state dimension. Crucially, they identify the regime of low instability complexity as both practically central and the only setting where stabilization is plausible (high instability complexity systems require exponentially large controls to stabilize).

Method: The authors propose a unified online learning algorithm for general LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex/exploding modes). The algorithm's learnable parameter count scales as Õ(k), where k counts eigenvalues outside the real stable interval plus non-semisimple modes. They also prove a lower bound showing any filter-based predictor requires at least k filters. Theoretical analysis is complemented by experiments on high-dimensional systems.

Result: The main results are: (1) a unified online prediction algorithm achieving sublinear regret with Õ(k) parameters for any LDS; (2) a proof that systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls; (3) a lower bound establishing k as a valid complexity measure for filter-based predictors; (4) experimental validation showing sharp outperformance over prior methods on high-dimensional systems at equal parameter budgets.

Conclusion: Prediction for stabilization is meaningful precisely when instability complexity k is small. The proposed algorithm achieves optimal parameter scaling in this regime, with k serving as a tight complexity measure. This bridges theory and practice for online LDS prediction under realistic constraints.

Abstract: Motivated by the challenge of stabilizing a general unknown linear dynamical system (LDS) from observations, we study the natural prerequisite of online prediction. Our goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics rather than the full hidden -- state dimension. We focus on the practically central regime of systems with low instability complexity -- eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, together with non-semisimple modes-potentially embedded in an otherwise stable real spectrum of much higher dimension; we write $k$ for this count. This regime is the primary setting in which stabilization is plausible: we show that many systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. Thus, prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when the instability complexity is small. Within this regime, we introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of $\widetilde{O}(k)$. Finally, we prove a lower bound showing that $k$ is a valid complexity measure: any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters. Experiments corroborate our theory: on a high-dimensional system, our predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget.

</details>


### [216] [Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation for Large Language Model Uncertainty Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02182)
*Jijie Zhang,Zhe Ren,Quan Zhang,Dandan Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DALorRA is a variational Bayesian sparse framework that performs uncertainty quantification at the rank level of LoRA by stochastically masking rank dimensions, achieving excellent calibration without sacrificing reasoning accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs fine-tuned for specific tasks suffer from overconfidence, which undermines trustworthy deployment. Existing LoRA methods may provide superfluous model capacity through redundant rank-one components, motivating a need for uncertainty quantification that is lightweight and effective.

Method: DALorRA operates on the insight that LoRA aggregates multiple rank-one components. It imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions within the LoRA framework, creating a variational Bayesian sparse approach. During training, this enables Bayesian regularization of model capacity; during inference, it provides ensemble-like calibration by leveraging the stochastic rank-level masks.

Result: Extensive experiments show that DALorRA achieves excellent calibration of LLMs while preserving reasoning accuracy, effectively mitigating the overconfidence problem inherent in task-specific fine-tuning.

Conclusion: DALorRA shifts uncertainty quantification from dense parameter space to a lightweight rank-level paradigm, offering a simple yet effective solution to the overconfidence problem in fine-tuned LLMs without compromising their reasoning performance.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning capabilities, but their task-specific fine-tuning is notoriously plagued by overconfidence, severely hindering trustworthy deployment. We propose Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a simple and effective variational Bayesian sparse framework that shifts the paradigm of uncertainty quantification from the dense parameter space to the lightweight rank level of low-rank adaptation (LoRA). With the insight that LoRA essentially aggregates multiple rank-one components that may provide superfluous model capacity, DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate DALorRA's excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy.

</details>


### [217] [Beyond the Performance Illusion: Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization for Spatially Correlated Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02055)
*Prathamesh Patil,Arpit Jain,Aswanth Krishnan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Random dataset splits fail in spatiotemporally correlated domains (e.g., aerial imagery, medical imaging), causing data leakage and hidden stratification. The paper proposes SASP for better validation splits and CDRO for robust training, together improving generalization, calibration, and failure-mode detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard i.i.d. random-split evaluation is inadequate for spatiotemporally correlated data, leading to (1) data leakage from correlated samples across train/val splits that inflates performance estimates, and (2) hidden stratification where aggregate metrics mask poor performance on minority subpopulations. These failures are prevalent in domains like aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging.

Method: The authors propose two complementary techniques: (1) Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that explicitly account for spatial and temporal correlation structures to minimize leakage while maintaining class balance; and (2) Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust optimization that stabilizes training under the stricter, more challenging splits produced by SASP.

Result: Across multiple benchmarks in spatiotemporally correlated domains, the SASP+CDRO combination consistently yields improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes that remain undetected under conventional random-split evaluation.

Conclusion: The i.i.d. assumption underlying standard evaluation protocols is fundamentally flawed for spatiotemporally correlated data. Adopting structure-aware partitioning and robust training remedies systematic evaluation failures and enables more trustworthy model assessment and deployment in real-world geospatial and temporal domains.

Abstract: Performance evaluation in AI systems commonly assumes that random dataset splits produce independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) subsets. We show that this assumption often breaks down in spatiotemporally correlated domains such as aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging, leading to two systematic failures: data leakage, where correlated samples span training and validation splits and inflate performance estimates, and hidden stratification, where errors on minority subpopulations are obscured by aggregate metrics. To address these issues, we propose a unified evaluation and training framework for spatially correlated data. We introduce Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that reduce spatiotemporal leakage while preserving meaningful class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training that stabilizes optimization under these stricter splits. Across multiple benchmarks, this combination yields consistently improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes that remain hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.

</details>


### [218] [SA-HGNN: Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network for EEG-Based Depression Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02063)
*Yang Li,Pan Hu,Yan Zhang,Wenfan Yang,Tao Wu,Lianbo Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes SA-HGNN, a model combining sample-adaptive graph construction, hyperbolic graph convolution, and attention pooling to better capture hierarchical functional connectivity in EEG-based depression recognition, outperforming existing methods on public datasets across both resting-state and task paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GNN-based EEG depression recognition methods struggle to capture the inherent hierarchical structure of functional connectivity in depressed brain networks, leading to inaccurate connection pattern extraction. Euclidean representations are insufficient for modeling such latent hierarchies.

Method: SA-HGNN consists of three modules: (1) Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction that dynamically builds personalized brain network topologies; (2) Hyperbolic Graph Convolution that leverages hyperbolic geometry to capture hierarchical relationships; (3) Attention Pooling that adaptively filters noisy EEG channels to preserve authentic hierarchical topology.

Result: Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets show superior performance over baselines across both resting-state and task-related paradigms, with demonstrated robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in depression.

Conclusion: SA-HGNN effectively models the hierarchical functional connectivity of depression-affected brain networks by combining hyperbolic geometry with sample-adaptive graph learning, validated through strong empirical results across multiple EEG paradigms.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely used to capture spatial functional connectivity patterns to improve electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression recognition performance. However, the functional connectivity of brain networks in patients with depression exhibits an inherent hierarchical structure, making it difficult to capture accurate connection patterns. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel model named Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN), which aims to accurately extract the authentic hierarchical structure of depression-affected brain networks. Specifically, the proposed model comprises three core modules. First, a Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction module dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies to capture more complex spatial relationships within the brain network. Second, hyperbolic graph convolution is employed to overcome the representation bottlenecks of Euclidean space, leveraging hyperbolic geometry to precisely capture latent hierarchical relationships within the brain network. Finally, an Attention Pooling module adaptively filters out highly redundant noise channels in EEG signals, effectively mitigating the interference of inherent noise on the authentic hierarchical topology. Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method across resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating its robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in brain networks of patients with depression.

</details>


### [219] [HERMES: A Multi-Granularity Labeling Substrate for Pre-training Data Mixtures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02266)
*Ziyun Qiao,Yue Min,Ruining Chen,Yujun Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HERMES introduces a hierarchical, data-derived labeling substrate using Learned Semantic Transform and residual vector quantization, enabling granularity-controllable document codes for data mixing. It demonstrates that optimal mixing strategies depend on granularity level, reframing data mixture design as navigating a reusable hierarchy rather than selecting fixed label sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing data-mixing methods rely on pre-partitioned corpora with fixed label systems (provenance, topic taxonomies, flat embedding clusters), which commit to one semantic axis at one granularity. Changing resolution requires rebuilding labels entirely. The authors argue the bottleneck is the rigid label system, not the mixer itself.

Method: HERMES uses a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization (RVQ) to annotate each document with a coarse-to-fine hierarchical code. The prefix length of this code controls granularity, supporting up to ~130k distinct cells. A specific mixing rule combining equal-subbucket coverage with size-proportional within-bucket quality selection (top-30%) is tested across granularity levels on a 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training setup.

Result: At coarse granularity, HERMES performs comparably to KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics. The hierarchical substrate reveals granularity-dependent mixing effects: at one prefix length, the combined mixing rule lifts a 16-task macro-average by +0.0253; at the next finer level (candidate pools contract ~5x), the same rule loses its measurable edge.

Conclusion: Data mixture design should be reframed from choosing among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy. The contribution lies in the hierarchical labeling substrate, not a superior clusterer.

Abstract: Most data-mixing methods assume the corpus has already been partitioned into groups, and the choice of those groups determines what a mixer can express. Existing labels, including provenance, topic or format taxonomies, and flat embedding clusters, commit to one semantic axis at one granularity; changing the resolution rebuilds the labels. We argue the bottleneck is the label system, not the mixer, and provide a hierarchical one. HERMES is a data-derived labeling substrate: a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization annotates each document once into a coarse-to-fine code whose prefix length controls granularity up to approximately 130k cells. At coarse granularity HERMES sits at a plateau with KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics, so the contribution is the substrate, not the clusterer. On 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training, the hierarchy exposes an interaction fixed-granularity pipelines cannot test: at one prefix length, a combined Stage-2 rule contrast, equal-subbucket coverage versus size-proportional within-bucket quality top-30%, lifts a 16-task capability macro-average by +0.0253; at the next finer level, the same rule loses its measurable edge as candidate pools contract approximately 5x. HERMES reframes data mixture design from choosing among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy.

</details>


### [220] [Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02088)
*Chelsea Maria John,Thibaut Lunet,Sebastian Götschel,Andreas Herten,Stefan Kesselheim,Daniel Ruprecht*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) that predicts time increments rather than full solutions for 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection, yielding a compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB), fast (7 ms inference) model with accuracy surpassing standard FNO baselines, while demonstrating that training data resolution fundamentally limits accuracy even when generalizing to finer meshes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard FNOs applied to Rayleigh-Bénard convection face accuracy limitations. The authors aim to improve prediction accuracy through a modified training strategy (predicting time increments) while maintaining compactness and inference speed, and to investigate how training data resolution affects generalization to finer grids.

Method: An improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architecture trained to predict time increments (Δt updates) rather than full-state solutions for two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection. The model is evaluated against a standard FNO baseline and tested for zero-shot super-resolution generalization to finer meshes, with systematic analysis of how training resolution constrains accuracy.

Result: The time-increment FNO achieves higher accuracy than the standard FNO baseline while being compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) with fast inference (7 ms). Accuracy matches previous benchmarks. Critically, while FNOs can generalize to finer discretizations, accuracy is fundamentally bounded by the resolution of the training data.

Conclusion: Predicting time increments with FNOs offers a simple yet effective modification that improves accuracy for Rayleigh-Bénard convection modeling. The resolution of training data is a hard constraint on achievable accuracy, even for mesh-invariant operator architectures like the FNO — super-resolution generalization does not overcome information lost at coarse training resolutions.

Abstract: We propose an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments instead of full solutions, achieving higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference), while maintaining similar accuracy as demonstrated in previous benchmarks. We show that although FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy remains limited by the resolution of the training data.

</details>


### [221] [Ask the Right Comparison:Bias-Aware Bayesian Active Top-$k$ Ranking with LLM Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02104)
*Jian Xu,Delu Zeng,John Paisley,Qibin Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM judges exhibit systematic biases (verbosity, position effects) that corrupt pairwise rankings. The paper introduces a Bayesian inference framework with judge-specific bias covariates and a top-k-aware active acquisition strategy, recovering true quality rankings on biased judges and achieving the correct top-k with far fewer comparisons than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM judges are increasingly used for pairwise comparison tasks (ranking, model selection, paper triage), but they are noisy and systematically biased toward verbose/well-formatted outputs and exhibit position effects. Naive aggregation of biased votes recovers a ranking of presentation style rather than true quality, motivating the need for debiased judgment methods.

Method: The approach has two components: (1) Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so data determine which biases each judge exhibits; (2) a top-k-aware active acquisition rule that selects the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about top-k membership rather than the full ranking.

Result: Evaluated on a controlled benchmark with ground-truth quality using 16 real LLMs (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus): naive aggregation plateaus at a wrong top-k on biased judges regardless of budget; bias-aware model recovers the correct top-k; top-k-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or D-optimal rules. Cheap/mid-tier judges exhibit strong verbosity bias (corrected recall from ~0.5–0.6 to 0.84–1.0), while frontier judges show little bias.

Conclusion: Bias in LLM judges is real, heterogeneous, and capability-dependent. The proposed bias-aware Bayesian framework effectively debiases cheaper judges, while frontier judges already rank accurately. The top-k-aware active acquisition strategy dramatically reduces the comparison budget needed to identify top-k items, making LLM-based judging more reliable and cost-effective.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as cheap, scalable judges that compare candidate outputs pairwise -- to rank responses, select models, or triage papers. Yet LLM judges are both noisy and systematically biased: they favor verbose or well-formatted answers and exhibit position effects, so simply aggregating their votes recovers a ranking of presentation, not of true quality. We study the practical goal of identifying the \topk{} items under a fixed comparison budget, and make two contributions. First, we cast judging as Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so that the data decide which biases a given judge actually exhibits. Second, we introduce a \topk-aware active acquisition rule that chooses the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about \topk{} \emph{membership}, rather than about the full ranking. On a controlled benchmark with known ground-truth quality, judged by sixteen real LLMs spanning open and proprietary families (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), naive aggregation plateaus at a wrong \topk{} on biased judges regardless of budget, while our bias-aware model recovers it; \topk-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or a global-uncertainty (D-optimal) rule. Bias is real but heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap and mid-tier judges carry a strong verbosity bias that our model corrects (lifting recall from $\sim$$0.5$--$0.6$ to $0.84$--$1.0$), whereas the frontier judges we tested show little bias and already rank accurately, so bias-aware modeling changes little there.

</details>


### [222] [Predictive Conformal Slip Monitoring: An Empirical Evaluation of Rolling Split Conformal Prediction for Pre-Incident Traction Loss Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02124)
*Varshith Roy Kotla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates a Rolling Split Conformal Prediction method for early warning of traction loss in motorsport, finding it fails completely — zero recall, zero precision against real incidents, with a 15.3% false-alarm rate — due to violated exchangeability assumptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional traction control only intervenes after adhesion loss occurs. The authors investigate whether a statistically principled, per-driver conformal prediction approach could provide pre-incident warning signals, enabling proactive rather than reactive intervention.

Method: Rolling Split Conformal Prediction is applied to non-conformity residuals from per-driver Random Forest models of expected slip behavior. Unlike prior work, vehicle speed is explicitly included as a feature (not implicit in the target denominator), all laps per driver are used (not just fastest), and evaluation uses real FIA Race Control incident labels and track-limits deletions. A rolling-volatility detector flags anomalous samples, benchmarked against a static 95th-percentile threshold baseline.

Result: Strictly negative. Across 19 drivers and 55,563 test samples, mean precision and recall are both essentially 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents. The detector flags 15.3% of all samples as anomalous — an unacceptably high false-alarm rate. The static baseline performs no better. Ljung-Box tests (p < 0.001 for all 19 drivers) confirm the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is universally violated.

Conclusion: The conformal-volatility approach offers no predictive utility for early traction-loss warning under these conditions. The fundamental failure is attributed to autocorrelated residuals breaking exchangeability. The authors frame this as a rigorous negative result and outline requirements for a genuinely predictive future approach.

Abstract: Conventional traction control architectures intervene only after the adhesion limit of a tire has already been breached. This paper investigates whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction , monitoring the volatility of non-conformity residuals from a per-driver Random Forest model of expected slip behavior , can serve as a statistically grounded pre-incident warning signal, ahead of gross traction loss. Unlike an earlier internal draft of this work, the evaluation reported here corrects a confound in the slip proxy (vehicle speed is included as an explicit model feature, not left implicit in the target's denominator), uses every racing lap for each driver rather than only the fastest lap, and is scored against real, timestamped incident labels extracted from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions rather than narrated post-hoc. The result is negative: across 19 drivers and 55,563 test-phase telemetry samples, the rolling-volatility detector achieves a mean precision of essentially 0.0 and mean recall of 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents, while flagging on average 15.3% of all samples as anomalous , too high a false-alarm rate for any early-warning use. A static 95th-percentile threshold baseline performs no better in any way that would justify the added complexity of the conformal-volatility formulation. Residual autocorrelation diagnostics show the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is violated for every driver (Ljung-Box p < 0.001, n = 19/19), which is one plausible driver of the high false-alarm rate. We report this as a methodologically rigorous negative finding, diagnose its likely causes, and outline what a genuinely predictive version of this approach would require.

</details>


### [223] [ART for Diffusion Sampling: Continuous-Time Control and Actor-Critic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02137)
*Yilie Huang,Wenpin Tang,Xun Yu Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ART-RL learns optimal timestep schedules for diffusion sampling by formulating schedule optimization as a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem, where a time-warping rate is learned to improve sample quality without changing the underlying sampler.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard diffusion sampling uses uniform or hand-crafted timestep schedules that are fixed and suboptimal. The authors aim to learn adaptive timestep allocation automatically, optimizing sample quality for a given computational budget.

Method: ART (Adaptive Reparameterized Time) formulates timestep allocation as a deterministic continuous-time control problem, treating the sampling clock speed as the control variable. ART-RL introduces an equivalent randomized formulation using Gaussian policies, transforming schedule learning into a continuous-time RL problem. Policy evaluation and improvement characterizations are derived, along with trajectory-based moment identities, yielding implementable actor-critic updates for learning the optimal time-warping schedule.

Result: Across controlled low-dimensional settings and image generation tasks, ART-RL consistently improves sample quality over strong baseline schedules (uniform, hand-crafted) at matched computational budgets. Learned schedules generalize broadly — transferring without retraining across different sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

Conclusion: ART-RL provides a principled, plug-and-play method for learning optimal timestep schedules in diffusion sampling, demonstrated to be both effective and broadly generalizable, requiring only a change to the timestep grid while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline intact.

Abstract: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

</details>


### [224] [Probing Chemical Language Models: Effects of Pre-training and Fine-tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02140)
*Anna Karnysheva,Dietrich Klakow,Ji-Ung Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper systematically probes chemical language models (CLMs) for 78 molecular substructures across pre-trained and randomly initialized models, finding that pre-training improves molecular structure awareness in upper layers, ring structures are encoded even without training, and fine-tuning preferentially affects task-relevant substructures in alignment with chemical theory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the widespread use of chemical language models trained on linearized representations like SMILES, it remains poorly understood which chemically meaningful substructures these models actually encode internally. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically probing CLMs to reveal what molecular substructure knowledge is learned, where in the model it resides, and how fine-tuning alters these representations.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic probing study targeting 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained CLMs and six randomly initialized models. They employ probing classifiers to detect whether specific substructure information is encoded in the hidden representations at different layers. Additionally, they analyze how fine-tuning on two chemical downstream tasks affects the learned substructure representations, comparing changes before and after fine-tuning.

Result: Pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness, especially in upper layers. Randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer, suggesting inherent inductive biases. Fine-tuning on downstream tasks affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than irrelevant ones, indicating that representational changes follow chemical theory.

Conclusion: CLMs learn chemically meaningful substructure representations through pre-training, with upper layers being most informative. The presence of ring structure encoding in untrained models suggests architectural or tokenization biases. Fine-tuning induces chemically plausible, task-specific representational changes, reinforcing the utility of CLMs for molecular tasks.

Abstract: Chemical language models (CLMs) are trained with linearized representations such as SMILES, yet it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode. To foster a better understanding of CLMs, we conduct a systematic study and probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models. We furthermore study how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks affects the learned representations of molecular substructures. Our results show that pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness of CLMs, particularly in the upper layers. Moreover, randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Our analysis on two chemical downstream tasks further reveals that, interestingly, fine-tuning affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than others, indicating that the changes in the representations follow chemical theory.

</details>


### [225] [Predicting Early Stages Of Alzheimer's Disease And Identifying Key Biomarkers Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02142)
*Debopriya Ghosh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a stacking ensemble machine learning model combined with an artificial neural network to detect early-stage Alzheimer's disease using clinical, neuropsychological, and neuroimaging data from the ADNI dataset, employing iterative imputation, Borderline SVM-SMOTE for class imbalance, and feature selection to identify key biomarkers for early diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no complete cure, and early symptoms are often mistaken for normal aging, leading to late diagnosis. Early detection is critical for better disease management, motivating the development of a machine learning-based diagnostic tool using multimodal data.

Method: The study uses ADNI dataset with three modalities: clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging measures. Missing values are handled via iterative imputation, class imbalance is addressed using Borderline SVM-SMOTE, and feature selection is performed with wrapper-based and embedded methods. A stacking ensemble classifier combining Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM is developed, alongside an artificial neural network, with performance evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.

Result: The abstract does not report specific numerical results, but states that the models were compared across precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics to identify the best classifier and important biomarkers for early AD diagnosis.

Conclusion: The study aims to determine the best-performing classifier for early Alzheimer's detection and to identify significant biomarkers that can aid in early diagnosis, though explicit concluding findings are not detailed in the abstract.

Abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a brain disorder that develops slowly and mainly affects memory, thinking, language, and daily activities. It is one of the most common causes of dementia and creates many difficulties for patients as well as their families. In the early stage, the symptoms are often mild and may look like normal ageing. For this reason, many people are diagnosed late, when the disease has already progressed. At present, there is no complete cure for AD. Still, early detection can help doctors manage the condition better and take suitable steps at the right time. In this study, a machine learning model is proposed to detect the early stages of Alzheimers disease using clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging-related measures. The data used in this work is collected from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). As the dataset has missing values, iterative imputation is applied to fill them. The dataset also has class imbalance, which is handled using Borderline SVM-SMOTE. After that, feature selection is carried out using wrapper-based and embedded methods so that only important features are used for training. The selected features are divided into training and testing sets, and feature scaling is applied. A stacking ensemble model is developed using Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers. Along with this, an artificial neural network is also trained on the same dataset. The performance of these models is compared using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. This study aims to find the best classifier and also identify important biomarkers that may help in the early diagnosis of Alzheimers disease.

</details>


### [226] [Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02512)
*Wentao Zhang,Liliana Hotsko,Woojeong Kim,Pengyu Nie,Stuart Shieber,Yuntian Deng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PAW (Program-as-Weights) proposes compiling natural-language function specifications into parameter-efficient neural adapters (LoRA-style) that run on a small frozen interpreter model, matching the performance of 32B-scale direct prompting while using 1/50th the memory and running locally at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many fuzzy programming tasks (log alerting, malformed JSON repair, search ranking) resist rule-based solutions and are increasingly delegated to LLM APIs, incurring costs, latency, and privacy/reproducibility concerns. The authors seek to replace per-input LLM calls with a compile-once, run-locally paradigm.

Method: PAW trains a 4B compiler model on FuzzyBench (10M examples) that translates a natural-language function specification into parameter-efficient adapter weights (e.g., LoRA) for a frozen, lightweight interpreter (0.6B Qwen3). The compiler is invoked once per function definition; subsequent function applications use the adapted interpreter cheaply and offline.

Result: A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter running PAW programs matches the performance of directly prompting Qwen3-32B, while using roughly 1/50th the inference memory and achieving 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3.

Conclusion: PAW reframes foundation models from per-input problem solvers into tool builders, enabling compact, reusable, locally-executable neural functions that preserve locality, reproducibility, and cost efficiency.

Abstract: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally-executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

</details>


### [227] [Dynamic Neural Graph Encoding of Inference Processes in Deep Weight Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02166)
*Di Wu,Huan Liu,Zhixiang Chi,Yuanhao Yu,Konstantinos N. Plataniotis,Yang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes DNG-Encoder, a dynamic graph-based approach that represents neural network parameters while preserving the sequential nature of layer-by-layer inference, achieving ~10% improvement over SOTA on INR classification (CIFAR-100-INR).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for analyzing neural network weight spaces overlook the inherent sequential, layer-by-layer nature of neural network inference. Handling high-dimensional weight spaces efficiently while capturing this temporal/sequential processing dynamic remains an open challenge.

Method: Introduces a novel dynamic graph representation of neural network parameters that captures temporal dynamics of inference. The Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these dynamic graphs while preserving sequential processing structure. Additionally, INR2JLS leverages DNG-Encoder to map Implicit Neural Representations into a joint latent space for downstream tasks like INR classification.

Result: The approach demonstrates significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR benchmark.

Conclusion: Dynamic graph representations that respect the sequential nature of neural network inference provide a more effective framework for weight-space analysis, enabling substantial gains in downstream tasks such as INR classification.

Abstract: The rapid advancements in using neural networks as implicit data representations have attracted significant interest in developing machine learning methods that analyze and process the weight spaces of other neural networks. However, efficiently handling these highdimensional weight spaces remains challenging. Existing methods often overlook the sequential nature of layer-by-layer processing in neural network inference. In this work, we propose a novel approach using dynamic graphs to represent neural network parameters, capturing the temporal dynamics of inference. Our Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these graphs, preserving the sequential nature of neural processing. Additionally, we also leverage DNG-Encoder to develop INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space) for facilitate downstream applications, such as classifying Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Our approach demonstrates significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR.

</details>


### [228] [An Optimisation Framework for the Well-Conditioned Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02194)
*Joseph Webb,Sadok Jerad,Coralia Cartis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSGNAR is a second-order optimization framework for PINNs that uses a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton method with adaptive regularization and step-length control, achieving unprecedented accuracy (relative L2 errors down to 3×10⁻¹⁶) and speed across diverse PDE problems, with robustness to architecture, precision, and hyperparameter choices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs have struggled to match the precision of classical PDE solvers due to a severely ill-conditioned loss landscape that hinders optimization. Existing first-order methods (e.g., Adam, L-BFGS) are inadequate for navigating this pathological loss terrain, motivating the need for a scalable second-order approach that can effectively confront the ill-conditioning.

Method: The authors propose DSGNAR, which combines: (1) a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton (GN) model — using randomized sketching to approximate both the GN matrix and its update directions, reducing the computational and memory cost of full second-order methods; and (2) an adaptive ratio strategy that jointly controls Tikhonov regularization and step length, enabling stable and efficient convergence despite extreme ill-conditioning.

Result: DSGNAR achieves relative ℓ₂ errors as low as 3×10⁻¹⁶ in double precision. It improves state-of-the-art results by five orders of magnitude on Burgers' equation and eight orders on a high-dimensional Poisson problem, while being faster. In single precision, it solves Burgers' equation to 4.75×10⁻⁷ relative error in under 10 seconds. The method is robust across architectures, arithmetic precisions, and initial hyperparameters.

Conclusion: Second-order optimization, when made scalable via sketching and stabilized via adaptive regularization/step-length control, can overcome the ill-conditioning bottleneck in PINN training, closing the accuracy gap with classical solvers while retaining the flexibility of neural network-based PDE solving.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising route to solve partial differential equations, yet they have struggled to reach the precision of classical solvers. The obstacle is increasingly understood to be one of optimisation, owing to the severely ill-conditioned loss landscape. We present $\textbf{DSGNAR}$: Doubly-Sketched Gauss-Newton with Adaptive Ratio, a scalable second-order optimisation framework that confronts this ill-conditioning and, in doing so, obtains unprecedented accuracy and speed. $\textbf{DSGNAR}$ couples a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton model with a novel strategy that carefully controls both regularisation and step length. Across a suite of problems spanning nonlinear, chaotic, multi-scale, high-dimensional, and Navier-Stokes, the framework greatly improves on the state of the art: able to attain relative $\ell_2$ errors as low as $3\times10^{-16}$ in double precision, improve contemporary results by five orders of magnitude on the canonical Burgers' equation, and as much as eight orders on a high-dimensional Poisson problem, while remaining markedly faster. We further show that, in single precision, solutions at the limit of round-off error can be obtained very quickly: Burgers' equation to $\ell_2^{\text{rel}} = 4.75 \times 10^{-7}$ in under ten seconds. The framework is also robust to the choice of architecture, arithmetic precision, and initial hyperparameters.
  The code is available at https://www.github.com/wephy/physics-informed-neural-networks

</details>


### [229] [Online Resource Allocation with Continuous Random Consumption: Regret under Degeneracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02196)
*Jiawei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies online resource allocation with continuous reward and consumption size distributions. It identifies the "active weighted-mass exponent p" as the key parameter governing regret: when p > 1, regret scales as T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}; when p = 1, regret is only O((log T)^2). A sample-path marginal policy achieves these bounds without requiring fluid non-degeneracy, handling both primal degeneracy and dual non-uniqueness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classic online resource allocation models often assume deterministic sizes or rely on fluid relaxation non-degeneracy (e.g., unique dual optimum, strict complementarity). Real-world settings feature continuously distributed rewards and consumption sizes, where the fluid relaxation may be degenerate — both primal degeneracy and dual non-uniqueness can occur. The authors seek to characterize regret in this more challenging, realistic regime and to design policies that achieve optimal rates without non-degeneracy assumptions.

Method: The authors model requests arriving sequentially, each with an observable type, random reward, and random scalar size that scales a fixed resource-consumption vector. They define the "active weighted-mass exponent p," which quantifies the density of requests whose value-to-size ratios lie near the optimal acceptance cutoff. A sample-path marginal policy is proposed — it tracks the fluid solution along each sample path, making accept/reject decisions based on current resource consumption relative to the fluid benchmark. Regret analysis is conducted by relating the deviation from the fluid trajectory to the weighted mass near the cutoff, yielding both lower bounds (via information-theoretic arguments for all p > 1) and matching upper bounds.

Result: The main results are: (1) For p > 1, every online policy incurs regret Ω(T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}). (2) The proposed sample-path marginal policy matches this lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors. (3) When p = 1, the same policy achieves O((log T)^2) regret. Concrete examples: size and value-to-size ratio independent and uniform yield p = 1; size and reward independent and uniform yield p = 2. The policy thus attains o(√T) regret across the entire regularity class without any fluid non-degeneracy assumption.

Conclusion: The active weighted-mass exponent p fully characterizes the difficulty of online resource allocation with continuous randomness. The problem transitions from "hard" (regret growing as a power of T) when p > 1 to "easy" (poly-logarithmic regret) when p = 1. The proposed policy is near-optimal across this spectrum and robust to degeneracies in the fluid relaxation, significantly broadening the applicability of online allocation theory.

Abstract: We study online resource allocation when both rewards and consumption sizes may be continuously distributed. Requests arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected irrevocably under fixed resource capacities. Each request belongs to one of finitely many observable types; conditional on an observable request type, both the reward and the scalar size are random, and the realized size scales a fixed type-specific resource-consumption vector. The model allows the deterministic fluid relaxation to be degenerate.
  We show that additive regret is governed by the size-weighted mass of requests whose value-to-size ratios lie near the active acceptance cutoffs. We formalize this quantity through an active weighted-mass exponent p. When p > 1, this cutoff mass is thin, and the problem is genuinely hard: every online policy must incur regret of order at least $T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}$, and this holds for every p > 1. A sample-path marginal policy matches this lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors; and when p = 1, so that the mass grows linearly near the cutoff, it attains $O((\log T)^2)$ regret. For example, if the size and the value-to-size ratio are independent and uniformly distributed, then p = 1; if instead the size and the reward are independent and uniformly distributed, then p = 2. Thus the policy achieves $o(\sqrt{T})$ regret throughout this regularity class without any fluid non-degeneracy assumption, allowing both primal degeneracy and dual non-uniqueness.

</details>


### [230] [Self-explainable Operator Learning for Discovering Spatial Patterns in Functional Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02203)
*Mojgan Alishiri,Amirhossein Arzani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a self-explainable operator learning framework that reformulates operator learning as a linear combination of integral equations, enabling direct interpretability by decomposing input domains into subdomains and linking specific input regions to output predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural network-based operator learning models are opaque black-boxes, and existing explainability methods rely on post-hoc tools external to the model. There is a need for inherently interpretable operator learning that provides physically meaningful insight into predictions without external tools.

Method: The authors reformulate operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed via integral equations. By exploiting additive decomposability, they partition the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals to quantify each region's contribution to the final prediction. This yields a self-explainable structure where interpretability is embedded directly in the operator.

Result: Demonstrated on function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in fluid flow problems (blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics), the framework shows the operator prioritizes regions with strong feature gradients. Comparisons with post-hoc methods show qualitative agreement, with the key advantage of built-in explainability.

Conclusion: The framework offers a mathematically transparent, physically interpretable approach that builds trust for scientific ML applications by embedding explainability directly into the operator structure, eliminating reliance on external interpretability tools.

Abstract: Operator learning has emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex physical systems in functional spaces. However, their neural network-based architectures make them opaque models, obscuring the reasoning behind their predictions. In this work, we introduce a self-explainable operator learning framework that overcomes this challenge by reformulating operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed through integral equations. Exploiting the additive decomposability of these integral equations, we divide the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals to evaluate the contribution of each region to the final prediction. This decomposition enables direct interpretability where the model explains both inputs and outputs by linking specific input regions to corresponding output patterns, thereby revealing which spatial features drive predictions. We demonstrate the framework on function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in fluid flow problems involving blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics. The results show that the operator most often prioritizes regions with strong feature gradients, providing physically meaningful insight into the model's decision-making process. Comparisons with established post-hoc explainability methods demonstrate qualitative agreement while highlighting the key advantage of the proposed approach: explainability is embedded directly within the operator structure itself and does not require an external tool. Therefore, our framework provides a mathematically transparent and physically interpretable approach to uncover relationships within data, fostering trust in machine learning for scientific applications by enabling more informed data-driven analysis of physical systems.

</details>


### [231] [Generalization in offline RL: The structure is more important than the amount of pessimism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02288)
*Max Weltevrede,Matthijs T. J. Spaan,Wendelin Böhmer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Pessimism in offline RL does not inherently prevent optimal generalization in CMDPs; rather, generalization depends on whether the pessimism structure respects the symmetries of the optimal solution. The authors prove symmetric pessimism (even if overly pessimistic) can outperform mildly pessimistic asymmetric approaches, and advocate for applying data augmentation via a consistency loss during policy extraction instead of training on augmented datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the prevailing assumption that overly conservative pessimism in offline RL hinders generalization. The authors aim to show that pessimism's structure (specifically, whether it respects problem symmetries) matters more than its magnitude for generalization in contextual MDPs.

Method: The authors provide theoretical analysis proving that an overly pessimistic but symmetric value function can generalize better than a mildly pessimistic non-symmetric one in CMDPs. They connect pessimism structure to dataset coverage structure, and propose applying data augmentation through a consistency loss during policy extraction rather than standard offline training on augmented data. Empirical validation uses IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.

Result: A mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic, symmetric one. Data augmentation applied via a consistency loss during policy extraction outperforms the standard practice of offline training on an augmented dataset, as validated on a rotationally symmetric reacher task with IQL and CQL.

Conclusion: Generalization in offline RL for CMDPs depends on whether the pessimism structure respects underlying optimal solution symmetries, not the degree of pessimism. Enforcing symmetric value functions may require data augmentation, best applied through consistency loss at policy extraction rather than during offline training on augmented data.

Abstract: While pessimism counteracts overestimation bias in offline reinforcement learning (RL), being overly conservative has been associated with hindering certain forms of generalization. However, in this paper we demonstrate that being overly pessimistic does not inherently prevent optimal generalization in contextual MDPs (CMDPs). Instead, we argue successful generalization depends not on the amount of pessimism, but whether the pessimistic structure respects the underlying symmetries of the optimal solution. We prove that a mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic, symmetric one. In offline RL, the structure of the pessimism is determined by the structure of the dataset coverage. As such, enforcing a symmetric value function can be non-trivial, and might require techniques such as data augmentation (DA). Inspired by our theoretical results, we argue that DA can best be applied through a consistency loss during policy extraction, rather than the common practice of (regular) offline training on an augmented dataset. This is empirically validated using IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.

</details>


### [232] [Optimizing Visual Generative Models via Distribution-wise Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02291)
*Ruihang Li,Mengde Xu,Shuyang Gu,Leigang Qu,Fuli Feng,Han Hu,Wenjie Wang*
