# cs.CR [[Back]](#toc)

### [243] [Embedding Inference Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01276)
*Cedric Fitiavana Raelijohn,Sébastien Gambs,Jean-Francois Rajotte*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces an Embedding Inference Attack (EIA) that allows an adversary to identify which embedding model is being used in a black-box IR system by observing only the unordered set of retrieved documents, without access to rankings or similarity scores. The attack uses tailored queries that remain discriminative even with rerankers and bypass LLM input filters in RAG systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embedding models in modern IR systems are typically hidden behind APIs, posing a security risk. Prior embedding inversion attacks assume white-box knowledge of the model. This work addresses the gap of model identification in a stricter black-box setting where only the unordered set of retrieved documents is visible, which is a necessary precursor to launching model-specific attacks.

Method: The authors design tailored queries that produce distinctive document retrieval patterns for different candidate embedding models. By observing which documents are returned (without ranking or scores), the adversary matches the observed retrieval set against expected patterns for each known candidate model, enabling identification. The method is tested against defense mechanisms including rerankers, LLM-based input filtering in RAG systems, and similarity thresholds.

Result: The tailored queries successfully discriminate among candidate embedding models in the black-box setting. The attack remains effective when a reranker is introduced as a defense. On a real RAG system, crafted queries bypass the LLM's tendency to reject non-well-formed inputs. Proposed mitigations like similarity thresholds show some effectiveness but are also evaluated.

Conclusion: Black-box embedding model identification is feasible through carefully constructed queries, exposing a new security vulnerability in IR and RAG systems. This has implications for the design of more robust defenses in deployed retrieval systems.

Abstract: Embedding models are essential components of modern Information Retrieval (IR) systems, yet they are typically hidden behind APIs. Recent works have shown that dense IR system can lead to security vulnerabilities such as embedding inversion attacks. However, such attacks usually require that the attacker knows the embedding model for the attack to be applicable. In this paper, we study IR systems under a black-box setting in which the adversary observes only the unordered set of retrieved documents, without ranking or similarity scores. We demonstrate that in such contexts, tailored queries allow an adversary to identify which embedding model is in use from a set of known model candidate, which we coin as an embedding inference attack (EIA). We also show that certain queries remain discriminative even when the system includes a reranker as a potential defense mechanism. We further validate our method on a real Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, in which the tailored queries bypass the LLM's tendency to reject inputs it does not recognize as well-formed questions. Finally, we propose and evaluate other mitigation strategies such as similarity thresholds.

</details>


### [244] [Cognitive Firewall: A Proactive, Zero-Trust, Multi-Gate Framework for LLM Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01277)
*Michele Guida,Ruslan Shikhhamzayev,Sindhuja Penchala,Stefano Iannucci,Jiacheng Li,Shahram Rahimi,Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The Cognitive Firewall is a runtime safety framework that inserts an independent oversight model between users and LLMs, decomposing safety assessment into four categorical gates (intent, zero-trust context, consistency, and output risk). Gate decisions use escalation-based combination, allowing any confident danger signal to block interactions. It achieves ≤2% attack success on three jailbreak benchmarks and 14% on the hardest human-crafted set, with 8% over-refusal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM safeguards evaluate prompts or responses as isolated messages, making them vulnerable to multi-turn jailbreak strategies where harmful intent is decomposed across turns and no single message appears clearly unsafe. These methods cannot recover accumulated intent, verify asserted authority, or detect decomposed harmful objectives.

Method: The Cognitive Firewall interposes an independent oversight model between user and target model, implementing four categorical safety gates: (1) Intent Gate — identifies the operational objective of a request; (2) Zero Trust Context Gate — treats claimed roles/permissions as unverified evidence; (3) Consistency Gate — detects escalation and decomposition across dialogue turns; (4) Output Risk Gate — inspects candidate responses before release. Gate decisions are combined via escalation rather than score averaging, so any confident danger signal can block an interaction while preserving an auditable rationale.

Result: Evaluated on four jailbreak benchmarks and a benign safety test set, the Cognitive Firewall reduced attack success to ≤2% on three attack sets and 14% on the hardest human-crafted set, with an 8% over-refusal rate on benign content.

Conclusion: Decomposed, conversation-level oversight significantly improves proactive containment and auditability for LLM safety compared to isolated message-level evaluation, demonstrating that multi-gate escalation-based architectures are effective against diverse jailbreak strategies.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be induced to produce harmful content through multi turn strategies in which no single user message appears clearly unsafe. Existing runtime safeguards commonly evaluate prompts or responses as isolated messages, which limits their ability to recover ac-cumulated intent, verify asserted authority, or detect harmful objectives decomposed across a dialogue. This paper presents the Cognitive Firewall, a proactive runtime oversight framework that interposes an independent oversight model between a user and a protected target mod l. The framework decomposes safety assessment into four categorical gates: an intent gate that identi-fies the operational objective of a request, a zero trust context gate that treats claimed roles and permissions as unverified evidence, a consistency gate that detects escalation and decomposition across turns, and an output risk gate that inspects candidate responses before release. Gate decisions are combined through escalation rather than score averaging, allowing any confident danger signal to block an interaction while preserving an auditable rationale. Experiments on four jailbreak benchmarks and a benign safety test set show that the Cognitive Firewall substantially reduces attack success across single turn, multi turn, authority based, and human crafted attacks. It lowers attack success to 2 percent or below on three attack sets and to 14 percent on the most difficult human crafted set, while maintaining an 8 percent over refusal rate. These results indicate that decomposed, conversation level oversight can improve proactive containment and auditability for LLM safety.

</details>


### [245] [Generative AI and Federated Learning for Intrusion Detection Systems: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01305)
*Jiefei Liu,Abu Saleh Md Tayeen,Pratyay Kumar,Qixu Gong,Wenbin Jiang,Huiping Cao,Satyajayant Misra,Jayashree Harikumar*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This survey systematically reviews the convergence of generative AI and federated learning for intrusion detection systems, categorizing applications by model type (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, LLMs) and task objectives, while identifying open challenges in synthetic data quality, adversarial risks, non-IID distributions, and domain-specific LLMs for network security.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IDS development is hindered by evolving attack behaviors, scarce realistic datasets, incomplete traffic records, class imbalance, and privacy constraints on centralized data collection. Generative AI and federated learning offer promising solutions to these long-standing limitations.

Method: A structured literature survey that (1) summarizes representative IDS research directions (adversarial ML, anomaly detection, IoT-IDS, explainable IDS, benchmarks), (2) categorizes generative AI applications by model families (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, LLMs) and task objectives (anomaly detection, synthetic data generation, augmentation, imputation, adversarial generation, alert explanation), and (3) reviews FL-integrated generative IDS studies with a discussion of open challenges.

Result: The survey identifies that generative models support six key IDS tasks and that FL enables privacy-preserving distributed training, but significant gaps remain in synthetic data fidelity, realistic traffic generation, dual-use adversarial risks, handling non-IID client data, communication efficiency, standardized federated IDS benchmarks, and adapting LLMs for network security.

Conclusion: Generative AI and FL together form a promising paradigm for next-generation IDS, but realizing practical deployments requires addressing fundamental challenges in data quality, adversarial robustness, and domain-specific model adaptation.

Abstract: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are essential for monitoring network traffic and identifying malicious activities in modern cyber-physical, Internet of Things (IoT), enterprise, and distributed network environments. However, developing reliable IDS models remains challenging because attack behaviors evolve over time, realistic datasets are difficult to obtain, traffic records may be incomplete, attack classes are often imbalanced, and privacy constraints limit centralized data collection. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) and Federated Learning (FL) provide new opportunities to address these limitations. Generative models can support anomaly detection, synthetic traffic generation, data augmentation, data imputation, adversarial traffic generation, and IDS alert explanation. FL enables distributed IDS training without directly sharing local network traffic, making it suitable for privacy-sensitive and geographically distributed environments. This survey provides a structured review of generative AI and FL techniques for IDS. We first summarize representative IDS research directions, including adversarial machine learning, anomaly-based detection, IoT-oriented IDS, explainable IDS, and benchmark datasets. We then categorize generative AI applications in IDS according to model families and task objectives, covering autoencoder-based models, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), diffusion models, and Large Language Models (LLMs). Finally, we review emerging studies that integrate generative AI with FL-based IDS and discuss open challenges, including synthetic data quality, realistic traffic generation, dual-use adversarial risks, non-IID client distributions, communication-efficient model sharing, federated IDS benchmarking, and domain-specific LLMs for network security.

</details>


### [246] [An alternative approach towards attacks against fully-split PLWE instances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01340)
*Iván Blanco-Chacón,Rodrigo Martín Sánchez-Ledesma,Raúl Durán Díaz*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether root-based attacks on certain cryptosystems can be generalized by constructing isomorphisms from known vulnerable instances to fully-split polynomial rings. The authors prove that no new vulnerabilities arise under a fully-split setting: the only possible isomorphisms between fully-split polynomial rings are of a specific form, and applying them always distorts samples such that they become indistinguishable, thus preventing attack generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Following prior work by the authors on root-based attacks, the motivation is to rigorously determine whether these attacks can be extended to a broader class of instances by constructing explicit isomorphisms from vulnerable configurations to fully-split polynomial rings. The goal is to either find new vulnerabilities or formally prove that such generalization is impossible.

Method: The authors first construct an explicit isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings and polynomial rings where prior root-based attacks are known to apply. They then demonstrate that applying this isomorphism to samples from a distinguishing problem distorts the samples in a way that renders them useless for distinguishing. Finally, they provide a formal proof that any isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings must take the specific form they constructed, thereby ruling out alternative isomorphisms that might yield new attacks.

Result: Under the fully-split setting, no new vulnerabilities are introduced via isomorphism-based generalization of root-based attacks. The explicit isomorphism always distorts samples into an indistinguishable form, and the classification result shows that no other isomorphism structure exists that could circumvent this limitation.

Conclusion: The isomorphism-based approach to extending root-based attacks to fully-split polynomial rings is fundamentally limited and does not yield new distinguishing attacks. This provides a formal barrier to generalizing the previous root-based attack methodology in this setting.

Abstract: In the present work we address some key questions regarding the generalization of root-based attacks presented in a recent work by the authors. In particular, we analyze potential root-based attacks extensions via the construction of explicit isomorphisms from vulnerable instances, and provide a formal proof that this approach will not yield any new vulnerabilities under a fully-split setting. To do so, we first construct an explicit isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings and polynomial rings where previous attacks apply and show that the application of such an isomorphism will always distort the samples in a way that the resulting samples cannot be used to distinguish. Then, we prove that any isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings must be of the form of the constructed isomorphism.

</details>


### [247] [Chameleon: Recovering Cyber-Physical Systems from Memory Corruption Attacks via ML Surrogates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01356)
*Mohsen Salehi,Karthik Pattabiraman*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Chameleon is a framework that uses ML-based surrogate models to automatically recover cyber-physical systems from memory corruption attacks by replacing compromised software compartments at runtime, enabling continued operation in safety-critical tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory corruption defenses either terminate/halt CPS execution (catastrophic for safety-critical tasks) or degrade to simplified defaults/reboot. Neither approach preserves full operational capability while surviving attacks.

Method: Chameleon trains ML-based surrogates at compartment granularity that replicate original compartment behavior without the same vulnerabilities. Upon attack detection, the compromised compartment is swapped with its trained surrogate. Implemented using LLVM and evaluated on seven robotic vehicles (simulated and real).

Result: Surrogates closely approximate original compartments (average R²=0.96), successfully recover systems from real-world memory corruption attacks, and complete tasks with low performance and memory overhead.

Conclusion: Chameleon demonstrates that ML-based surrogates can effectively replace compromised CPS components, enabling resilient recovery without termination, rebooting, or degraded fallback behavior.

Abstract: Cyber-physical systems (CPSs) are increasingly deployed in every aspect of our lives and can be compromised through memory corruption vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to hijack the control flow and take over the system. Existing techniques mostly focus on detecting such attacks but respond by terminating or halting execution upon attack detection, which is not acceptable in CPSs used in safety-critical tasks, as interrupted tasks can have catastrophic consequences. Other techniques replace compromised CPS components with simplified defaults that degrade system behavior, or reboot the system upon attack detection.
  We propose Chameleon, a novel framework for automatically recovering CPSs from memory corruption attacks using machine learning (ML)-based surrogates trained at compartment granularity that nearly replicate their original compartments' behavior but do not have the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. Upon attack detection, Chameleon replaces the compromised compartment with its trained surrogate. We implemented Chameleon using the LLVM compiler and evaluated its efficiency and effectiveness on seven different robotic vehicles (RVs), including simulated and real ones. We found that Chameleon can generate surrogates that closely approximate the original compartments (with an average R$^2$=0.96), successfully recover the system despite real-world memory corruption attacks unlike prior approaches, and complete their tasks while incurring low performance and memory overhead.

</details>


### [248] [From Forgeries to Foundation Models: A Systematic Survey of Identity Document Attack and Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01442)
*Gourab Das,Pavan Kumar C,Raghavendra Ramachandra*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This survey unifies Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis under a single identity verification threat model. It traces detection methods from heuristics to foundation models, audits public datasets (2019–2025) revealing a Reality Gap, identifies Script-Dependent Generative Instability in non-Latin script inpainting, and demonstrates via zero-shot benchmarking that even the strongest models fail under security-oriented conditions (APCER >25%). The paper concludes with directions for forensically grounded, privacy-preserving, and legally accountable identity verification systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI has fundamentally shifted identity document forgery capabilities, enabling high-fidelity synthesis and field-level manipulation with minimal expertise. Existing detection benchmarks fail to reflect this evolving threat, and the fragmented treatment of physical presentation, digital injection, and generative synthesis attacks obscures their shared forensic failure modes. A unified threat model and evaluation framework is urgently needed.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic survey that: (1) proposes a unified threat model spanning Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis; (2) traces the evolution of detection methodologies from rule-based heuristics to forensic localization, injection-aware pipelines, foundation models, and few-shot frameworks; (3) audits public datasets from 2019–2025 to quantify the Reality Gap; (4) analyzes large multimodal models for identity document manipulation, introducing the concept of Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI); and (5) performs zero-shot benchmarking of publicly available models on unseen synthesized ID cards under security-oriented operating conditions.

Result: Key findings include: (1) a persistent Reality Gap between benchmark conditions and operational deployment across public datasets (2019–2025); (2) Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) as a recurring typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting by large multimodal models; (3) even the strongest publicly available models achieve APCER values above 25% under security-oriented operating conditions in zero-shot benchmarking on unseen synthesized ID cards, indicating severe limitations in cross-domain generalization.

Conclusion: Current detection systems are insufficient for real-world deployment against GenAI-augmented identity document forgery. Future work must focus on forensically grounded detection methods, privacy-preserving verification architectures, and legally accountable frameworks that can bridge the Reality Gap and handle cross-domain generalization challenges, particularly for non-Latin scripts and unseen synthesis techniques.

Abstract: Identity document forgery has undergone a fundamental capability shift: generative AI tools now enable high-fidelity document synthesis and field-level manipulation with minimal technical expertise, while detection methods remain constrained by benchmarks that do not reflect this threat. The resulting attack surface spans physical presentation, digital injection, and fully generative synthesis, introducing distinct forensic failure modes that require a unified threat model and evaluation framework. This survey provides, to our knowledge, the first unified treatment of Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis within a single identity verification threat model. We trace detection methodologies from rule-based heuristics through forensic localisation, injection-aware pipelines, foundation models, and few-shot frameworks. A systematic audit of public datasets from 2019--2025 exposes a persistent Reality Gap between benchmark conditions and operational deployment. We further analyse large multimodal models for identity document manipulation, identifying Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) as a recurring typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting. Finally, zero-shot benchmarking on unseen synthesised ID cards shows that even the strongest publicly available models achieve APCER values above 25% under security-oriented operating conditions, highlighting substantial limits in cross-domain generalisation. We conclude by outlining future directions toward forensically grounded, privacy-preserving, and legally accountable identity verification systems.

</details>


### [249] [Hamm-Grams: An Algorithm for Mining Regular Expressions of Bytes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01445)
*Derek Everett,Edward Raff,James Holt*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes hamm-grams, a robust variant of n-gram features for malware detection that uses fixed-length regular expressions with single-character wildcards, constructed via a novel locality-sensitive hashing and clustering algorithm, and demonstrates their effectiveness in classification tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional n-gram features used in machine learning–based malware detection are inherently brittle — small modifications to malware (e.g., obfuscation, insertion, or deletion of bytes) can dramatically alter n-gram signatures. There is a need for more robust static features that can tolerate minor variations while preserving discriminative power.

Method: The authors introduce hamm-grams: fixed-length regular expressions with single-character wildcards (e.g., "ab?d"). They develop an efficient algorithm to discover common hamm-grams using (1) a new locality-sensitive hash (LSH) function designed to produce collisions between strings with small Hamming distance, and (2) a clustering step within hash buckets to determine optimal wildcard placements, making the feature extraction computationally feasible at scale.

Result: Hamm-gram features demonstrate clear advantages over traditional n-grams in both malware classification and detection tasks, showing improved robustness to adversarial perturbations while maintaining or improving classification accuracy.

Conclusion: Hamm-grams represent a more resilient alternative to conventional n-gram features for static malware analysis. By tolerating small byte-level variations via wildcards, they mitigate the brittleness problem inherent in exact-match n-grams, making machine learning–based malware systems more robust to evasion.

Abstract: Malware poses a critical and ever-evolving threat, and robust and effective systems for detecting and classifying malware are of essential importance. $n$-grams features are among the common static features used in effective machine learning systems for malware, but these features are inherently brittle. We propose an algorithm for constructing more robust features, hamm-grams, which are a special class of regular expressions having a fixed length and single-character wildcards. We devise an efficient algorithm for finding common hamm-grams using a new locality-sensitive hash designed to produce collisions among pairs of small Hamming distance and a clustering within hash buckets to place wildcards. We then demonstrate the advantages of these features in malware classification and detection tasks.

</details>


### [250] [Overthink-Triggered Slowdown Attacks on LVLM-Based Robotic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01518)
*Qiang Han,Jie Wu,Bo Chen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper identifies and validates that LVLMs in robotic systems are vulnerable to overthinking-induced slowdown attacks, where adversarially crafted scene text triggers excessively long reasoning traces. The authors propose a three-stage framework to discover transferable triggers, achieving up to 6.96x latency amplification, with physical printed triggers still causing 4.74x slowdown.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LVLMs integrated into robotic systems can exhibit overthinking — generating excessively long reasoning traces that increase inference time. An adversary can exploit this by embedding crafted scene text into the robot's visual environment, deliberately slowing decision-making and causing safety risks. This attack works under black-box conditions, making it a serious, practical threat that warrants systematic investigation.

Method: The authors propose a three-stage framework: (1) Construct a diverse corpus of reasoning-intensive scene text and extract overthinking-correlated lexical features from short response prefixes. (2) Perform an efficient black-box search using a prefix-based proxy score to filter candidates, then confirm top candidates with full latency measurements. (3) Evaluate black-box transferability by testing a fixed pool of triggers on unseen images across multiple LVLMs, measuring latency amplification and attack success rates.

Result: Across three representative LVLMs, all discovered triggers produce slowdown ratios exceeding 1.0x, with the strongest single trigger reaching 6.96x latency amplification. Physical printing of text triggers still causes up to 4.74x slowdown. Triggers transfer effectively between different LVLM models and consistently induce significant latency increases in robotic systems.

Conclusion: LVLMs in robotic systems are systematically vulnerable to overthinking-based slowdown attacks via adversarially crafted scene text. The discovered triggers are transferable across models and effective even when physically printed, highlighting a practical safety concern for deployed robotic systems that warrants further attention and mitigation strategies.

Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have been increasingly integrated into robotic systems. However, these models may exhibit overthinking behaviors, where they generate excessively long reasoning traces, incurring an excessive inference time. This overthinking behavior poses a serious risk to robotic systems, as the adversary can deliberately trigger overthinking to slow down the decision making of a victim robotic system, causing a variety of safety issues (i.e., an overthinking-induced slowdown attack). To initiate this attack, an adversary can embed carefully crafted, human-readable scene text into the visual scene observed by a victim robotic agent, causing significant inference delays even under a strict black-box setting. Therefore, the embedded scene text serves as a significant "trigger" for the attack.
  This work systematically identifies and validates transferable triggers of overthinking in robotic systems by introducing a three-stage framework. First, we construct a diverse corpus of reasoning-intensive scene text and extract overthinking-correlated lexical features from short response prefixes. Second, we perform an efficient black-box search guided by a prefix-based proxy score while selectively confirming a small set of top candidates with full latency measurements. Third, we evaluate black-box transfer using a fixed pool of triggers on unseen images and multiple LVLMs, reporting latency amplification and attack success rates under standard thresholds. Across three representative LVLMs, all triggers yield slowdown ratios greater than 1.0x, with the strongest single-trigger case reaching 6.96x. The physical printing of the text trigger still causes up to 4.74x latency amplification. These results demonstrate that our discovered triggers are transferred between multiple LVLM models and consistently cause significant slowdowns in robotic systems.

</details>


### [251] [LIB-TRAP: Standard Cell Library Hardware Trojan Risk Assessment and Prevention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01526)
*Harish Kumar Dharavath,Md Muhtasim Alam Chowdhury,Rozhin Yasaei,Soheil Salehi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a novel hardware Trojan attack vector where standard cell libraries themselves are tampered, enabling malicious foundries to replace deactivated Trojan cells with activated ones during fabrication. The authors demonstrate this attack by converting the Saed32nm and Sky130nm standard cell libraries into malicious versions and testing them on AES-128, Ethernet, and WISHBONE DMA benchmark circuits, showing the attack is stealthy against design-level feature-based detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hardware Trojan research focuses primarily on inserting Trojans in the space between standard cells, neglecting the vulnerabilities posed by the standard cells themselves — the fundamental building blocks of digital designs. The fabless manufacturing model's inherent trust assumptions make standard cell libraries a critical but underexplored attack surface.

Method: The authors propose a threat model where a tampered standard cell library is provided to the design house, with deactivated HT cells that are swapped for activated versions by the foundry during fabrication. They convert open-source standard cell libraries (Saed32nm, Sky130nm) into malicious libraries using open-source and industry-standard EDA tools, then synthesize three benchmark circuits (AES-128 encryption core, Ethernet controller, WISHBONE DMA engine) with both clean and Trojan-infected libraries across Synopsys 32nm and SkyWater 130nm technologies. Stealthiness is evaluated by extracting design-level features (cell count, area, dynamic/static power) for binary classification.

Result: The malicious libraries successfully mask the presence of arbitrary hardware Trojans from IC designers. The attack vector proved effective and stealthy across multiple benchmark designs and technology nodes, with design-level features such as total cell count, total area, dynamic power consumption, and static power failing to reliably distinguish between clean and Trojan-infected synthesized circuits.

Conclusion: Standard cells represent a significant and underappreciated attack surface for hardware Trojan insertion. The demonstrated attack vector — tampering standard cell libraries — is both practical and difficult to detect using conventional design-level metrics, exposing a critical gap in current hardware security practices that must be addressed.

Abstract: Vulnerabilities inherent to the fabless semiconductor manufacturing model have significantly increased the risk of malicious Hardware Trojan (HT) insertion, posing severe threats to hardware security. Several HT mitigation and detection strategies have been developed, and existing works explore the insertion of HTs in the space between standard cells in an integrated circuit. However, there is a lack of research into the vulnerabilities posed by the building blocks of most digital designs on the market today, the standard cells. This work investigates a novel threat model in which standard cells are considered untrusted. Our proposed threat model provides the design house with a tampered standard cell library. The intended netlist is synthesized and implemented using the tampered library. During fabrication, a nefarious foundry replaces the library's deactivated HT cells with activated counterparts. Using open-source and industry-standard Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools, existing standard cell libraries, Saed32nm and Sky130nm, are converted into malicious libraries capable of masking the presence of arbitrary HTs from IC designers. The malicious library is then applied and characterized in multiple standard benchmark designs. To demonstrate the efficacy and stealthiness of this standard cell-based attack vector, three benchmark circuits, an AES-128 encryption core, an Ethernet controller, and a WISHBONE DMA engine, were synthesized using both clean and Trojan-infected libraries across Synopsys 32nm and SkyWater 130nm technologies. Design-level features, including total cell count, total area, dynamic power consumption, and static power, were extracted from these synthesized circuits to serve as inputs for binary classification

</details>


### [252] [VeriChat: An Agentic Conversational AI Assistant for Hardware Security Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01668)
*Dipayan Saha,Khan Thamid Hasan,Shams Tarek,Sujan Kumar Saha,Mark Tehranipoor,Farimah Farahmandi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: VeriChat is a domain-specialized conversational assistant for hardware security verification that uses a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent workflow to provide context-aware security guidance while minimizing hallucinations. It integrates with open-source EDA tools (Icarus Verilog, Yosys, SymbiYosys) for direct RTL analysis and achieves 87.73% faithfulness, outperforming proprietary models, with demonstrated capability in autonomous hardware Trojan detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hardware security verification is a complex, multi-stage process requiring security-focused guidance that current verification environments lack. While conversational AI could provide on-demand assistance, general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini are unreliable due to hallucination risks and reliance on static, outdated knowledge. There is a need for a domain-specialized, trustworthy assistant that supports existing verification workflows without replacing them.

Method: VeriChat employs a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent architecture with three specialized agents collaborating to minimize hallucinations and improve response transparency and reliability. It integrates open-source EDA tools — Icarus Verilog, Yosys, and SymbiYosys — to perform syntax checking, synthesis analysis, simulation, and formal verification directly on user-provided RTL designs. The system is evaluated using a comprehensive methodology with a Faithfulness metric.

Result: VeriChat achieves a Faithfulness score of 87.73%, significantly outperforming leading proprietary models. The framework is demonstrated through a hardware Trojan detection case study on an AES S-Box IP, where VeriChat autonomously identifies, simulates, and formally proves a covert key-leakage vulnerability via a multi-turn conversational workflow.

Conclusion: VeriChat demonstrates that a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent conversational system specialized for hardware security verification can provide reliable, context-aware guidance while avoiding the hallucination pitfalls of general-purpose chatbots. Its integration with open-source EDA tools enables end-to-end autonomous security analysis, as evidenced by the successful detection and formal verification of a hardware Trojan in an AES S-Box IP.

Abstract: Hardware security verification is a multi-stage process in which engineers must navigate complex design analyses, threat considerations, and verification strategies. They often need security-focused guidance, yet current verification environments provide little structured support for such assistance. Although conversational AI could offer such on-demand assistance, directly using general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini is risky due to their tendency to hallucinate and their reliance on static, outdated knowledge. We present VeriChat, a domain-specialized conversational assistant designed to support, rather than replace, existing verification workflows by providing context-aware security guidance. VeriChat employs a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent workflow in which three specialized agents collaboratively minimize hallucinations while improving the transparency and reliability of the response. Beyond question answering, VeriChat integrates open-source EDA tools, including Icarus Verilog, Yosys, and SymbiYosys, to perform syntax checking, synthesis analysis, simulation, and formal verification directly on user-provided RTL designs. Evaluated using a comprehensive methodology, VeriChat achieves a Faithfulness score of 87.73%, significantly outperforming the leading proprietary models. We demonstrate the framework through a hardware Trojan detection case study on an AES S-Box IP, where VeriChat autonomously identifies, simulates, and formally proves a covert key-leakage vulnerability through a multi-turn conversational workflow.

</details>


### [253] [Beyond Gradient-Based Attacks: Adversarial Robustness and Explainability Stability in Cybersecurity Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01679)
*Mona Rajhans,Vishal Khawarey*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper extends adversarial attack evaluation on cybersecurity classifiers to Random Forest and XGBoost, introducing the Explainability Stability Index (ESI) to measure TreeSHAP attribution drift. Key finding: prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct axes — XGBoost shows near-perfect robustness to ZOO attacks yet suffers severe SHAP drift, necessitating joint measurement of both properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Security analysts depend on SHAP-based explanations to triage alerts from cybersecurity classifiers. Adversarial attacks threaten both prediction integrity and explanation reliability, yet prior work focused narrowly on differentiable models (MLPs). The authors aim to extend evaluation to tree-based ensemble models (RF, XGBoost) widely used in practice, and to quantify the overlooked dimension of explanation stability under attack.

Method: The authors evaluate five adversarial attacks (including three black-box methods: ZOO, Square Attack, and a query-efficient approach) on Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers across four tabular security datasets (phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021). They introduce the Explainability Stability Index (ESI), a [0,1]-scaled scalar metric measuring TreeSHAP attribution drift, reported alongside the Robustness Index (RI). A two-axis framework (gradient dependence, query efficiency) categorizes attack behavior, and a step-size ablation addresses a PGD anomaly on z-score normalized data.

Result: ZOO (gradient-based black-box) yields degenerate results on XGBoost (RI ~0.98) due to piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, creating a false appearance of robustness. Square Attack reveals genuine vulnerability (RI ~0.36). Yet ZOO still drives substantial SHAP drift: XGBoost ESI ~0.06–0.16 vs. 0.14–0.29 for RF, demonstrating that prediction robustness and explanation stability are independent. The two-axis framework explains the attack ranking and provides practical guidance for tree ensemble evaluation.

Conclusion: Prediction robustness and explanation stability must be jointly measured in adversarial evaluations of tree-based cybersecurity classifiers. The ESI provides a standardized metric for this purpose. The two-axis framework (gradient dependence, query efficiency) offers actionable guidance for selecting and interpreting attacks, and the PGD anomaly underscores the importance of careful normalization in tabular adversarial settings.

Abstract: Adversarial attacks on cybersecurity classifiers pose a dual threat: degrading predictions and destabilising the SHAP-based explanations that security analysts rely on to understand and triage alerts. We extend our prior MLP conference study to Random Forest and XGBoost across four tabular security datasets (phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021), evaluating five attacks including three black-box methods applicable to non-differentiable tree models. We introduce the Explainability Stability Index (ESI), a scalar metric computed from TreeSHAP attribution drift under adversarial perturbation, reported on the same [0,1] scale as the Robustness Index (RI). A key finding is that gradient-based black-box attacks (ZOO) produce degenerate results against XGBoost (apparent RI ~0.98) due to piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, while score-based Square Attack reveals genuine vulnerability (RI ~0.36). These degenerate perturbations still drive substantial attribution drift: XGBoost ESI ~0.06-0.16 despite near-perfect ZOO robustness, versus 0.14-0.29 for RF, showing that prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct axes requiring joint measurement. A two-axis framework (gradient dependence, query efficiency) explains the observed attack ranking and yields practical guidance for tree ensemble evaluation. A step-size ablation explains a counterintuitive PGD anomaly on z-score normalised tabular data.

</details>


### [254] [Pmeta-TLA: Backdoor Attacks for Speech Classification Models via Meta-Learning with Timbre Leakage Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01702)
*Yueming Huang,Wenhan Yao,Fen Xiao,Xiarun Chen,Weiping Wen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Timbre Leakage Attack (TLA), a stealthy backdoor attack for speech classification models that embeds timbre information at the frame level in self-supervised features, and Pmeta-TLA, a meta-learning framework with Projected Conflicting Gradients for efficient multi-backdoor injection. The approach achieves superior attack efficacy, stealthiness, and robustness with lower cost compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current speech classification models are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, but existing speech triggers can be detected by deep neural network defenders. There is a pressing need to explore more stealthy and potent attack vectors to expose security risks before they can be exploited in the wild.

Method: The authors propose two components: (1) TLA (Timbre Leakage Attack) — a trigger that disseminates timbre information at the frame level within deep self-supervised speech features, producing poisoned samples that sound natural to humans; (2) Pmeta-TLA — a multi-backdoor injection training strategy that uses meta-learning combined with Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) to embed multiple backdoors simultaneously, enabling TLA as a multi-target attack tool.

Result: Experiments on data-poisoning backdoor attacks in keyword spotting tasks across multiple deep neural network models show that the proposed TLA and Pmeta-TLA achieve superior attack efficacy, enhanced stealthiness, greater robustness, and reduced attack cost compared to baseline methods.

Conclusion: TLA and Pmeta-TLA expose critical vulnerabilities in speech classification systems by demonstrating that frame-level timbre-based triggers can bypass both human perception and neural network defenses, while meta-learning enables efficient multi-backdoor deployment. This underscores the urgent need for more robust defenses in speech models.

Abstract: Recently, speech classification methods have gained widespread adoption in intelligent gadgets. Current study indicates that backdoor attacks provide a substantial security concern to these models, underscoring the pressing necessity to investigate additional potential attack techniques to expose and prevent such risks. This work discusses the vulnerability of current speech triggers to detection by deep neural network defenders and introduces the Timbre Leakage Attack (TLA). The suggested trigger disseminates timbre information at the frame level within the deep self-supervised features, producing poisoned samples that appear natural to human perception. Furthermore, we introduce Pmeta-TLA, an innovative training mechanism for embedding numerous backdoors one time. This method proposes a multi-backdoor injection training strategy using meta-learning and Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) and introduces TLA as a multi-target attack tool within it. We performed tests on data-poisoning backdoor attacks in keyword spotting tasks utilizing some deep neural network models. Experimental results indicate that the proposed strategy attains superior Attack efficacy, enhanced stealthiness, robustness, and a reduced attack cost relative to baseline methods.

</details>


### [255] [Trust Boundary Semantic Gaps: A Multi-dimensional Analysis and Mitigation for Security-by-Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01711)
*Doyeon Kim,Jin-Young Choi,Junghee Lee*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces the concept of Trust Boundary Semantic Gap (TBSG) — where syntactically valid artifacts crossing trust boundaries still violate semantic security requirements. The authors analyze 75 security incidents (2014–2025), propose a four-dimensional analysis model (MDTBSG: Identity, Spatial, Temporal, Interpretation), and develop TBSAM, a design-time framework for identifying, prioritizing, and mitigating TBSGs. They validate the framework through a retrospective analysis of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST attack.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional trust-boundary defenses rely on format, protocol, and signature validation, which only ensure syntactic correctness. These mechanisms fail to guarantee that an artifact satisfies the receiving domain's semantic security properties. This "gap" between syntactic validation and semantic security requirements enables attacks where properly signed/authenticated artifacts (e.g., updates, tokens) still lead to compromise. The authors seek to formalize and address this underexamined class of vulnerabilities.

Method: The authors analyzed 75 publicly reported security incidents (2014–2025) at the boundary level to identify patterns of semantic misalignment. From this empirical study, they developed MDTBSG, a four-dimensional analysis model (Identity, Spatial, Temporal, Interpretation) for classifying semantic gaps. They then built TBSAM (Trust Boundary Semantic Analysis and Mitigation), a design-time framework that: (1) identifies TBSGs from design specifications, (2) prioritizes them, (3) traces propagated gaps to their originating boundary, and (4) maps each gap to candidate architectural controls. The framework was validated via a retrospective reconstruction of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain attack.

Result: The analysis of 75 incidents revealed recurring patterns of semantic misalignment across trust boundaries, captured in the four MDTBSG dimensions. Applying TBSAM to the SolarWinds/SUNBURST case demonstrated the framework's ability to make receiving-domain assumptions explicit, distinguish locally originating gaps from propagated ones, and identify architectural controls capable of interrupting the attack path. The results show that syntactic validation alone is insufficient at trust boundaries.

Conclusion: Syntactic validation (format, protocol, signature checks) is necessary but not sufficient for trust-boundary security. The TBSG concept formalizes the gap between what syntactic checks establish and what semantic security properties require. Making trust-boundary assumptions explicit through frameworks like TBSAM can complement Security-by-Design practices, enabling designers to identify and mitigate semantic gaps before deployment.

Abstract: Modern systems use format-, protocol-, and signature-based mechanisms before accepting artifacts across trust boundaries. These mechanisms are necessary: they show that an artifact is well formed, protocol-compliant, or properly authenticated. They do not, however, show that the artifact satisfies the semantic security properties required by the receiving domain. A signed update or an authenticated token may therefore be accepted yet enable compromise. We call this condition a Trust Boundary Semantic Gap (TBSG): an artifact crosses a trust boundary and passes correctly implemented syntactic validation, but the assertions established by that pass are insufficient to satisfy the receiving domain's security requirements. TBSG concerns what remains unestablished after a syntactic pass, not absent checks or implementation bugs. Analyzing 75 publicly reported security incidents (2014-2025) at the boundary level, we organize semantic misalignment into a four-dimensional analysis model: Identity, Spatial, Temporal, and Interpretation (MDTBSG). Building on it, we develop Trust Boundary Semantic Analysis and Mitigation (TBSAM), a design-time framework that identifies TBSGs from design specifications, prioritizes them, traces propagated gaps to their originating boundary, and maps each to candidate architectural controls. We apply TBSAM to a retrospective reconstruction of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain attack, showing how it makes receiving-domain assumptions explicit, separates locally originating from propagated gaps, and identifies controls that interrupt the path. These results suggest that syntactic validation, while necessary, is not sufficient at trust boundaries, and that making trust-boundary assumptions explicit can complement Security-by-Design.

</details>


### [256] [Resilient Liquid Democracy: Mitigating Voting Power Imbalances via Secure Delegation Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01730)
*Zhuolun Li,Evangelos Pournaras*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a secure liquid democracy mechanism using sealed delegation (via decentralized timed-release encryption) to prevent herding and coercion, combined with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots to handle delegate failures. Formal proofs of secrecy and receipt-freeness are provided, and empirical evaluation on real datasets reveals that delegation improves accuracy only under large, unrepresentative abstention, while sealed formation primarily reduces power concentration and fallback mechanisms sharply reduce vote loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing liquid democracy systems use transparent delegation, which creates three problems: (1) popularity-driven herding where voters follow high-weight delegates, (2) verifiable coercion since delegation choices are visible, and (3) systemic fragility when highly-backed delegates abstain, causing cascading vote loss. The authors aim to resolve the tension between informed expertise routing and systemic robustness.

Method: The authors design a cryptographic protocol featuring: (1) sealed delegation using decentralized timed-release encryption to hide delegation choices during the formation phase, preventing herding and coercion while maintaining final auditability; (2) ranked multi-delegation allowing voters to specify backup delegates; (3) personal fallback ballots so votes are not lost if all delegates abstain. They formally prove pre-reveal secrecy and resubmission receipt-freeness. The mechanism is evaluated on four real datasets: a municipal participatory-budgeting election with calibration survey, twenty additional participatory-budgeting elections, and 60,000 US voters with objective competence measures.

Result: Key findings: (1) Delegation's effect on representational accuracy follows a "recoverable-gap law" — it helps only when abstention is large and systematically unrepresentative, and is otherwise neutral or harmful. (2) Representative-style delegation is safer than delegating to a competence elite. (3) Sealed formation's benefit is primarily structural: it sharply reduces power concentration rather than directly improving accuracy. (4) Ranked multi-delegation with personal fallback ballots sharply reduces vote loss under realistic and targeted delegate failures, replicating across all 20 elections tested.

Conclusion: The sealed liquid democracy mechanism successfully addresses coercion, herding, and delegate-failure fragility through cryptographic hiding and fallback provisions. The empirical results caution that delegation is not a universal improvement for democratic accuracy; its benefits are conditional on the nature and scale of abstention, and structural safeguards (sealed delegation, fallbacks) are essential for robust deployment.

Abstract: Liquid democracy promises to improve collective decision-making by allowing voters to vote directly, delegate their voting power to trusted participants, or combine both approaches through fallback mechanisms. However, existing deployments typically rely on transparent delegation, which exposes voters to popularity-driven herding, makes coercion verifiable, and introduces systemic fragility when highly-backed delegates abstain. In this paper, we propose a secure liquid democracy mechanism that resolves the tension between informed expertise routing and systemic robustness. We introduce a sealed delegation regime using decentralized timed-release encryption, which cryptographically hides delegation choices during the formation phase to prevent herding and coercion, while restoring full public auditability for the final tally. To address delegate failures, we extend the protocol with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots. We formally prove pre-reveal secrecy and resubmission receipt-freeness for our protocol. Finally, we evaluate the mechanism on four real datasets, a municipal participatory-budgeting election with a calibration survey, twenty further participatory-budgeting elections, and 60,000 US voters with an objective competence measure. They show that whether delegation improves representational accuracy follows a recoverable-gap law; it helps only when abstention is large and systematically unrepresentative, and is otherwise neutral or harmful, with representative-style delegation safer than delegating to a competence elite. The benefit of sealed formation is primarily structural, sharply reducing power concentration rather than directly improving accuracy; and ranked multi-delegation with personal fallback ballots sharply reduces vote loss under realistic and targeted delegate failures, a result that replicates across all twenty elections.

</details>


### [257] [Knowledge Over Parameters: Evolving Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01742)
*Yuqiang Sun,Han Liu,Ying Li,Yiran Zhang,Zong Cao,Ziyun Guo,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: EvoVuln reformulates smart contract vulnerability detection as procedural knowledge evolution, using a Runtime with Inversion of Control architecture and a two-phase evolution pipeline to synthesize and refine detection logic from minimal labeled data (5 positive + 5 negative samples), achieving 71% macro F1 and enabling portable, low-cost model transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Smart contract vulnerabilities are predominantly logic bugs requiring structured procedural knowledge of attack patterns. Existing LLM-based detection methods are limited: prompt-based approaches depend on manually crafted rules, while fine-tuning demands large labeled datasets that are scarce in this domain. A method is needed that can automatically synthesize and refine detection logic from minimal labeled samples.

Method: EvoVuln proposes an automated framework with two core components: (1) An IoC Runtime that compiles detection rules into Executable Policies, strictly decoupling deterministic control flow from LLM semantic reasoning to ensure logical adherence and produce diagnostic telemetry for error localization. (2) A two-phase evolution pipeline: Cold Start bootstraps and stress-tests an initial rule using auto-synthesized corner cases; Few-Shot Evolving then grounds the policy in real-world semantics using only 5 vulnerable and 5 safe examples per vulnerability type, via abductive semantic debugging without parameter updates.

Result: Across five real-world vulnerability types, EvoVuln achieves a 71% macro-average F1-score, outperforming all baselines. The evolved procedural knowledge is portable across models: a lightweight, low-cost model surpasses a much larger zero-shot model by 19 percentage points, and transfers to other LLMs without retraining. The one-time evolution cost is under $50.

Conclusion: EvoVuln demonstrates that procedural knowledge evolution with minimal supervision is a viable and cost-effective paradigm for smart contract vulnerability detection, offering strong performance, cross-model portability, and eliminating the need for large labeled datasets or parameter fine-tuning.

Abstract: Smart contract vulnerabilities are predominantly logic bugs whose detection requires structured, step-by-step procedural knowledge of attack patterns and contract semantics. Existing LLM-based methods struggle to generate this knowledge automatically: prompt-based methods rely on manually crafted detection rules, while fine-tuning requires massive labeled datasets that are inherently scarce in this domain. We present EvoVuln, an automated framework that reformulates vulnerability detection as a procedural knowledge evolution problem, synthesizing and refining detection logic using only a minimal number of labeled samples.
  To achieve this, EvoVuln introduces two key mechanisms. First, a Runtime with an Inversion of Control (IoC) architecture compiles detection rules into Executable Policies. This strictly decouples deterministic control flow from LLM semantic reasoning, ensuring faithful logical adherence and producing dense diagnostic telemetry for precise error localization. Second, a two-phase evolution pipeline refines the rule via abductive semantic debugging without any parameter updates: Cold Start bootstraps and stress-tests an initial rule using auto-synthesized corner cases; Few-Shot Evolving then grounds the policy in real-world semantics using only five vulnerable and five safe examples per vulnerability type.
  Evaluated across five real-world vulnerability types, EvoVuln achieves a 71% macro-average F1-score, outperforming all baselines. The evolved procedural knowledge is portable across models: it enables a lightweight, low-cost model to surpass a much larger zero-shot model by 19 percentage points, and transfers to other LLMs without retraining, at a one-time evolution cost under $50.

</details>


### [258] [Has This Checkpoint Been Abliterated? A Two-Signal Audit and Its Failure Map](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01854)
*Gabriel Hurtado*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A threshold-free audit combining activation refusal-gap and weight-recovery energy separates abliterated (refusal-stripped) checkpoints from benign ones at AUROC 0.95 across 273 models, enabling pre-deployment detection with balanced accuracy 0.89 on held-out families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current runtime guardrails evaluate model outputs, not the model artifact itself, making them unable to detect whether an open-weight checkpoint has had its refusal mechanism stripped prior to deployment. A pre-deployment audit is needed.

Method: Two complementary internal signals are combined: (1) a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap that provides refusal-specificity, and (2) a weight-recovery energy measuring the base-to-candidate weight difference that provides recall. These are negatively correlated and label-complementary. Their z-scores are summed into a single threshold-free score. Evaluated on a registry of 273 checkpoints (Qwen, DeepSeek-distilled Qwen, Llama, Gemma) comprising 57 public abliterations and 37 benign fine-tunes, merges, and instruction-tunes.

Result: The combined z-sum achieves AUROC 0.95, significantly outperforming either signal alone (0.84 for refusal-gap, 0.90 for weight energy). A Youden-calibrated threshold transfers to held-out families at balanced accuracy 0.89 (FPR 0.11), missing only 4 of 57 abliterations. Two failure modes are identified: a spoofed reference evades detection with no training (ΔW=0, ρ=1), and a white-box owner can train past the threshold while remaining guard-unsafe.

Conclusion: The audit is effective as a triage mechanism, not tamper-proofing. It requires an attested reference checkpoint and its claims are bounded by the evaluated registry. It cannot defend against spoofed references or adaptive white-box adversaries.

Abstract: Can a platform tell, before deployment, whether an open-weight checkpoint has had its refusal mechanism stripped? Runtime guards cannot: they score generations, not the artifact. We combine two cheap internal signals, a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap and a weight-recovery energy of the base-to-candidate weight difference, into a threshold-free checkpoint audit. The two are negatively correlated and label-complementary: the gap supplies refusal-specificity and the weight energy supplies recall. On a 273-checkpoint registry spanning Qwen, DeepSeek-distilled Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, their z-sum separates 57 public abliterations from 37 benign fine-tunes, merges, and instruction-tunes at AUROC 0.95, significantly above either signal alone (0.84, 0.90), and a Youden-calibrated threshold transfers to held-out families at balanced accuracy 0.89 (FPR 0.11), missing only 4 of 57. We then map two failures, in order of severity: a spoofed reference evades both axes with no training (ΔW=0, \r{ho}=1 by construction), and a white-box owner trains a checkpoint past the threshold while it stays guard-unsafe and coherent. The audit is effective triage, not tamper-proofing: it presumes an attested reference, and its claims are bounded by the registry we evaluate it on.

</details>


### [259] [Behind the Refusal: Determining Guardrail Activation via Behavioral Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02121)
*William Hackett,Peter Garraghan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a black-box methodology to detect whether an AI system has a guardrail, identify what content it blocks, and distinguish guardrail blocks from LLM rejections — achieving 100% detection accuracy and 98% F1 on block/rejection classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Researchers conducting adversarial testing against production AI systems cannot easily tell whether a blocked response comes from a guardrail or the LLM's own safety alignment. This distinction matters because bypass techniques differ significantly between the two, impacting attack strategy. No prior methodology exists for black-box guardrail reconnaissance.

Method: The authors propose a black-box reconnaissance methodology that monitors HTTP, lexical, and timing signals from target AI systems. With zero prior knowledge and black-box access only, the approach systematically probes the system with benign and malicious prompts, then analyzes behavioral differences in response patterns to infer guardrail presence, blocked content categories, and distinguish guardrail blocks from LLM rejections.

Result: The methodology detects guardrail presence with 100% accuracy, with statistically significant behavioral separation between benign and malicious interactions (q < 0.001). It identifies blocked content categories and distinguishes guardrail blocks from LLM rejections on unseen prompts with an average F1 score of 98%.

Conclusion: The proposed guardrail reconnaissance methodology is highly effective, enabling black-box adversarial testers to reliably detect guardrails, map their blocked categories, and differentiate guardrail intervention from native LLM refusal — a critical capability for realistic AI security assessments.

Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) and agentic systems become integrated into real-world applications, ensuring their safety and security is critical. Guardrail systems that detect and block malicious instructions sent to and from an LLM are an essential component of AI security. However, researchers conducting black-box adversarial emulation against production AI systems often struggle to determine whether a guardrail block or an LLM rejection has occurred. This distinction is important because the techniques used to bypass guardrails can differ substantially from those used to bypass LLM safety alignment, and has a material impact on attack technique selection and optimization. We propose the first black-box guardrail reconnaissance methodology, which detects the presence of a guardrail within a target AI system through behavioral monitoring of HTTP, lexical, and timing signals, assuming only black-box access and zero prior knowledge of the guardrail or AI system. Experiments demonstrate that our approach detects guardrail presence with 100% accuracy, with statistically significant behavioral separation between benign and malicious interactions (q < 0.001). Our approach further identifies the content categories a guardrail is designed to block, and distinguishes guardrail blocks from LLM rejection on unseen prompts with an average F1 score of 98%.

</details>


### [260] [Cloak and Detonate: Scanner Evasion and Dynamic Detection of Agent Skill Malware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02357)
*Zimo Ji,Congying Xu,Zongjie Li,Yudong Gao,Xin Wei,Shuai Wang,Shing-Chi Cheung*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Existing static scanners for LLM coding agent skills are vulnerable to payload-preserving evasion (SkillCloak bypasses 80-96%). The authors propose SkillDetonate, a runtime sandbox auditor using OS-level information-flow tracking, achieving 97% detection at 2% FPR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM coding agents increasingly use third-party skills from public marketplaces, creating a software supply-chain attack surface. Existing defenses rely on static scanning (pattern matching or LLM-as-judge), but it is unclear whether they can withstand adaptive, payload-preserving evasions that alter appearance while retaining malicious semantics.

Method: The paper has two phases: (1) SkillCloak, an evasion framework with two strategies — Structural Obfuscation (rewriting payload indicators into semantically equivalent forms) and Self-Extracting Skill Packing (hiding malicious components at install-time, restoring them at runtime). Tested across 8 scanners and 1,613 real-world malicious skills. (2) SkillDetonate, a behavior-centric runtime auditor that sandboxes skills and detects malicious effects via OS-boundary information-flow evidence, combining on-demand closure lift (observing materialized instructions during execution) with marker-based taint analysis (tracking sensitive-data flows across agent context, files, processes, and network operations).

Result: SkillCloak: SFS Packing bypasses every scanner at >90%; Structural Obfuscation bypasses >80% on most static scanners and reaches 96% on a hybrid scanner. SkillDetonate: detects 97% of attacks at 2% false-positive rate; sustains 87% detection on real-world malicious skills.

Conclusion: Appearance-based auditing is insufficient for securing LLM agent skill marketplaces. Behavior-centric runtime auditing with OS-level information-flow tracking provides a robust alternative, achieving high detection rates with low false positives against both synthetic and real-world malicious skills.

Abstract: LLM coding agents increasingly rely on third-party agent skills from public marketplaces, which execute with the agent's privileges and create a software supply-chain attack surface: a malicious skill can steal credentials, exfiltrate source code, or install backdoors. Existing defenses use static skill scanners based on pattern matching or LLM-as-judge analysis, but it remains unclear whether they withstand adaptive evasions that preserve malicious behavior while changing payload appearance.
  This paper first presents an adversarial study of existing skill scanners through SkillCloak, a payload-preserving evasion framework that keeps the attack semantics intact while transforming their visible form. SkillCloak uses two complementary strategies: Structural Obfuscation, which rewrites visible payload indicators into semantically equivalent forms, and Self-Extracting Skill (SFS) Packing, which hides malicious components from the install-time view and restores them during agent execution. Across eight scanners and 1,613 in-the-wild malicious skills, SFS Packing bypasses every scanner at over 90%, while Structural Obfuscation bypasses over 80% on most static scanners and reaches 96% on a hybrid scanner, showing that appearance-based auditing is insufficient.
  Motivated by this finding, we propose SkillDetonate, a behavior-centric runtime auditor that executes skills in a sandbox and detects malicious effects through OS-boundary information-flow evidence rather than install-time appearance. SkillDetonate combines on-demand closure lift, which observes instructions materialized during execution, with marker-based taint analysis, which tracks sensitive-data flows across the agent context, files, processes, and network operations. The results show that SkillDetonate detects 97% of attacks at a 2% false-positive rate and sustains 87% detection on real-world malicious skills.

</details>


### [261] [SoK: A Taxonomy for Cybersecurity Incident Response Influence Factors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02451)
*Thomas Biege,Marius Brockhoff,Jonas Kaspereit,Fabian Ising,Lea Gröber,Sebastian Schinzel*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper presents a systematic literature review (n=417 academic, n=40 grey literature) spanning 1999–2024 that develops the "Cybersecurity Incident Response Influencing Factor Taxonomy" (CIR-IF Taxonomy). The taxonomy organizes factors affecting organizational incident response preparedness and response across multiple domains. When compared against seven established frameworks and the NIST SP 800-61r3 incident response profile, the CIR-IF Taxonomy offers richer, more rigorous, and more systematically organized coverage of incident response drivers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite growing literature on cybersecurity incident response, no unified framework exists to systematically organize accumulated knowledge across the multiple relevant domains (technology, HCI, organizational theory, human factors). This fragmentation hinders researchers from identifying underexplored areas and targeting empirical/theoretical investigations effectively.

Method: A systematic review of 417 academic publications and 40 non-scientific (grey literature) publications was conducted. Factors influencing organizational incident response were extracted and synthesized into the CIR-IF Taxonomy. The resulting taxonomy was then systematically compared against seven established scientific frameworks and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework elements referenced in NIST SP 800-61r3's incident response profile.

Result: The CIR-IF Taxonomy was derived, classifying all existing empirical findings from 1999 to mid-2024. Comparative analysis demonstrated that the CIR-IF Taxonomy provides richer, more rigorous, and more systematically organized coverage of incident response influencing factors than existing frameworks, including the NIST SP 800-61r3 profile.

Conclusion: The CIR-IF Taxonomy fills a critical gap by offering a comprehensive, integrative, multi-domain framework for incident response factors. It enables researchers to better identify research gaps and provides practitioners with a systematically organized reference for improving organizational incident response preparedness.

Abstract: Cybersecurity incident response has emerged as a critical area of interest for both researchers and practitioners. The corpus of literature on cybersecurity incident response is expanding, yet a unified framework for systematically organizing the accumulated knowledge remains absent. The aspects of incident response span multiple domains, including technology, human-computer interaction, organizational theory, and human factors. A comprehensive, integrative perspective on these factors can enable researchers to identify underexplored areas and more effectively target their empirical and theoretical investigations. Our study systematizes the factors that influence organizational preparedness for and response to cybersecurity incidents. Through a systematic review of academic literature (n = 417) and non-scientific publications (n = 40), we derived the "Cybersecurity Incident Response Influencing Factor Taxonomy" (\textit{CIR-IF Taxonomy}). Existing empirical findings were classified within this taxonomy, providing a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of knowledge from the period 1999 to mid-2024. The taxonomy categories were systematically compared with seven established scientific frameworks and with the \textit{NIST Cyber Security Framework} elements referenced in the \textit{NIST Special Publication 800-61r3} incident response profile. The results of this comparison show that the \textit{CIR-IF Taxonomy} delivers a richer, more rigorous, and more systematically organized view of the factors that drive and shape incident response.

</details>

### [262] [Benchmarking Code Improvement with Progressive, Adaptive, and Interactive Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01360)
*Cuong Chi Le,Aashish Yadavally,Minh Le-Anh,Tien N. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PAIR-Bench introduces a progressive, feedback-guided benchmark for evaluating how LLMs iteratively refine incorrect code, using structured hinting with controlled failure-region and hint-depth parameters to assess repair trajectories rather than just binary pass/fail outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM evaluation for code generation and repair relies solely on binary functional correctness (pass/fail), which is too coarse. It ignores partial progress, how models use feedback, whether they introduce regressions, and the refinement trajectory — all critical aspects of real-world iterative code improvement.

Method: PAIR-Bench employs progressive hinting with two control dimensions: (1) failure-region control, which groups hidden failing tests into distinct failure scenarios to target specific bugs, and (2) hint-depth control, which varies the granularity of information revealed — from coarse symptoms to implementation-level guidance. The benchmark evaluates repair trajectories using progressive metrics that capture targeted repair success, generalization beyond hints, preservation of correct behavior, and the amount of assistance required.

Result: PAIR-Bench enables measurement of whether a model repairs targeted failures, generalizes beyond the provided hint, preserves already-correct behavior, and quantifies the level of assistance needed — providing a finer-grained assessment than binary pass/fail metrics.

Conclusion: PAIR-Bench offers a more nuanced, multidimensional evaluation framework for LLM code-improvement capabilities by focusing on the refinement process rather than solely on final outcomes, addressing a significant gap in current code-generation benchmarks.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on code generation and program repair using binary functional correctness: a generated program or patch either passes or fails a test suite. This protocol is simple but coarse, as it ignores partial progress, feedback use, regressions, and the refinement trajectory through which models often improve code. We introduce PAIR-Bench, a progressive and adaptive benchmark for evaluating code improvement: transforming an incorrect or incomplete program into a more correct one through feedback-guided refinement. PAIR-Bench uses progressive hinting, a structured feedback protocol with two controls. Failure-region control determines what the feedback targets by grouping hidden failing tests into failure scenarios, while hint-depth control determines how much repair-relevant information is revealed, from coarse symptoms to implementation-level guidance. This design enables PAIR-Bench to measure whether a model repairs targeted failures, generalizes beyond the hint, preserves already-correct behavior, and how much assistance it requires. By evaluating repair trajectories progressive metrics rather than only final pass/fail outcomes, PAIR-Bench provides a finer-grained assessment of LLM code-improvement capability.

</details>


### [263] [A global predicted-fMRI drive signal from TRIBE does not predict YouTube replay heatmaps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01400)
*Barada Sahu,Shivesh Pandey*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A state-of-the-art multimodal brain-encoding model (TRIBE) was used to predict fMRI responses to YouTube videos. The predicted cortical engagement signals showed no evidence of forecasting real-world re-watch behavior as measured by YouTube's "most replayed" heatmaps. The null result held across multiple control analyses, with apparent effects in music videos attributed to a genre-specific artifact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While deep multimodal brain-encoding models achieve high accuracy in predicting fMRI responses to naturalistic video, it remains unknown whether these predicted neural signals can forecast real-world behavioral engagement — specifically, which moments in videos viewers choose to re-watch.

Method: The authors applied TRIBE (the winning model of the 2025 Algonauts challenge, combining Llama-3.2, V-JEPA2, and Wav2Vec-BERT) to 48 YouTube videos. Predicted cortical responses were reduced to a per-second engagement curve via global field power (GFP). These curves were correlated against each video's "most replayed" heatmap data. Position-controlled partial correlations, raw correlations, comparisons against loudness/motion baselines, six cortical-network readouts, and an autocorrelation-preserving permutation test were all employed.

Result: The pooled position-controlled partial correlation was +0.058 (95% CI [-0.04, 0.15]; t(47)=1.21, p=0.23), indistinguishable from zero and not significantly above loudness (+0.04, paired p=0.74) or motion baselines. Moderate correlations found for music videos were driven by an intro/onset-replay artifact specific to that genre and did not generalize. The null result held across all six cortical-network readouts and under permutation testing.

Conclusion: Despite TRIBE's high internal prediction accuracy of fMRI responses, its predicted cortical engagement does not forecast real-world re-watch behavior. Apparent predictive effects in music videos are artifactual. The authors release code, video IDs, and an acquisition method compatible with YouTube's SABR-only streaming.

Abstract: Deep multimodal brain-encoding models now predict fMRI responses to naturalistic video with high accuracy. Whether their predicted neural signals also forecast behavioral engagement is unknown. We run TRIBE, the winning model of the 2025 Algonauts brain-encoding challenge (Llama-3.2 + V-JEPA2 + Wav2Vec-BERT), on 48 YouTube videos and reduce its predicted cortical response to a per-second engagement curve, the global field power.
