Correlated against each video's "most replayed" heatmap, a passively-collected proxy for which moments viewers return to, the curve shows no evidence of predicting re-watch behavior. The pooled position-controlled partial correlation is +0.058 (95% CI [-0.04, 0.15]; one-sample t(47)=1.21, p=0.23), indistinguishable from zero and not significantly above simple loudness and motion baselines (loudness +0.04, paired p=0.74). The raw correlation is also near zero; the moderate values reported for music videos reflect a genre-specific intro/onset-replay artifact rather than content prediction, and do not generalize. The null holds across six cortical-network readouts and under an autocorrelation-preserving permutation test. We release the code, the video-ID manifest, and an acquisition method that works despite YouTube's SABR-only streaming.

</details>


### [264] [GPUAlert: A Zero-Instrumentation Process-Boundary Monitor for Diagnosing GPU Training-Job Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01409)
*Parv Agarwal,Asif Ekbal*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: GPUAlert is a command-line wrapper that monitors GPU training jobs, emails structured failure notifications with classified causes and logs, and achieves 0.997 macro-F1 on failure classification with ~3ms overhead, all without requiring any changes to the training script.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPU training jobs fail frequently (~40% on large clusters), but operators typically discover failures only hours later upon reconnection. Existing solutions like experiment trackers require script modifications and cloud connectivity, while scheduler mail hooks provide only a single status line without cause or logs.

Method: GPUAlert implements three reliability primitives: (1) a pre-launch log guarantee that establishes durable storage before the child process can crash, (2) notifier isolation ensuring the wrapper's exit code depends solely on the child's status, and (3) a non-silent artifact budget that bounds attachment size without silently dropping output. Failure classification uses an ordered-rule classifier trained on a labelled corpus of 474 GPU training logs across 15 failure classes.

Result: The ordered-rule classifier achieves 0.997 macro-F1 on 12 hardware-reproduced classes, substantially outperforming unordered keyword matching (0.830) and exit-code inspection (0.133). Wrapper overhead is ~3ms per job. The pre-launch guarantee preserves logs where shell redirects yield nothing, and the wrapper returns the child's exit code unchanged across all 15 failure modes even when the SMTP relay is unreachable.

Conclusion: GPUAlert provides a lightweight, zero-code-change solution for reliable GPU training job monitoring with high-accuracy failure classification, robust log preservation, and guaranteed exit-code fidelity, addressing a critical gap in production ML infrastructure.

Abstract: GPU training jobs fail often, roughly two in five on large production clusters, yet the operator typically learns of a failure only by reconnecting hours later. Experiment trackers require editing the training script and maintaining a cloud connection; the scheduler's mail hook delivers a single status line with no cause and no logs. GPUAlert is a command-line wrapper that monitors any training command at the process boundary, and with no change to that command, emails a structured notification on completion carrying a classified failure cause, durable logs, and output artifacts. The tool is organized around three reliability primitives: a pre-launch log guarantee that establishes the durable destination before the child process can crash, notifier isolation that makes the wrapper's exit code a pure function of the child's status regardless of whether the email succeeds, and a non-silent artifact budget that bounds attachment size without ever dropping output silently. We release a labelled corpus of 474 GPU training logs across 15 failure classes and a reproducible evaluation harness. On the twelve hardware-reproduced classes, the ordered-rule classifier reaches 0.997 macro-F1, against 0.830 for unordered keyword matching and 0.133 for exit-code inspection. Wrapper overhead is a constant approximately 3ms per job; the pre-launch guarantee preserves a log where a shell redirect yields nothing; and across all 15 failure modes the wrapper returns the child's exit code unchanged even when the SMTP relay is unreachable.

</details>


### [265] [Adoption and Impact of Command-Line AI Coding Agents: A Study of Microsoft's Early 2026 Rollout of Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01418)
*Emerson Murphy-Hill,Jenna Butler,Alexandra Savelieva*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A study of Microsoft's 2026 rollout of CLI coding agents (Claude Code, Copilot CLI) across tens of thousands of engineers found adoption spread through social networks, retention correlated with coding activity rather than demographics, and adopters merged ~24% more pull requests — with the effect persisting over four months.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations need to understand who will adopt and retain agentic CLI tools, and whether these tools produce measurable output gains, because token spend at scale can reach millions of dollars annually. Misjudging adoption or impact risks expensive rollouts without improving engineering velocity.

Method: Observational study of tens of thousands of Microsoft engineers during an early-2026 rollout. Adoption patterns were tracked through social network analysis; retention was modeled against coding activity and demographic variables; output was measured via a counterfactual difference-in-differences approach using merged pull requests as the productivity proxy across a four-month window.

Result: Three key findings: (1) first use spread primarily through social networks; (2) retention was associated more with engineers' coding activity than with demographic factors; (3) adopters merged approximately 24% more pull requests than they would have otherwise, with the lift persisting across the full four-month observation window.

Conclusion: CLI coding agents are neither uniformly adopted nor mere novelty effects. Organizations should treat visible peer use as central to their rollout strategy to maximize adoption and retention, and the sustained ~24% PR lift suggests genuine productivity benefits that can justify the token expenditure.

Abstract: Organizations rolling out agentic command line tools like Anthropic's Claude Code and GitHub's Copilot CLI need to know who will try them, who will keep using them, and whether the tools produce enough output to justify their cost. At organizational scale, token spend can run into millions of dollars annually, so misreading adoption, retention, or impact can make a rollout expensive without changing engineering velocity. Studying tens of thousands of engineers at Microsoft over its early-2026 rollout, we find that first use spread primarily through social networks, retention was associated more with engineers' coding activity than with demographics, and adopters merged roughly 24% more pull requests than they would have otherwise. We use merged pull requests as our proxy for output -- acknowledging that a merged PR is not the same as the value it delivers -- and the lift persists across our four-month window. These results suggest that CLI coding agents are neither uniformly adopted nor mere novelty effects and that organizations should treat visible peer use as central to rollout strategy.

</details>


### [266] [Risk Architecture for AI-Native Engineering Teams: An Organizational Framework for Agentic System Governance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01421)
*Laxmipriya Ganesh Iyer*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Traditional software risk frameworks (ownership by feature, escalation by severity, assurance by test coverage) break down for agentic AI systems due to probabilistic outputs, autonomous multi-step actions, and silently mutating risk surfaces. This paper provides a profile taxonomy for team types, a failure-mode taxonomy including a novel "dependency-boundary determinism mismatch" cluster, and a methodology for scoring how well each profile's risk architecture handles defined scenarios. Key finding: coverage degrades monotonically as teams move toward AI-native operation, with the most severe uncovered failures occurring at organizational boundaries where probabilistic AI outputs meet deterministic dependencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing software risk frameworks assume deterministic behavior, discrete auditable change events, and clear component-to-owner mappings — all three assumptions are violated by agentic AI systems. While AI risk literature exists at the policy level (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) and the threat taxonomy level (OWASP), there is a gap at the engineering management layer where roles, decision rights, and escalation structures are defined. This paper aims to fill that gap.

Method: The paper contributes three artifacts: (i) a seven-dimension profile distinguishing pure software-engineering, hybrid, and AI-native teams; (ii) a six-cluster failure-mode taxonomy including a newly identified cluster (dependency-boundary determinism mismatch); and (iii) a synthetic framework-adequacy methodology that scores each profile's risk architecture on detection, containment, and escalation across a defined scenario set. Evaluation produces derived coverage claims (not observed behavioral data) since the object of study is framework adequacy.

Result: Coverage degrades as teams move from pure software engineering to AI-native operation, monotonically in the median and abruptly in the count of uncovered high-consequence failures appearing only at the AI-native step. Degradation concentrates in specific failure-mode categories. The most severe, least-covered failures arise not inside AI-native teams but at organizational boundaries where probabilistic outputs are consumed by determinism-assuming dependencies.

Conclusion: The paper identifies a critical organizational boundary problem: the mismatch between probabilistic AI outputs and deterministic consuming systems creates the most severe and least-covered failure modes. This suggests engineering management risk frameworks for agentic AI must address cross-boundary escalation structures, not just internal team practices.

Abstract: Engineering management research has produced mature frameworks for software risk: ownership by feature, escalation by severity, and assurance by test coverage. These frameworks implicitly assume deterministic behavior, discrete and auditable change events, and clear component-to-owner mappings. Teams that build and operate agentic AI systems violate all three assumptions at once: outputs are probabilistic, systems take autonomous multi-step actions, and the risk surface mutates silently between deployments. Existing AI risk literature addresses this from above (policy frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001) or below (threat taxonomies such as OWASP's agentic AI guidance), but not at the layer where an engineering manager (EM) operates: roles, decision rights, and escalation structures. This paper contributes (i) a seven-dimension profile distinguishing pure software-engineering, hybrid, and AI-native teams; (ii) a six-cluster failure-mode taxonomy including a previously unarticulated cluster, dependency-boundary determinism mismatch; and (iii) a synthetic framework-adequacy methodology scoring how well each profile's risk architecture detects, contains, and escalates a defined scenario set. Because the object of study is framework adequacy rather than human behavior, the evaluation yields derived rather than observed coverage claims. Coverage degrades as teams move from pure software engineering to AI-native operation, monotonically in the median and abruptly in the count of uncovered, high-consequence failures appearing only at the AI-native step. The degradation concentrates in specific failure-mode categories, and the most severe, least-covered failures arise not inside AI-native teams but at the organizational boundary where their probabilistic outputs are consumed by determinism-assuming dependencies.

</details>


### [267] [From Anatomy to Smells: An Empirical Study of SKILL.md in Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01456)
*David Boram Hong,Aaron Imani,Iftekhar Ahmed*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: First systematic study of SKILL.md files as software artifacts, analyzing 238 real-world Agent Skills to derive a taxonomy of semantic components, identifying skill smells as violations of authoring best practices, and revealing that over 99% of skills contain at least one smell — highlighting a significant gap between recommended and actual authoring practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite rapid adoption of Agent Skills (which provide on-demand domain knowledge to LLM agents via SKILL.md files), no empirical understanding exists of how these files are authored in practice or whether established authoring guidelines are followed, creating a knowledge gap about this emerging software artifact.

Method: A three-phase approach: (1) qualitative analysis of 238 real-world SKILL.md files to derive a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level semantic components; (2) multivocal literature review of 29 sources to synthesize best practices for authoring SKILL.md files; (3) development of an automated detector applied to real-world skills to identify violations ("skill smells") and track their persistence across skill evolution.

Result: The taxonomy captures 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level semantic components. Over 99% of real-world SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell, and once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear as skills evolve — indicating systemic deviations from best practices.

Conclusion: There exists a substantial gap between recommended and actual authoring practices for SKILL.md files. This motivates the development of automated remediation techniques and increased developer awareness to address skill smells as an emerging software quality concern in the Agent Skills ecosystem.

Abstract: Agent Skills provide on-demand domain knowledge to LLM agents without requiring model retraining. Each Agent Skill is defined by a mandatory SKILL.md file containing metadata and an unstructured Markdown body whose contents are left entirely to the skill author. Despite the rapid adoption of Agent Skills, little is known about how these files are authored or whether existing authoring guidelines are followed in practice. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of SKILL.md files as a software artifact. We qualitatively analyze 238 real-world skills and derive a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level semantic components. We then conduct a multivocal literature review of 29 sources to identify best practices for authoring SKILL.md files and introduce skill smells as violations of these practices. Finally, we develop an automated detector and apply it to real-world skills, finding that over 99% of SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell, and once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear as skills evolve. These findings reveal a substantial gap between recommended and actual authoring practices, motivating the development of automated techniques to remediate skill smells while increasing developer awareness of this emerging quality issue.

</details>


### [268] [Insights from GitHub Community on the Matter Standard: Developer Perspectives and Challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01494)
*Muhammad Hassan,Carl Gunter,Susan Landau,Masooda Bashir*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Analysis of 13,000+ GitHub issues from Project CHIP reveals four recurring problem areas in Matter IoT standard adoption: Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform/Network challenges, highlighting needs for improved test infrastructure, cross-vendor guidance, and documentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Matter aims to solve IoT interoperability issues, but little empirical evidence exists on how developers actually experience the standard during implementation and integration. This gap hinders targeted improvements to the ecosystem.

Method: Mixed-methods empirical study mining over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP GitHub repository, combining topic modeling (computational) with qualitative analysis to categorize and characterize contributor-reported problems.

Result: Four recurring concern areas were identified: (1) Testing — challenges with test infrastructure and automation; (2) Interoperability — cross-vendor compatibility and specification conformance issues; (3) Development — codebase complexity, build systems, and tooling friction; (4) Platform and Network — platform-specific bugs and network-layer problems. These manifest throughout the codebase and tooling evolution.

Conclusion: The findings reveal systematic rather than incidental challenges in Matter's ecosystem, pointing to concrete opportunities to refine test infrastructure, strengthen cross-vendor guidance, and improve documentation as the standard matures.

Abstract: Matter seeks to resolve longstanding interoperability problems in the Internet of Things (IoT), yet little is known about how developers experience the standard in day to day work. This paper examines over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP GitHub repository to understand the kinds of problems contributors report when implementing and integrating Matter. Using topic modeling and qualitative analysis, we identify four recurring areas of concern, Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform and Network, and describe how they manifest in the evolution of the codebase and tooling. The findings reveal systematic technical and integration challenges and point to concrete opportunities to refine Matter's test infrastructure, cross vendor guidance, and documentation as the standard continues to mature.

</details>


### [269] [Kani: A Model Checker for Rust](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01504)
*Rémi Delmas,Zyad Hassan,Qinheping Hu,Rahul Kumar,Felipe R. Monteiro,Thanh Nguyen,Adrián Palacios,Celina Val,Michael Tautschnig,Justus Adam,Daniel Schwartz-Narbonne,Carolyn Zech*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Kani is an open-source model checker for Rust that uses bounded model checking (via CBMC) to verify memory safety, functional correctness, and panic-freedom. It supports unbounded verification through contracts and has been deployed at scale in production CI, verifying over 16,000 harnesses per code change in the Rust standard library.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Rust's ownership type system guarantees memory safety in safe code, several critical properties remain unverified: the soundness of unsafe operations (e.g., raw pointer dereferences), functional correctness, and absence of runtime panics. Existing tools focus primarily on bug-finding rather than providing formal correctness guarantees for these properties.

Method: Kani compiles proof harnesses from Rust's MIR (Mid-level Intermediate Representation) into CBMC's bit-precise verification engine, enabling automatic checking of safety properties without user annotations. For unbounded verification, it introduces a specification language supporting function contracts, loop contracts, quantifiers, and function stubbing, allowing users to lift verification from bounded to unbounded correctness guarantees.

Result: Case studies on industrial Rust projects demonstrated that contracts upgraded verification from panic-freedom to full functional correctness, uncovering six previously unknown bugs. Kani operates at production scale, with over 16,000 harnesses verified per code change in the Rust standard library verification campaign.

Conclusion: Kani demonstrates that bounded model checking, augmented with a contract-based specification language, can provide practical correctness guarantees for real-world Rust code at scale, bridging the gap between Rust's type-level safety and full program correctness.

Abstract: Rust's ownership type system prevents memory errors in safe code, but certain desirable properties remain orthogonal to compilation: the soundness of unsafe operations (e.g., raw pointer dereferences), functional correctness, and absence of runtime panics. We present Kani, an open-source model checker for Rust that pushes bounded model checking beyond bug-finding to provide correctness guarantees for these properties. Kani compiles proof harnesses from Rust's Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) into CBMC's bit-precise verification engine, automatically checking a comprehensive set of safety properties with no user annotation. To extend verification from bounded to unbounded, Kani provides a specification language comprising function contracts, loop contracts, quantifiers, and function stubbing. We demonstrate feasibility through case studies on industrial Rust projects, where contracts upgraded verification from panic-freedom to functional correctness, uncovering six previously unknown bugs. Kani operates at scale in production CI, with over 16,000 harnesses verified per code change in the Rust standard library verification campaign.

</details>


### [270] [A Capacity-Aware Parr Model for Agile Projects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01562)
*Pedro E. Colla*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A refactored Parr model is proposed as a capacity-aware forecasting layer for agile projects, combining normalized latent effort demand with observed/planned capacity trajectories to forecast progress, completion time, and capacity deficits without assuming fixed internal activity paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical software effort distribution models (PNR family, Parr curve) assume flexible staffing patterns, limiting their direct applicability in agile environments where team capacity is fixed, partially fixed, or externally constrained, as the original curves may prescribe staff demand the organization cannot allocate.

Method: The authors refactor Parr's model into a compact, capacity-aware forecasting layer: a normalized Parr-shaped latent effort demand is combined with an observed or planned capacity trajectory. The model uses a small parameter set (total effort K, Parr shape parameter, origin constant c for nonzero initial staffing, and capacity trajectory). A discrete sprint formulation, calibration from ordinary Scrum records, and a rolling-origin validation protocol against simple management baselines are provided.

Result: The model forecasts aggregate progress, completion time, capacity deficit, and capacity slack under resource-restricted conditions without assuming the same internal activity path is followed, using minimal parameters and standard Scrum data.

Conclusion: The capacity-aware refactoring of the Parr model offers a practical, lightweight forecasting layer for agile projects, filling the gap between classical effort distribution theory and real-world capacity-constrained agile delivery.

Abstract: Classical software effort distribution models, including the PNR family and Parr alter native curve, were designed to describe the time distribution of development effort under an implied staffing pattern. Their direct use in agile environments is limited when team capacity is fixed, partially fixed, or externally constrained, the original curve may prescribe a staff demand that the organization cannot allocate. This paper proposes a compact refactoring of Parr model as a capacity-aware forecasting layer for agile projects. The contribution is deliberately narrower than a full causal theory of project dynamics. A normalized Parr shaped latent effort demand is combined with an observed or planned capacity trajectory. The resulting model forecasts aggregate progress, completion time, capacity deficit, and capacity slack without assuming that the same internal activity path is followed under resource restriction. The model uses a small parameter set such as total effort K, a Parr shape parameter, an origin constant c that can match nonzero initial staffing, and the capacity trajectory. A discrete sprint formulation is provided, together with a calibration method from ordinary Scrum records and a rolling origin validation protocol against simple management baselines.

</details>


### [271] [A Single Patch Is Not Enough: Deterministic Fusion of Repair Candidates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01597)
*Boyang Yang,Xiangliang Hu,Luyao Ren,Yanjun Chen,Bach Le,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé,Haoye Tian*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PatchFusion proposes a deterministic, test-free post-generation method that fuses shared edit atoms across candidate patches to construct a final repair. It outperforms existing selectors on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Defects4J benchmarks while remaining far cheaper than test-based or LLM-based alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing pass@k evaluations overstate real-world utility because developers apply a single final patch (pass@1). Current post-generation methods—ranking, test filtering, or LLM judging—fail to deterministically reuse shared edit-atom evidence across candidates to both select and construct the optimal patch. The pass@k-to-pass@1 gap thus remains underaddressed.

Method: PatchFusion operates in three stages: (1) fusing whole-diff agreement into a repair neighborhood, (2) selecting an auditable representative, and (3) applying evidence-constrained fusion (ECF) to retain repeated edit atoms and prune unsupported parts. It is fully deterministic and consults no test outcomes at decision time. The authors also introduce PatchFuseBench, a fixed-pool benchmark across three datasets.

Result: PatchFusion solves 426/500 bugs (SWE-bench Verified), 236/300 (SWE-bench Multilingual), and 87/371 plausible patches (Defects4J), outperforming all matched candidate-pool selectors. It recovers 41 and 27 bugs that no single source solves. ECF ablation adds +5/+6/+9 solved bugs with no regression. Gains remain stable under pool resampling. It reaches 96.2% and 89.7% of the candidate-reachable ceiling on the two SWE-bench benchmarks at orders-of-magnitude lower cost.

Conclusion: Cross-candidate evidence fusion is a viable and superior alternative to test-based or LLM-based post-generation selection. PatchFusion narrows the pass@k-to-pass@1 gap deterministically and cost-efficiently, suggesting that reusing shared edit atoms across candidate pools is a promising direction for practical automated program repair.

Abstract: Modern LLM coding agents are commonly evaluated using pass@k, but developers typically apply a single final patch in real-world settings. This pass@k-to-pass@1 gap is a post-generation problem: a candidate patch pool may contain a correct patch, but the system must decide which one to suggest to developers. Existing post-generation approaches mainly rank whole candidates, filter them with tests, or query an LLM judge, but none deterministically reuse shared edit-atom evidence to both select and construct the final patch. Thus, we propose PatchFusion, a deterministic atomic evidence fusion approach for candidate patches that consults no test outcome at decision time. PatchFusion first fuses whole-diff agreement into a repair neighborhood, selects an auditable representative, and then applies evidence-constrained fusion (ECF) to retain repeated edit atoms and prune unsupported parts. To evaluate this setting, we build PatchFuseBench, a fixed-pool benchmark covering SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Defects4J candidate patches.
  On PatchFuseBench, PatchFusion solves 426/500 bugs on SWE-bench Verified and 236/300 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and reaches 87/371 plausible patches on Defects4J, outperforming every matched candidate-pool selector on all three. PatchFusion recovers 41 and 27 bugs that no single source solves (30 and 18 more over the best single source). Ablation studies show that ECF adds +5/+6/+9 solved bugs by recovering in-pool repairs that selection misses, with no observed regression, and that PatchFusion's gains remain stable as candidate pools are resampled. On these complementary multi-source pools, cross-candidate evidence recovers more correct patches than the test-based and LLM-based selectors we evaluate, at orders-of-magnitude lower cost, reaching within 96.2% and 89.7% of the candidate-reachable ceiling on the two SWE-bench benchmarks.

</details>


### [272] [AgentFlow: Building Agent Dependency Graphs for Static Analysis of Agent Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01640)
*Shenao Wang,Xinyi Hou,Yanjie Zhao,Xiao Cheng,Haoyu Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentFlow is a static analysis framework that constructs Agent Dependency Graphs (ADGs) from LLM agent programs to recover framework-induced dependencies. It enables Agent Bill of Materials generation and prompt-to-tool risk detection, outperforming existing AST-based tools across 5,399 real-world programs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agent programs combine conventional code with framework-specific semantics (agent constructors, tool decorators, handoff declarations), creating "agent dependencies" that are invisible to traditional static analysis tools. Existing dependency tracking cannot recover these framework-induced semantics, hindering governance, security auditing, and supply-chain transparency for agent software.

Method: AgentFlow introduces the Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic typed graph with nodes representing agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies, and typed edges capturing component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow dependencies. The framework performs static analysis across five agent frameworks and supports downstream analyses including Agent BOM generation and taint-style prompt-to-tool risk detection. Evaluation uses AgentZoo, a corpus of 5,399 real-world agent programs.

Result: AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based tools, generates more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs.

Conclusion: The ADG provides a practical and effective foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software, filling a critical gap left by conventional static analysis approaches that cannot reason about framework-induced agent semantics.

Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly developed as source-code applications built on agent frameworks. These agent programs combine conventional host-language code with framework-defined semantics for models, prompts, tools, memory, and multi-agent orchestration logic. As a result, their behavior depends not only on traditional control and data flows, but also on a new class of agent dependencies. Such dependencies are often expressed as framework-induced semantics, such as agent constructors, tool decorators, and agent handoff declarations, making them difficult to recover with existing static analysis or dependency tracking tools. In this paper, we present AgentFlow, the first static analysis framework for recovering and analyzing agent dependencies from agent programs. AgentFlow constructs an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic graph representation that represents agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies as typed nodes, and captures their component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow dependencies as typed edges. Built on ADGs, AgentFlow supports a range of analyses for agent governance and security, including Agent Bill of Materials (BOM) generation and prompt-to-tool risk detection. We implement AgentFlow for five representative agent frameworks and evaluate it on AgentZoo, a corpus of 5,399 real-world agent programs. Our evaluation shows that AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based agent static analysis tools, generates more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs. These results show that ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software.

</details>


### [273] [When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01641)
*Xinyi Hou,Shenao Wang,Yanjie Zhao,Haoyu Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM agents suffer from Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs)—unbounded iterative execution causing cost exhaustion and resource drain. The authors propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool that uses an Agent IR and Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to detect IALs. Evaluated on 6,549 repositories, it found 68 confirmed IAL failures across 47 projects with 91.9% precision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly use iterative execution (planning, tool use, state updates, collaboration), but this creates IALs—failures where agents repeatedly execute model calls, tools, transitions, or handoffs without bounded feedback. These loops cause cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context window overflow, and repeated external side effects. No existing tool systematically detects such failures in real-world agent code.

Method: IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool, abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework-independent Agent IR, constructs an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover both explicit and framework-induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state-growing operations without an effective bound.

Result: Evaluated on 6,549 LLM agent repositories, IAL-Scan reported 74 potential findings. Manual review confirmed 68 true IAL failures across 47 projects, yielding 91.9% precision.

Conclusion: IALs represent a distinct and practically significant failure mode in LLM agent systems. Static analysis via IAL-Scan is effective at detecting these loops across diverse frameworks, enabling developers to identify and mitigate unbounded execution paths before deployment.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on iterative execution to solve tasks through planning, tool use, state updates, and agent collaboration. While this design enables flexible automation, it also creates a new class of failures: an agent may repeatedly execute model calls, tools, workflow transitions, or agent handoffs when the feedback path is not effectively bounded. We call this problem Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs). IALs are not ordinary programming loops; they arise from the interaction between agent logic, framework semantics, runtime observations, and termination mechanisms. Such failures can amplify a single request into long running model and tool execution, causing cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context growth, and repeated external side effects. We propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool for detecting IAL failures in real-world LLM agent projects. IAL-Scan abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework independent Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover explicit and framework induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state growing operations without an effective bound. We evaluate IAL-Scan on 6,549 LLM agent repositories. It reports 74 potential findings, among which manual review confirms 68 IAL failures across 47 projects, achieving 91.9% precision.

</details>


### [274] [Refploit: Facilitating Exploit Construction via Code-Agent Trajectory Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01760)
*Zirui Chen,Zhipeng Xue,Jiayuan Zhou,Xing Hu,Xin Xia,Xiaohu Yang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Refploit is an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework that leverages failed exploit-generation attempts to iteratively refine and reproduce vulnerability exploits from unstructured public references. It uses differential execution to validate exploits and analyzes failed trajectories to derive corrective constraints, achieving 80.2% reproduction rate on 172 Java exploit references—a 64.3% relative improvement over initial trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public exploit references for Java library vulnerabilities are often incomplete or unstructured, making automatic reproduction into runnable exploits difficult. Existing code agents frequently generate superficially successful exploits that bypass actual vulnerable logic (e.g., replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented stubs), yielding false positives. A method is needed to recover from these failures by intelligently reusing partial progress from failed attempts.

Method: Refploit operates in a two-phase loop: (1) Differential execution validation — it compares the behavior of the generated exploit against a patched vs. unpatched version of the library to determine whether the vulnerable logic is actually triggered. (2) Trajectory recovery — when validation fails, Refploit analyzes the agent's reproduction progress, identifies trajectory segments corresponding to completed subtasks and misleading directions, and derives constraints that guide focused re-generation. This constraint-guided recovery is repeated until a validated exploit is produced.

Result: Evaluated on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets (172 exploit references, 143 vulnerabilities) using DeepSeek-V4-Flash as the base LLM, Refploit reproduced 138 exploits (80.2% success rate). This represents a 64.3% relative improvement over initial agent-generated trajectories. It outperformed the state-of-the-art exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents like Codex with GPT-5.4. The framework also demonstrated generality by improving a different code agent when adapted to it.

Conclusion: Failed agent trajectories contain recoverable subtask progress and valuable negative signals. By systematically validating exploit effectiveness and guiding recovery through constraint derivation from failed trajectories, Refploit substantially improves automatic vulnerability reproduction. Its strong performance and cross-agent generality suggest trajectory recovery is a broadly applicable paradigm for code-generation agents dealing with complex, under-specified tasks.

Abstract: Vulnerability exploits play a crucial role in assessing the downstream impact of Java library vulnerabilities. While some vulnerabilities are accompanied by disclosed exploit references, automatically reproducing such references into runnable exploits remains challenging because they are often incomplete, unstructured, or only describe partial reproduction steps. Recent code agents provide a promising way to automate this process, but our study shows that their generated exploits often appear successful without triggering the actual vulnerable logic, such as replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions. To address this, we propose Refploit, an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework for facilitating vulnerability reproduction from public exploit references. The key insight is that a failed agent trajectory is not entirely useless. It may have already completed some reproduction subtasks while also revealing misleading directions that should be avoided. Refploit first validates an agent-generated exploit through differential execution. When the exploit is ineffective, Refploit analyzes its reproduction progress, locates the trajectory segments associated with the reproduction progress, and derives constraints to guide focused recovery. We evaluate Refploit on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets, covering 172 exploit references for 143 vulnerabilities. Under DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit successfully reproduces 138 exploits, achieving a reproduction rate of 80.2%. It achieves a 64.3% relative improvement over the initially generated trajectories and outperforms both the SOTA exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents such as Codex with GPT-5.4. We further adapt Refploit to another code agent and observe consistent improvements, demonstrating its generality.

</details>


### [275] [KRCA: An Efficient Root Cause Analysis System in Hyper-Scale Microservice Systems via Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01788)
*Jiamin Jiang,Jingfei Feng,Yu Luo,Qingliang Zhang,Yongqian Su,Wenwei Gu,Shenglin Zhang,Tianyu Cui,Yao Wu,Jielong Huang,Nan Qi,Dan Pei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: KRCA is an end-to-end Root Cause Analysis system for hyper-scale microservices that uses a multi-stage pipeline combining API-level drilldown, skeleton-based causal graphs, and a memory-augmented multi-agent framework to localize root cause services and classify failure types, achieving significant accuracy gains and a 77.3% reduction in diagnosis time in production at Kuaishou.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hyper-scale microservice systems, composed of numerous independently evolving, loosely coupled services, experience unavoidable failures. Existing RCA methods fail to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale, creating a need for efficient, accurate, and production-grade root cause analysis that can quickly localize root cause services and classify failure types for SREs.

Method: KRCA employs a multi-stage pipeline: (1) API-level drilldown to narrow the search space by isolating suspicious services; (2) instantiation of a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics as a high-recall structural prior; (3) a memory-augmented multi-agent framework that verifies causality and generates the final failure report. The approach balances structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning for both diagnostic accuracy and real-time efficiency.

Result: KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 for root cause service localization and 0.79 for failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at least 31% in absolute gains. Deployed in Kuaishou's production environment for over six months, it reduced average diagnosis time by 77.3%.

Conclusion: KRCA demonstrates that combining structured causal priors with multi-agent reasoning is a highly effective approach for RCA in hyper-scale microservice systems, offering both superior accuracy and substantial operational efficiency gains in real-world production environments.

Abstract: Hyper-scale microservice systems have become the standard infrastructure for large-scale Internet companies. These systems consist of numerous loosely coupled microservices that evolve independently through continuous development and deployment. Such complexity makes failures unavoidable, necessitating efficient Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to help Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) quickly localize root cause services and classify failure types. However, existing RCA methods often struggle to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale of these systems. In this paper, we present KRCA, an end-to-end RCA system designed for hyper-scale microservice systems. To manage the vast search space, KRCA employs a multi-stage pipeline that begins with an API-level drilldown to isolate suspicious services. It then instantiates a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics to serve as a high-recall structural prior, before utilizing a memory-augmented multi-agent framework to verify causality and generate the final failure report. By combining structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning, KRCA employs balances diagnostic accuracy with the efficiency requirements of real-time production use. Experimental results show that KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 and 0.79 for root cause service localization and failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at lease 31% in absolute gains. KRCA has been deployed in Kuaishou's production environment for over six months, reducing the average diagnosis time by 77.3%.

</details>


### [276] [Archer: Towards Agentic Review for Compiler Optimizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01808)
*Yunbo Ni,Shaohua Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Archer is an automated agentic code review tool for LLVM compiler optimizations that uses obligation-guided analysis and deterministic validation to find semantic bugs. Evaluation on 398 recent LLVM PRs reveals 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs contain miscompilation bugs, exposing a critical review capacity gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern compilers like LLVM are updated frequently, but expert reviewer capacity is severely limited, causing delayed integration and subtle semantic bugs (e.g., miscompilations) slipping into the codebase. General-purpose code review agents struggle with compiler complexity, motivating a specialized automated review approach.

Method: The authors present Archer, an agentic code review tool specifically for compiler optimizations targeting LLVM. Archer constrains the review process bidirectionally: (1) obligations are used to guide the agent's analysis, and (2) a deterministic validation guard ensures only findings with executable evidence are admitted.

Result: On 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs from the last two months, Archer found that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs contain semantic bugs (miscompilations), demonstrating a significant gap in critical review capacity within large compiler projects.

Conclusion: Archer demonstrates practical value as an automated supplementary reviewer for compiler projects, revealing that a substantial fraction of both open and already-merged PRs contain semantic bugs, and highlighting the urgent need for automated review tooling in large-scale compiler development.

Abstract: Modern compilers are frequently updated, but expert review capacity is highly limited, leading to delayed integration and, in some cases, subtle semantic bugs entering the compiler codebase. Automating the code review process with modern general code review agents may be feasible, but it faces critical challenges due to compiler complexity. In this paper, we use LLVM as our target compiler and present Archer, the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations. Archer constrains the agentic review process from both ends by using obligations to guide analysis and a deterministic validation guard to admit only findings backed by executable evidence.
  We evaluated Archer on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs in LLVM from the last two months. The review results are shocking and concerning: Archer discovers that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs are buggy, i.e, introducing semantic bugs such as miscompilations in LLVM. Our findings expose a critical gap in the capacity for critical review in large compiler projects and demonstrate the practical value of Archer as an additional reviewer.

</details>


### [277] [Decoupling Code Complexity from Newcomer Participation: A Causal Study of AI Coding Agent Adoption in OSS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01810)
*Weiwei Xu,Xuanning Cui,Hengzhi Ye,Minghui Zhou*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Using difference-in-differences on 1,888 open-source projects that adopted AI coding agents (with 603 in the main analysis), the study finds no evidence that AI agents crowd out newcomers — newcomer inflow, onboarding, and retention remain unchanged — despite a modest increase in code complexity (+3–11% across metrics). The feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is growing concern that AI coding agents (e.g., Cursor, Claude Code) may crowd out newcomers from open-source projects by automating simple beginner tasks and making code harder to read, thereby threatening the pipeline of future contributors. The paper seeks to provide a causal answer to this concern.

Method: The authors identify 1,888 GitHub projects that adopted an AI coding agent via their first commit of a configuration file. They apply a difference-in-differences design comparing adopters against matched non-adopting control projects, restricting the main analysis to 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. Outcomes include newcomer inflow, onboarding/retention metrics, good-first-issue labels (as a correlational beginner-task measure), and code complexity (cognitive and cyclomatic metrics). Multiple estimators and trend specifications are used, including conservative ones.

Result: No significant decline in newcomer inflow, onboarding, or retention after AI agent adoption — point estimates range from a small increase to a slight, insignificant dip under the most conservative specification. Good-first-issue labels also show no decline (though parallel trends could not be tested). Code complexity increases significantly: ~11% on a cognitive metric for Python and +3–4% in cyclomatic complexity across all languages. However, in fixed-unit subsets where complexity rose, newcomer participation did not decline, indicating the complexity effect is decoupled from newcomer outcomes.

Conclusion: In established open-source projects, adopting AI coding agents makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out human newcomers. The feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

Abstract: Open-source projects depend on a steady inflow of newcomers. A growing concern is that AI coding agents (tools such as Cursor and Claude Code that write code from natural-language instructions) will crowd them out, by absorbing the simple tasks that beginners start with and by making code harder to read. We give this concern a causal answer. Using GitHub code search we identify 1,888 projects that adopted an agent, signaled by their first commit of a configuration file. We apply difference-in-differences against matched non-adopting controls, restricting the main analysis to the 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. We find no evidence of crowding-out: across estimators newcomer inflow shows no significant decline after adoption (point estimates run from a small increase to, under the most conservative trend specification, a slight and insignificant dip), onboarding and retention are unchanged, and a sparse, correlational beginner-task measure (good-first-issue labels, which we cannot test for parallel trends) shows no decline. The feared mechanism is real but decoupled: adoption raises per-function code complexity (about +11% on a cognitive metric for Python, a quarter of the prior estimate, and +3 to 4% in cyclomatic terms across all languages), yet in fixed-unit subsets where complexity rose (Python on the cognitive metric, and all languages on the cyclomatic metric), newcomer participation does not decline. These results suggest that, in established open-source projects, adopting an AI coding agent makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out the human newcomers that a project depends on: the feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

</details>


### [278] [Understanding Software Defect Prediction: A Large-scale Empirical Study Across Uncertainty Quantification and Performance Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01842)
*Ranjun Peng,Xuan Xie,Rubing Huang,Wenbin He,Zhijie Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A large-scale study of 16 classifiers across 36 within-project and 32 cross-project datasets reveals that uncertainty quantification (UQ) metrics correlate inconsistently with performance and calibration, are highly context-dependent, and transfer poorly across projects. Researchers should evaluate UQ against specific objectives and independently assess calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SDP classifiers output probabilities used for prioritization and risk communication, but it is unclear whether common probability-based UQ metrics reliably indicate predictive performance and calibration quality. Prior work lacked systematic, large-scale empirical evidence on these relationships, especially across different prediction settings (WPDP vs. CPDP).

Method: The authors conducted a large-scale empirical study evaluating five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics across 16 representative classifiers. They analyzed correlations under two settings: WPDP (36 benchmark datasets) and CPDP (32 feature-compatible datasets), stratifying results by classifier category and dataset collection.

Result: Under WPDP, UQ metrics correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC or F1; correlations varied across classifier types and datasets. Performance and calibration were related but not interchangeable — classifiers with strong discrimination could still have large calibration error. Under CPDP, many UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating unreliable transfer of uncertainty signals.

Conclusion: UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives rather than treated as a universal proxy. Calibration must be assessed independently using multiple metrics. Transferred probabilities in CPDP settings require revalidation before informing quality-assurance decisions.

Abstract: Software defect prediction (SDP) classifiers produce probabilities used for inspection prioritization, threshold tuning, and risk communication. Probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) characterizes prediction confidence, but whether common UQ metrics reliably indicate performance and calibration remains unclear. We conducted a large-scale empirical study of probability-based UQ for SDP. We evaluated five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics for 16 representative classifiers. We analyzed these relationships under two prediction settings: within-project defect prediction (WPDP), using 36 benchmark datasets, and cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), using 32 feature-compatible datasets. Results showed that UQ was highly context-dependent. Under WPDP, UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC, F1 score, and other metrics; these correlations also varied across classifier categories and dataset collections. Performance and calibration were related but not interchangeable; classifiers with strong discrimination could still exhibit large calibration error. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating that uncertainty signals do not reliably transfer across projects. Thus, UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives. Calibration should be assessed independently using multiple metrics. Transferred probabilities should be revalidated before guiding quality-assurance decisions.

</details>


### [279] [Technical Debt Friction for Maintenance Prioritization: An Industrial Multi-Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01850)
*Simeon Tverdal,Phu Nguyen,Arda Goknil,Antonio Martini,Markus Borg,Adam Tornhill*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a multi-case industrial study investigating "technical debt friction" — a prioritization concept for identifying where technical debt most severely impacts maintenance and evolution. Through structured walkthroughs with practitioners across multiple cases, the authors found that friction analysis aligned with known problematic areas and predicted future maintenance needs, though its practical relevance is context-dependent. The study suggests friction distributions may reveal broader maintenance patterns beyond individual refactoring candidates, and the concept is most effective when combined with contextual knowledge and complementary socio-technical views.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional software analytics (code health, hotspots, coupling) provide valuable signals but fail to capture the experienced burden of change that slows software evolution in practice. Organizations need more effective ways to prioritize maintenance and refactoring efforts for maximum practical benefit. The concept of "technical debt friction" is proposed to bridge this gap by quantifying how strongly technical debt impedes maintenance activities.

Method: A multi-case industrial study employing structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners. Analysis artifacts included code health metrics, hotspots, coupling measures, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views. The study examined: (1) how practitioners interpret technical debt friction, (2) whether friction analysis aligns with perceived maintenance pain points and refactoring needs, and (3) what broader insights friction provides beyond individual refactoring candidates. Both file-level and exploratory project-level analyses were conducted.

Result: Practitioners found technical debt friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, particularly when combined with complementary technical and socio-technical views. At the file level, friction frequently aligned with known problematic areas and, in several cases, with files that later received maintenance attention. However, practical relevance was strongly context-dependent. Exploratory project-level analysis suggested that friction distributions may reveal broader maintenance and evolution patterns.

Conclusion: Technical debt friction is a promising decision-support concept for prioritizing maintenance and refactoring efforts, but it is most effective when used alongside contextual knowledge and supporting evidence rather than in isolation.

Abstract: Software-intensive organizations need effective ways to identify where maintenance and refactoring efforts will yield the greatest practical benefit. Although software analytics such as code health, hotspots, and coupling provide valuable signals, they do not always capture the experienced burden of change that slows software evolution in practice. This paper presents a multi-case industrial study of technical debt friction as a prioritization-oriented concept for identifying where technical debt most strongly affects maintenance and evolution. We investigate how practitioners interpret the concept, whether friction-related analysis aligns with perceived maintenance pain points and refactoring needs, and what broader maintenance and evolution insights friction can provide beyond individual refactoring candidates. To this end, we conducted structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners across multiple industrial cases using analysis artifacts including code health, hotspots, coupling, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views. Our findings show that practitioners generally considered technical debt friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, especially when interpreted together with complementary technical and socio-technical views. At the file level, friction often aligned with known problematic areas and, in several cases, with files that later received maintenance attention, although its practical relevance depended strongly on context. In addition, our exploratory project-level analysis suggests that friction distributions may reveal broader maintenance and evolution patterns. These results indicate that technical debt friction is promising as a decision-support concept, but most effective when used with contextual knowledge and supporting evidence.

</details>


### [280] [Regression Accumulation in Multi-Turn LLM Programming Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01855)
*Yonghui,Huang,Lin Ma,Amjed Tahir,Qian Zhang,Liwen Xiao,Lysa Xiao*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM multi-turn coding conversations suffer from "regression accumulation": later code suggestions frequently break requirements satisfied in earlier turns. Testing 6 LLMs on 26,016 instances across 8-turn chains, 40–73% of tasks lost previously correct behavior. Cross-Turn Conflict is the dominant failure mode. A Verification Gate strategy (checking new code against prior tests with rollback and retry) consistently improved all models, raising final-turn quality significantly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-assisted coding is inherently iterative, yet existing evaluations focus on single-turn correctness. In multi-turn settings, LLMs may regress on previously satisfied requirements when generating new code — a phenomenon termed "regression accumulation." Understanding and mitigating this is critical for reliable LLM-assisted software development.

Method: The authors constructed 542 tasks by extending HumanEval+ and MBPP+ benchmarks into 8-turn requirement-evolution chains. Six LLMs were evaluated across 26,016 turn instances. At each turn, code was tested against all prior benchmark tests to detect regressions. Additionally, 384 failure cases were manually analyzed and labeled by four independent annotators to build a taxonomy of multi-turn regression bugs. The Verification Gate mitigation strategy was evaluated: after each code generation, the new code is checked against all prior tests; if any fail, the model rolls back and retries.

Result: Regression accumulation was observed in all six models, with 40–73% of tasks losing previously correct behavior across the full 8-turn conversation. Final-turn quality was consistently lower than initial-turn quality, especially when later turns introduced input validation or broader input types. Cross-Turn Conflict emerged as the primary failure category. The Verification Gate strategy was the only approach that consistently improved all models, boosting DeepSeek-V3 final-turn quality from 75.8% to 87.9% and Llama-3.1-8B from 31.6% to 47.3%.

Conclusion: Strong single-turn performance can overestimate reliability in multi-turn coding scenarios. Future LLM coding evaluations and tooling should explicitly test for regression accumulation — verifying that later code suggestions preserve earlier requirements — and should incorporate Verification Gate mechanisms as a practical mitigation.

Abstract: In LLM-assisted software development, coding is often iterative. We study regression accumulation in multi-turn LLM programming conversations, where later code suggestions may break requirements introduced in earlier turns. Reliability therefore depends not only on satisfying the current request, but also on preserving previously satisfied behavior.
  We construct 542 tasks from HumanEval+ and MBPP+ and extend each task into an 8-turn requirement-evolution chain. We evaluate six LLMs on 26,016 turn instances (542 x 6 x 8). At each turn, we test whether the current code still passes earlier benchmark tests. We also analyze 384 failure cases from the failure population and build a taxonomy of multi-turn regression bugs through independent four-annotator labeling.
  Our results show that regression accumulation appears across all six models: 40% to 73% of tasks lose previously correct behavior over the full conversation. Final-turn quality is lower than initial-turn quality across models, especially when later turns add input validation or broader input types. Manual analysis shows that Cross-Turn Conflict, where later code conflicts with earlier requirements, is the main failure class. We further find that Verification Gate, which checks new code against prior tests and triggers rollback and retry, is the only strategy that consistently improves all models, raising final-turn quality from 75.8% to 87.9% on DeepSeek-V3 and from 31.6% to 47.3% on Llama-3.1-8B.
  These findings suggest that strong single-turn performance can overestimate reliability in multi-turn coding conversations. Future evaluation and tool design should test whether later code suggestions preserve earlier requirements and should include Verification Gate mechanisms.

</details>


### [281] [An Exploratory Study on LLM-Generated Code and Comments in Code Repositories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01867)
*Yongyi Ji,Jiaji Wang,Yi Zhou,Fuxiang Chen,Hongji Yang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates the prevalence, characteristics, and bug association of LLM-generated code and comments across company- and community-maintained repositories from 2021–2025, using detector-based proxy analysis to identify likely AI-generated content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite widespread LLM adoption in software development (20–30% of code at large tech companies), skepticism persists regarding debugging overhead and comment quality. The authors aim to empirically characterize LLM-generated code/comments, compare company vs. community repositories, and assess whether LLM-generated code correlates with bugs.

Method: The authors conduct large-scale experiments on active repositories (2021–2025) using multiple detection tools and techniques that identify code and comments likely generated by LLMs. They analyze temporal trends, distribution across file types, intra-repository clones, grammatical correctness of comments, differences between company- and community-maintained projects, and overlap with human-labelled bugs.

Result: (1) LLM-detected code decreased over time and concentrated in test cases, while LLM-detected comments remained stable. (2) LLM-detected code exhibits substantial intra-repository clones; LLM-detected comments show lower grammatical correctness. (3) Company repositories have higher percentages of LLM-detected code and comments. (4) Only a small fraction of human-labelled bugs are associated with LLM-detected code.

Conclusion: LLM-generated content in repositories follows distinct patterns: code is declining and concentrated in tests with high cloning, comments are grammatically weaker, corporate adoption outpaces community use, and bug risk from LLM code appears minimal — suggesting concerns may be overstated.

Abstract: The use of LLMs in software development has become increasingly widespread on tasks such as code generation and summarization. Reports from large technology companies showed that around 20% to 30% of their code are generated by LLMs. However, there remains skepticism about the practical usage of LLM-generated code and comments, such as concerns on more time for debugging the generated code and the unnaturalness of the generated comments. In this paper, we study the code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs and their characteristics, the differences between company- and community-maintained repositories, and how likely bugs are associated with LLM-generated code. We conduct extensive experiments on active company- and community-maintained repositories from 2021 to 2025 using various tools and techniques that detect code and comments generated by LLMs. Based on our detector-based proxy analysis, the results suggest that code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs decreased over time and appeared frequently in test cases, while that of comments remains relatively stable. Proxy results further suggest that code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs shows substantial intra-repository code clones, whereas comments exhibit a relatively low proportion of grammatically correct sentences. In addition, the company-maintained repositories show a higher percentage of code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs, and only a small percentage of the human-labelled bugs are detected as being likely associated with LLM-generated code.

</details>


### [282] [Understanding Build Reproducibility in the F-Droid Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01890)
*Denise Nanni,Julien Malka,Stefano Zacchiroli,Théo Zimmermann,Gabriele d'Angelo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An empirical study of build reproducibility in the F-Droid Android app ecosystem, examining both historical trends and temporal decay. While bitwise reproducibility rates have improved over time for new app versions, and 94% of successfully rebuilt apps remain bitwise identical, rebuildability itself degrades significantly due to missing dependencies (76% of failures).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: F-Droid rebuilds apps from source and verifies bitwise reproducibility at publishing time, but provides no guarantee that reproducibility persists over time. As ecosystems evolve, this reproducibility may degrade, threatening software preservation and security. No prior empirical study had quantified this temporal decay.

Method: The authors analyzed historical reproducibility logs from F-Droid and conducted a large-scale rebuild experiment: attempting to rebuild 18,904 app versions (spanning September 2018 to February 2026) that had been previously confirmed as bitwise reproducible, then measuring both rebuild success rate and bitwise reproducibility among successes.

Result: Overall bitwise reproducibility rates for newly published apps have steadily increased over time. The rebuild experiment achieved an 83% success rate; missing dependencies accounted for 76% of failures. Among successfully rebuilt apps, 94% remained bitwise reproducible (yielding identical artifacts).

Conclusion: Bitwise reproducibility largely holds for apps that can still be rebuilt, but rebuildability is highly sensitive to temporal decay — primarily due to disappearing dependencies. This exposes a critical vulnerability in F-Droid's long-term reproducibility guarantees.

Abstract: The security of open source applications benefits considerably from the possibility of rebuilding their source and verifying the output. F-Droid, a prominent distribution for open source Android applications, systematically rebuilds them from source and tests their bitwise reproducibility at app publishing time. However, F-Droid offers no guarantee that app reproducibility will continue to hold in the future. As software ecosystems evolve, reproducibility may degrade, with potential negative consequences for software preservation and security. We present the first empirical study of build reproducibility in the F-Droid app ecosystem. Analyzing historical reproducibility logs, we find that the overall bitwise reproducibility rate has been steadily increasing over time (as new versions of apps are published). We then evaluate how reproducibility holds in time for fixed app versions, by attempting to rebuild 18 904 app versions that F-Droid had previously confirmed bitwise reproducible, published between September 2018 and February 2026, achieving an 83% rebuild success rate, and identify missing dependencies as the dominant cause of failure, accounting for 76% of non-rebuildable cases. Among successfully rebuilt apps, 94% are also bitwise reproducible-i.e., they still yield bitwise identical artifacts upon rebuild. Together, these results show that while bitwise reproducibility largely holds for apps that can be rebuilt, rebuildability itself is highly sensitive to temporal decay.

</details>


### [283] [AI Writes Faster Than Humans Can Review: A Longitudinal Study of an Enterprise 2x Mandate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01904)
*Hao He,Shyam Agarwal,Yegor Denisov-Blanch,Pavel Azaletskiy,Sanmi Koyejo,Bogdan Vasilescu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A longitudinal case study of an enterprise "2x" mandate at an AI-forward company shows per-capita pull request throughput doubled to 2.09x baseline by April 2026. Using staggered difference-in-differences with 802 developers and ~196k PRs, the gain is linked to AI adoption and accumulated use—not the mandate itself. Gains are broadly shared across seniority, concentrated in newer code, and accompanied by a restructuring of code review toward automation, with automated review overtaking human review while merge/revert rates held steady.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite enterprises increasingly mandating AI coding tools and claiming large productivity gains, there is scarce longitudinal, quantitative evidence on how such mandates actually unfold in practice. The authors aim to fill this gap with a rigorous case study.

Method: A quantitative case study using a panel of 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests from January 2024 to April 2026. The primary outcome is per-capita merged PR throughput. A staggered difference-in-differences design is employed to link within-developer throughput gains to AI adoption timing and accumulated usage intensity, with the mandate treated as a catalyst rather than a direct causal driver.

Result: Per-capita throughput reached 2.09x the pre-mandate baseline by April 2026. The within-developer gain is associated with AI adoption and grows with accumulated use; the mandate acted catalytically. Gains are broadly shared across seniority levels but concentrated in newer code and not separable across model generations. Code review was restructured: per-reviewer load roughly doubled, automated review surpassed human review in volume, while merge and revert rates remained stable.

Conclusion: The evidence strongly implicates an adoption-and-use channel for productivity gains rather than the mandate itself as a direct driver. AI coding tools can substantially boost enterprise developer throughput without degrading code quality metrics, while fundamentally shifting code review practices toward automation.

Abstract: Enterprises increasingly mandate AI coding tools and report large productivity gains, yet longitudinal evidence on how such a mandate unfolds is scarce. In this paper, we present a quantitative case study of a documented enterprise "2x" mandate at a mid-sized, AI-forward company that has been committed to doubling merged pull requests per engineer since mid-2025. In a panel of 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests (January 2024-April 2026), per-capita throughput eventually doubled, reaching 2.09x the pre-mandate baseline in April 2026, among the largest gains reported from a field deployment of AI coding tools to our knowledge. A staggered difference-in-differences design links the within-developer share of this gain to AI adoption and to a further gain that grows with accumulated use, with the mandate acting as a catalyst rather than a direct driver. Because adoption and usage intensity were not randomly assigned, we read this evidence as strongly implicating an adoption-and-use channel rather than as exact causal attribution. The gain is broadly shared across seniority yet concentrated in newer code and not separable across model generations. Adoption also restructured code review around automation: per-reviewer load roughly doubled and automated review overtook human review, while merge and revert rates held steady.

</details>


### [284] [Beyond Textual Repository Exploration: Dual-Modal Structural Reasoning for Agentic Issue Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01929)
*Jiayi Zhang,Kai Huang,Yang Liu,Chunyang Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: DUALVIEW introduces a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework that enhances agentic program repair by augmenting repository exploration with visual graph representations (MCG, FCG, CHG, PDG), enabling agents to reason over persistent structural views rather than reconstructing dependencies from sequential textual observations, yielding consistent improvements on SWE-bench Pro and Verified across diverse agent architectures and model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic program repair systems rely on sequential, text-based code navigation, which forces agents to repeatedly reconstruct structural information (module organization, call relationships, dependency chains) across interaction steps. This leads to exploration drift and incomplete localization, especially in large-scale, long-horizon repositories with complex long-range dependencies.

Method: DUALVIEW represents repository structure through four complementary graph views: Module Coupling Graph (MCG), Function Call Graph (FCG), Class Hierarchy Graph (CHG), and Program Dependence Graph (PDG). These are exposed via a queryable interface that provides both visual and textual responses, allowing agents to directly reason over persistent visual representations of code dependencies rather than reconstructing structure from fragmented textual observations.

Result: DUALVIEW consistently improves issue-resolution performance across different agent architectures and model families on SWE-bench Pro and Verified. Ablation studies confirm that gains stem from both textual structural information and visual externalization of repository dependencies, with the latter particularly benefiting long-horizon repository exploration.

Conclusion: Visual reasoning via dual-modal structural scaffolding substantially enhances repository exploration for issue-resolution agents. Persistent, queryable graph-based representations mitigate the limitations of sequential text-based navigation, enabling more effective understanding of complex codebases and reducing exploration drift.

Abstract: Recent advances in agentic program repair have significantly improved issue resolution by enabling iterative repository exploration. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on sequential, text-based code navigation, which fundamentally limits their ability to reason over large-scale long-horizon repositories with complex and long-range dependencies. As issue-resolution agents traverse repositories through fragmented textual observations, structural information such as module organization, call relationships, and dependency chains must be repeatedly reconstructed across interaction steps, often leading to exploration drift and incomplete localization. We present DUALVIEW, a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework that brings visual reasoning into repository exploration for issue-resolution agents. DUALVIEW represents repository structure through four complementary graph views: Module Coupling Graph (MCG), Function Call Graph (FCG), Class Hierarchy Graph (CHG), and Program Dependence Graph (PDG), and exposes them through a queryable interface with visual and textual responses. Rather than reconstructing repository structure from a sequence of textual observations, agents can directly reason over persistent visual representations of code dependencies, enabling more effective exploration and understanding of long-horizon codebases. We evaluate DUALVIEW on SWE-bench Pro and Verified. Results show that DUALVIEW consistently improves issue-resolution performance across different agent architectures and model families. Further ablation studies demonstrate that the gains arise not only from textual structural information but also from visual externalization of repository dependencies, which better supports long-horizon repository exploration.

</details>


### [285] [Underspecification does not imply Incoherence: The Risks of Semantic Collapse in Coding Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01953)
*Cedric Richter,Mike Papadakis*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLMs tend to collapse onto a single incorrect interpretation of underspecified prompts, producing coherent but misaligned code. This "detrimental semantic collapse" affects 10%+ of standard benchmarks and increases 5× with injected underspecification, undermining methods that rely on incoherence to detect ambiguity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work assumes that prompt underspecification leads to incoherence—an LLM producing semantically diverse outputs when queried multiple times. The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that LLMs may instead consistently converge on a single but incorrect interpretation, creating a blind spot in existing disambiguation and correctness estimation techniques.
