Method: The authors evaluate LLMs on code generation benchmarks (MBPP, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench) by repeatedly sampling from the same underspecified prompt and measuring semantic diversity of outputs. They also deliberately inject underspecification issues (ambiguity, incompleteness, contradiction) into benchmark prompts and measure the rate of detrimental semantic collapse—defined as consistent generation of coherent but behaviorally misaligned code across multiple samples.

Result: Detrimental semantic collapse affects over 10% of tasks in MBPP, 3% in HumanEval, and 32% in LiveCodeBench. When underspecification is deliberately injected, the collapse rate rises over 5×. This demonstrates that incoherence is an unreliable proxy for detecting underspecification, exposing a fundamental blind spot in current methods.

Conclusion: LLMs exhibit a previously unrecognized failure mode—detrimental semantic collapse—where they consistently produce coherent but incorrect code under underspecification rather than displaying semantic diversity. This calls into question evaluation and disambiguation techniques that assume incoherence signals ambiguity, and highlights the need for new approaches to detect and mitigate this behavior.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly effective at generating code when task descriptions are clear and precise. Yet, in practice, user-provided task descriptions are often ambiguous, incomplete, or contradictory, leaving critical aspects of the intended program behavior underspecified. In such cases, multiple behaviorally distinct interpretations may satisfy the description equally well, yet semantically differ in ways that matter/affect the user intent. A natural expectation, often assumed by researchers, is that prompt underspecification manifests as incoherence: When asked multiple times, an LLM produces multiple semantically distinct implementations reflecting the ambiguity of the task description. In this paper, we challenge this assumption. We find that LLMs frequently collapse onto a single incorrect interpretation of the task description, consistently generating coherent but behaviorally misaligned code. We term this failure mode detrimental semantic collapse and find that it affects over 10% of tasks in MBPP, 3% in HumanEval, and 32% of LiveCodeBench, all benchmarks assumed to be well-specified. By deliberately injecting underspecification issues in the benchmark prompts, the rate rises to over 5 times, exposing a fundamental blind spot in disambiguation and correctness estimation techniques that rely on incoherence as a proxy for prompt underspecification.

</details>


### [286] [Epic-Organized vs. Requirement-Aligned Gherkin: An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Acceptance Criteria Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01980)
*Shahbaz Siddeeq,Mateen Abbasi,Jussi Rasku,Zheying Zhang,François Christophe,Tommi Mikkonen,Pekka Abrahamsson*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Comparing epic-organized vs. requirement-aligned LLM-generated Gherkin BDD scenarios, the epic-organized (Timeless) approach achieved comparable semantic coverage (94.3% vs 92.9%) while significantly outperforming the baseline on expert-rated Correctness, Executability, and Completeness, suggesting higher perceived quality without sacrificing coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated authoring of Gherkin BDD acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. The paper investigates whether organizing LLM generation around epics (rather than aligning directly with individual requirements) can improve the quality and coverage of generated Gherkin scenarios.

Method: The authors propose Timeless, an epic-organized LLM pipeline that uses JSON-constrained generation to produce Gherkin scenarios. They compare it against a naive zero-shot LLM baseline using four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation includes structural validity metrics, automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings, and blind expert assessment by four researchers rating Correctness, Executability, and Completeness on Likert scales.

Result: Timeless achieved 100% structural validity (vs. 99% baseline), 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate (vs. 92.9% baseline), and superior expert ratings: Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50). TF-IDF underestimated epic-organized coverage, suggesting lexical metrics miss coverage when scenarios paraphrase at higher abstraction levels.

Conclusion: Epic-organized generation improves perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage. However, the authors caution that broader replication across diverse datasets and domains is necessary before generalizing this finding.

Abstract: Automated authoring of Gherkin Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. This study investigates whether epic-organized LLM-generated Gherkin produces higher quality and coverage than requirement-aligned generation. We compare our Timeless (an epic-organized LLM pipeline) approach against a naive large language model (LLM) baseline on four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation covers structural metrics, automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings, and blind expert assessment by four researchers. In our evaluation, the JSON-constrained pipeline produced structurally valid scenarios across all generated outputs, while the zero-shot baseline achieved 99% structural validity. Semantic coverage was comparable to the baseline, with Timeless achieving 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate compared with 92.9% for the baseline. TF-IDF produced lower coverage scores for the epic-organized output, suggesting that lexical metrics may miss coverage when scenarios paraphrase requirements at a higher level of abstraction. Expert raters prefer the epic-organized strategy on Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50). Overall, the results suggest that epic-organized generation can improve perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, although broader replication is needed before generalizing this finding.

</details>


### [287] [Benchmarking Quantum Software Testing with Scalable Quantum Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02029)
*Yuechen Li,Minqi Shao,Xiyuan Li,Jianjun Zhao,Kai-Yuan Cai*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Qolumbina is a benchmark infrastructure for quantum software testing that curates 40 test-ready quantum programs from open-source repositories, proposes QST-oriented characterization criteria, and enables controlled, reproducible empirical evaluation of QST approaches at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing QST research lacks standardized benchmarks: current studies rely on small, hard-coded, or circuit-level programs, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories with no clear selection criteria. This hampers fair comparison, systematic reproducibility, and rigorous empirical evaluation reflective of real-world quantum software development.

Method: The authors built Qolumbina by curating 40 quantum programs from open-source repositories. They applied systematic selection, refactoring, specification writing, test case creation, unit test development, and standardized interfaces to transform raw programs into test-ready subjects. They also defined QST-oriented criteria characterizing programs along four dimensions: functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. Two recent QST approaches were evaluated in controlled experiments to demonstrate feasibility.

Result: The empirical study showed that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Controlled experiments with two QST approaches demonstrated feasibility for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, while revealing backend-dependent effects that influence QST result interpretation.

Conclusion: Qolumbina provides a systematic, reproducible benchmark infrastructure that enables rigorous evaluation of quantum software testing techniques on realistic, scalable programs, addressing a critical gap in the QST research landscape.

Abstract: Quantum software testing (QST) checks whether quantum programs behave according to their intended specifications. A key requirement for QST research is a benchmark that supports rigorous empirical evaluation on programs that are testable and better reflect current software development practices. However, existing studies heavily rely on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories without clear selection criteria, which limits fair comparison and systematic reproducibility. To this end, we present Qolumbina, a benchmark infrastructure for controlled QST experiments on scalable quantum programs. Qolumbina curates 40 programs from open-source repositories, turns them into test-ready subjects through systematic selection, refactoring, specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. We also propose QST-oriented criteria to characterize quantum programs along functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. Using these criteria, our empirical study shows that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Through controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches, we demonstrate the feasibility of using Qolumbina for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, and highlight backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.

</details>


### [288] [Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02052)
*Shuhan Liu,Yukai Zhao,Xing Hu,Kui Liu,Xiaohu Yang,Xin Xia*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: BOUND is a lightweight model editing framework that reduces package hallucination in LLMs by treating it as a package-validity boundary editing problem, using risk-aware localization and LoRA adapters to reinforce valid packages while suppressing hallucinated ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs frequently hallucinate non-existent package names during software engineering tasks, which poses a significant security risk as attackers can exploit these hallucinations by registering malicious packages under hallucinated names, creating supply chain attack vectors. Existing approaches lack effective, localized mitigation strategies.

Method: BOUND frames mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem with three components: (1) a risk-aware localization strategy that identifies modules responsible for package hallucination, (2) lightweight LoRA adapters applied to those modules, and (3) a boundary-aware training objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated ones, and preserves locality behavior.

Result: On package recommendation tasks, BOUND reduces Package-HR by 79.9% on edit prompts and 65.4% on unseen prompts. Generalization results show Package-HR reductions of 12.8% in code generation and 34.0% in pip install recommendation.

Conclusion: BOUND effectively refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs, significantly reducing package hallucinations across multiple tasks while preserving valid package recommendations, thereby improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in software engineering tasks, such as code generation, library recommendation, and dependency configuration. However, recent studies show that LLMs may suffer from package hallucination, where they generate non-existent or invalid package names. These hallucinations can be exploited in software supply chain attacks, as attackers may register malicious packages under hallucinated names. Therefore, mitigating package hallucination is important for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development. In this paper, we introduce BOUND, a lightweight localized model editing framework for mitigating package hallucinations in LLMs. BOUND formulates package hallucination mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem, where the boundary refers to the model's ability to distinguish valid packages from hallucinated package names under a given task context. It first locates modules related to package hallucination through a risk-aware localization strategy, and then edits these modules with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated packages, and preserves locality behavior. Experimental results show that BOUND effectively reduces package hallucinations while preserving valid package recommendations. In the package recommendation task, BOUND reduces package-level hallucination rate (Package-HR) by 79.9% on edit prompts and by 65.4% on unseen prompts. The learned package-validity boundary further generalizes to other package-related tasks, reducing Package-HR by 12.8% in code generation and by 34.0% in pip install recommendation. These results show that BOUND refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs and improves the reliability of package-related outputs.

</details>


### [289] [Prompt Coverage Adequacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02057)
*Florian Tambon,Michael Konstantinou,Cedric Richter,Charles Chenouard,Mark Harman,Mike Papadakis*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel testing metric that measures how well test suites satisfy prompt requirements by leveraging LLM attention mechanisms, demonstrating over 30% more fault-detection effectiveness than traditional code coverage in LLM-driven software development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs and autonomous agents are shifting software development from writing code to expressing intents via prompts. Traditional code coverage criteria are inadequate for this paradigm because prompts, not code, have become the primary development artifacts. New testing approaches are needed that operate at the prompt level.

Method: The authors propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, which uses attention mechanisms of LLMs to measure how well a test suite satisfies the requirements expressed in a prompt. They instantiate this criterion using an attention boosting approach and evaluate it across two datasets and multiple LLMs.

Result: Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and can uncover over 30% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation.

Conclusion: Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to the emerging paradigm of LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria.

Abstract: In recent years, it has become increasingly evident that large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents raise the level of abstraction in software development by shifting the focus from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals. This paradigm shift introduces new challenges, particularly in how testing should be guided when prompts, rather than code, become primary development artifacts. To address this challenge, we propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion designed to support the testing of code generated from task descriptions. Prompt Coverage Adequacy serves as an analog to traditional code coverage, but operates at the level of prompts used in LLM and agent-based programming. Specifically, it measures how well a given test suite satisfies the requirements expressed in a prompt by leveraging the attention mechanisms of LLMs. We evaluate a simple instantiation of this criterion, based on attention boosting, across two datasets and multiple LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and can uncover over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation. These findings suggest that Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to the emerging paradigm of LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

</details>


### [290] [HTTP REST API Structure Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02442)
*Ran Dubin,Amit Dvir*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: HRAL is an unsupervised anomaly detection system that learns API behavior from network traffic without requiring documentation. It achieves 82.07% recall and 87.24% F1-score, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is sparse, and reaches 100% detection when combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: APIs are critical to modern software but pose significant security risks. Existing security approaches often depend on predefined rules or comprehensive API documentation (e.g., OpenAPI specs), which are frequently unavailable or incomplete in real-world settings. There is a need for an approach that can secure APIs without relying on documentation.

Method: HRAL (HTTP REST API Learning) is an unsupervised anomaly detection method that models API endpoint structure and behavior directly from network traffic. It learns normal API usage patterns without predefined rules or documentation, then flags deviations as potential threats. Evaluation spans varying levels of OpenAPI documentation completeness, and the system is also tested in combination with signature-based rules (OWASP ModSecurity CRS).

Result: HRAL achieves average recall of 82.07% and F1-score of 87.24%. It significantly outperforms existing techniques when API documentation is limited and approaches the effectiveness of systems using full API documentation. When combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS, detection reaches 100%.

Conclusion: HRAL is highly effective in real-world, partially documented API environments and shows strong potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions, particularly when documentation is scarce or incomplete.

Abstract: Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) are essential in software development, enabling web services, mobile apps, and microservices. However, their widespread use introduces significant security risks, highlighting the importance of API security. This paper presents HTTP REST API Learning (HRAL), a novel unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models the structure and behavior of API endpoints directly from network traffic, without relying on predefined rules or documentation. HRAL enables robust detection of malicious activity by understanding how APIs behave and flagging deviations as potential threats. We evaluate HRAL across varying levels of OpenAPI documentation detail and compare it with existing techniques. HRAL achieves strong performance, with an average recall of 82.07% and an F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Moreover, our results approach the effectiveness of full API document definitions. When combined with signature-based rules such as the OWASP ModSecurity CRS, our system achieves 100% detection. These results highlight HRAL's effectiveness in real-world, partially documented API environments and its potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions.

</details>


### [291] [File-Level Copying Is an Implicit Dependency in Open Source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02059)
*Runzhi He,Audris Mockus,Wenhao Yang,Minghui Zhou*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: File-level copying across open-source repositories is a pervasive, ungoverned practice that breaks supply-chain visibility. A large-scale mixed-method study reveals distinct copy forms (vendoring, hardware sync, scaffolding, UI assets, direct reuse) with form-specific security and license risks that are invisible to traditional dependency scanners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: File-level copying undermines the four signals that package managers provide for declared dependencies: provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance. The scale, forms, and consequences of this unmanaged reuse across the open-source ecosystem are poorly understood, leaving significant supply-chain risks unquantified and unaddressed.

Method: A mixed-method study using World of Code (WoC), a large-scale OSS infrastructure. From a 0.1% commit sample, 690,500 copy events were extracted, and 3,912 rationale-bearing commits were manually labeled for intent. Copy events were classified into 13 axial forms. Security risk was assessed via CVE matching across the full-WoC graph; license risk was evaluated through pre-validation candidate detection and manual verification (inter-rater reliability kappa = 0.752).

Result: Copy forms are unreliable proxies for intent: 78% of hardware/driver copies are fork-maintenance, while 70% of dependency-vendoring copies signal upstream bypass. Copied sources are stale (median 155 days; 38.5% >1 year old), with only 4.3% documenting origin and 2.0% recording a version. Vendored dependencies carry 88% of 17,314 CVE-risk commits (80% CVSS ≥ 7.0, upstream-fix adoption 47–84%). Direct source-code reuse accounts for 66% of 41,777 license-violation candidates, with 39 verified high-star violations. Both risk types propagate to packaged software and evade metadata-based scanners.

Conclusion: Copy-form taxonomy reveals that visibility gaps are form-specific and concentrated. Vendored dependencies harbor critical security vulnerabilities with slow fix adoption, while direct source-code reuse concentrates license violations. These risks are invisible to existing dependency scanners, necessitating new tooling and governance mechanisms for file-level reuse.

Abstract: File-level copying is a widespread but ungoverned form of software reuse. Copying files across repositories reduces supply-chain visibility: it removes the four observable signals a package manager provides for a declared dependency (provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance) with no mechanism to restore them. To characterize the scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse, we present a mixed-method study of copying across the entire open-source ecosystem using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, we extract 690,500 copy events and retain 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. We show that the 13 axial copy forms, spanning vendored dependencies, hardware/driver synchronization, scaffolding, UI assets, and direct source-code reuse, are unreliable proxies for developer intent: among rationale-bearing commits, hardware/driver copies are predominantly fork-maintenance work (78%), while dependency-vendoring copies more often signal upstream bypass (70%) than offline availability. These visibility gaps are form-specific: security and license risk concentrate in complementary copy forms. Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days; 38.5% over one year old) and seldom record a recoverable origin (4.3% documented), let alone a checkable version (2.0% versioned); even vendored copies record where they came from only 10% of the time. Security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits in the full-WoC graph, 88% in the dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS >= 7.0 and upstream-fix adoption is only 47%-84%. License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse: 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in the source-code form, with 39 verified high-star violations (kappa = 0.752). Both risks reach packaged software and are invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone.

</details>


### [292] [Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02294)
*Zimo Ji,Zekai Zhang,Congying Xu,Zongjie Li,Yudong Gao,Shuai Wang,Shing-Chi Cheung*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: UnderSpecBench evaluates coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) on 2,208 DevOps prompts varying in instruction specificity. Results show 55.8–67.8% of runs violate action boundaries — agents guess rather than fail under ambiguity — revealing that completion-centric benchmarks overstate safe autonomy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed autonomously on production infrastructure, where completing a task is not sufficient for safety — wrong actions can cause severe consequences. Existing benchmarks emphasize task completion but neglect how agents behave under benign yet underspecified instructions, leaving a critical evaluation gap around action-boundary violations.

Method: The authors introduce UnderSpecBench, a benchmark of 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. Each task preserves identical environment and ground-truth safe action while varying instructions along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius, yielding 2,208 prompt variants. Evaluation uses deterministic, side-effect-based oracles to classify outcomes into Safe Success, Wrong Target, OverScope, and non-action categories (clarification, refusal, deferment). Five agent × model configurations (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex) are tested.

Result: 55.8–67.8% of runs violate at least one action boundary. Underspecification does not primarily cause failure — it causes agents to guess. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. These patterns hold across all tested agent–model configurations.

Conclusion: Completion-centric evaluation overstates safe autonomy in coding agents. The findings motivate layered mitigations at the model, harness, and system layers to address boundary-violating guesswork under underspecified instructions.

Abstract: LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed to act autonomously on real production infrastructure. They execute shell commands, modify repositories, and call operational APIs. However, completing a task is not sufficient for safety. A wrong action can cause severe consequences. Existing agent benchmarks largely emphasize task completion, leaving open how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions.
  We present UnderSpecBench, a benchmark for measuring action-boundary violations in coding agents (i.e., Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode) on DevOps tasks. UnderSpecBench includes 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior and organized across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. To isolate underspecification from task difficulty, each task keeps the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying the instruction along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius. The resulting 2,208 prompt variants are evaluated with deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that separate Safe Success, Wrong Target, and OverScope outcomes; non-action runs are further classified as clarification, refusal, or deferment.
  Across five agent x model configurations using OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex, the evaluation results show that underspecification does not mainly make agents fail; it makes them guess. 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. These findings show that completion-centric evaluation can overstate safe autonomy and motivate mitigations at the model, harness, and system layer.

</details>


### [293] [Guiding Human Validation of LLM-Generated Code via Verifiable Literate Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02333)
*Ziqi Yuan,Wenhao Lu,Hao Wu,Dunhong Jin,Chuan Wu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Vibe coding generates code via natural language, but validating intent alignment is hard. This paper proposes Verifiable Literate Programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework using unambiguous NL documentation as an intermediate layer between prompts and code. It combines a literate language with deterministic translation, LLM-based mismatch detection with trace links, and model-checking-based verification of derived properties. VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%–73.2% to 65.4%–93.5%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated code from natural-language prompts often fails due to underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations. Existing validation methods (LLM-assisted automated testing, partial user involvement via prompts/test cases) are inadequate—they suffer from prompt ambiguity, model fallibility, and overlook corner cases. A bug study revealed that detailed human feedback is essential for reliable code generation.

Method: VLP introduces three core techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation; (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection using trace links between prompts and documentation to focus review on suspicious lines; (iii) a verification module that derives API-usage checks and formal properties from user-validated documentation and verifies them against generated code via model checking.

Result: VLP improves code pass@1 from a baseline range of 28.7%–73.2% to 65.4%–93.5%, with reasonable user effort required.

Conclusion: VLP demonstrates that a human-in-the-loop approach centered on unambiguous NL documentation can effectively bridge the intent-code gap in LLM-based code generation, making reliable validation accessible to users across all programming skill levels.

Abstract: Vibe coding democratizes software development by allowing users to generate code via natural-language (NL) interaction with large language models (LLMs). However, the code is reliable only when it faithfully implements the user's intent, which is difficult and labor-intensive for users to validate. Existing validation methods either rely on LLM-assisted automated testing, which suffers from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility, or involve users only in partial software artifacts such as prompts and test cases, which may overlook corner cases and program details. Motivated by a bug study of LLM-generated code, we find that detailed human feedback is essential, as failures often stem from underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations.
  This paper presents verifiable literate programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework designed to make the review/validation process of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels. At its core, VLP proposes unambiguous NL-based documentation as a readable intermediate layer between prompts and code. The documentation demonstrates concrete program semantics and enables users to provide feedback on potential intent-code mismatches. It supports human-involved, end-to-end repair and validation via three techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection that uses trace links between prompts and documentation to focus users' review effort on suspicious documentation lines, and (iii) a verification module that leverages user-validated documentation to derive API-usage checks and formal properties, which are then verified against the generated code using model checking. Our evaluation shows that VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.

</details>


### [294] [Developers' Experience with Generative AI Beyond Productivity Assessment -- Insights from an Empirical Mixed-Methods Field Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02337)
*Charlotte Brandebusemeyer,Kerim Zunic,Thomas Zimmermann,Tobias Schimmer,Bert Arnrich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A mixed-methods study of professional developers using GenAI coding assistants in natural work settings reveals that satisfaction is high for repetitive tasks, but combining in-code suggestions with chat-based prompting within a single task reduces benefits. Task-specific interaction type selection matters, and cognitive load stems from AI interaction while productivity depends on output quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on AI-powered coding assistants has focused narrowly on output quality and productivity gains, overlooking developers' well-being and interaction experiences. There is a need for developer-centered, real-world studies to understand how professionals naturally engage with GenAI tools.

Method: A developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study combining controlled data collection sessions with natural work periods, investigating how professional developers engage with GenAI in their authentic work environments.

Result: Developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, especially for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, reporting efficiency and productivity gains. Both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve efficiency and reduce perceived workload, but combining them within a single task diminishes benefits. Cognitive load arises from AI interaction during development-heavy tasks, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Participation increased developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI.

Conclusion: A rule-of-thumb for selecting GenAI interaction type based on task characteristics is proposed. The findings underscore the value of real-world, mixed-methods study designs for understanding GenAI tools and developer experiences holistically.

Abstract: With the growing adoption of AI-powered coding assistants, organizations and developers are increasingly seeking to optimize their interaction with these tools. Prior research has largely focused on output quality and productivity gains, with limited attention paid to developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This paper presents a developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study to investigate how professional developers engage with Generative AI (GenAI) in their natural work environment. Controlled data collection sessions are combined with natural work periods. Results show that developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, particularly for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, and report perceived efficiency and productivity gains. Copilot interaction type preferences differ by task type and complexity: While both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve task efficiency and reduce perceived workload, combining these interaction types within a single task diminishes benefits. We propose a rule-of-thumb for selecting an interaction type based on task characteristics. During development-heavy tasks, results indicate that perceived cognitive load arises from AI interaction, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Participation in this study positively influenced developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools. These findings demonstrate the value of real-world, mixed-methods study designs to understand GenAI tools and developers' experiences with them.

</details>


### [295] [SkillFuzz: Fuzzing Skill Composition for Implicit Intents Discovery in Open Skill Marketplaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02345)
*Jinwei Hu,Yi Dong,Youcheng Sun,Xiaowei Huang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: skillfuzz is an execution-free fuzzing approach that discovers implicit intents in LLM agent skill marketplaces by using contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to identify skill compositions where individually benign skills combine to redirect agents toward unintended objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In open skill marketplaces for LLM-based agents, marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. However, individually benign skills can interact when co-activated, producing emergent implicit intents that redirect agents toward unintended objectives. Detecting these is difficult because the harmful effect only emerges through composition, execution environments may be unavailable at admission time, and the combinatorial space of co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size.

Method: skillfuzz formulates implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions. It extracts structured skill contracts from skill documents and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. The approach is execution-free: it uses planning artifacts to expose agent intent before execution and employs deviations from a skill-free baseline as a differential oracle to detect implicit intents without running code.

Result: Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, skillfuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space those alternatives require.

Conclusion: Implicit intents in multi-skill LLM agents represent a significant and previously underexplored security risk in open skill marketplaces. skillfuzz demonstrates that contract-guided MCTS can effectively and efficiently discover these emergent malicious behaviors without requiring execution, offering a practical admission-time auditing tool for marketplace operators.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly automate software engineering tasks through reusable skills, natural-language instruction documents that guide planning and execution. Open skill marketplaces enable users to assemble agents by co-activating community-contributed skills, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. As a result, individually benign skills may interact to redirect an agent toward unintended objectives, which we term implicit intents. Detecting such intents is challenging because the effect emerges only through skill composition, execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and the space of possible co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size. In this paper, we formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, where skill compositions are the unit under test, planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Based on this formulation, we propose skillfuzz, the first execution-free testing approach that extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, skillfuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space they require.

</details>


### [296] [Understanding Agent-Based Patching of Compiler Missed Optimizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02370)
*Batu Guan,Zirui Wang,Shaohua Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates how well coding agents can patch compiler missed optimizations in LLVM, finding that agents struggle to generalize beyond the reported test case to cover the full developer-intended scope. The authors introduce historical-knowledge augmentation via retrieval and distillation from prior LLVM optimization PRs, which improves generalization alignment with developer patches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compiler missed optimizations are pervasive and costly to fix, requiring significant developer effort. The key insight is that patching a missed optimization is fundamentally a generalization problem—fixing not just the reported case but similar cases sharing the same root cause. Prior work has not systematically studied whether AI coding agents can handle this generalization challenge.

Method: The authors construct a benchmark from real-world LLVM missed optimization issues. They compare agent-generated patches against developer-written reference patches along the dimension of optimization scope (how broadly the patch applies to similar cases). They further propose historical-knowledge augmentation techniques that retrieve and distill information from prior LLVM optimization pull requests to guide agent patch generation toward developer-aligned generalization.

Result: Coding agents often successfully optimize the given example cases, but many generated patches either cover only a subset of the developer-intended scope, partially overlap with it, or in some cases over-generalize beyond the reference patch. Historical-knowledge augmentation improves developer-aligned generalization and yields practical benefits on real-world IR.

Conclusion: Patching compiler missed optimizations requires generalization beyond the specific reported case, which remains a significant challenge for current coding agents. Leveraging historical PR knowledge effectively nudges agents toward better-aligned and more practical optimization patches.

Abstract: Compiler missed optimizations refer to cases in which compilers failed to optimize certain code. It takes many compiler developers' efforts to implement or patch such missed optimizations. In this paper, we present a systematic study of how well agents patch compiler missed optimizations. We identify a significant challenge that patching a missed optimization requires more than just fixing the reported case, and instead requires generalizing to similar cases. We construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues and compare agent-generated patches with patches from developers in terms of optimization scope. Our results show that coding agents often optimize the given examples, but many generated patches either cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it; in some cases, they further generalize beyond the reference patch. We further introduce historical-knowledge augmentation techniques that leverage prior LLVM optimization pull requests through retrieval and distillation, showing that they improve developer-aligned generalization and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world IR.

</details>


### [297] [Reasoning effort, not tool access, buys first-try reliability in agentic code generation: an observational study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02436)
*Achint Mehta*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The study tested whether adding capabilities (browser-based testing tools, design-oriented prompts) to agentic coding assistants improves software quality. Ninety agent runs built the same application. Results showed frontier models dominate, a testing tool increased cost without improving function, higher reasoning effort dramatically improved first-try success, and a design prompt improved visual quality without affecting function.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly given extra capabilities like testing tools and design-oriented prompts under the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study directly tests that assumption, addressing a gap in empirical evidence on whether these additions actually improve outcomes.

Method: Ninety independent agent runs built the same application (a real-time retrospective board) from a single detailed specification. Each run was scored on a fixed 14-criterion functional rubric (42-point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs spanned multiple model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels (High vs. xHigh), a browser-based testing tool, and two design-oriented prompts. A criterion-level and cost analysis were conducted.

Result: Capability tier dominated: frontier models clustered near the ceiling, while a low-cost local model scored 24–37 points. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first-try in 44% of runs. The testing tool raised cost 42–68% without improving functional scores or reliability. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first-try perfect runs from 28% to 89% and cut corrective prompts ~5-fold, at 9–29% more cost. A design-oriented prompt raised visual quality (4.5 vs. 3.0 on a 5-point scale) without improving function; a one-paragraph paraphrase reproduced the entire lift.

Conclusion: The practical lesson is to match the fix to the failure: most first-run failures stem from weak reasoning (remedied by stronger models or more reasoning effort), not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch. Adding tools without addressing reasoning gaps increases cost without benefit.

Abstract: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly given extra capabilities, such as browser based testing tools and design oriented system prompts, on the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study tested that assumption directly. Ninety independent agent runs built the same application, a real time retrospective board, from one detailed specification, each scored on a fixed 14 criterion functional rubric (42 point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs spanned several model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels, a testing tool, and two design oriented prompts. Capability tier dominated: frontier models clustered near the ceiling while a low cost local model fell to 24 to 37 points. A criterion level analysis revealed what run totals conceal. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first try in 44 percent of runs, with its failure rate shifting sharply across model generations while mean totals moved less than a point. The testing tool raised cost by 42 to 68 percent without improving functional score or reliability, even on interface visible criteria. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first try perfect runs from 28 percent to 89 percent and cut corrective prompts about five fold, for 9 to 29 percent more cost. A design oriented prompt raised visual quality, 4.5 versus 3.0 on a 5 point scale, without lifting function, and a one paragraph paraphrase of its directive reproduced the entire lift. The practical lesson is to match the fix to the failure: most first run failures came from weak reasoning, which a stronger model or more effort prevents, not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch.

</details>


### [298] [TestEvo-Bench: An Executable and Live Benchmark for Test and Code Co-Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02469)
*Jiale Amber Wang,Kaiyuan Wang,Pengyu Nie*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TestEvo-Bench is a novel benchmark for evaluating test automation agents on test-code co-evolution tasks sourced from real commits, featuring execution-grounded metrics and a live-updating pipeline. Experiments with SOTA agents show up to 77.5% success on generation and 74.6% on update tasks, but performance degrades on recent tasks and under cost constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing test generation/update benchmarks isolate tests from the code change and rely on static metadata that doesn't verify executability or semantic relevance. This prevents rigorous evaluation of whether a test automation agent truly understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite.

Method: TestEvo-Bench is mined from 152 open-source Java projects, yielding 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records. Each task is anchored to a real commit history, packaged with environment configuration, and supports execution-grounded metrics (pass rate, coverage, mutation score). The benchmark is live, with timestamps and periodic automated mining to enable restricting evaluation to tasks postdating a model's training cutoff. Four SOTA agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, SWE-Agent with Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro) were evaluated.

Result: Agents achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rates are materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drop significantly under limited per-task cost budgets.

Conclusion: TestEvo-Bench provides a more realistic, execution-grounded evaluation framework for test-code co-evolution. While SOTA agents show promising results, their degradation on recent data and under cost constraints highlights remaining challenges and the benchmark's utility for driving progress in test automation.

Abstract: Software tests and code evolve together: a code change should be followed by new or updated tests that record the new software behavior. Yet existing test generation and update benchmarks often isolate the test from the code change, and rely on static metadata that does not verify whether a test is executable or semantically tied to the code change. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a test automation agent understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite.
  We introduce TestEvo-Bench, a benchmark of test and code co-evolution tasks mined from software repositories, with two tracks: in test generation, the agent shall write new tests to capture the new software behavior; in test update, the agent shall adapt failing existing tests to the changed software behavior. Each task is anchored to a real commit history and packaged with environment configuration to support execution-grounded metrics such as pass rate, coverage, and mutation score. TestEvo-Bench is also a live benchmark: each task records the timestamp of the test and code changes, and new tasks are periodically mined by our automated pipeline, so evaluation can be restricted to tasks postdating a model's training cutoff to reduce data leakage risk. The current snapshot contains 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks, curated from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records across 152 open-source Java projects. We experiment with four state-of-the-art agents that combine strong harnesses (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and SWE-Agent) with strong foundation models (Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro). Results show that they achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rate is materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drops significantly under limited per-task cost.

</details>

# cs.MA [[Back]](#toc)

### [299] [Cache Merging as a Convergent Replicated State for Multi-Agent Latent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01308)
*Carlos Baquero,Luís Brito*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: CanonicalMerge introduces a commutative, associative, idempotent merging scheme for multi-agent KV-caches using mean K-norm ordering, achieving byte-identical results under input permutation and matching best-case BagMerge accuracy with structural guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent latent reasoning via KV-cache concatenation (BagMerge) is non-commutative and sensitive to input ordering, with the best order being unpredictable across regimes, latent-step budgets, and model scales. This motivates a convergent replicated state approach that eliminates ordering sensitivity.

Method: CanonicalMerge orders KV-caches by mean K-norm at a middle layer, producing byte-identical merged caches under any input permutation (verified up to arity N≤5). The replicated state is modeled as a set of content-addressed latent fragments merged via set union (a state-based CvRDT: commutative, associative, idempotent, absorbing). CanonicalMerge serves as the deterministic render of this state.

Result: On partitioned-reasoning benchmarks, CanonicalMerge matches the best BagMerge ordering across all regime-by-budget-by-ordering cells without requiring knowledge of optimal ordering, with negligible accuracy loss. On HotpotQA multi-document QA, it outperforms training-free output-fusion baseline PackLLM by 45 points at matched budget. At k>2, the approach transports latent traces but does not compose them, motivating future work.

Conclusion: CanonicalMerge provides an unconditional structural guarantee of permutation invariance for multi-agent KV-cache merging, placing cache-level merging in a distinct and superior regime compared to output-level fusion, while highlighting the need for composition mechanisms at higher agent counts.

Abstract: Multi-agent latent reasoning composes agents' KV-caches into one context for a final agent. Prior work (Agent Primitives) does this by concatenating caches along the sequence axis with RoPE re-encoding, which we call BagMerge. BagMerge is non-commutative, and the best input ordering is unpredictable, shifting with the regime, the latent-step budget, and the model scale. We make this exchange a convergent replicated state. First, CanonicalMerge fixes the layout by content: ordering caches by mean K-norm at a middle layer renders the merged cache byte-identical under any input permutation, verified algorithmically (arity N<=5) and bit-for-bit on real Qwen3-1.7B and 4B state. Second, we separate the replicated state from decode-time layout: the state is a set of content-addressed latent fragments whose merge is set union, a state-based CvRDT (commutative, associative, idempotent, absorbing), and CanonicalMerge is its deterministic render. Because the render is byte-equivalent, every N=2 accuracy number carries over unchanged and re-delivered duplicates are absorbed rather than re-concatenated. On a partitioned-reasoning benchmark, CanonicalMerge matches the best BagMerge ordering in every regime-by-budget-by-ordering cell without knowing which order is best, trading a small, statistically insignificant accuracy margin for an unconditional structural guarantee. The behaviour transfers to real multi-document QA (HotpotQA), while the closest training-free output-fusion baseline (PackLLM) loses by 45 points at matched budget, placing cache-level merging in a regime distinct from output-level fusion. Finally, at k>2 the approach transports and colocates latent traces but does not by itself compose them, which we characterize to motivate future work.

</details>


### [300] [Simulation Based Reward Function Validation for Multi-Agent On Orbit Inspection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01367)
*Patrick Quinn,Bala Prenith Reddy Gopu,George M. Nehma,Madhur Tiwari*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper proposes a generalized reward function for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) in spacecraft inspection tasks, using 3D reconstruction analysis to evaluate arbitrary image collections rather than fixed inspection points, and derives broader insights for inspection planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MARL approaches for spacecraft inspection rely on reward functions tied to reaching predetermined inspection points, limiting flexibility. The authors aim to develop a generalized reward function that can evaluate images taken at arbitrary locations, giving agents full control over image acquisition timing and positioning.

Method: The authors design a generalized reward function informed by 3D reconstruction analysis of inspected objects in orbit. This reward function accommodates an arbitrary number of images captured at arbitrary locations, enabling trained agents to autonomously decide when and where to collect images rather than being constrained to predefined waypoints.

Result: The generalized reward function yields insights into best practices for the MARL inspection task and provides key takeaways applicable to broader spacecraft inspection problems beyond the MARL context.

Conclusion: A flexible, reconstruction-informed reward function improves MARL-based spacecraft inspection by decoupling agent behavior from fixed inspection points, offering lessons transferable to the wider inspection domain.

Abstract: A proposed method for the control of groups of inspection spacecraft is Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). While MARL has already been employed for this purpose in previous work, the reward functions used focus on reaching a finite set of predetermined inspection points around the target. In this work, we study and develop a generalized reward function for the MARL inspection task informed by the analysis of 3D reconstructions of inspected objects in orbit. Because the reward function is generalized such that any number of images at arbitrary locations may evaluated, we also allow trained agents to have complete control over when images are collected. With this approach, we gather insights into best practices for not only the specific MARL inspection task, but also gain key takeaways informative to the broader inspection task outside of a MARL context.

</details>


### [301] [Congestion-Based Slot Pricing in a Railway Auction Game](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01822)
*Bill Roungas,Sebastiaan Meijer*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A multi-agent auction system for allocating congested railway slots among heterogeneous operators uses congestion-based pricing with corrective penalties to mitigate large-agent dominance. Experiments with domain experts show the correction mechanism triggers as designed, but large operators persist with high-request strategies, suggesting pricing alone is insufficient to neutralize strategic dominance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Railway slot allocation under deregulation, where heterogeneous strategic agents (train operators of varying sizes) compete for discrete, congested resources. The core challenge is that large operators can strategically dominate auctions, and the authors aim to design a mechanism that mitigates this dominance while maintaining transparency and congestion sensitivity.

Method: A multi-agent repeated game with incomplete information, implemented as a real-time web-based environment where human participants control operators. The auction mechanism features: (1) a congestion-based base price that scales with aggregate demand, and (2) an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalizes the highest-requesting agent and rewards the lowest-requesting agent. Two structured sessions were conducted with domain experts, with live marginal-cost and competitor feedback.

Result: The congestion mechanism responded to aggregate demand as designed, and corrective incentives were actively triggered. However, large-operator agents persisted with high-request strategies despite penalties. Post-session debriefs revealed participants' decisions were role-driven (not personal disposition), with strategic motives including preserving market presence and raising rivals' costs, operating alongside short-term profit maximization.

Conclusion: Corrective pricing is necessary but not sufficient to neutralize strategic dominance in asymmetric multi-agent settings. The findings highlight the need for complementary mechanism design elements beyond pricing adjustments, and the authors call for analytical validation and larger-scale multi-agent experiments.

Abstract: We present a multi-agent system for studying the allocation of discrete, congested resources among heterogeneous strategic agents, motivated by the problem of railway slot allocation under deregulation. Multiple operator-agents, differing in size and capacity, interact through a shared auction mechanism over repeated rounds under time-constrained decision-making. The mechanism combines a congestion-based base price that increases with aggregate demand with an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalises the agent requesting the most slots and rewards the agent requesting the fewest, and is designed to mitigate strategic dominance by large agents while preserving transparency and congestion sensitivity. We formulate the interaction as a repeated game with incomplete information and implement the system as a real-time, web-based multi-agent environment in which human participants control individual agents and observe live marginal-cost and competitor feedback.
  We report exploratory observations from two structured sessions with domain experts acting as operator-agents. The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed and the corrective incentives are actively triggered, but agents representing large operators persist with high-request strategies despite the penalty, suggesting that corrective pricing is necessary but not sufficient to neutralise strategic dominance in this multi-agent setting. A post-session debrief indicates that participants' decisions were driven by the assumed agent role rather than personal disposition, and provides qualitative support for strategic motives, such as preserving market presence and raising rivals' costs, operating alongside short-term profit maximisation. We discuss implications for multi-agent mechanism design under asymmetric budgets and outline directions for analytical validation and larger-scale multi-agent experiments.

</details>


### [302] [CausalSteward: An Agentic Divide-Conquer-Combine Copilot for Causal Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01936)
*Nicholas Tagliapietra,Gian Lorenzo Marchioni,Moritz Willig,Juergen Luettin,Lavdim Halilaj,Kristian Kersting*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: CausalSTeward (CAST) is a multi-agent, human-in-the-loop framework for learning large causal models from high-dimensional data by iteratively partitioning variable clusters, then fusing prior knowledge with data-driven methods (retrieval augmented generation, conditional independence tests) to address causal identifiability challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning causal models from high-dimensional real-world data is challenging because core causal assumptions are often violated, leading to identifiability issues. Although substantial prior knowledge exists, effectively integrating it into causal discovery remains an open problem.

Method: CAST employs a divide-and-conquer, multi-agent collaborative approach: large variable clusters are iteratively partitioned and analyzed separately. The framework fuses prior knowledge with data-driven techniques using retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and conditional independence tests, all within a human-in-the-loop paradigm.

Result: The paper uses the CAST framework to examine the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning within multi-agent systems and investigates how human-in-the-loop interaction contributes to accurate and trustworthy causal model assembly.

Conclusion: Human-in-the-loop multi-agent frameworks like CAST offer a promising direction for assembling large-scale causal models by combining prior knowledge, data-driven testing, and iterative decomposition, while also revealing current boundaries of causal reasoning in such systems.

Abstract: Learning causal models from high-dimensional data is a significant challenge, particularly in real-world settings where violations of core assumptions lead to causal identifiability issues. Although massive amounts of prior knowledge are available, and contain valuable causal information, effectively integrating this knowledge into the causal discovery process remains an open problem. We introduce CausalSTeward (CAST), a novel human-in-the-loop framework for interactively assembling large causal models. CausalSteward is a multi-agent collaborative system that tackles high-dimensional causality through a divide-and-conquer approach where large clusters of variables are iteratively partitioned and then separately analyzed. Our framework fuses prior knowledge with a data-driven approach by using tailored tools such as retrieval augmented generation and conditional independence tests. Finally, we use this work to examine the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning in multi-agent frameworks, and how the human-in-the-loop can contribute to accurate and trustworthy results.

</details>


### [303] [AgentsCAD: Automated Design for Manufacturing of FDM Parts via Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning and Geometric Feature Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02448)
*Emmanuel George,Christopher Keefe,Peter Pak,Amir Barati Farimani*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: AgentsCAD is a multi-agent system that uses LLMs and graph learning to automatically detect and fix DFAM issues (specifically overhangs) in FDM parts by parsing STEP files, analyzing geometry, and proposing modifications verified by a vision-language model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 3D printing slicers can detect defects like steep overhangs but cannot modify the underlying geometry to fix them. This creates a gap between defect identification and automated geometry correction, requiring manual DFAM interventions.

Method: A multi-agent pipeline: (1) STEP file parsing and overhang detection above 45°; (2) face-adjacency topology graph construction with optional GraphSAGE semantic labeling (trained on MFCAD++ with 59,665 parts); (3) Claude Sonnet agent for design reasoning and modification recommendations (reorientations, fillets, chamfers); (4) GPT-4o vision-language verifier inspecting rendered views; (5) output of modified STEP file and human-readable report.

Result: A birdhouse model test case showed the system correctly diagnoses overhangs, selects appropriate mitigation strategies, and proposes physically valid corrections, partially solving the geometry-to-language translation problem for LLM-driven CAD modification.

Conclusion: AgentsCAD demonstrates that bridging B-Rep geometry with LLM reasoning via a multi-agent architecture can automate targeted DFAM modifications, though the geometry-to-language translation problem is only partially solved.

Abstract: Parts manufactured with Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) often require Design for Additive Manufacturing (DFAM) modifications to ensure printability, structural integrity, and reduced post-processing. Current slicers identify defects such as steep overhangs but are unable to modify the underlying geometry. This work presents AgentsCAD, a multi-agent system that bridges raw boundary-representation (B-Rep) geometry and Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning to automate targeted DFM. The workflow begins by parsing a STEP file. The agentic system detects overhangs above a 45°threshold, constructs a face-adjacency topology graph, and optionally injects semantic feature labels from a GraphSAGE model trained on MFCAD++ (59,665 parts), before dispatching a Claude Sonnet design-reasoning agent that recommends reorientations, fillets, chamfers, and similar modifications. A GPT-4o vision-language verifier inspects rendered views to confirm geometric integrity. Outputs include a modified STEP file and a human-readable report. A test case on a birdhouse model demonstrates that the system correctly diagnoses overhangs, selects appropriate defect mitigation strategies, and proposes physically valid corrections, partially solving the geometry-to-language translation problem central to LLM-driven CAD modification.

</details>


### [304] [Adoption and Ecosystem Health: A Longitudinal Analysis of Open-Source Multi-Agent Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02453)
*Xi Zhang,Papi Menon,Vivian Chu,Koray Cosguner*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper evaluates the health of 15 open-source AI agent frameworks using quantitative metrics beyond GitHub stars—specifically contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and contributor retention—finding that star-based popularity is unreliable and that metrics like contributor density offer a more robust basis for framework selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of open-source AI agent frameworks since ChatGPT's launch has made framework selection difficult for engineering teams. Popularity signals like GitHub stars are easily inflated by hype cycles and inorganic activity, obscuring genuine ecosystem health. The authors aim to provide more reliable, data-driven metrics for evaluating framework adoption and sustainability.

Method: The authors analyzed 15 major open-source AI agent framework repositories from late 2022 to early 2026, using 808,042 stars, 73,997 pull requests, 86,241 commits, and 987,330 user profiles. They assessed ecosystem health along three dimensions—awareness, adoption, and retention—and introduced metrics including contributor density (contributors per 1,000 stars), cross-framework contribution mapping, and retention curves over time.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Star counts reflect hype cycles and inorganic activity—AutoGPT garnered 111,967 stars in one month but had a contributor density below 9 per 1,000 stars versus LangChain's 41; lower-profile frameworks like Pydantic-AI showed higher contributor density. (2) Visibility and engagement diverge—MetaGPT and LangFlow had contributor density ratios below 5 despite high visibility; openai-agents-python's limited contributor base suggests institutional backing alone does not ensure community depth. LangChain attracted 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors, functioning as shared infrastructure. (3) Contributor retention drops most steeply in the first 30 days and stabilizes near 90 days.

Conclusion: Ecosystem health is better measured by contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention than by stars alone. These metrics provide engineering teams with a more robust basis for evaluating and selecting open-source AI agent frameworks.

Abstract: Since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, open-source agentic frameworks have proliferated, making framework selection important for engineering teams while obscured by popularity signals such as GitHub stars. This paper analyzes 15 major open-source AI agent framework repositories from late 2022 to early 2026, using 808,042 stars, 73,997 pull requests, 86,241 commits, and 987,330 user profiles to assess ecosystem health across awareness, adoption, and retention. Three findings emerge. First, headline popularity is unreliable. Star counts reflect hype cycles and inorganic activity. AutoGPT gained 111,967 stars in one month but converted fewer than 9 contributors per 1,000 stars, defined as contributor density in this research, compared with LangChain's 41. Lower-profile frameworks such as Pydantic-AI show higher contributor density, indicating deeper adoption. Second, mapping awareness against adoption shows that visibility and engagement diverge. MetaGPT and LangFlow have contributor density ratios below 5 even with their high visibility. Openai-agents-python's limited contributor base suggests institutional backing alone does not ensure community depth. By analyzing cross-framework contribution, we discover that LangChain functions as a shared infrastructure, attracting 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors. Third, retention drops most steeply in the first 30 days of initial contribution and stabilizes near 90 days. Overall, ecosystem health is better measured by contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention than by stars alone. These metrics offer teams a more robust basis for framework evaluation.

</details>
