### [305] [STRUCTSURVEY: Structured Agentic Retrieval for Automated Survey Paper Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01243)
*Paolo Pedinotti,Enrico Santus*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: STRUCTSURVEY is a hierarchical multi-agent framework that improves automated scientific survey generation by constructing graph-based representations of entities, relations, and taxonomies during retrieval, shifting structural reasoning earlier in the pipeline. It outperforms embedding-only baselines on ROUGE recall and LLM-as-a-Judge ratings for structure, depth, and synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid growth of scientific publications makes manual survey writing increasingly difficult. Existing LLM-based automated survey generation methods retrieve unstructured data and require models to infer conceptual, methodological, and taxonomic relations from raw text at generation time, which burdens the generation phase and limits structural coherence.

Method: STRUCTSURVEY is a hierarchical multi-agent framework that shifts structural reasoning from the generation stage to the retrieval stage. It dynamically constructs graph-based representations capturing entities, relations, and topical taxonomies during retrieval. Evaluation uses a new reference-grounded benchmark of ACL survey papers designed for reproducible long-form scientific summarization.

Result: Compared to embedding-only retrieval baselines, STRUCTSURVEY improves ROUGE-1 recall by +2.9 and ROUGE-2 recall by +1.0 on average, without reducing precision. It also achieves higher LLM-as-a-Judge ratings for logical structure, depth, and synthesis.

Conclusion: Explicit structural retrieval yields surveys that more closely resemble human-written organization and reasoning, demonstrating that incorporating graph-based entity and taxonomic representations into the retrieval stage meaningfully enhances the quality of long-form scientific summarization.

Abstract: The rapid growth of scientific publications makes it increasingly difficult to track and synthesize research progress. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can support automated survey generation, existing methods retrieve unstructured data and require models to infer conceptual, methodological, and taxonomic relations from raw text at generation time. We introduce STRUCTSURVEY, a hierarchical multi-agent framework that shifts structural reasoning from generation to retrieval by dynamically constructing graph-based representations of entities, relations, and topical taxonomies. We evaluate STRUCTSURVEY on a new reference-grounded benchmark of ACL survey papers for reproducible long-form scientific summarization. Compared with embedding-only retrieval baselines, STRUCTSURVEY improves ROUGE-1 recall by +2.9 and ROUGE-2 recall by +1.0 on average, without reducing precision. It also improves LLM-as-a-Judge ratings for logical structure, depth, and synthesis, showing that explicit structural retrieval yields surveys closer to human-written organization and reasoning.

</details>


### [306] [Retrieval-Augmented Generation to Support Railways Engineering Tasks: A Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01244)
*Andrea Gerardo Russo,Federico Ruggeri,Ivan Tomarchio,Davide Bombini,Nicolò Donati,Gianmarco Pappacoda,Paolo Torroni,Giuseppe-Emiliano La Cara*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper presents an industrial case study on designing and deploying a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system for consulting complex railway technical regulations, offering a human-centered approach applicable to other regulated industries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The increasing volume and complexity of technical regulations pose significant challenges for professionals in regulated industries, necessitating efficient and accurate information retrieval systems that can handle domain-specific regulatory documentation.

Method: A case study methodology documenting the end-to-end process — from design through deployment — of building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system tailored for railway domain technical regulations, employing a human-centered implementation approach that integrates LLM capabilities with domain expertise.

Result: The paper reports on the successful industrial deployment of a RAG system for railway regulation consultation, demonstrating a replicable model for balancing technological capabilities with domain expert involvement in highly regulated technical environments.

Conclusion: A human-centered RAG approach for technical documentation consultation is both feasible and valuable across regulated industries, with the railway sector case study providing transferable insights for other domains requiring regulatory compliance and precise information retrieval from complex documentation.

Abstract: The growing number and complexity of technical regulations represent an important challenge for all professionals in regulated industries. This paper describes a case study, from design to deployment, of building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system for the consultation of complex technical regulations in the railway domain. Although developed for the railway sector, this testimony of an industrial experience is of particular value for technical domains where regulatory compliance and accurate information retrieval from complex documentation are essential requirements. It also constitutes a human-centered approach for implementing LLM-powered technical documentation consultation across various regulated industries, balancing technological capabilities with domain expertise.

</details>


### [307] [Bi-NAS: Towards Effective and Personalized Explanation for Recommender Systems via Bi-Level Neural Architecture Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01387)
*Longfeng Wu,Yao Zhou,Tong Zeng,Zhimin Peng,Bhanu Pratap Singh Rawat,Lecheng Zheng,Giovanni Seni,Dawei Zhou*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Bi-NAS is a bi-level neural architecture search framework that jointly optimizes cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions for recommendation, augmented by LLM-based zero-shot explanation generation, achieving both improved accuracy and explanation quality across four real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing recommender systems struggle to provide effective, evaluable explanations across diverse scenarios. Enhancing explanation quality is critical for user engagement, trust, and decision-making, yet jointly optimizing the underlying architecture for both recommendation accuracy and explanation generation remains underexplored.

Method: The authors propose Bi-NAS, a bi-level neural architecture search framework that simultaneously optimizes intra-layer (cross-attention mechanisms) and inter-layer (feature interaction functions) design spaces. Additionally, they integrate Large Language Models with zero-shot prompting to generate personalized, user-aligned explanations that reflect both user feature preferences and item quality scores.

Result: Extensive evaluations on four real-world datasets show that Bi-NAS boosts recommendation accuracy and significantly improves explanation effectiveness, delivering clear and reliable insights to users.

Conclusion: Bi-NAS demonstrates that jointly searching architectural components for both recommendation and explanation, combined with LLM-based generation, yields a system that is both more accurate and more transparent, advancing the state of explainable recommender systems.

Abstract: Recommender systems are vital in helping users navigate vast amounts of information, offering personalized suggestions and effective explanations for these recommendations. While previous efforts have attempted to provide such explanations, evaluating their effectiveness across various scenarios remains a challenge. Enhancing these explanations is essential for improving user engagement, trust, and decision-making. To facilitate effective explanations within the recommender system, we propose a Bi-level Neural Architecture Search (Bi-NAS) framework to optimize explanations. This approach simultaneously refines cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions by exploring both intra-layer and inter-layer design spaces. Furthermore, we integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance explanation generation, leveraging zero-shot prompting to produce more effective and personalized justifications. By aligning user feature preferences with item quality scores, our approach ensures that explanations reflect both user intent and item attributes, improving transparency and reasoning depth. Extensive evaluations on four real-world datasets demonstrate that Bi-NAS not only boosts recommendation accuracy but also significantly improves the effectiveness of explanations for recommender systems, providing users with clear and reliable insights into the suggestions they receive.

</details>


### [308] [CoPersona: Collaborative Persona Graphs for Robust LLM Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01485)
*Yangtian Zhang,Leyao Wang,Hiren Madhu,Ngoc Bui,Walter Roznyatovskiy,Rex Ying*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: CoPersona is a graph-based collaborative personalization framework that addresses sparse and skewed user histories in LLM personalization by decomposing interactions into facet-level representations and leveraging peer signals through a multiplex persona graph with dual-branch inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world LLM personalization suffers from sparse and skewed user interaction histories, where most users have few interactions and even frequent users' logs are incomplete and biased. This makes weakly observed user attributes hard to infer, causing brittle personalization when test requests involve under-supported facets. Existing methods lack mechanisms to borrow signals from similar users to fill these gaps.

Method: CoPersona decomposes user interaction histories into multiple facet-level representations instead of operating in a single unstructured global space. It constructs a multiplex persona graph that explicitly models peer-to-peer, facet-level alignment among users. At inference time, a dual-branch architecture combines non-parametric peer retrieval with parametric graph reasoning to effectively leverage peer information for personalization.

Result: Experiments across multiple domains and model scales show consistent improvements over strong baselines, validating CoPersona's effectiveness for robust LLM personalization.

Conclusion: Collaborative personalization via facet-level decomposition and graph-based peer signal transfer is an effective approach to overcome the limitations of sparse, skewed user histories, leading to more robust LLM personalization.

Abstract: Real-world LLM personalization is often constrained by sparse and skewed user histories: most users provide only a handful of interactions, while even frequent users' logs capture an incomplete and biased view of their preferences. As a result, weakly observed user attributes are difficult to infer, leading to brittle personalization when test-time requests shift toward under-supported facets. Motivated by this limitation, we present CoPersona, a graph-based collaborative personalization framework that completes sparse user profiles by borrowing signals from behaviorally similar peers. However, directly transferring signals is difficult because uneven facet coverage introduces bias into interaction histories, obscuring user similarity in the unstructured global space. To address this issue, CoPersona decomposes interaction histories into multiple facet-level representations and explicitly models peer-to-peer, facet-level alignment through a multiplex persona graph. To effectively leverage peer information at inference time, we employ a dual-branch architecture that combines non-parametric peer retrieval with parametric graph reasoning. Experiments across multiple domains and model scales demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, validating CoPersona as an effective approach for robust LLM personalization.

</details>


### [309] [IntentTune: Using user demand and personalization to resolve "unknown" query intents for e-commerce search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01530)
*Rachith Aiyappa,Ishita Khan,Chester Palen-Michel,Jayanth Yetukuri,Samarth Agrawal,Mehran Elyasi,Shuang Zhou*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: IntentTune is a framework that resolves ambiguous e-commerce queries by leveraging user-specific behavioral signals (search history, browsing) to infer latent intent like gender and age, outperforming population-level demand patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many real-world e-commerce queries are under-specified (e.g., "watch," "shirt"), lacking explicit attributes like gender or age group. This ambiguity hinders query intent detection and downstream retrieval. The paper aims to determine whether user-specific behavioral signals or population-level demand patterns are more effective at resolving such ambiguous intents.

Method: IntentTune is introduced as a framework for resolving ambiguous query intents using two signal sources: (1) user-specific behavioral signals — search history, browsing activity, and profile attributes; and (2) population-level demand patterns aggregated across all users. Experiments are conducted on real-world e-commerce data, comparing the efficacy of these signal types for inferring gender, age group, product category, and size intent from under-specified queries.

Result: Population-level demand patterns alone are insufficient to reliably infer intent for under-specified queries. User-specific behavioral signals — particularly prior search queries — significantly outperform both population-level statistics and static profile information across all intent dimensions: gender, age group, product category, and size.

Conclusion: User-specific behavioral signals, especially prior search queries, are the most effective source for resolving under-specified query intents in e-commerce search, and IntentTune successfully leverages these signals to improve intent inference accuracy.

Abstract: Understanding user intent is fundamental to delivering relevant search results in e-commerce. However, substantial fraction of real-world queries are under-specified (e.g., "watch" or "shirt"), lacking explicit attributes such as gender or age group. This ambiguity poses a significant challenge for query intent detection models in e-commerce search systems, which must accurately infer latent user intent (e.g., age, gender) to support effective downstream retrieval. We introduce IntentTune, a framework for resolving ambiguous or under-specified query intents by leveraging either (1) user-specific behavioral signals including search history, browsing activity, and profile attributes or (2) population-level demand patterns aggregated across all users. Through experiments on real-world e-commerce data, we first demonstrate that population-level demand patterns alone are insufficient to reliably infer intent in under-specified queries. We then demonstrate that user-specific behavioral signals -- particularly prior search queries -- outperform both population-level statistics and static profile information for inferring gender, age group, product category, and size intent from underspecified queries.

</details>


### [310] [Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Academic Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01852)
*Valentin J. J. Kreileder,Johannes Reisinger,Andreas Fischer*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This study evaluates cluster-based semantic chunking against fixed-size and recursive chunking in RAG systems using long academic theses, finding no performance advantage for the semantic approach and revealing that RAGAs faithfulness metrics may be unreliable in this context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether cluster-based semantic chunking — a more sophisticated document segmentation strategy — yields measurable improvements in retrieval quality and answer accuracy over simpler baseline chunking methods (fixed-size and recursive) when applied to long, structured academic documents in RAG pipelines.

Method: The authors implemented a RAG system with three chunking strategies (fixed-size, recursive, and cluster-based semantic chunking) and evaluated performance on long academic theses using the RAGAs (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment) framework, comparing results across both fixed/generic questions and document-specific questions.

Result: Cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler fixed-size or recursive chunking strategies under the tested configuration. Performance varied substantially between fixed and document-specific questions, likely due to document formatting and preprocessing effects. Additionally, the RAGAs faithfulness metric demonstrated limited reliability in this experimental setup.

Conclusion: More complex semantic chunking does not guarantee better RAG performance for structured academic documents; simpler chunking methods remain competitive. Caution is warranted when relying on RAGAs faithfulness as an evaluation metric, and question type (generic vs. document-specific) significantly influences outcomes.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems use the question-answering capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to access information outside their parameters. We evaluate if cluster-based semantic chunking improves retrieval and answer quality compared to fixed-size and recursive chunking evaluating on long, structured academic theses using the Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment (RAGAs) framework. RAGAs based faithfulness shows limited reliability in this setup. Performance on fixed versus document specific questions varied substantially, likely related to the formatting of documents and preprocessing. Under the tested configuration, cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler strategies.

</details>


### [311] [Planning over Matrix-Factorization MDPs for Candidate Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02115)
*Mikhail Trapeznikov,Maksim Utushkin*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper reformulates top-K recommendation retrieval as a Markov Decision Process over user-state dynamics induced by fold-in updates, showing that lightweight planning (even one-step lookahead) consistently outperforms static matrix factorization retrieval across multiple datasets, with cosine similarity proving essential over inner product to avoid popularity bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard matrix factorization retrieval treats all top-K recommendations as independent by computing a single static user vector and scoring items once. In reality, each recommended item alters the user's state, which should influence subsequent recommendations. The authors investigate when explicitly modeling and planning over these sequential user-state dynamics yields material gains over static retrieval, without retraining embeddings or changing the underlying representation.

Method: The authors cast top-K retrieval as an MDP over the implicit ALS posterior (the precision matrix A⁻¹ and user latent vector u). Actions are item selections, and state transitions are computed via a closed-form rank-one fold-in update after each recommended item. The trajectory reward combines a relevance term (cosine similarity between user state and item) with a posterior-alignment term. They compare three retrieval strategies under fixed embeddings: (1) static top-K scoring, (2) one-step lookahead planning, and (3) horizon-K Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Evaluation uses two protocols: per-user leave-last-n split and a stricter global time split across five datasets.

Result: Dynamics-aware planning outperforms static retrieval on all five datasets under the leave-last-n protocol. Gains persist on MovieLens-1M and VK-LSVD under the stricter global time split. A single step of lookahead captures most of the improvement, making MCTS largely unnecessary. Crucially, cosine similarity as the relevance measure is essential for these gains; inner-product similarity entangles relevance with item popularity and nullifies the planning benefit.

Conclusion: Lightweight planning over fold-in user-state dynamics offers a practical, retraining-free layer on top of fixed collaborative filtering embeddings that improves top-K retrieval. The approach is most effective when relevance is measured via cosine similarity rather than inner product, and a single lookahead step suffices, making it computationally feasible for production recommenders.

Abstract: For a recommender service, we view the customer journey as a chain of item recommendations: a useful item changes the user's state and therefore what should be retrieved next. Standard matrix-factorization retrieval ignores this -- it builds one user vector and returns the top-$K$ items by a static score, treating them as independent. We ask a narrow question: when is it worth planning over the user-state dynamics that fold-in induces? To answer it we propose casting top-$K$ retrieval as an MDP over the implicit-ALS posterior $(A^{-1},u)$, where an action is an item and the transition is a closed-form rank-one fold-in, and the trajectory reward combines a relevance similarity with a posterior-alignment term. Under the same fixed embeddings we compare static retrieval, one-step planning, and horizon-$K$ MCTS across five datasets and two protocols: a per-user leave-last-$n$ split and a stricter global time split. Dynamics-aware planning tends to overcome static retrieval on all datasets under leave-last-$n$, and the gains hold on MovieLens-1M and the VK-LSVD slices under the global time split. A single step of lookahead already captures most of the gain, so the lightweight planning layer turns static top-$K$ scoring into a short decision and improves retrieval over fixed collaborative-filtering embeddings, with no retraining and no change to the representation. These gains depend on measuring relevance with cosine rather than inner-product similarity, which is otherwise entangled with item popularity.

</details>


### [312] [Bringing Agentic Search to Earth Observation Data Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02387)
*Minghan Yu,Youran Sun,Chugang Yi,Yixin Wen,Haizhao Yang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: NASA's agentic search system uses LLMs and the NASA EO Knowledge Graph to match natural-language queries to geoscience datasets/tools. A fine-tuned neural scorer combined with BM25 via score fusion yields 5x improvements in Recall@10 and MRR. Adding a zero-shot LLM reranking stage further boosts MRR by 28%, demonstrating complementarity between supervised retrieval and LLM reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NASA holds thousands of geoscience datasets and tools (Worldview, Giovanni, Science Discovery Engine, Harmony), but finding the right resource is difficult even for domain experts. The motivation is to leverage knowledge graphs and LLMs to build an accessible, natural-language-driven search system that substantially amplifies the latent value of structured knowledge for the geoscience community.

Method: (1) Derive NASA-EO-Bench: an open benchmark of 47k query-dataset pairs (21k task-based queries) from the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (NASA EO-KG). (2) Fine-tune a neural scorer on NASA-EO-Bench, outperforming cosine and BM25 baselines. (3) Apply score fusion combining the neural scorer with BM25, improving Recall@10 and MRR by over 5x. (4) Add a zero-shot agentic reranking stage using LLM reasoning on a stratified N=200 subset, with no additional training.

Result: The fine-tuned neural scorer beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Score fusion of neural scorer + BM25 raises Recall@10 and MRR by over 5x. Zero-shot agentic reranking lifts MRR by an additional 28% on the N=200 stratified subset, demonstrating that LLM reasoning is complementary to supervised retrieval.

Conclusion: In the era of LLMs, the latent value of knowledge graphs can be substantially amplified through agentic search. A hybrid pipeline—supervised neural retrieval with BM25 fusion, plus zero-shot LLM reranking—delivers strong performance for domain-specific resource discovery. The system is deployed as a public service for the geoscience community, and NASA-EO-Bench is released as an open benchmark.

Abstract: NASA and its data centers hold thousands of geoscience datasets and tools like Worldview, Giovanni, the Science Discovery Engine, and Harmony. Finding the right one is hard even for domain experts. We present an agentic search system, deployed as a public service for the geoscience community, that takes a natural-language research query and returns the matching datasets and tools. We demonstrate that, in the era of large language models, the latent value of knowledge graphs (KGs) can be substantially amplified through agentic search. From the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (NASA EO-KG) we derive NASA-EO-Bench, an open benchmark of 47k query-dataset pairs (21k task-based queries). A neural scorer fine-tuned on NASA-EO-Bench beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Further combining it with BM25 via score fusion raises both Recall@10 (R@10) and MRR by over 5x. On top of this supervised pipeline, we add a zero-shot agentic reranking stage that, without any additional training, lifts MRR by 28% on a stratified N=200 subset, showing that LLM reasoning is complementary to supervised retrieval.

</details>


<div id='cs.HC'></div>

# cs.HC [[Back]](#toc)

### [313] [ExPerT: Personalizing LLM Responses to Users' Domain Expertise via Query-Wise Semantic and Keystroke Behavioral Cues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01242)
*Yeji Park,Jiwon Tark,Taesik Gong*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ExPerT is a query-wise personalization framework that adapts LLM responses based on users' domain expertise by combining semantic analysis of query text with behavioral keystroke dynamics, achieving 65.7% lower expertise inference error and 17.52% higher response satisfaction compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM personalization methods rely on static user profiles or text-only signals, failing to capture how a user's expertise varies across different queries. A user may be an expert in one domain but a novice in another, and current systems cannot dynamically adapt to this query-specific expertise variation.

Method: ExPerT employs two components: (1) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that jointly interprets query text and keystroke dynamics (typing patterns) using in-context LLM prompting to infer the user's expertise level for that specific query domain; (2) an expertise-conditioned response generation module that tailors detail level, terminology, and conceptual complexity of the LLM's response accordingly.

Result: In a user study with 40 participants and 1,270 queries, ExPerT reduced expertise inference error by 65.7% over the strongest baseline (MAE: 0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved response satisfaction by 17.52% on a 5-point Likert scale (from 3.71 to 4.36).

Conclusion: Integrating behavioral signals (keystroke dynamics) with semantic query analysis enables significantly more accurate query-level expertise inference and substantially improves user satisfaction with personalized LLM responses, validating the effectiveness of query-wise dynamic personalization.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by end users, yet existing personalization methods relying on static profiles or text-only signals fail to capture query-specific expertise variation. We present ExPerT, a query-wise personalization framework that adapts LLM responses to users' query domain expertise by combining semantic and behavioral cues. ExPerT consists of two key components: (i) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that jointly interprets query text and keystroke dynamics via in-context LLM prompting, and (ii) an expertise-conditioned response generation that adapts the level of detail, terminology, and conceptual complexity. Our user study with 40 participants and 1270 queries demonstrated that ExPerT reduced expertise inference error by 65.7% compared to the strongest baseline (MAE = 0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved response satisfaction by 17.52% (from 3.71 to 4.36) on a 5-point Likert scale.

</details>


### [314] [Mitigating Confirmation Bias through Hand-Drawing Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01359)
*Chenyu Lin,Cindy Xiong,Icy Zhang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Hand-drawn construction videos of bar charts reduce confirmation bias and improve data interpretation accuracy compared to static charts, especially when data conflicts with prior beliefs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data visualization interpretation is frequently distorted by viewers' prior beliefs (confirmation bias), undermining informed decision-making. The authors sought to explore whether an embodied pedagogical approach — showing the dynamic construction process of a visualization — could counteract this cognitive bias.

Method: A controlled experiment comparing two conditions: static bar charts versus videos depicting the hand-drawing construction of bar charts. Both conditions were tested across contexts that either aligned with or challenged participants' prior beliefs, measuring interpretation accuracy, belief-consistent errors, and belief-overriding responses.

Result: Hand-drawn construction videos significantly improved participants' ability to interpret data accurately, even when the data contradicted their prior beliefs. The approach reduced belief-consistent errors and increased the likelihood of belief-overriding responses compared to static charts.

Conclusion: Exposing the construction process of a visualization fosters more accurate reasoning and mitigates confirmation bias. This opens a promising design space for bias-mitigating data interfaces grounded in embodied cognition principles.

Abstract: Understanding data visualizations is essential for informed decision-making, yet interpretation is often shaped and even distorted by prior beliefs. We investigate whether an embodied pedagogical approach, in which viewers observe the dynamic hand-drawing of a visualization, can mitigate confirmation bias and improve interpretation accuracy. We conducted a study comparing static bar charts to videos in which charts are constructed through hand-drawing, across contexts that either align with or challenge participants' prior beliefs. The results indicate that hand-drawn videos helped participants accurately interpret data, even when the data conflicted with their prior beliefs. This approach also reduced belief-consistent errors and increased belief-overriding responses. These findings suggest that exposing the construction process of a visualization supports more accurate reasoning and mitigates the influence of confirmation bias. Consequently, this work introduces a promising design space for bias-mitigating data interfaces.

</details>


### [315] [Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01506)
*Tomohiro Nagashima,Lisa Siegrist,Niklas Scholz,Shintaro Sato,Martina Vincoli,Man Su*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A speed-dating study with 16 students and 15 teachers in Germany revealed significant misalignments in views on student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classrooms, particularly regarding trust in AI and social-emotional aspects of learning. Teacher-student relationships outside AI use emerged as a key shaping factor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work has not fully examined whether teachers' and students' views on AI in K-12 classrooms align or diverge, despite the critical importance of multi-stakeholder perspectives as AI technologies become integrated into school settings.

Method: A speed-dating study using storyboards was conducted with 16 school students and 15 school teachers in Germany. The study employed explicit pair-matching analysis to systematically investigate alignments and misalignments between student and teacher views on student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classrooms.

Result: Students and teachers held misaligned views on several key topics, most notably: (1) the degree of trust placed in AI, and (2) the social and emotional dimensions of student learning with AI. Additionally, teacher-student relationships established outside of AI use were found to significantly shape both stakeholders' views and interactions with AI in the classroom.

Conclusion: The study illustrates that preferences in teacher-student-AI interactions are complex and contingent upon dynamic relational dynamics among stakeholders. The authors discuss potential reasons for misalignments and propose strategies to bridge these perspective gaps.

Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based technologies have been integrated into school classrooms where multiple stakeholders (with different roles) interact with each other, it is critical to deeply understand stakeholder views in the classroom. In particular, prior work has not fully uncovered how teachers' and school students' views might or might not align well with each other, especially in K-12 classrooms. We conducted a speed-dating study using storyboards with 16 school students and 15 school teachers in Germany to investigate alignments and misalignments between their views on student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classroom. Through an explicit pair-matching analysis, we found that students and teachers had misaligned views on several key topics, including how much they trust AI and social and emotional aspects of student learning with AI. Findings also revealed the importance of teacher-student relationships outside of AI use that shape stakeholders' views and interactions. We discuss potential reasons for the observed misaligned views and strategies to fill the perspective gaps. This study illustrates the complexities of preferences in teacher-student-AI interactions that depend on the dynamic relations among the stakeholders.

</details>


### [316] [OrchestrXR: A Multi-Agent System for Idea-to-Prototype XR Study Authoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01588)
*Shuqi Liao,Chenfei Zhu,Karthik Ramani,Voicu Popescu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: OrchestrXR is a multi-agent human-AI workflow that supports researchers in transforming early-stage XR study ideas into runnable Unity prototypes through structured, controllable stages: study design, scene generation, and interaction generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The process of turning an initial XR study idea into a functional prototype is fragmented across study design, 3D scene construction, and interaction logic implementation. Existing approaches lack a unified, controllable pipeline that preserves researcher intent throughout the workflow.

Method: OrchestrXR employs a multi-agent human-AI workflow with three structured stages: (1) study design using structured schemas, (2) scene generation, and (3) interaction generation. It features multi-agent orchestration and interactive human-agent interfaces, producing a Unity-based prototype while allowing researcher oversight and control at each stage.

Result: A user study with 12 XR researchers demonstrated that OrchestrXR effectively supports early-stage XR study authoring, with strong preservation of researcher intent across all stages of the workflow.

Conclusion: OrchestrXR offers a viable and effective approach for early-stage XR study prototyping by combining multi-agent AI orchestration with human-in-the-loop control, addressing the fragmentation problem in XR study authoring.

Abstract: Extended Reality (XR) has become an important interaction paradigm in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). XR studies are used to investigate interaction, perception, and user behavior in immersive environments, and typically involve experimental tasks, 3D scenes, and interactive logic. However, turning an initial XR study idea into a runnable prototype remains fragmented across study design, scene construction, and interaction implementation. We present OrchestrXR, a multi-agent human-AI workflow for early-stage idea-to-prototype XR study authoring. Rather than treating XR study creation as one-shot generation, OrchestrXR supports a controllable workflow across study design, scene generation, and interaction generation through structured schemas, multi-agent orchestration, and interactive human-agent interfaces, producing a Unity-based prototype from a researcher's idea. A user study with 12 XR researchers suggests that OrchestrXR provides effective support for early-stage XR study authoring with strong intent preservation across stages.

</details>


### [317] [Made to Feel: How Designers Bring Emotions into Affective Visualization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01593)
*Yixin Bai,Ziyi Wang,Keke Wu,Fumeng Yang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper explores how visualization practitioners incorporate emotion into their design work through interviews with 15 practitioners. It identifies three functional roles of emotion (entry, engagement, outcome), three facets of how designers work with emotion (data, design, audience) with corresponding design strategies, and ethical considerations. Key findings reveal that affective intent often emerges organically during design rather than being pre-planned, emotional impact stems from cumulative design choices rather than isolated visual elements, and evaluation remains a critical challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While affective visualization has gained increasing attention in the visualization research community, prior work has focused on viewer experiences and theoretical frameworks, leaving a significant gap in understanding how practitioners actually bring emotions into their visualization design process. This study aims to fill that gap by empirically investigating designers' practices, strategies, and challenges.

Method: The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 visualization practitioners. Interview data were analyzed using hybrid thematic analysis, combining inductive and deductive coding approaches to identify patterns and themes related to emotional design in visualization.

Result: The analysis yielded three main thematic contributions: (1) a taxonomy of three emotion functions — entry (attracting viewers), engagement (sustaining attention), and outcome (leaving a lasting impression or motivating action); (2) three facets of emotion work — data (emotional qualities of the data itself), design (visual encoding choices), and audience (understanding viewer context), along with concrete design strategies for each; and (3) a set of ethical considerations designers navigate. Two emergent insights were that affective intent often arises iteratively during design rather than being predetermined, and that emotional impact is an emergent property of aggregated design decisions, not attributable to single visual elements. Practitioners identified evaluation of emotional impact as a persistent and unresolved challenge.

Conclusion: Emotion in visualization design is a complex, emergent, and ethically nuanced practice. The findings provide an empirically grounded framework for understanding how practitioners operationalize affect, and underscore the need for the research community to develop better methods and metrics for evaluating emotional dimensions of visualization.

Abstract: Affective visualization is increasingly studied in visualization research, yet how designers bring emotions into their visualization work remains unexplored. This paper addresses this gap through semi-structured interviews with 15 visualization practitioners. Using hybrid thematic analysis, we identify: (1) three functions that emotions can serve for viewers (entry, engagement, outcome); (2) three facets of how designers work with emotion (data, design, audience), along with design strategies; and (3) ethical considerations in the design process. We also observe that affective intent often emerges during the design process rather than being planned from the outset, and that emotional impact arises from accumulated design choices rather than isolated visual elements. Finally, we highlight evaluation as a key challenge identified by our participants.

</details>


### [318] [Evaluating Glanceable Multi-Device Family Health Tracking with Smartwatches and Home Displays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01618)
*Lucas M. Silva,Evropi Stefanidi,Aehong Min,Franceli L. Cibrian,Jesus A. Beltran,Cassie Zeiler,Sabrina E. B. Schuck,Kimberley D. Lakes,Gillian R. Hayes,Daniel A. Epstein*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A 9-week study with 12 families (44 participants) compared smartwatch-only, home display-only, and combined designs for family mood and goal tracking. Results showed home displays significantly increased tracking frequency, children tracked more consistently than adults, and multi-device redundancy accommodated diverse family routines and preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While ubiquitous computing has explored personal health tracking devices extensively, there is limited understanding of multi-device designs for family informatics, where health management is inherently collaborative and requires coordination across family members with different routines, mobility patterns, and device preferences.

Method: A within-subjects, 9-week field study with 44 participants from 12 families, who alternated between three conditions: smartwatch-only, home display-only, and a combined multi-device design for tracking moods and goals. Data collection included log analysis of tracking behavior (frequency, timing, location) and qualitative interview analysis.

Result: Log analysis: Home display presence significantly increased mood and goal tracking frequency vs. smartwatch-only. Tracking peaked in afternoons, dropped on weekends, occurred 2.6X more at home. Children tracked more consistently than adults across all conditions, with overall mood tracking declining over time. Interview analysis: Smartwatch glanceability enabled opportunistic tracking and awareness while apart; home displays served as reminders during family routines and engaged non-participant members who avoided wearables. Multi-device redundancy accommodated diversity in family routines, mobility patterns, and device preferences.

Conclusion: Multi-device family informatics systems should be designed for inclusivity, glanceability, and adaptability, accommodating heterogeneous preferences within families through redundant yet complementary ubiquitous data sharing across smartwatches and home displays.

Abstract: While ubiquitous computing research has explored diverse devices for personal health tracking, we know less about multi-device designs for family informatics, where health management is inherently collaborative. To understand how families adopt and perceive ubiquitous access to shared health data across contexts, we evaluated smartwatch-only, home display-only, and combined designs for tracking moods and goals, domains central to family health behavior regulation. 44 people across 12 families alternated between these designs over nine weeks. Log analysis revealed that mood tracking and goal reporting were significantly more frequent with the home display present compared to smartwatch-only use, despite an overall decline in mood tracking over time. Tracking peaked in afternoons, dropped on weekends, and occurred 2.6X more at home, with children tracking more consistently than adults across all designs. From interview analysis, we learned how family data glanceability on smartwatches supported opportunistic tracking and awareness while apart, whereas displays reminded families to self-track and collaborate during home routines including members that avoided wearables (e.g., non-participants). Multi-device redundancy accommodated diversity in routines, mobility patterns, and device preferences among members in the same family. We discuss opportunities for multi-device family informatics that accommodates different preferences through inclusive, glanceable, and adaptable ubiquitous data sharing.

</details>


### [319] [From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01692)
*Yuming Feng,Yuan Tian,Erica Zhao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: AITutor is an AI tutoring system for junior-high math that translates pedagogical mechanisms into UI features. A field study with 12 students preparing for the Zhongkao revealed that students resist Socratic dialogue under time pressure, instead using "answer-first" shortcuts as diagnostic checkpoints. Features like layered worked examples and metacognitive scaffolding lowered reasoning repair costs. The authors contribute the "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop" framework for designing AI that supports reasoning inspection, repair, curriculum verification, and delayed retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs integrated into educational technology risk reducing mathematical learning to mere answer generation — students may bypass genuine reasoning by prompting for solutions. The authors aim to investigate how to design AI tutoring systems that structurally support reasoning processes rather than simply outputting answers, particularly for junior-high students under the high-stakes pressure of the Zhongkao exam.

Method: A three-phase approach: (1) a generative study to design AITutor by translating pedagogical mechanisms (Socratic dialogue, worked examples, scaffolding) into concrete UI features; (2) a usability study; and (3) a 12-participant field deployment with mixed-methods triangulation — analyzing 7,379 telemetry events, 8 contextual observations, and 10 interviews with junior-high students preparing for the Zhongkao.

Result: Students actively resisted traditional Socratic dialogue under time pressure, instead repurposing "answer-first" shortcuts as vital diagnostic checkpoints. Layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, and metacognitive scaffolding demonstrably lowered the interaction cost of reasoning repair. The study surfaced nuanced behavioral patterns around how students inspect, repair, and verify their mathematical reasoning in authentic exam-preparation contexts.

Conclusion: The authors contribute the "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop," a design framework with actionable implications for building AI systems that structurally support inspection, local repair, curriculum verification, and delayed retrieval of mathematical reasoning. The work challenges the assumption that Socratic dialogue is universally effective, showing that under time pressure, students adapt AI tools in pragmatically rational ways that designers should accommodate rather than resist.

Abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into educational technology threatens to reduce mathematical learning to mere answer generation. This paper presents a generative study, usability study, and 12-participant field deployment of AITutor, an interactive system that translates theoretical pedagogical mechanisms into concrete user interface features. We explore how junior-high students preparing for high-stakes exams (Zhongkao) interact with AI tutoring. Through mixed-methods triangulation (7,379 telemetry events, 8 contextual observations, 10 interviews), we reveal that students actively resist traditional Socratic dialogue under time pressure, repurposing "answer-first" shortcuts as vital diagnostic checkpoints. We demonstrate how features like layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, and metacognitive scaffolding lower the interaction cost of reasoning repair. We contribute a "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop," offering actionable implications for designing AI that structurally supports the inspection, local repair, curriculum verification, and delayed retrieval of mathematical reasoning in the wild.

</details>


### [320] [Adapting CCDF Plots for Visualizing Ordinal Regression Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01747)
*Abhraneel Sarma*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes modified Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots as an intuitive visualization method for communicating results from cumulative-link ordinal regression models, addressing a key barrier to the adoption of these statistically more appropriate models for ordinal data like Likert items.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite cumulative-link ordinal regression models being statistically superior to linear models/ANOVA for ordinal data (making fewer assumptions), their adoption in Visualization, HCI, and psychology remains limited. The author posits that the primary barrier is not statistical complexity but rather the difficulty in visually representing and intuitively communicating the results from such models.

Method: The author proposes modified Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots as a visualization technique tailored for ordinal regression outputs. The paper demonstrates how these plots can convey the same substantive takeaways that researchers typically extract from metric-assuming analyses, but in a manner faithful to the ordinal nature of the data.

Result: The paper demonstrates that mCCDF plots enable researchers to intuitively communicate key findings from ordinal regression models, bridging the gap between statistical rigor and interpretability that has historically hindered adoption of these models.

Conclusion: mCCDF plots offer a viable solution to the communication barrier surrounding ordinal regression models. By making results from these models as interpretable as those from traditional metric-based analyses, the approach may encourage broader adoption of more appropriate statistical methods for ordinal data.

Abstract: Cumulative-link ordinal regression models are an alternative approach for analysing ordinal data such as Likert items, which are widely used in Visualization (and other related fields like HCI, psychology etc.). There are many researchers who are strong proponents of this approach, as it makes less stringent assumptions about the data, compared to the more commonly used linear model or ANOVA. Yet, ordinal regression models have seen limited adoption. I posit that one possible reason for this might be due to the difficulty in visually representing the results from such models, and in communicating the key takeaways in an intuitive manner. I propose the use of (modified) Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots to visualize the results of ordinal regression models, and demonstrate how the same takeaways that researchers present from analyses which treat ordinal data as metric can be easily communicated using mCCDFs.

</details>


### [321] [A Social Norms Approach to Youth Social Media Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01807)
*JaeWon Kim*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Youth desire authentic, trusting social media interactions but fail to achieve them due to normative constraints rather than individual choice. The dissertation argues that platform norms create pluralistic ignorance, design interventions are shaped by existing norms, and the narrow societal definition of "social media" limits innovation. The research involves co-designing an independent, evidence-based platform with youth that signals trust-building as its core purpose.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A persistent gap exists between what young people say they want from social media (authentic self-expression, less judgment, interpersonal trust) and how they actually behave on these platforms. The author argues this disconnect stems not from individual failings but from normative structures — platform norms, peer perception, and perceived behavioral expectations — that constrain youth engagement.

Method: The dissertation adopts a social norms framework structured around three interrelated theoretical claims. The methodology is participatory and design-based: engaging youth directly in the co-design and co-construction of an independent, evidence-based social platform whose features are intentionally designed to signal norms of trust and authentic connection.

Result: Three key claims emerge: (1) Platform norms drive pluralistic ignorance, where youth conform to norms they privately reject. (2) Design interventions cannot be evaluated in isolation; their efficacy depends on the surrounding normative environment, meaning privacy and other relational goals must be reframed as social norms rather than individual settings. (3) The societal conflation of "social media" with a handful of dominant platforms constrains both policy and design imagination to harm-reduction rather than proactive re-envisioning.

Conclusion: The path forward lies in building an independent social platform co-designed with youth, where every feature consistently communicates that fostering trusted connections is the platform's raison d'être, thereby establishing a distinct normative environment from the outset.

Abstract: Young people consistently say they want authentic self-expression, less judgment, and more interpersonal trust on social media, yet they rarely manage to engage that way. My dissertation argues that the obstacle is normative rather than individual: how youth engage is governed less by personal choice than by platform norms, peer perception, and beliefs about how others behave. I take a social norms approach to youth social media design organized around three claims. First, platform norms constrain individual behavior, producing a pluralistic ignorance in which youth enact norms they privately reject. Second, design interventions are themselves shaped by existing norms, so whether a feature works depends on the environment around it, which means relational goals such as privacy must be treated as social norms rather than individual settings. Third, a societal norm about what ``social media'' is -- equating it with a few mainstream platforms -- confines policy and design to mitigating those platforms rather than actively envisioning supportive alternatives. Together these claims motivate my dissertation research: engaging youth directly in designing and building an evidence-based independent platform whose features consistently signal that building trusted connections is what the space is for.

</details>


### [322] [Visual Analytics of Neighborhood Attribute Profiles for Exploring Structural Equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02163)
*Kohei Arimoto,Masahiko Itoh*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes a visual analytics method using dimensionality reduction to explore the true manifold structure of node attribute profiles in attributed networks. Applied to inter-firm transaction data, it reveals that structural roles form non-linear, density-biased manifolds, challenging the assumption that nodes with identical semantic labels share similar structural roles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current representation learning methods for attributed networks implicitly assume a uniform and continuous feature space, which may obscure the true topological structure of high-dimensional node attribute profiles. The authors aim to visually investigate whether this assumption holds and what the actual feature space topology looks like.

Method: A visual analytics approach employing dimensionality reduction to project nodes' neighborhood attribute profiles from high-dimensional space into a visually interpretable low-dimensional representation, enabling direct inspection of the feature space's manifold structure. The method is applied to inter-firm transaction networks.

Result: Analysis of the feature space topology against industry classifications yielded three findings: (1) supply chain hierarchies exhibit continuous transitions rather than discrete boundaries; (2) categories that are semantically identical under general classifications can be clearly separated by actual transaction network structure; (3) a single industry label may fragment into multiple distinct regions in the feature space.

Conclusion: The assumption that identical semantics imply similar structural roles may be invalid. The authors suggest the need for new similarity metrics that respect the underlying manifold topology rather than relying on uniform, continuous feature space assumptions prevalent in existing representation learning methods.

Abstract: Exploring similar nodes in attributed networks represents a key challenge in data mining. While recent representation learning methods embed networks into low-dimensional vectors, they often implicitly assume a uniform and continuous feature space. This paper proposes a visual analytics approach using dimensionality reduction to help clarify the true topological structure of high-dimensional feature spaces formed by nodes' neighborhood attribute profiles. Analyzing inter-firm transaction networks indicates that structural roles can form complex, non-linear manifolds with density biases. Comparing this feature space with industry classifications suggested: (1) supply chain hierarchies transition continuously; (2) categories treated identically under general semantics can be clearly separated by actual transaction networks; and (3) a single industry label may fragment into multiple regions. These findings suggest potential limitations in assuming identical semantics imply similar structural roles and highlight the possible need for new similarity metrics aligned with manifold topology.

</details>


### [323] [Synthetic Contact with AI Reduces Cross-Partisan Animosity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02181)
*Benjamin Lira,Noah Castelo,Stefano Puntoni,Olivier Toubia*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: AI chatbots representing the political outgroup can reduce affective polarization: brief synthetic conversations correct misperceptions about outgroup attitudes, warm feelings toward opponents, and increase willingness to engage in real cross-partisan contact—though effects largely fade within a week.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-partisan animosity has surged while meaningful intergroup contact remains scarce due to active avoidance. The authors investigate whether AI chatbots can serve as a scalable, low-barrier substitute for the face-to-face contact people shun.

Method: Five preregistered studies (N=3,960 U.S. partisans) using within-person and between-group experimental designs. Participants engaged in brief (~10 min) conversations with AI chatbots embodying outgroup political views on topics such as environmental consumption and immigration. Measures included perceived outgroup attitudes, affective warmth, and behavioral choice (opting into real cross-partisan conversation). One study tested durability over one week; content analysis compared outgroup bots to control chatbots.

Result: (1) Partisans showed lower avoidance of AI outgroup partners vs. human ones. (2) A single conversation corrected large misperceptions (Democrats overestimated Republican anti-environmentalism by >1 SD) and increased warmth. (3) Effects were driven by information provision, not mere social engagement. (4) On immigration, chatbot contact increased real cross-partisan conversation choice by 6 pp. (5) Warmth gains largely dissipated after one week, with small residual effects among extreme partisans.

Conclusion: Synthetic contact via outgroup AI chatbots is a scalable, behaviorally meaningful, and broadly acceptable intervention for reducing partisan animosity. However, effects are mostly transient, suggesting the need for repeated or reinforced exposure to sustain benefits.

Abstract: Americans' warmth toward members of the opposing political party has fallen sharply over the past three decades -- yet meaningful cross-partisan contact remains scarce, in part because people actively avoid it. Across five preregistered studies (total N = 3,960 U.S. partisans), we test whether brief conversations with AI chatbots representing the political outgroup can substitute for the contact people shun. Synthetic contact first lowers the barrier to entry: partisans would endure almost twice as long contemplating their own mortality to avoid a human outgroup partner as an AI one. These conversations then correct the misperceptions that fuel division. At baseline, Democrats placed Republicans more than a standard deviation past their actual position on environmental consumption attitudes -- enough to flip the average Republican from supportive to opposed -- and a single ten-minute conversation with an outgroup chatbot corrected those beliefs and warmed affect in a within-person study of both parties. A three-arm experiment ruled out pure engagement and sociality as drivers. Synthetic contact also moved behavior, in a sample of both parties and on a more affectively charged issue: participants who spoke with an outgroup bot about immigration were six percentage points more likely than controls to choose to have a real conversation with a partisan from the other side. A final study tested whether these gains last: the warmth effect replicated immediately in a new sample; most of it faded within a week, with a small residual concentrated among the most extreme partisans. Analyzing conversation content showed that information, more than friendliness, distinguishes outgroup bots from control chatbots. Together, these findings establish synthetic contact as a scalable, behaviorally consequential, and -- unlike face-to-face contact -- widely acceptable form of cross-partisan engagement.

</details>


### [324] [What Types of Human-AI Teams Exist?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02198)
*Nathan Hughes,Ibrahim Habli*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper systematically analyzes 53 human-AI teaming studies, categorizing them into five distinct clusters based on psychological taxonomies of teaming, revealing that disparate team types are studied under the same label, raising concerns about the transferability of insights across papers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite growing interest in human-AI teaming, the literature spans multiple domains with no clear understanding of what types of teams are actually being studied or how they compare. This lack of taxonomic clarity threatens the generalizability and cumulative value of research findings.

Method: The authors conducted a systematic analysis of 53 papers on human-AI teams, applying psychological taxonomies of teaming to derive a classification framework. They categorized the studies into five clusters: AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, and Group Equanimity, based on holistic team-level characteristics.

Result: The analysis revealed five distinct clusters of human-AI team types, each with unique combinations of team-level characteristics. These disparate team configurations are all studied under the umbrella term "human-AI teaming," suggesting that findings may not be directly transferable between studies from different clusters.

Conclusion: The authors call into question the assumed transferability of insights across human-AI teaming studies and provide practical guidance, including a taxonomy for identifying team types, a reporting checklist for researchers, and recommendations for synthesizing the field more coherently.

Abstract: Human-AI teaming has received increasing attention in the literature. However, the range of studies conducted in multiple domains make it difficult to understand what types of teams are being studied, and in what ways are they similar/different from one another. In this study, we analyse 53 papers on human-AI teams and categorise them into five main clusters based on psychological taxonomies of teaming; AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, and Group Equanimity. Each cluster represents a unique combination of holistic team-level characteristics, indicating there are multiple disparate team types studied under the same definition. In turn, this raises the question of whether insights are truly transferable between papers. We conclude with guidance on how to identify the types of human-AI teams studied, a checklist for reporting a human-AI team in research work, and ways in which the field can be further synthesised.

</details>


### [325] [Personality Without Persons? A Psychometric Critique of Big Five Testing in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02325)
*Kim Zierahn,Cristina Cachero,Anna Korhonen,Nuria Oliver*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates whether Big Five personality inventories—developed for humans—are valid for LLMs. Testing 244 models across 49 families, the authors find that adapted items can achieve content validity, but the inventories fail to capture meaningful inter-model differences (only 3% of variance), the five-factor structure collapses (four facets merge, r ≥ .92), and alignment training shifts scores toward social desirability. They conclude Big Five scores do not measure a human-personality-equivalent construct in LLMs and call for LLM-native evaluation frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human personality inventories like the Big Five are increasingly used to characterize, compare, and govern LLMs despite being developed and validated exclusively for humans. No systematic psychometric evaluation has established whether these instruments apply meaningfully to LLMs. This gap risks producing misleading characterizations that inform benchmarking and governance decisions.

Method: A systematic psychometric evaluation was conducted in three phases: (1) Content validity assessment of five candidate Big Five inventories, with expert review to select the most suitable; (2) Administration of the winning inventory to N = 244 LLMs from 49 model families, analyzing variance decomposition to assess inter-individual differences; (3) Factor analysis to test whether LLM responses recover the expected five-factor structure, plus comparison of base vs. instruction-tuned model variants to examine effects of alignment training.

Result: (1) LLM-adapted Big Five items achieved sufficient content validity, but original human-developed items did not. (2) Between-model variability was very low, accounting for only 3% of total score variance; most variance was attributable to within-model item-level noise. (3) The five-factor structure did not replicate: four of the five Big Five facets collapsed into a single dimension (r ≥ .92). (4) Alignment training systematically shifted scores toward socially desirable traits in instruction-tuned models compared to base models.

Conclusion: Big Five personality scores in LLMs do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality. Applying human personality frameworks to LLMs without validation yields misleading characterizations. The field needs evaluation frameworks developed specifically for LLMs rather than uncritically adopting human constructs.

Abstract: Human personality inventories are increasingly used to characterize large language models (LLMs), compare systems, and inform downstream governance claims. Yet, these inventories were developed and validated for humans, and it remains unclear whether they apply to LLMs. We present a systematic psychometric evaluation of Big Five personality measurements in LLMs. We ask three research questions: Do Big Five inventories a) appropriately describe LLMs, b) capture inter-individual differences across models, and c) reflect internal factors consistent with human personality. We assess content validity of five candidate Big Five inventories and administer the winning inventory to N = 244 different models spanning 49 model families. First, we found that Big Five items adapted for LLMs can reach sufficient content validity, while original human-developed items did not. Second, Big Five inventories did not capture meaningful differences between LLMs: We found low variability between models, accounting for only 3% of total score variance. Third, LLMs responses did not recover the Big Five five-factor structure with four of the Big Five facets collapsing into one (r >= .92). Direct comparisons between base and instruction-tuned model variants suggested that alignment training systematically shifted Big Five scores toward socially desirable traits. These findings demonstrate that Big Five scores do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs. Applying human personality frameworks to LLMs produces misleading characterizations used to benchmark, compare, and govern LLMs. We highlight the need for evaluation frameworks that are developed for LLMs, rather than adopting human constructs without validation.

</details>


### [326] [Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02361)
*Zirui Shan,Vanessa Echeverria,Yuheng Li,Yi-Shan Tsai,Roberto Martinez-Maldonado*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A within-subjects study (n=60) found that GenAI-assisted data comics outperform conventional visualizations for student information retrieval and comprehension, particularly insight tasks, while raising engagement. However, concerns about AI-driven misinformation and ownership persist.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Students struggle with interpreting visualizations due to limited visualization literacy. Data comics show promise for improving engagement and understanding, but empirical evidence is scarce partly because creating them is labor-intensive. GenAI offers a scalable solution to this creation bottleneck, motivating an empirical comparison of conventional visualizations vs. GenAI-assisted data comics.

Method: A within-subjects experimental design with 60 university students. Participants completed information retrieval and comprehension tasks using both conventional visualizations and data comics (created with GenAI assistance). Performance was measured across task types, controlling for participants' prior visualization literacy levels. Subjective feedback on engagement, ease of understanding, and ethical concerns was also collected.

Result: Students consistently performed better with data comics, especially on insight comprehension tasks, regardless of their prior visualization literacy. Data comics were rated as more engaging and easier to understand. However, participants raised concerns about GenAI-driven misinformation and issues of content ownership.

Conclusion: Data comics represent a potentially effective tool for data communication in education. GenAI can help overcome the creation barrier, but ethical concerns — particularly around misinformation and ownership — must be addressed before widespread adoption.

Abstract: In today's data-driven world, students often struggle with interpreting visualisations due to limited visualisation literacy. Data comics have emerged as a promising medium to enhance engagement and understanding, but their educational value has seen little empirical examination, partly due to the effort required to create them. Recent advances in Generative AI (GenAI) offer a scalable solution to this challenge. We conducted a within-subjects study with 60 university students, comparing conventional visualisations with data comics, created with assistance from GenAI tools, across information retrieval and comprehension tasks. Students consistently performed better with data comics, particularly in insight comprehension tasks, independent of prior visualisation literacy. Students also commented data comics as more engaging and easier to understand, though concerns were raised about GenAI-driven misinformation and ownership. Our findings highlight the potential of data comics as a potentially effective tool for data communication in education, while underscoring the need to address ethical concerns related to AI-assisted creation.

</details>


### [327] [Physical surfaces make touch interactions in virtual reality precise, efficient, and bimanual](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02430)
*Wen Ying,Seongkook Heo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates how different levels of hand-grounded haptic feedback (none, vibrotactile/pressure, and a portable physical surface) affect precision-demanding touch interactions in VR. The physical surface condition yielded the best selection precision, tracing efficiency, sketch quality, and bimanual hand use, driven by users' enhanced sense of confidence and control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mid-air gestures in VR lack tactile feedback and a physical reference surface (haptic grounding), creating significant challenges for precise and efficient touch interactions in tasks like selecting, tracing, and sketching.

Method: A user study comparing three levels of hand-grounded haptic feedback: (1) No Haptic Feedback (visual-only), (2) Tactile Feedback (vibrotactile and pressure cues upon virtual surface contact), and (3) Physical Surface (a portable, tangible surface). Tasks requiring high precision — selecting, tracing, and sketching — were evaluated.

Result: Portable physical surfaces produced the best selection precision, tracing efficiency, and sketch quality. Participants also exhibited increased bimanual hand utilization when using the physical surface, and reported a preference for physical surfaces due to greater confidence and control.

Conclusion: Providing a portable physical surface as haptic grounding significantly improves precision touch interactions in VR compared to tactile-only or no haptic feedback. The enhanced performance and user preference stem from improved confidence and motor control afforded by a tangible reference.

Abstract: Virtual reality (VR) systems can enable convenient hand-based interactions across diverse work scenarios. However, mid-air gestures lack tactile feedback and a physical reference surface to support the hand. This absence of haptic grounding can cause significant challenges in achieving precise and efficient touch interactions. This paper investigates the effect of different types of hand-grounded haptic feedback on the touch performance of VR tasks that demand high precision, such as selecting, tracing, and sketching. We compared three levels of haptic feedback: 1) No Haptic Feedback, where only visual feedback was provided; 2) Tactile Feedback, where users received vibrotactile and pressure feedback upon touching a virtual surface; 3) Physical Surface, where users interacted with a portable and tangible surface.
  Our study found that portable physical surfaces enabled the best selection precision, tracing efficiency, and sketch quality. Furthermore, participants showed increased bimanual hand utilization when engaging with a physical surface during tasks. These observed behaviors corresponded to participants' preference for interacting with physical surfaces, attributed to a better sense of confidence and control.

</details>


### [328] [When Do LLM Personas Support Visualization Design? A Cross-Model Study of Color Assignment and Chart Choice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02455)
*Shahreen Salim,Klaus Mueller*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: LLM personas show personality-color coupling that is highly dependent on model configuration and concept type, while chart-idiom preferences are driven more by task context than personality traits. The findings frame LLM personas as exploratory probes, not human substitutes, and call for multi-model testing and no-persona baselines in visualization research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM personas are increasingly used as proxies for diverse users in early-stage visualization design, but it is unclear whether persona-conditioned outputs reflect genuine, stable personality effects or are merely artifacts of model selection and task framing. This uncertainty threatens the validity of using LLMs for user-centered visualization research.

Method: The authors evaluated 43 Big Five personality profiles across three model configurations (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5-mini) on two visualization-relevant tasks: (1) color assignment for six concepts (abstract and concrete) and (2) chart-idiom preference ratings across task contexts. They compared personality-driven variance against model-identity-driven variance, and benchmarked trait-aligned cluster rankings against a no-persona baseline.

Result: Personality-color coupling was absent in GPT-4o-mini, consistent in GPT-4.1-mini, and partial (2/6 concepts) in GPT-5-mini. For abstract concepts, personality explained more hue variance than model identity; for concrete concepts, effects were smaller and comparable. In chart choice, trait-aligned clusters produced stable top-idiom rankings across all nine cluster-context combinations, but the no-persona baseline recovered the same top choice in 8/9 model-context cells.

Conclusion: LLM personas should be treated as exploratory probes rather than surrogates for human participants in visualization design. The study recommends multi-model testing, disaggregating results by concept type (abstract vs. concrete), and always including no-persona baselines to disentangle task-driven effects from personality-driven signals.

Abstract: Large language model personas are increasingly used to approximate diverse users during early-stage visualization design, but it remains unclear whether persona-conditioned outputs reflect stable personality effects or artifacts of model choice and task framing. We examine this question across two visualization-relevant tasks: color assignment for abstract and concrete concepts, and chart-idiom preference ratings across task contexts. Using 43 Big Five profiles across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, and GPT-5-mini, we find that personality-color coupling is highly model-configuration dependent: absent in GPT-4o-mini for all six concepts, consistent in GPT-4.1-mini across all six, and partial in GPT-5-mini for two of six. Concept type further shapes the signal: for abstract concepts, personality explains more hue variance than model identity, while concrete concepts show smaller and comparable effects. In chart choice, trait-aligned cluster aggregation produces stable top-idiom rankings across all nine cluster-context combinations, but a no-persona baseline recovers the same top choice in 8 of 9 model-context cells, indicating that task context drives rank-1 selection more than personality. These findings position LLM personas as exploratory probes for visualization design, not substitutes for human participants, and motivate multi-model testing, concept-type disaggregation, and no-persona baselines in future studies.

</details>
